item.title: [SCMP] Can Connie Chan become San Francisco’s first Asian-American in Congress?
item.description:
On a recent warm Thursday evening, supporters drift into San Francisco’s United Irish Cultural Centre to hear Connie Chan, who is running for California’s 11th congressional district.

Born in Hong Kong, Chan attended elementary school in Taiwan before immigrating to the United States at 13. Now a San Francisco supervisor, she hopes to succeed long-time Democratic powerhouse Nancy Pelosi, who announced her retirement and endorsed her.

The 48-year-old politician would be the first Asian-American to represent the city in Congress.
item.content:encoded:
On a recent warm Thursday evening, supporters drift into San Francisco’s United Irish Cultural Centre to hear Connie Chan, who is running for California’s 11th congressional district.

Born in Hong Kong, Chan attended elementary school in Taiwan before immigrating to the United States at 13. Now a San Francisco supervisor, she hopes to succeed long-time Democratic powerhouse Nancy Pelosi, who announced her retirement and endorsed her.

The 48-year-old politician would be the first Asian-American to represent the city in Congress.

But Chan faces a strong adversary in Scott Wiener.

While she entered local politics in 2020, Wiener has been a fixture in San Francisco Democratic circles since 2004, building strong ties with Asian-Americans, championing “yes in my backyard” (Yimby) housing policies and establishing himself as a formidable fundraiser.

As Chan takes the stage, she recounts her life story, her hands moving in a slightly practised fashion for emphasis. She speaks of the hard work, love of freedom and her family’s arrival with almost nothing before finding her way as a volunteer interpreter and social activist.

“That is our job, our job for San Francisco, for the United States, to be the conscience not only for the nation but the conscience for this world,” she says to enthusiastic applause in the large, half-full hall with ageing chandeliers, parquet flooring and large Palestinian, Irish and American flags.

“We must stand in solidarity and make sure that we send, all of us in Congress, that we’re ready to pass that vote with conscience to say no more wars and no more genocide,” she adds, addressing a crowd heavily weighted towards union labour, Arab-Americans and older whites. “We are ready to vote for peace around the world.”

Will Nancy Pelosi’s successor take a different approach to China?

San Francisco has long been a hub of liberalism and multiculturalism, and it remains to be seen whether Pelosi's successor adopts her views on China honed during her 38 historic years in Congress as the nation’s first female speaker and an outspoken critic of Beijing’s human rights record.

Some say San Francisco politics have moved on from the stance Pelosi embraced in the 1990s, with neither candidate likely to make geopolitics as central as she did.

But Chan devoted nearly a third of her speech to Gaza, Ireland and oppression. Others argue that even if US-China tensions intensify, Chan would have deeper cross-cultural roots in finessing any trans-Pacific tensions.

Pelosi was not one to hide her views. She was a long-standing critic of Beijing’s human rights record, opposing preferential trade treatment for China and speaking out against its treatment of Tibetans, Uygurs and Hong Kong activists. In 2022, she became the first sitting US House speaker to visit Taiwan in a quarter century.

Beijing was quick to react. During and after her visit, China suspended military talks; conducted unprecedented live-fire military drills, including missiles launched over the island; sent warplanes and ships across the Strait’s median line; and imposed an import ban on hundreds of Taiwanese products.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

“Connie would be able to advocate those dynamics with a level of care and competency that other candidates would not be able to and, to be quite honest, that Pelosi wouldn’t have been able to or wasn’t able to do,” said Vincent Pan, co-executive director of the activist group Chinese for Affirmative Action.

“I just don’t think that, on this issue, Scott would be able to do so. Again, it’s not a direct criticism. It’s just stating a fact.”

Asian-American voters could prove decisive in San Francisco race

The contest is significant for several reasons, Chinese-American community members say. As enthusiastically supported as Pelosi was in winning 20 elections, San Francisco has never had an Asian-American representative in Congress, despite Asians making up a third of the city’s population.

“Our communities are super threatened by the Trump administration, so that necessitates new leadership that can address what we’re facing,” said Russell Jeung, Asian-American studies professor at San Francisco State University and co-founder of activist group Stop AAPI Hate.

“Connie Chan’s advocacy, her use of language, makes a strong statement that Asian-Americans are part of the system, have a stake in the community. And what people are realising is that Asians are not just a swing vote but actually a dominant voting bloc.”

One concern is that recent Chinese immigrants vote at lower rates than other groups, especially if they do not speak English and have little experience with democracy.

“Having an Asian-American candidate sort of draws their attention and then educates them,” Jeung added. “We don’t have the socialisation into the American system.”

In June’s primary, dominated by three Democratic candidates, Wiener garnered 41 per cent of the vote against Chan’s 30 per cent.

But after tech entrepreneur Saikat Chakrabarti dropped out, lending his support to Chan, the race has tightened. Ultimately, a lot of the outcome will depend on Asian-American turnout, say local operatives.

An October 16-19 University of Southern California poll has Wiener leading by 6 percentage points, within the margin of error. Betting site Kalshi shows a wider margin, giving Wiener 79 per cent odds against Chan’s 22.

“It is and was quite a hill to climb for Connie,” said Malcolm Yeung, chief executive of San Francisco’s Chinatown Community Development Centre.

“Scott’s reputation, which is incredibly well deserved, is that he’s a monster campaigner,” Yeung added. “He works harder than virtually any other politician. He shows up at every event, talks to every constituent.”

Key issues in this heart of the Silicon Valley race include development and artificial intelligence.

Wiener is seen as more pro-growth, more aligned with property and tech firms and a long-time advocate of the “yes in my backyard” housing stance.

Chan’s base includes public sector and construction unions and opponents of data centres and gentrification.

Chan supporter Jordan Mar, a political organiser, said a Chinese-American representative in Congress is long overdue given the city’s long history of migrant workers singled out for exclusion.

He voted for Wiener in past state races, Mar said, but Chan’s concerns over artificial intelligence (AI), data centres and lost opportunities swayed him.

“I think he takes too much Anthropic money,” he said, referring to the San Francisco-based AI model developer. “It’s not necessarily about strong ethnic identity, but I think we need strong regulations to support housing.”

Given that both candidates are progressive Democrats, the advertising has been civil without the rancour seen in Texas, Ohio and other scorched-earth races.

As a long-time Yimby, Wiener has sought to paint Chan as something of a regressive Nimby – short for “not in my backyard” – while she has hit him on his ties to corporate interests.

Political insiders say Pelosi, who has ties to both candidates, endorsed Chan for several reasons, including her own long-standing support in Chinatown, her advocacy for female candidates and Chan’s backing from construction unions.

Wiener also “got ahead of the game a little bit” by announcing his candidacy and appealing to her backers before Pelosi formally bowed out, said one source.

“That’s a no-no, especially with Nancy,” he added.

Chan and Wiener divide San Francisco’s Chinese community

As always, however, Chinese communities are complex, encompassing people from mainland China, Taiwan and Hong Kong, recent immigrants and multigenerational families, and residents across the economic spectrum.

Even as Asian-Americans feel obliged to support one of their own, many prefer Wiener’s policies and more pro-business stance.

“In the Chinese community, a lot of people don’t want to speak up because Chinese are supposed to support Chinese,” said Nancy Yu Law, owner of a tea shop and active in the Chinatown History and Culture Association that has several hundred Chinese shop owners. “A lot of people don’t necessarily agree with what she has done, but we don’t want to say we don’t support her. It’s tricky.”

Yu Law recounts a recent fundraising event attended by several of her Chinese business friends.

“Somehow Pelosi shows up. Oh, wow – and they were stunned. And when they asked for a group photo, all my friends left. But they did sponsor her US$1,500,” Yu Law said. “And they say ‘no way, I have lots of business in China’.”

The shopkeeper added that if Chan is elected as Pelosi’s successor, business owners are concerned she could mirror her mentor’s Taiwan visits and human rights campaigns. “My friends do not want to take a picture with Nancy Pelosi.”

Back at the Irish cultural hall, as she mingles in the crowd dressed in a tweed jacket and a thick black belt, Chan counters that her lived experience makes her an ideal trans-Pacific bridge.

“Chinatown is a gateway between Asia and the diverse Asian-American population, which gives me deep understanding,” she said. “It’s not a monolithic community. I understand our different Asian heritage, how complex we are as Asian-Americans.”

item.title: [SCMP] How a Democratic-controlled Congress could reshape US policy on China
item.description:
A Democratic takeover of either chamber of the US Congress could bring tougher scrutiny of President Donald Trump’s dealings with Beijing, even as lawmakers are likely to maintain a broadly hawkish stance towards China, analysts said.

A change in control could shift the emphasis of congressional oversight, with the Democratic Party seeking greater accountability for the administration’s China policy after Trump’s Republican Party largely gave him room to manoeuvre, said Sarah Trister, a former lead staff member on the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific.

“I would not expect congressional Democrats to come in and seek to fully reframe the China relationship,” she said.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic takeover of either chamber of the US Congress could bring tougher scrutiny of President Donald Trump’s dealings with Beijing, even as lawmakers are likely to maintain a broadly hawkish stance towards China, analysts said.

A change in control could shift the emphasis of congressional oversight, with the Democratic Party seeking greater accountability for the administration’s China policy after Trump’s Republican Party largely gave him room to manoeuvre, said Sarah Trister, a former lead staff member on the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific.

“I would not expect congressional Democrats to come in and seek to fully reframe the China relationship,” she said.

But winning a majority in the coming midterm elections would give Democrats tools to challenge the administration’s decisions, including the power to compel testimony and obtain documents.

“They’re going to use their power if they do take the majority; they’ll have subpoena power,” said Trister, now a managing director at consulting firm FGS Global.

Trister said both parties largely agree that China poses security and economic risks, although Democrats favour what she described as “strategic decoupling”.

Technology, trade, Taiwan, artificial intelligence and tariffs are among the issues analysts expect to draw scrutiny, as Trump pursues warmer ties with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

How Democrats see the China AI question

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre, said that the Democrats are not of one mind on China right now.

There are “members of the more traditional moderate wing of the Democrats, like Chuck Schumer, who have been advocating for tougher, say, export controls and have been pretty vocal in criticising Trump for relaxing export controls or not being tougher”, he said.

But the landscape among party members differs. Some in the more progressive wing have more mixed views on this topic, according to Chan, and may be interested in “trying to work with China on AI”.

If Democrats take control of Congress, he predicts they may try a two-pronged approach on AI and technology, a hot-button issue for both parties.

“On the one hand, try to close the export control loopholes and push forward things like Match,” Chan said, referring to the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act.

At the same time, Democrats could “build some more communication channels with China on AI and try to come up with different ideas”, he added.

Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, thinks if Democrats take back one or two chambers of Congress, they “will be even more energised” around a US-China collaboration on AI.

“There are a number of other prominent Democratic senators who have said that the United States and China need to collaborate,” he noted.

“Not because we trust China, not because we will trust China, but just because the stakes of getting this issue wrong are too high.”

Democrats vow to rein in Trump’s trade war

The approach to tariffs, a cornerstone of Trump’s second term agenda, could see a shift under a Democratic-led Congress, according to Josh Lipsky, vice-president and chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council.

He said Democrats had vowed to try to rein in tariffs if they won control of Congress.

He predicted Democrats would pass bills seeking to restore Congress’s authority over trade, including measures requiring congressional approval to maintain tariffs and restricting the use of certain statutes to impose them.

Trump would veto any such legislation that reached his desk, Lipsky said, but the bills could establish a policy framework for 2028 and beyond.

On China, however, some tariffs could remain in place, he said.

“Look at the 100 per cent EV tariffs [President Joe Biden] put on China, right?” he said. “That prevented what Europe is experiencing right now: a flood of cheap Chinese EVs [electric vehicles] into our markets.”

The current Congress is also debating bipartisan legislation to codify a ban on Chinese-made connected vehicles.

The debate over which tariffs to retain, alongside China’s retaliation involving critical minerals, will play out over the next two years, Lipsky said.

Will the US become more aggressive on Taiwan?

Taiwan remains one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relations, with arms sales and provisions in the annual US defence bill among the key areas of congressional attention.

Bonnie Glaser, a China expert at the German Marshall Fund, said a Democratic victory could give the party greater influence over Taiwan policy through control of the defence authorisation and spending processes, as well as the Senate agenda.

That could allow Democrats to push for requirements on the delivery of previously approved weapons, notifications of new arms sales, the use of Taiwan security funds and reports on delays, as well as explanations for suspending or conditioning arms sales, she said.

“If the Democrats control both chambers, there could be a push to legislate constraints on administration policy. For example, there could be momentum to pass the Six Assurances to Taiwan Act, which has bipartisan cosponsors,” Glaser said.

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with the mainland, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force and is committed to supplying the island with defensive weapons.

Leadership reshuffle on key congressional committees

A Democratic majority would put the party in line to take control of key congressional committees, handing leadership positions to lawmakers with differing priorities on China.

In the House, Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, would be positioned to replace Republican Brian Mast as chairman. Ami Bera of California would likely take over the East Asia and Pacific subcommittee from Republican Young Kim.

If Democrats also win the Senate, Chris Coons of Delaware could succeed retiring Jeanne Shaheen as the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee and potentially become its chairman.

The Congressional-Executive Commission on China, currently led by Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and the congressman Chris Smith, could also come under Democratic leadership, with the congressman Jim McGovern or Senator Jeff Merkley among the potential choices. Both have long criticised Beijing’s human rights record.

One of the most closely watched changes could come at the House Select Committee on China, which is a temporary congressional body.

Glaser said it would likely survive a change in party control, though its priorities could shift towards human rights issues.

Ro Khanna of California, the committee’s top Democrat, would be positioned to succeed Republican John Moolenaar as chairman.

Wyne said if Khanna did become chairman, he could take the committee in a “potentially much more productive direction”, adding that the ranking member is clear-eyed about various challenges that China poses to US national interests.

He also argues that the overall direction of congressional policy towards China is unlikely to change significantly, though a combination of factors could give Democrats more political room to challenge the administration’s approach.

“A confluence of factors – Trump’s unorthodoxy on China policy, warming American sentiment towards China, and growing anxiety among US allies and partners over Washington’s unreliability and unpredictability – could create more political space for members of the next Congress to advocate alternative approaches,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Let them play: the Hong Kong playgrounds teaching children to take risks
item.description:
A climbing frame, a two-metre slide and a handful of seats made to resemble animals that bounce around on a spring: Hong Kong playgrounds often leave children – and their guardians – underwhelmed, but those championing a new era of play hope to fix that.

Spanning 15,000 sq ft, the OC Commons Playground, situated next to the Olympian City shopping complex in Tai Kok Tsui, is part of a recent wave of playgrounds in Hong Kong – both public and private – that hark back to the free, unstructured play that was briefly encouraged during the late 1960s and 70s. Its bamboo-shaped poles with footholds, trampoline-helmed hills and metal plates that chime when stepped on have been designed to develop mobility, cognition, sensory awareness, problem-solving skills and tolerance for risk. But this example remains an outlier, and unless greater diversity in design is encouraged across the city, play areas may remain shackled to a predictable homogeneity that fails to ignite the imagination of children or test their appetite for risk.

Introduced in 1929, Hong Kong’s first urban playgrounds were havens for rowdy, unsupervised children amid economic hardship. After the Pacific War (1941-45) during World War II, as the colonial government began building housing estates for a mushrooming population, playgrounds opened at the bases of residential blocks, many offering little more than the four “S”s: slides, see-saws, swings and sandpits. Although they were prominent fixtures across the city’s public-housing developments, playgrounds were often treated as an afterthought by architects and engineers.
item.content:encoded:
A climbing frame, a two-metre slide and a handful of seats made to resemble animals that bounce around on a spring: Hong Kong playgrounds often leave children – and their guardians – underwhelmed, but those championing a new era of play hope to fix that.

Spanning 15,000 sq ft, the OC Commons Playground, situated next to the Olympian City shopping complex in Tai Kok Tsui, is part of a recent wave of playgrounds in Hong Kong – both public and private – that hark back to the free, unstructured play that was briefly encouraged during the late 1960s and 70s. Its bamboo-shaped poles with footholds, trampoline-helmed hills and metal plates that chime when stepped on have been designed to develop mobility, cognition, sensory awareness, problem-solving skills and tolerance for risk. But this example remains an outlier, and unless greater diversity in design is encouraged across the city, play areas may remain shackled to a predictable homogeneity that fails to ignite the imagination of children or test their appetite for risk.

Introduced in 1929, Hong Kong’s first urban playgrounds were havens for rowdy, unsupervised children amid economic hardship. After the Pacific War (1941-45) during World War II, as the colonial government began building housing estates for a mushrooming population, playgrounds opened at the bases of residential blocks, many offering little more than the four “S”s: slides, see-saws, swings and sandpits. Although they were prominent fixtures across the city’s public-housing developments, playgrounds were often treated as an afterthought by architects and engineers.

A major advancement in playground design came in the 60s, when features such as cement bridges, mazes and tunnels were fitted into the play areas of residential developments in Kennedy Town and Tsuen Wan, and on the Kai Tak Estate, writes arts practitioner Helen Fan Lok-yi, in her book The Abstract Playscapes of Hong Kong (2023). But the most representative sculptural play space arrived in 1969, when American artist Paul Selinger’s Shek Lei Playground introduced Kwai Chung to monumental forms that resembled a perforated belt, toppled chess pieces and cylinders stacked like waves: installations that were intended to stimulate free play and exploration. Although Selinger “failed in replicating his Shek Lei Playground model in Hong Kong”, writes Fan, “he influenced subsequent Hong Kong designers to experiment with mixing art, landscaping and play”.

In the late 70s and early 80s, however, mounting lawsuits over playground injuries in the United States cast doubt on the safety of sculptural playgrounds, a cautiousness that spread to Hong Kong. As the city tended to import its play equipment from the West, standardised, certified, mass-produced equipment prized for durability and ease of maintenance became the norm. Shek Lei Playground met its unheralded end in the 90s.

According to Fan, the shift suited Hong Kong families, who were increasingly hiring foreign domestic helpers to care for their children. In a rapidly developing city where parents were rarely supervising playground time, creativity came second to safety.

Nonetheless, in 1987, the non-governmental, non-profit Playright Children’s Play Association was established to promote and safeguard children’s right to play. Soon after, in 1989, Playright opened Hong Kong’s first “accessible” play area, King’s Park Children’s Playground, in Yau Ma Tei. Designed to include children with physical, sensory or developmental disabilities, it brought a rack of tubular audio instruments, a “touch wall”, strong sculptural qualities and diverse textures to engage young visitors.

In 2018, Playright introduced the city’s first “inclusive” playground – one that fosters shared social integration as well as multi-ability play – in Tuen Mun. Here, the recreational facilities include a water-play zone, an undulating area, trampolines and musical playthings, such as percussion instruments. Between those two openings, the term “free play” had become popular among parents and educators, who believed benefits such as enhanced concentration and interest in learning would follow when children could choose their own tools, ways to play, playmates and activity areas.

One year later, then-chief executive Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor announced the revitalisation of more than 170 public play areas managed by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department (LCSD) by 2024, “to make [Hong Kong’s] public play spaces more innovative and fun as well as to meet the aspirations of local residents”. Only 18 have been revamped so far, though, officials having cited the Covid-19 pandemic and the time needed to consult residents and process their requests as reasons for the delays.

Jacky Chan Wai-hin, head of play-environment development at Playright, which has been a consultant on at least one of the government’s 170 projects, says playgrounds support social well-being and resilience, and they also make sense for property developers eager to extend the duration of customer visits to shopping centres.

Since its Playright-designed OC Commons Playground opened earlier this year, Olympian City has seen a 10 per cent rise in footfall, attracting families from as far away as Tung Chung, says Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer at Sino Group.

“OC Commons is in a great location because it’s right next to a mall that, in this case, acts more like a community living room, where people do more than just shop, but hang out,” says Chan. “Olympian City also has indoor bathrooms and resting spots that are paramount to a good playground.”

Other shopping plazas banking on the appeal of playgrounds include the Tsz Wan Shan Shopping Centre, where, in 2020, a water-play zone and climbing nets were added to the fifth floor. A year later, the 18,000 sq ft Moko Park reopened in Mong Kok’s Moko mall, boasting Hong Kong’s longest climbing wall and slides of varying heights.

Alan Cheung Kwok-lun, co-founder and managing director of One Bite Design Studio and the creative mind behind T Town’s The Wonderful Town of Play, in Tin Shui Wai, says the growing involvement of private developers with strict marketing goals adds pizzazz: “Private sectors’ No 1 priority is the ‘wow factor’; they want Hong Kong’s tallest, longest something whereas government playgrounds don’t care for marketing gimmicks.”

T Town’s 32,000 sq ft, Hong Kong Wetland Park-themed playground opened in December last year on the roof of the mall. Since its debut, footfall on the building’s second floor, connecting to the playground, has doubled, according to Katherine Lo Yan-kay, director of asset management (Hong Kong) at Link Asset Management, the developer behind T Town, drawing unprecedented numbers of visitors from nearby Yuen Long and Tuen Mun.

Like OC Commons, The Wonderful Town of Play has an adventure tower, a rope pyramid, a trampoline and a tyre swing. Cheung’s design also incorporates facts and graphics about the nearby conservation park and its wildlife: a large model of a black-faced spoonbill is perched above the vertical climber, for instance, and a three-dimensional hopscotch game, Mudskipper Jump, is paired with an information plaque about the amphibious fish.

While Cheung understands children are unlikely to visit a playground to learn about wetland species, the theme gives the space a distinct identity and offers guardians something to read while they are supervising their charges. Such intergenerational touches – even those as simple as increased shade and seating areas – are crucial to sustaining the relevance of a playground, he says. “Why can’t teenagers and adults play as well? We have this misconception because our society hasn’t catered to this demographic in our playground designs,” he says. “For the elderly, this could mean including simple workout equipment placed in spots where they can see their grandchildren. Meanwhile, teenagers may want nooks where they can hang out.”

A sense of ownership also encourages repeat visits. Another of Cheung’s projects – Siu Hei Court Play Space, a Tuen Mun playground refurbished in 2020 – is decorated with tiles adorned with artwork by nursery-school and kindergarten students. Although the play area may not be suitable for them just yet, Cheung hopes that by “making the space feel relevant”, those children will return as regular visitors when they are older.

Ownership also informs the 2024 Well-being Design Guide, a framework launched by the Housing Bureau and the Hong Kong Housing Authority. It intends, with the aid of feedback from residents, to transform public housing from blocks of basic shelter into vibrant communities.

In some cases, the reference suggests switching out drab playground sets for what Housing Department chief architect Tim Li Man-wai calls “communal fitness playscapes”, which welcome cross-generational activities rather than serving only as a children’s playground. Li sees this shift not as a loss of play space, but as a way to maximise use. He points to Yip Wong Estate, in Tuen Mun, where, instead of a conventional basketball court, netless rims were installed at various heights against a colourful, numbered wall. “Older children come here for basketball competitions, but the lower rims also invite young kids who may otherwise be deterred by the high hoops. Here, they can see who can dunk a ball into a hoop with a higher number, or a specific colour; they can really stretch their imagination,” says Li.

Before the new initiative, Li explains, residents’ feedback was collected through district councils, and projects tended to conform to a top-down approach. Now, discussions, interviews and workshops are conducted from the ground up, to identify pain points and possible remedies. “Society is changing, and so should the way we engage with our people when designing their living spaces. Before, residents didn’t have time to engage with us – they were likely too busy making a living and were happy with just a roof over their heads. However, with more public spaces and a widespread use of social media, people are more willing to voice their concerns.

“When residents are a part of the design process, they have ownership about what appears in that space and are therefore more accepting of the final product,” he says.

Ownership implies users’ trust in the designers to improve their lives. But designers, too, must have faith that their spaces will be treated with respect. Before its relaunch in 2021, Yi Pei Square Playground, in Tsuen Wan, shared space with a four-metre-wide emergency-vehicle access. A meaningful redesign meant removing the gate that separated it from shops.

“Park-goers and nearby residents were worried that, if we removed the gate, shop owners would spill their belongings into the park area,” says Kay Chan Wan-ki, a freelance product designer and community-interaction planner who worked on the redesign. “But we believed that people’s sense of discipline and respect for the common good would improve if they had well-designed public spaces that met their needs.”

Following the redesign, frequent policing by officials kept the shopkeepers in line.

“You can’t please everyone, but ultimately, it was a change for the better,” says Kay Chan.

Despite the innovation evident in parts of the city, she laments a continuing lack of creativity, adventure and nature in play. Playright’s Jacky Chan shares her concerns, adding that the city’s acceptance of, and education around, unconventional playgrounds must keep pace with the LCSD’s refurbishments, or risk a return to boring uniformity.

“A playground is not a stand-alone place. First, the public must get used to these new designs. Asians have a concept of ‘as safe as possible’, but those in the West believe in ‘as safe as necessary’. A safe playground isn’t meant to eliminate all risks – only the lethal, seriously dangerous ones. Little bumps and bruises are inevitable when children explore.”

Chan’s optimism is fuelled by past victories: “When sandpits first appeared in Hong Kong’s playgrounds, they were littered with cigarette butts and – in some cases – needles. This rarely happens any more, which is a great example of public education making enormous strides.”

Acceptance is one challenge, but construction and administration are quite another. “We face barriers from developers, the government, management and operational teams, because when these non-conventional playground facilities malfunction, it’s not just replacing a loose nail,” says Chan. “We must also look at workmanship, construction companies and suppliers. Do they have the know-how to make these new-age playgrounds? Only a few fields are related to playground design: architecture, landscape design and engineering. We can instil these concepts of risk, adventure and free play in students [of those disciplines] early on.”

Last December, Playright opened Hung Hom’s Dream Together Playground, which is anything but ordinary. As one of a rotating theme, until October 14, the park hosted a “pirate ship”, whose wooden bow was scribbled with children’s paintings, its flag and mast a sparkly sheet of tarp and an upside-down table. Scattered throughout were arm hooks fashioned out of tinfoil and half bottles, swords carved out of wood and “cannons” made from hole-punchers and plastic lids. Its outdoor expanse included sandpits and structures that were meant to be deconstructed and reassembled for all sorts of play. High steps and slim balancing beams pushed children beyond their comfort zone.

Chan calls this style of playground “half-and-half”, wherein children are tasked with co-creating their version of fun. Colouring on the floor is as encouraged as crafting a pulley system to deliver make-believe takeaway boxes. Since every visitor is a co-creator, the settings keep refreshing. (Another thing that’s unusual about the Dream Together Playground is that there is a charge to enter parts of the 23,680 sq ft site; HK$240 for one child-and-adult pair covers on-site supervision staff, materials and the costs of periodically changing the theme of the space.)

“Playright has been pushing this project for the past 20 years,” says Chan. “A playground like this is very rare in our city, but it’s a start.”

item.title: [SCMP] First Look: Yurt, Hong Kong’s ‘first modern Central Asian restaurant’
item.description:
While Hongkongers scout remote destinations for their first holiday in 2026, a journey of discovery for the palate is now on offer closer to home. Yurt, newly opened on SoHo’s Elgin Street, is bringing the hitherto unexplored flavours of Central Asia to the heart of the city, proving you don’t need a boarding pass to be an adventurous gourmand.

In a dining scene that prides itself on diversity, Central Asia has remained conspicuously absent from the many menus on offer in Hong Kong. For the founders behind Yurt, filling that gap has been a project a long time in the making.

“This idea has been in the back of all our minds for years, even before we met,” they share. The catalyst was when Xeniya Tregubenko was introduced to fellow Kazakh native Ali Nuraly through a mutual friend early last year. What started as a casual chat quickly touched on a common dream – to introduce Central Asian flavours to Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
While Hongkongers scout remote destinations for their first holiday in 2026, a journey of discovery for the palate is now on offer closer to home. Yurt, newly opened on SoHo’s Elgin Street, is bringing the hitherto unexplored flavours of Central Asia to the heart of the city, proving you don’t need a boarding pass to be an adventurous gourmand.

In a dining scene that prides itself on diversity, Central Asia has remained conspicuously absent from the many menus on offer in Hong Kong. For the founders behind Yurt, filling that gap has been a project a long time in the making.

“This idea has been in the back of all our minds for years, even before we met,” they share. The catalyst was when Xeniya Tregubenko was introduced to fellow Kazakh native Ali Nuraly through a mutual friend early last year. What started as a casual chat quickly touched on a common dream – to introduce Central Asian flavours to Hong Kong.

For both, Yurt marks a distinctive new life chapter. For Tregubenko, a seven-year Hong Kong resident, the restaurant is about “putting down permanent roots” for her culture in her adopted city. For Nuraly, a more recent arrival, it signals “the exciting beginning of my entrepreneurial journey”.

Although the pair were confident in the appeal of their plan, Nuraly admits that taking the first concrete step towards opening Yurt was daunting. “Introducing a completely unknown cuisine … it was a leap of faith,” he says.

The greater challenge, however, was one of cultural translation. “It’s one thing to cook the dishes; it’s another to bring the spirit,” Nuraly explains.

The man tasked with helping achieve this goal is head chef Marat Zakaryayev, another native of Kazakhstan whose culinary experience runs from Almaty to London. “My goal is for the first-time taster to understand our homeland through its flavours,” he says.

Completing this culinary bridge is pastry chef Anna Lobanova. Formerly pastry chef at Whey, she now works from her base in Kazakhstan to create desserts that are authentically Central Asian yet designed to resonate locally.

Diners walking into Yurt get an immediate sense of Central Asia with a warm, cosy dining room featuring atmospheric decor and lighting along with objects from the region. As Tregubenko explains, it is filled with gifts and mementos brought by members of the city’s Central Asian community who have come to support the space. The result is an atmosphere that feels deeply personal – less like the opening of a commercial venture and more like the founding of a communal home.

The opening menu offers a concise, narrative-driven tour of the steppes through dishes from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. A meal begins with baursak – the essential welcome of home-made, fluffy fried dough. Its name translates to “striving for unity”, and it’s a staple of the dastarkhan or traditional banquet table in Kazakh and Kyrgyz culture.

Zakaryayev is keenly aware of the differences in topography between Hong Kong and Central Asia: “One shaped by the sea and rivers, the other by mountains and endless steppe.”

The head chef has embraced this opportunity to work with ingredients that would be less familiar back home – even if featuring seafood on the menu does not come naturally. One thoughtful appetiser of sea bass with pumpkin and mung bean purée, for example, incorporates local ingredients while remaining rooted in Central Asian spices and palate.

Mains present the pillars of Central Asian cuisine, starting with beshbarmak. Described as “the dish of celebration”, it features hand-pulled noodles and tender meat in a soulful broth. It is joined by pilaf, a fragrant rice dish with beef, raisins and quail eggs that serves as a flavourful ode to Uzbekistan.

The final act is a dessert that bridges the vastness of Asia, balancing the sweet-tart flavour of Kazakhstan’s famed Aport apple against a rich, umami-forward home-made cheesecake and cheese caramel, thoughtfully adapted to a “sweet but not too sweet” profile suitable for local palates.

Yurt’s founders have taken to publicising the concept as the “first modern Central Asian restaurant” in Hong Kong – and they are aware of the responsibility that comes with claiming such a mantle. “We’re the first chapter of this cuisine for many, and we take that very seriously,” says Tregubenko.

The team’s determination to present an authentic version of their native cuisine is what led them to include horse meat on the menu – a traditional and respected protein across the steppe. The founders initially grappled with the decision, aware of the potential for misunderstanding. Ultimately, they chose cultural integrity over compromise, offering it as an add-on sausage served with their signature beshbarmak.

“We felt like if we shied away, if we didn’t showcase this one key element of our cuisine, we’d be watering down our own culture,” Tregubenko explains. “It’s an act of cultural honesty and integrity for us.”

That same commitment has led Nuraly and Tregubenko to operate Yurt as a halal establishment, positioning it as one of Hong Kong’s few refined halal dining spots. That commitment extends beyond the preparation of the food to the drinks menu as well. They “focus on crafting exceptional non-alcoholic pairings”, ensuring the experience remains celebratory and inclusive, even if it can be a “challenge” to explain to certain guests why they don’t serve alcohol.

An initial positive response suggests a healthy appetite for this previously unfamiliar cuisine. Nuraly says they’ve seen “overwhelming support” from the local Central Asian community, who have been introducing friends and inquisitive local explorers. Their target audience, he says, is simply “the curious”.

Looking forward, the founders hope Yurt will evolve into a broader cultural hub – a “living bridge” for music and art from the region. For now, they’ve built a different kind of destination. As they put it: “If the yurt in the steppe is a movable home, then Yurt the restaurant is a home that found its place.”

It’s a home that invites Hong Kong’s ever-curious diners to pull up a chair and embark on a journey to Central Asia, no passport required.

item.title: [SCMP] Why the Philippines remains a hotspot for transnational drug syndicates
item.description:
Transnational drug syndicates in the Philippines continue to thrive despite decades of crackdowns targeting street-level dealers, with analysts warning that regional suppliers, financiers and trafficking networks have largely eluded enforcement efforts.

Former drug officials and security analysts say the country’s drug trade remains closely connected to a wider regional supply chain, with criminal groups relying on local partners, maritime routes and established distribution networks to move methamphetamine across Southeast Asia.

A foiled attempt to smuggle US$55 million worth of methamphetamine aboard a private jet in Laos, allegedly bound for the Philippines, has brought renewed attention to these cross-border operations, prompting a House investigation into suspected Philippine connections.
item.content:encoded:
Transnational drug syndicates in the Philippines continue to thrive despite decades of crackdowns targeting street-level dealers, with analysts warning that regional suppliers, financiers and trafficking networks have largely eluded enforcement efforts.

Former drug officials and security analysts say the country’s drug trade remains closely connected to a wider regional supply chain, with criminal groups relying on local partners, maritime routes and established distribution networks to move methamphetamine across Southeast Asia.

A foiled attempt to smuggle US$55 million worth of methamphetamine aboard a private jet in Laos, allegedly bound for the Philippines, has brought renewed attention to these cross-border operations, prompting a House investigation into suspected Philippine connections.

At least five transnational drug networks operate in the Philippines, according to Mark Anthony Santos, chairman of the House committee on dangerous drugs, who cited information from an unnamed senior police official.

Chinese and Chinese-Filipino trafficking groups, as well as Mexican and West African drug cartels, including the Sinaloa cartel, dominated the country’s drug black market, Santos said.

“Drug syndicates do not operate solely through street-level distribution. They exploit private aircraft, maritime routes, financial intermediaries, and gaps in coordination among jurisdictions. Even when a shipment is intercepted, the people financing and organising the operation may remain beyond the reach of investigators,” Santos said in a statement on October 22.

“Authorities must look beyond intercepted shipments, follow the money, and work with foreign law enforcement to identify and dismantle the syndicates behind the drug trade.”

Among the major networks operating in the region is Sam Gor, an alliance of Chinese criminal groups linked to the crystal meth trade. It is estimated to control 40 per cent to 70 per cent of the regional drug market, operating through partners and criminal groups.

At a briefing earlier this month, Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) director general Isagani Nerez confirmed that Sam Gor comprised an alliance of five major Chinese triad groups: the 14K Triad, Bamboo Union, Big Circle Gang, Sun Yee On and Wo Shing Wo, whose leaders are believed to be based in Hong Kong and Taiwan.

This Week in Asia has reached out to PDEA for comment.

Sam Gor is reportedly also present in Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, New Zealand, Australia, South Korea, Japan, mainland China and Taiwan.

An evolution

Former drug officials and analysts said the potential Philippine connection to the foiled shipment in Laos, as well as the presence of transnational drug cartels in the country, reflected a long-standing problem dating back decades.

“These connections have existed for many years, particularly in the methamphetamine trade, where regional suppliers have historically relied on local Chinese and Filipino-Chinese groups for domestic distribution,” a former Philippine drug official, who requested anonymity, told This Week in Asia.

“The Philippines’ geographical location, extensive coastlines, maritime borders, and significant domestic demand make it vulnerable to these activities.”

Jeremy Douglas, deputy director of operations at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, agrees that the Philippines has long remained a major market for illicit drugs – mostly methamphetamine, known locally as shabu – from the Golden Triangle, the mountainous border region where Thailand, Myanmar and Laos converge near the Ruak and Mekong rivers.

The presence and activities of transnational organised crime groups in the Philippines have been observed for at least the past 10 to 20 years, according to Dr Rohan Gunaratna, a professor of security studies at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Nanyang Technological University.

“What we are seeing today is largely a continuation and evolution of criminal networks that have long operated across the region,” he said.

Gunaratna called the Southeast Asian drug trade ecosystem “highly dynamic, interconnected and adaptive”.

“It operates through a regional supply chain in which different countries play different roles, from manufacturing and precursor sourcing to transport, wholesale distribution and consumption,” he said.

Chinese transnational criminal organisations are significant actors in this ecosystem as their influence extends well beyond the direct trafficking of drugs, according to Gunaratna. “Their networks and business relationships enable them to connect production facilities with wholesale distributors and established criminal groups in destination markets.”

The region’s major drug markets included Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam, Gunaratna said, although the scale and nature of consumption and trafficking varied across countries.

“Beyond Southeast Asia, Australia and other Asia-Pacific markets also remain important destinations for regional drug supplies,” he said.

The Philippines’ drug trade

The methamphetamine trade in the Philippines has historically been connected to the wider regional supply chain controlled by Chinese transnational criminal organisations, including networks associated with Sam Gor, according to Gunaratna.

He said Chinese transnational criminal groups played a significant role in establishing the meth trade in the Philippines during the 1990s. Over time, methamphetamine became the country’s dominant illicit drug market.

“At the higher levels, these networks have played a significant role in the sourcing and moving methamphetamine supplies, while local Chinese and Filipino-Chinese criminal groups have traditionally handled domestic wholesale distribution and retail networks,” he said.

Regional suppliers and local distribution networks did not necessarily work as a unified organisation, but through interconnected relationships and supply arrangements, he added.

Aside from its extensive coastline and several islands, the Philippines’ weak governance and corruption among law enforcement personnel and government officials created opportunities for organised criminal groups to operate, Gunaratna said.

He pointed to the Zamboanga-Basilan-Sulu-Tawi-Tawi corridor, which connects the southern Philippines with maritime areas bordering Malaysia and Indonesia, as an area of concern.

“Its geography, combined with informal maritime routes and limited enforcement coverage in certain areas, creates opportunities for the movement of illicit commodities across national boundaries,” Gunaratna said, adding that the Philippines primarily served as a destination and distribution market for drugs, and occasionally a transshipment point for markets such as Australia.

These operations predate former president Rodrigo Duterte’s administration, which launched a controversial war on drugs from 2016 to 2022 that left thousands dead.

But targeting lower-level players in the domestic market “does not necessarily translate into dismantling the larger regional supply chains, which operate across multiple jurisdictions”, said the former drug official.

“The drug problem was significant then, and it is now; the fundamentals of the regional drug market, the use and demand and the supply remain a major challenge the Philippines and [its] neighbours are still grappling with,” Douglas said.

item.title: [SCMP] Will diversifying fuel imports be enough to fix Indonesia’s energy shortfall?
item.description:
Indonesia is looking beyond Singapore for petrol supplies as it seeks to reduce its dependence on a single source, but analysts say diversifying imports will do little to address the country’s fuel production shortfall without faster refinery modernisation and investment in alternative fuels.

Indonesia has long sourced petroleum products from Singapore, including RON 90 petrol, which has a minimum octane rating of 90 and is marketed domestically as Pertalite. Singapore’s geographic proximity, advanced blending facilities and extensive storage capacity have made it a key supplier to Indonesia.

Jakarta is now trying to diversify away from Singapore and is looking for alternative suppliers such as China and India, according to Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Bahlil Lahadalia.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia is looking beyond Singapore for petrol supplies as it seeks to reduce its dependence on a single source, but analysts say diversifying imports will do little to address the country’s fuel production shortfall without faster refinery modernisation and investment in alternative fuels.

Indonesia has long sourced petroleum products from Singapore, including RON 90 petrol, which has a minimum octane rating of 90 and is marketed domestically as Pertalite. Singapore’s geographic proximity, advanced blending facilities and extensive storage capacity have made it a key supplier to Indonesia.

Jakarta is now trying to diversify away from Singapore and is looking for alternative suppliers such as China and India, according to Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Bahlil Lahadalia.

“We know that we import RON 90 fuel from a neighbouring country, so starting tomorrow I will be leaving for several countries, including India, China and other countries, to get certainty about supplies,” Bahlil told reporters on Monday.

The ministry has yet to provide an update on Bahlil’s trips. It did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

According to Bahlil, the government does not want to “rely on a single source of supply”, considering that nearly 60 per cent of Indonesia’s fuel imports currently come from Singapore.

Data from statistics agency BPS showed that 28.36 per cent of Indonesia’s oil and gas imports in the first half of this year came from Singapore.

Bahlil said the shift to China and India was also a precaution in case Singapore retaliated against Jakarta’s decision to cut natural gas exports to the city state by 31 million standard cubic feet per day. Indonesia currently supplies gas to Singapore with a total volume of 409.5 MMSCFD.

“Before we take any step, it is impossible not to consider or take everything into account,” he said.

Bahlil revealed on October 23 that the subsidised Pertalite reserves covered consumption for just 18 days, while reserves for the non-subsidised fuel stood at over 20 days.

Insufficient refinery capacity

The move to seek alternative partnerships highlights Indonesia’s fuel production gaps, as its refining capability cannot keep up with growing domestic demand.

Indonesia’s current refinery capacity sits at about 1 million barrels per day, but daily domestic consumption requires 1.6 million barrels, according to Fabby Tumiwa, executive director of the Institute for Essential Services Reform. Singapore offset the gap by up to 400,000 barrels per day, he said.

“Singapore’s fuel production is well-suited to our fuel needs. We also know that Singapore is a regional refining and trading hub. The trading ecosystem there is very liquid, making it easy to buy fuel on the spot or long-term market,” Fabby told This Week in Asia.

“From an energy security perspective, relying on a single source with large volumes is unsafe. We must diversify, both the products and sources.”

Fabby said “not all refineries in Indonesia operate continuously”, while some new refinery projects planned by state-owned oil and gas company Pertamina “simply cannot proceed due to lack of financing or investors”.

The United States’ Energy Information Administration estimated the average utilisation rate of eight Indonesian refineries in 2024 at 79 per cent, the latest data available.

“It’s not that Indonesia lacks refineries. The question is whether the capacity and configuration of the available refineries can produce the type and volume of petrol the public needs,” said Iwa Garniwa, rector of the PLN Institute of Technology in Jakarta.

During former president Joko Widodo’s first term, Indonesia announced seven new refinery projects to boost domestic fuel production; only one, the massive refinery upgrade project in Balikpapan, has materialised.

Bahlil said last week the Balikpapan refinery, which cost Jakarta US$7.4 billion to build, would meet up to a quarter of domestic fuel demand.

Muhammad Baron, Pertamina’s vice-president of corporate communication, said in a statement to This Week in Asia that the Balikpapan refinery underlined the government’s efforts to “reduce dependence on fuel imports by increasing refinery capacity and optimising domestic resources”.

“[The Balikpapan refinery] increases crude oil processing capacity and refinery capabilities to process residues into higher-value products, producing Euro V-quality fuel,” Muhammad said.

Euro V petrol indicates a cleaner fuel standard that limits emissions of sulphur, carbon monoxide and particulate matter.

Iwa said the future of other refinery projects depended on “significant capital investment”, whether foreign or domestic.

“Investors need to take into account crude oil prices, processing margins, exchange rates, domestic fuel prices and the risk of policy changes. If the project’s economics are unattractive or the risk allocation is unclear, investors may delay their investment decision,” Iwa said.

He pointed to the long-delayed construction of the New Grass Root Refinery in Tuban, East Java, a joint project between Kilang Pertamina Internasional and Russian oil giant Rosneft. The project, expected to process up to 300,000 barrels of crude per day, has languished in the planning stage since 2015.

“The Tuban project’s experience demonstrates that changing geopolitical conditions and partner issues can affect project timelines,” Iwa said.

For now, the government could meet the rising Pertalite demand by sourcing it from countries such as South Korea, Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates, Iwa said.

Alternative fuels

Aside from building new refineries, Muhammad said Pertamina “continues to increase domestic oil production, optimise its use as a raw material for refineries, and increase processing efficiency and reliability”.

Pertamina was also developing a domestic bioethanol supply as a petrol blending component to support the government’s implementation of the B50 biofuel programme, he added.

The B50 blend consists of 50 per cent crude palm oil and 50 per cent fossil diesel.

As Indonesia aims for fuel self-sufficiency by 2028, Fabby urged the government to begin cultivating more bioethanol-producing crops such as sugar cane, sorghum and corn.

“If we work hard, E10 might be achievable by 2028,” Fabby said, referring to a fuel blend of up to 10 per cent renewable bioethanol and 90 per cent fossil fuel.

“However, targeting E50 by 2028 will be quite difficult, as it requires a surge in bioethanol production, vast areas of land and [considerable] time since crops cannot grow overnight.”

item.title: [SCMP] Saviour or stopgap? Malaysia’s South Korean jets arrive to relieve ageing fighters
item.description:
Malaysia received its first South Korean-made light combat jet on Friday under a nearly 4 billion ringgit (US$990 million) procurement, in what analysts describe as welcome relief for an ageing air force still years away from replacing its frontline fighters.

The FA-50M Block 20 jet arrived at the air force base in Labuan, off Borneo, with a second expected in Kuantan on the peninsula’s east coast next Monday. They are the first of 18 aircraft ordered from Korea Aerospace Industries under a deal formalised in May 2023.

The remaining aircraft are scheduled to arrive in stages through March 2028 – beginning the first fleet renewal in 19 years since the delivery of Russian-built Sukhoi Su-30MKMs in 2007.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia received its first South Korean-made light combat jet on Friday under a nearly 4 billion ringgit (US$990 million) procurement, in what analysts describe as welcome relief for an ageing air force still years away from replacing its frontline fighters.

The FA-50M Block 20 jet arrived at the air force base in Labuan, off Borneo, with a second expected in Kuantan on the peninsula’s east coast next Monday. They are the first of 18 aircraft ordered from Korea Aerospace Industries under a deal formalised in May 2023.

The remaining aircraft are scheduled to arrive in stages through March 2028 – beginning the first fleet renewal in 19 years since the delivery of Russian-built Sukhoi Su-30MKMs in 2007.

Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin said on Friday that the acquisition would enhance Malaysia’s capabilities “particularly in carrying out its air defence responsibilities”.

“The procurement is particularly important as the existing Hawk aircraft are scheduled to be decommissioned in 2028,” he said, according to state news agency Bernama.

During Monday’s budget debate, the minister also outlined plans to deploy three Turkish-made Anka-S surveillance drones at Labuan and establish a squadron to operate and support them to improve intelligence gathering over the South China Sea.

The FA-50Ms will replace ageing British-built Hawks and be used to train future fighter pilots, taking on some duties performed by the Sukhois and American-made F/A-18D Hornets. The South Korean-built jets feature advanced radar for tracking targets and a targeting pod to guide precision strikes.

Patrol pressure

Malaysia’s maritime interests in the South China Sea span two geographically separated regions – including the Borneo states of Sabah and Sarawak, where offshore oil and gas operations have drawn objections from Beijing.

Beijing claims much of the South China Sea, overlapping with maritime claims by Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Brunei and Taiwan. China maintains that its activities in the disputed waters are lawful, while Malaysia considers the waters where it conducts energy exploration to fall within its own maritime jurisdiction.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has insisted that Malaysian exploration will continue despite Chinese protests, while remaining open to negotiations.

The competing positions came into focus in May 2021, when Malaysia scrambled Hawks from Labuan after detecting 16 Chinese military transport aircraft approaching Sarawak. Malaysia said the planes had entered its airspace while China maintained they were on routine training, had not entered another country’s territorial airspace and were exercising their right to overflight under international law.

Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said the FA-50M would give Malaysia a more capable aircraft for such encounters. “While the aircraft might be a lightweight jet, it remains useful for projection of presence.”

The Philippines uses the same family of jets for its South China Sea patrols. Manila ordered another 12 FA-50s from Seoul last year in a deal worth about US$700 million, adding to a regional market for Korean aircraft that includes Indonesia and Thailand.

However, compared to larger multirole fighters, the new jets had limitations in their sensors, weapons payload and range, Koh said.

“It’s at best an interim, stopgap measure before the [air force] introduces next-generation fighter jets that would augment and eventually replace the existing Su-30MKM and F/A-18D,” he said. “The most feasible approach would be to try to extend the service lifespan and continue to modernise the Sukhois and Hornets for as long as possible.”

The air force also needed “a fundamental relook at its procurement policy that accounts fully for a long-term, sustainable service of the assets”, including maintenance and repairs, he said.

Replacement dilemma

Malaysia abandoned an attempt to acquire second-hand Kuwaiti Hornets earlier this year over delivery timing and uncertainty about long-term maintenance and support.

Khaled said in July that the government was considering bringing its replacement fighter procurement forward into the 2026–2030 development plan – subject to funding. The Hornets and Sukhois would need to be retired by around 2035, the minister said.

A Hornet crash at Kuantan in August last year also put the fleet under scrutiny, although investigators attributed the accident to a bird strike.

Kuala Lumpur-based defence analyst Zaki Salleh said the FA-50Ms could reduce the older fighters’ workload by taking on patrol, pilot training and suitable strike missions, saving operating costs and strain on their airframes.

“The arrival of the first two aircraft does not mean they can be immediately deployed for actual operational missions,” he said. Pilots and ground crews still needed to be trained, and aircraft systems had to be integrated into the air defence network before regular operations.

The toughest balance will be ensuring training at Kuantan did not compromise readiness to respond from Labuan, or vice versa, according to Zaki. He said maintenance providers would be crucial to “minimising the time aircraft spend in hangars undergoing maintenance and maximising their operational availability”.

Malaysia’s CAP55 air force development blueprint envisages 36 light combat aircraft, twice the current order, to meet its training and operational needs.

Hoo Chiew Ping, a senior fellow at the East Asian International Relations Caucus, said the Korean purchase was significant because “securing budgets for high-end, advanced multi-role combat aircraft remains exceedingly difficult”.

Since a renewed industrial cooperation agreement in 2025, Malaysia’s defence relationship with Seoul had been expanding beyond aircraft sales, she said. “Training of technical experts is provided along with the sales of FA-50M, and the delivery is on time. These further solidify South Korea’s position as a credible defence partner of Malaysia.”

The successful delivery was encouraging Malaysian interest in South Korea’s KF-21 fighter, Hoo added. Turkey has also offered cooperation on its Kaan programme, although Malaysia has yet to announce its choice of replacement aircraft.

“If structured properly, a well-managed technology transfer and co-production contract for the KF-21 would not only elevate Malaysia’s combat capabilities beyond the legacy Hornet, but also ensure smooth interoperability with the US during the joint military exercises,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Unwritten rules’ become newest target in Communist Party’s war on corruption
item.description:
The Communist Party of China has pledged to vigorously crack down on the “unwritten rules” that enable corruption in the party, deepening its long-running campaign to keep officials in line.

At a Friday press conference, senior officials described the important takeaways from the 20th Central Committee’s Fifth Plenum, which concluded the day before. They underscored President Xi Jinping’s assertion that corruption remains a serious challenge that requires sustained pressure and targeted action against the informal practices that undermine formal rules.

The four-day conclave concluded with the adoption of the “Decision of the CPC Central Committee on Several Major Issues Concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance.”
item.content:encoded:
The Communist Party of China has pledged to vigorously crack down on the “unwritten rules” that enable corruption in the party, deepening its long-running campaign to keep officials in line.

At a Friday press conference, senior officials described the important takeaways from the 20th Central Committee’s Fifth Plenum, which concluded the day before. They underscored President Xi Jinping’s assertion that corruption remains a serious challenge that requires sustained pressure and targeted action against the informal practices that undermine formal rules.

The four-day conclave concluded with the adoption of the “Decision of the CPC Central Committee on Several Major Issues Concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance.”

In a rare move, the document singled out “unwritten rules” as a prominent problem to tackle.

Unwritten rules refer to the implicit understanding that those with power must be compensated in exchange for jobs, services, promotions, contracts, land leases or even to access social welfare or admission to schools. This can take the form of money, sex or the exchange of favours.

These rules have long permeated Chinese society and persist despite the party’s 14-year-long anti-corruption campaign. Measures to stamp out wrongdoing include regulations banning what were formerly commonplace practices, like extravagant business entertainment and gift-giving.

“For a period of time, some unwritten rules have existed to varying degrees both inside and outside the party, undermining the authority and enforcement power of party rules and discipline, which has drawn strong reactions from cadres and the public,” said Xie Chuntao, executive vice-president of the Central Party School.

“The decision emphasises starting by establishing clear rules and puts forward corresponding measures in advancing openness in party and government affairs, strengthening education and guidance, correcting related disorderly phenomena and establishing and improving institutional mechanisms,” Xie said.

Tang Fangyu, the director of the party’s Central Policy Research Office, said that the decision represented the plenum’s most important outcome and that its drafting was led by Xi.

“He personally planned the process, provided continuous guidance, set the direction, and played a decisive role,” Tang said. The work involved soliciting opinions from localities and government departments, commissioning research on key topics, collecting more than 1,000 suggested revisions and further refinements during the plenum discussions, ensuring the document reflected the collective will of the party, he said.

In August, Xi also chaired a symposium with non-party figures to solicit opinions on the draft decision. During this, he underscored the need for heightened risk awareness amid “prolonged governance, periods of peace and complex environments,” state news agency Xinhua reported on Friday.

The decision calls for maintaining high pressure so officials “dare not, cannot and do not want to” engage in corruption, while addressing the symptoms and causes of illicit behaviour.

Soon after Xi took the helm in 2012, state media rolled out a campaign calling for codified rules and laws to replace unwritten rules, warning they had twisted societal values, bred injustice and allowed corruption to permeate different sectors.

In 2014, the fourth plenum of the 18th Central Committee vowed to “resolutely eliminate all kinds of unwritten rules, never permit leniency beyond the law and never allow cases to be handled based on connections, personal relationships or money”. The party’s mouthpiece People’s Daily also published an article that year with the headline: “We must dare to declare war against unwritten rules”.

However, Xi has repeatedly stated that the problem remains a persistent threat. In an October article in Qiushi, the party’s flagship theoretical journal, the president wrote that “when formal rules are not firmly upheld, unwritten rules inevitably flourish; when unwritten rules prevail, formal rules become mere decorations”.

He said that this allowed “political brokers and fraudsters” to rely on personal connections to get ahead in the party.

To curb unwritten rules, he stressed toughening up the enforcement of formal rules, increasing transparency in party and government affairs and strictly punishing violations while holding leaders accountable.

Xi’s speech at the fifth plenum of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) in January gave some examples of these unwritten rules.

“Some cadres rely on personal connections rather than the organisation, and trust relationships rather than laws and discipline,” Xi said, adding that transactions conducted through personal connections allowed “bribes to drive out legal funds” and that informal instructions written by powerful officials could supersede official government decisions.

An article published by Xinhua in June said that unwritten rules could jeopardise public interests, erode government credibility and destroy the foundation of Communist Party rule.

While the party corruption watchdog has occasionally used the specific term “unwritten rules” in its statements about corrupt officials, the details provided by the CCDI often point indirectly to the “unwritten rules” of bribery through money, sex or advantages for family members.

A recent high profile example is Ma Xingrui, formerly a Politburo member and Xinjiang Communist Party chief.

In July this year, the CCDI accused him of “improperly accepting gifts and money, helping relatives buy houses at discounted prices” and engaging in “power-for-sex and money-for-sex transactions”.

Ma also condoned efforts by his relatives to profit from his influence, “fostering rampant corruption across his family”, it said, adding he accepted huge amounts of money and property through his family members and associates.

Ma also sought “benefits for others in cadre selection and appointment, and improperly arranged jobs for others, personally and through relatives,” it added.

The CCDI said in April that Yi Huiman, the former chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, also traded his power for money and sex.

In a documentary produced by the CCDI in 2017, Jin Daoming, the former anti-corruption chief of Shanxi, said that he tried to turn down bribes when he first arrived in the northern province, but he was told that he would offend others. Eventually, Jin – a 20-year veteran of the corruption watchdog – was given a life sentence for accepting 123.7 million yuan (US$18.6 million) in bribes.

Unwritten rules are so entrenched in China’s social fabric that they are not limited to high ranking officials. An article published by the CCDI in 2023 said supervision should be extended to grassroots cadres who use the little power they have to obtain bribes — in the names of “gratitude money,” “company shares, and “loans” — in exchange for contracts for village infrastructure or changing how land can be used.

Beyond party discipline, the plenum’s decision focused on improving the quality of cadres through rigorous education, selection and supervision, according to Huang Jianfa, vice-minister in charge of daily operations at the Central Organisation Department.

It stressed upholding the correct criteria for selecting officials, while demanding the party “resolutely remove those who are disloyal to the party, who say one thing and do another, and who abuse power for personal gain”, he added.

He noted that it also emphasised the need to balance strict oversight with support for officials, creating systems that both reward and protect officials who take the initiative and act responsibly.

Zhang Fuhai, a senior official with the CCDI, said at the press conference that the resolution would strengthen supervision.

This includes making party committees’ supervision more effective, enhancing supervision at the local level and bringing together various oversight bodies to work as a unified force.

The conclave also endorsed disciplinary penalties against 18 senior civilian and 16 military figures – all full or alternate members of the Central Committee – according to an official communique. The total of 34 marks a new high for recent plenary sessions.

The gathering had the lowest attendance in decades. Only 162 of the 205 full Central Committee members attended, representing a turnout of just 79 per cent. A total of 117 alternate members of the Central Committee were present at the session, compared with 147 last year.

The tough message and measures on discipline come a year ahead of the 21st national party congress, which will see major reshuffles at the top echelons of Beijing’s political and military establishment.

item.title: [SCMP] In Michigan Senate race, Trump’s softer China tone gives candidates room to look elsewhere
item.description:
Two years ago, Mike Rogers stood before the Republican National Convention and warned that it was “impossible to build an EV without getting into bed with the Communist Party of China”.

The former US House Intelligence Committee chairman made opposition to Chinese investment a prominent theme of his 2024 Senate bid in Michigan, which he narrowly lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin.

Now, as Rogers runs again, US President Donald Trump’s softer approach towards Beijing has given candidates more room to focus elsewhere, some analysts argue, even as Chinese competition continues to shape the choices facing Michigan’s car industry.
item.content:encoded:
Two years ago, Mike Rogers stood before the Republican National Convention and warned that it was “impossible to build an EV without getting into bed with the Communist Party of China”.

The former US House Intelligence Committee chairman made opposition to Chinese investment a prominent theme of his 2024 Senate bid in Michigan, which he narrowly lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin.

Now, as Rogers runs again, US President Donald Trump’s softer approach towards Beijing has given candidates more room to focus elsewhere, some analysts argue, even as Chinese competition continues to shape the choices facing Michigan’s car industry.

A South China Morning Post review of advertisements posted between the August 4 primary and October 20 found no mention of China in 19 distinct spots on Rogers’ YouTube and X accounts.

The pattern extends to his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, a doctor and former Detroit health director: none of the 18 ads on his campaign’s YouTube channel mention China either, including one attacking “bad trade deals”.

Mary Gallagher, dean of the University of Notre Dame’s Keough School of Global Affairs, said Trump’s less confrontational tone with China had reduced its political salience, allowing candidates to concentrate on concerns voters felt more immediately, including energy costs and trade friction with Canada.

David Dulio, a political scientist at Oakland University in Michigan, agreed that Trump’s approach had given candidates more room to focus elsewhere.

The domestic economy, the war with Iran and tariffs on Canada had become more immediate concerns for voters, he said. “I think it’s just a matter of there are bigger fish to fry.”

Yet China remains central to the industrial choices facing Michigan, the historic heart of American carmaking, where Ford Motor, General Motors and Chrysler helped build the industry.

Both candidates advocate protection against Chinese carmakers, while Ford is advancing a battery plant using technology licensed from CATL, the Chinese battery giant.

Their contest raises a question that restrictions on Chinese cars alone cannot answer: what role should Chinese technology play in sustaining American manufacturing?

Rogers and El-Sayed are competing for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, in a race that carries weight beyond Michigan.

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority going into the November 3 election, and the seat is one of two Democrats are defending in states Trump won in 2024.

Trump carried Michigan by 1.4 percentage points, yet Republicans have not won a Senate race there since 1994. Independent analysts rate the contest a toss-up, though El-Sayed has led narrowly in most recent polls.

The race is also a test for the Democratic Party’s left wing. El-Sayed, who was endorsed by progressive Senator Bernie Sanders, backs Medicare for All and higher taxes on the wealthy.

Rogers has sought to tie El-Sayed to the Democratic Socialists of America. El-Sayed rejects the socialist label, saying he believes in capitalism but that it “has to be regulated”.

Their advertising runs on separate tracks.

Rogers’ spots focus on energy prices, the Middle East and the tariff dispute with Canada, and attack El-Sayed on national security.

El-Sayed’s ads draw on his medical and public-health record and attack Rogers over corporate donors, drug-company money and his Florida home. In one, a United Auto Workers member asks: “Who needs two yachts?”

The ads converge on the war with Iran. Rogers called for it to end quickly in a late-September spot, while an El-Sayed ad posted on October 11 says the war “costs taxpayers a billion dollars a day” and accuses Rogers of “advocating for war after war”.

Matt Grossmann, a political-science professor at Michigan State University, offered a complementary explanation for China’s absence: campaigns emphasise issues that distinguish candidates and persuade voters, and other concerns can displace issues that featured in earlier campaigns.
