Agreement on protecting the car industry can leave China less prominent in advertising without making it less important to the state, he said.

Grossmann pointed to Canada’s direct connections to Michigan through families, travel and cross-border car production.

Dulio said Rogers’ criticism of tariffs on Canada served two purposes: addressing Michigan’s economic interests and showing independence from Trump.

El-Sayed had sought to tie Rogers to the president, he said, while Rogers was trying to reassure voters who disapproved of Trump that he was willing to disagree with him.

Gallagher also suggested that uncertainty over Chinese involvement in American supply chains gave candidates room to avoid categorical positions while companies and policymakers weighed the risks and benefits.

The debate stage nevertheless showed how strongly both candidates continued to frame China as an industrial competitor.

At their second and final debate, in Detroit on October 21, Rogers said the first federal policy he would pursue was a ban on Chinese companies building cars in the United States.

“That is the single number one existential threat to our automobile industry here,” he said, according to a debate transcript.

El-Sayed challenged him over Trump’s stated openness to Chinese carmakers building vehicles in the US, asking whether Rogers would stand up to the president on the issue.

But El-Sayed, too, said the country could not cede the future of its car industry to China. He proposed protecting and subsidising a US-built electric vehicle with a 300-mile range (483km) that would cost US$25,000.

Both candidates also address China on their campaign websites. In a May 7 statement supporting legislation to ban Chinese cars and auto parts, Rogers described China as the biggest threat to Michigan manufacturing.

El-Sayed’s foreign-policy platform advocates competition through research, development and economic strength, alongside cooperation with Beijing and enforcement of trade and intellectual-property rules.

“Our competition with China is not fated toward kinetic war,” it says.

A changed landscape

The two candidates are debating China against a different industrial backdrop from the one Rogers campaigned on two years ago.

Then, the flashpoint was Gotion High-tech’s proposed US$2.4 billion battery plant near Big Rapids, which Rogers opposed. The Chinese-linked project is no longer moving ahead.

Michigan’s economic development agency declared it dead in October 2025 and moved to recover US$23.6 million in state funding.

The dispute had upended politics in Green Charter Township, where residents raised concerns about the project’s scale, environmental impact and the company’s ties to China.

A different model has since gone ahead. Ford owns and operates its BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, but the plant runs on technology licensed from CATL.

Ford began making pre-production lithium iron phosphate cells at the plant in June and has said it expects to produce market-ready cells before the end of this year, according to The Detroit News. The cells are intended to power Ford’s forthcoming lower-cost electric pickup truck.

The plant’s future depends on demand for electric vehicles, and it is on EVs, along with Trump’s broader trade policy, that the candidates’ differences are clearest.

Rogers’ “Beating Heart” advertisement attacks El-Sayed’s position on petrol-powered cars and declares: “No EV mandates, ever.” China is not mentioned.

El-Sayed has backed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, a policy supported by the United Auto Workers union, which endorsed him in June.

At a Detroit Economic Club forum on October 20, he said he was “not against tariffs per se” but described the administration’s approach as chaotic and self-serving. He argued that tariffs should be tied to an industrial policy.

Rogers called Trump’s tariffs a mixed bag. He credited them with bringing car production back to Michigan from China and Mexico, but said tariffs on Canada may not have been well thought through.

Grossmann placed the campaign in the context of a broader national shift towards more positive views of trade.

He pointed to Gallup polling showing that 82 per cent of American adults viewed foreign trade as an opportunity for economic growth in February 2026, compared with 61 per cent in February 2024.

Grossmann described a “thermostatic” response in which public opinion can move against a policy direction as government pursues it more aggressively.

He suggested that fatigue with trade restrictions could make arguments used in earlier campaigns less effective.

For Michigan, the car industry’s political importance extends beyond those directly employed in it, Grossmann said. Family connections and its place in the state’s identity give its future a resonance that reaches beyond the factory floor.

In Marshall, the choices carry the prospect of new jobs. Ford said in June that it expected to employ 800 people at its battery plant by the end of the year, eventually rising to 1,700.

Yet the choices facing the industry are not necessarily the issues driving the campaign. Dulio said concerns about the domestic economy, petrol prices and trade with neighbouring Canada had pushed China down the voters’ agenda.

“It’s not that those issues aren’t important. It’s just that they have been superseded by more proximate and salient issues,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s wider yuan push: a gateway to the world?
item.description:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority. In the last of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing examines Hong Kong’s push to make the currency part of everyday life – from vending machines and retail payments to government spending and cross-border trade.

At Hong Kong’s Central Ferry Pier No 8, mainland Chinese tourist Lei is surprised to find that the digital currency e-CNY can be used to buy drinks from a vending machine.

Lei, a logistics worker in his twenties from Guangxi, had never encountered the digital currency and related payment system developed by the country’s central bank, the People’s Bank of China, in real life.
item.content:encoded:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority. In the last of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing examines Hong Kong’s push to make the currency part of everyday life – from vending machines and retail payments to government spending and cross-border trade.

At Hong Kong’s Central Ferry Pier No 8, mainland Chinese tourist Lei is surprised to find that the digital currency e-CNY can be used to buy drinks from a vending machine.

Lei, a logistics worker in his twenties from Guangxi, had never encountered the digital currency and related payment system developed by the country’s central bank, the People’s Bank of China, in real life.

Hong Kong has been testing the use of e-CNY in a pilot scheme, with the aim of making cross-border retail payments more convenient.

“I remember when I was in senior secondary school, my politics class talked about this,” he said of the e-CNY. “But we haven’t seen this in real life. I saw this for the first time today in Hong Kong.”

The excitement did not move him, however, to use the option; he went with Alipay instead.

As China seeks to expand international use of the yuan amid rising geopolitical uncertainties and growing import-export trade, the Hong Kong government has made wider use of the currency a priority in its annual policy address and the city’s first five-year plan, covering 2026-30.

From vending machines to government receivables and payments for cross-border bills, yuan settlements are gaining momentum – although consumer habits and currency unpredictability during conversion into Hong Kong dollars remain obstacles.

Government-led yuan adoption

Hong Kong has the world’s largest offshore yuan liquidity pool. As of July 31, renminbi deposits in the city had reached 1.3 trillion yuan.

In an interview with the SCMP earlier this month, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city had taken steps to pave the way for broader yuan use among businesses and residents.

For example, he said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city’s de facto central bank, had earlier injected more liquidity into the offshore renminbi market by expanding its renminbi business facility to 500 billion yuan.

“Another thing that we should do is about education,” he said. “Try to share more use cases of renminbi in the region, either in the form of trade settlement and others, in such a way that there is greater interest and eagerness across the region using renminbi.”

He conceded that bottlenecks in yuan adoption needed to be addressed.

Hui cited market feedback on insufficient direct quotes between local currencies and the yuan.

With Asian economies trading more heavily among themselves after the Covid-19 pandemic, and the renminbi offering lower interest rates than the US dollar, Hui said there were stronger reasons for regional businesses to raise financing and settle trades in the yuan without touching the dollar.

In June, the Monetary Authority signed a memorandum of understanding with Bank Indonesia, the country’s central bank, and the People’s Bank of China to establish a bilateral transaction framework for direct offshore renminbi-Indonesian rupiah trading, reducing exchange-rate risks and transaction costs for businesses.

“[Through this] there will be greater willingness for market participants to use RMB,” Hui said.

Yuxuan Tang, Asia head of rates and foreign exchange strategy at JP Morgan Private Bank, said global fragmentation could be manifested by the fact that rising geopolitical tensions and supply chain reconfiguration were encouraging countries and businesses to diversify their settlement arrangements.

Direct currency transaction frameworks, such as the mechanism between the offshore renminbi and rupiah mentioned in the policy address, could reduce transaction costs, limit foreign exchange risk and lessen operational dependence on a single settlement system.

“The broader implication is a gradual evolution towards a more multicurrency global financial system,” Tang said. “Over time, this could deepen regional currency liquidity pools and support the development of local financial markets.”

The current situation highlighted the transition of the offshore renminbi from a pure trade-settlement currency into an investment and diversification asset amid global fragmentation, Tang said.

Hong Kong authorities are also taking the lead in adopting more yuan in government revenue and expenditure.

On the revenue side, Hui said the government had recently changed the law to allow it to collect stamp duty in renminbi when mainland investors bought and settled Hong Kong-listed shares directly in yuan through renminbi-denominated stock counters under the cross-border Stock Connect scheme.

Trading in these stock counters is due to be rolled out by July next year.

Receiving stamp duty in yuan would also help the government manage exchange-rate risks, Hui said.

“When we have the RMB counters collecting stamp duty in RMB, it will also be an additional source of RMB,” he said.

“Having them directly deployed will be a way for us to avoid the need for managing the exchange-rate risk. Fundamentally, it is to manage use – RMB in and RMB out.”

On the expenditure side, settlement in yuan is already a reality.

The government has made renminbi payments for a cross-border infrastructure project, the Western Cross-River Link Bridge connecting two parks in Hong Kong and Shenzhen in the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone.

More significantly, it is discussing with mainland authorities the possibility of settling the 2027-29 Dongjiang water supply agreement in renminbi. The city paid HK$5.28 billion for Dongjiang water in 2025-26.

Through the Dongjiang-Shenzhen water supply scheme, Hong Kong has relied on water from the Dongjiang, or East River, for the past 60 years, supplying up to 80 per cent of the city’s fresh water.

Cross-border social welfare payments are also shifting to renminbi.

According to the Social Welfare Department, the government spent about 37.7 million yuan in the 2025-26 financial year on places at residential care homes in Guangdong province.

As of September, 1,600 Hong Kong seniors were staying in 29 homes for the elderly taking part in the department’s subsidised residential care services scheme in the province.

An additional 5.77 million yuan was paid out in medical subsidies to 762 elderly participants who opted to receive the funds in the currency.

Use cases

At the retail level, e-CNY is another point of focus. Hui revealed that the number of local retail outlets accepting the digital currency had jumped from 300 in May 2024 to about 5,200 currently.

“They cover a whole value chain in terms of retail stores, hotels, travel agencies, restaurants, convenience stores [and] supermarkets,” Hui said.

“So fundamentally, we try to provide at the more retail level as much convenience as possible, in such a way that for the users who are really ready and willing to use e-CNY, they can do that more conveniently in Hong Kong.”

As of January this year, 79,600 e-CNY wallets had been registered, according to data from the People’s Bank of China.

The city’s Faster Payment System (FPS), a real-time payment platform, mirrors this rapid growth.

Daily renminbi transaction volume on the system surged from about 30 million yuan across 700 transactions in the fourth quarter of 2018 to an average of 21,500 transactions worth about 1.1 billion yuan daily by the third quarter of this year, according to bureau data.

To further fuel the momentum, the Monetary Authority is actively preparing to link FPS directly with the mainland’s UnionPay, a bank card and payment system, in a move expected to enable seamless cross-border retail payments across a vast merchant network.

Despite the rapid growth of QR-code payments, a banking source pointed to a lingering hurdle in the city’s infrastructure: settlement banks automatically convert these renminbi payments into Hong Kong dollars for local merchants at the back end as goods are priced in the local currency.

Asked about the instant conversion, Hui said authorities were trying to develop an ecosystem in which banks encouraged merchant acceptance by expanding support, noting that the number of retail banks supporting e-CNY top-ups through FPS had risen from 17 to 19.

“So, what we try to do is really identify more players in the market that are ready and also willing to take on e-CNY in such a way that for people or for tourists who are coming here and also want to use it, they have the right means to do so,” Hui said.

Mainland tourists are believed to make up the largest group of e-CNY users in Hong Kong.

Mainlanders accounted for 78 per cent, or 31.9 million, of the tourists visiting the city in the first nine months of this year, according to the Hong Kong Tourism Board.

Hong Kong-based FreshUp, a major operator of vending machines, including those at the Central pier, is part of the private sector driving the wider use of the yuan in the city.

Founder and executive director David Lam said the company rapidly upgraded about 800 of its more than 5,000 machines to accept e-CNY.

In the weeks before the 15th National Games, co-hosted by Guangdong, Hong Kong, and Macau last November, there was a coordinated push to expand e-CNY acceptance and use in the city, mainly a bank- and merchant-led adoption campaign.

Appointed by Bank of China (Hong Kong), FreshUp spearheaded the roll-out in October last year.

“We helped them modify many things, such as installing QR-code scanners, ensuring back-end data accuracy, and integrating the API [application programming interface],” Lam said. “We spent a lot of effort on this project.”

He said the company had deployed the payment option across targeted tourist-heavy transport hubs.

“The response has been very good. It has achieved Bank of China’s expectations for the project,” Lam noted, declining to reveal exact transaction data.

By capturing what Lam described as “high-frequency, low-amount” daily transactions, these micro-purchases are quietly building consumer habits around the use of the digital yuan.

However, mainland tourist Mr Wu said more promotion and marketing was needed to raise awareness of e-CNY in the city, given the prevalence of Alipay and WeChat Pay. Alipay is owned by Ant Group, an affiliate of Alibaba Group Holding, which also owns the South China Morning Post.

“It has not been [widely] promoted,” said Wu, who is in his fifties. “Someone sent this [to me] previously but most people have not used it because Alipay and WeChat Pay are there already.”

Bank of China (Hong Kong) deputy chief executive Huabin Wang recently said that a growing range of renminbi products was among the advantages the city possessed that would ensure broad prospects as a global offshore renminbi hub.

“First, Hong Kong’s first five-year plan provides clearer guidance for the development direction of its renminbi business,” Wang said.

“Second, the city’s renminbi business ecosystem has become increasingly mature with its expanding range of offshore renminbi products.

“Third, Hong Kong has a unique advantage in telling the story of the international use of the renminbi, and its ability to reach emerging markets is strengthening.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore wields ‘quiet diplomacy’ in minister’s surprise visit to Indonesia amid haze tensions
item.description:
Singapore’s decision to send its top diplomat to Indonesia on a surprise visit, following days of terse exchanges over a regional haze, underscores a bid to defuse growing tensions and seek a direct channel to President Prabowo Subianto.

Analysts say Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan’s trip reflected his country’s preference for measured diplomacy amid rising nationalistic rhetoric in Indonesia, with the city state also mindful of containing any “negative fallout” as Jakarta grapples with local protests against the haze.

Balakrishnan met Prabowo at his private residence on Wednesday, a day after both states pledged deeper collaboration in tackling transboundary haze.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s decision to send its top diplomat to Indonesia on a surprise visit, following days of terse exchanges over a regional haze, underscores a bid to defuse growing tensions and seek a direct channel to President Prabowo Subianto.

Analysts say Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan’s trip reflected his country’s preference for measured diplomacy amid rising nationalistic rhetoric in Indonesia, with the city state also mindful of containing any “negative fallout” as Jakarta grapples with local protests against the haze.

Balakrishnan met Prabowo at his private residence on Wednesday, a day after both states pledged deeper collaboration in tackling transboundary haze.

Protests led by student leaders and civil society groups broke out in Jakarta on Wednesday over the government’s handling of forest fires that led to toxic haze blanketing parts of Indonesia and neighbouring countries.

Balakrishnan’s trip coincided with a rare meeting back home in which bosses of 10 locally registered firms were summoned to a session with three ministers in a display of tough action against those linked to the haze.

Singapore’s foreign minister had flown in “suddenly” and requested an audience with Prabowo, local media cited Indonesian Cabinet Secretary Teddy Wijaya as saying.

Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Balakrishnan said his trip was to ensure “high-level direct communication”.

“You can’t conduct diplomacy just by the phone or through the media, with all due respect. There’s face-to-face direct explanation, conveying concerns, and also looking for solutions,” he said.

The top diplomat declined to elaborate on the meeting’s details but said Prabowo and Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had already corresponded “at the highest level”.

Balakrishnan met his Indonesian counterpart Arrmanatha Nasir on Tuesday, and both announced the establishment of a joint task force to investigate companies linked to haze-creating forest fires in Indonesia.

Balakrishnan said the task force would ensure close coordination and data-sharing between both sides. “We expect, therefore, the deterrent impact of this joint task force to make a difference.”

Lina Alexandra, head of the international relations department at the Jakarta-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said the task force was a “good start” but would require high levels of inter-agency cooperation.

“I’m very hopeful, actually, but there must be follow-ups and more intensive cooperation for sure,” she said.

Consistent ‘quiet’ diplomacy

Balakrishnan’s visit was consistent with Singapore’s measured approach in dealing with its larger neighbour, which reflected the city state’s constraints as a small nation, observers said.

His request to meet Prabowo personally was a “clear signal of urgency” on Singapore’s part for de-escalation, as well as a nod to Jakarta that it understood the strategic implications of the situation and wanted to stabilise ties before potential deterioration, said Collins Chong, a foreign affairs analyst at the University of Malaya.

“Reaching Prabowo directly is important because he has the political authority to provide the necessary reassurance,” he added.

Longer-term existential challenges of energy and food security, and economic competitiveness had always been Singapore’s bigger and more pressing strategic concerns, Chong said.

“For a resource-constrained small state, maintaining stable relations with its immediate neighbours is a fundamental national security necessity,” Chong said, noting that Singapore had similarly offered help to Jakarta in previous haze episodes.

Tensions have been escalating in recent weeks, fuelled by allegations of economic sabotage and a reduction in gas supplies. Jakarta began cutting its gas line to Singapore on Saturday, citing rising domestic demand.

Former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi claimed last week that Singapore’s sovereign wealth funds Temasek and GIC were working behind the scenes to push global index MSCI to downgrade Jakarta’s market status, prompting swift denials from both firms.

Observers noted that Balakrishnan did not explicitly raise both incidents during his visit. On Tuesday, the minister said Singapore had “full confidence” in Indonesia – a sentiment he noted was reflected in its actions.

“Of course, as neighbours, we may not always agree on everything. But what matters is how we manage our differences and overcome challenges together,” said Balakrishnan, who spoke occasionally in Bahasa Indonesia.

“As the Indonesian saying goes, ‘Share the heavy burdens, and carry the lighter ones together’.”

Alan Chong, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), called the quote a “very diplomatic turn of phrase” and said, “I think the undeclared part of Balakrishnan’s visit to Jakarta is to actually sort out these issues and neutralise any negative fallout.”

He said Singapore had a precedent of using “quiet diplomacy” in its dealings with Indonesia, citing earlier incidents such as when then finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa suggested imposing a levy on ships passing through the Malacca Strait.

In response, Singapore reaffirmed on multiple occasions that transit through the strait was a right in accordance with international law.

Alexandra said she hoped the visit and the increased collaboration on tackling the haze would soothe bilateral tensions.

She suggested Indonesia “create a real mechanism to prevent such things from happening again so that these kinds of tensions can be avoided”.

Alan Chong warned that incidents such as the gas export cut – which Indonesia rationalised as a reaction to rising domestic demand – might occur with increasing frequency in the future as Prabowo continued nationalistic moves.

On Monday, Indonesia urged its umrah pilgrims to prioritise direct flights to Saudi Arabia over transit routes through Singapore, citing the potential to strengthen the country’s aviation industry.

“Singapore is a convenient target … and I think [Prabowo] expects Singapore to take it in stride,” Alan Chong said.

Balakrishnan’s visit marked a bid to remind the Indonesia leader “we have got a good relationship, and let’s not rock it further”, he added.

Dangers of online rhetoric

While the cost of compromise may rise with intensifying nationalistic sentiments, observers say it is unlikely to affect long-standing bilateral cooperation.

Balakrishnan on Wednesday acknowledged that recent weeks were a “period of concern, anxiety and anger” for residents in Singapore, when air quality had breached “very unhealthy levels”.

Many Singaporeans have taken their frustration online, with some calling for their government to take harsher legal measures against its neighbour. Indonesians have similarly accused Singapore-headquartered firms of contributing to the forest fires.

On Sunday, Calvin Cheng, a former Singapore nominated member of parliament, floated the idea of cutting undersea fibre-optic cables, sharing a graphic stating that 90 per cent of Jakarta’s internet traffic routes passed through Singapore.

Indonesia’s Communication and Digital Affairs Minister Meutya Hafid hit back on Tuesday, noting that most of the subsea cable system connecting to Singapore passed through Indonesian waters.

“Should they be severed, whether accidentally or intentionally, 80 per cent of Singapore’s connectivity capacity would be at risk of collapse,” she wrote on social media.

Meutya said global tech investors could exit Singapore if they lost Indonesia’s user base of 267 million people – a population 47 times that of Singapore.

Alan Chong slammed Cheng’s remark as “naive”.

“You can express unhappiness, but you do not threaten the severing of communications as a form of retaliation,” he said.

Unfriendly political rhetoric posed an “immediate danger” as it could create a cycle of nationalist reactions and risk neighbouring governments interpreting statements intended for a domestic audience, Collins Chong warned.

“This can narrow the political room for compromise and force both sides to demonstrate greater resolve, even when their underlying strategic interests favour cooperation,” he said.

Jefferson Ng, an associate research fellow at RSIS’ Indonesia Programme, said differences in economic principles and models between both states could have caused the “current turbulence”.

But he noted that both nations had established comprehensive cooperation across various issues. In July, leaders of the two countries signed 26 agreements which spanned areas such as economy, energy and defence.

“While online chatter and content have been at elevated levels in recent weeks due to frustrations on both sides, I think the overall bilateral relationship is very strong and will be able to weather the storm.”

Balakrishnan on Wednesday said political and polemic issues were bound to surface in the face of transboundary rows.

“It’s important for cool heads to prevail, for direct, honest, candid, constructive conversations to be had, and for us to look for a collective approach,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Japan is pushing for a more ‘proactive’ Southeast Asia amid great-power rivalry
item.description:
Japan wants a more united and proactive Southeast Asia as it sees Asean as a bulwark against an intensifying great-power rivalry, analysts say, while uncertainty over Washington’s long-term Indo-Pacific strategy has deepened Tokyo’s concerns about the region’s future.

Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi on Wednesday urged Southeast Asian nations to strengthen their collective response to emerging security threats, warning of a “rapidly deteriorating” security environment and shifts in the regional military balance that raised the risk of “dangerous miscalculations”.

“These crises do not merely adapt. They overlap and amplify one another,” Koizumi said at the Asean-Japan Defence Ministers’ Informal Meeting in Cebu.
item.content:encoded:
Japan wants a more united and proactive Southeast Asia as it sees Asean as a bulwark against an intensifying great-power rivalry, analysts say, while uncertainty over Washington’s long-term Indo-Pacific strategy has deepened Tokyo’s concerns about the region’s future.

Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi on Wednesday urged Southeast Asian nations to strengthen their collective response to emerging security threats, warning of a “rapidly deteriorating” security environment and shifts in the regional military balance that raised the risk of “dangerous miscalculations”.

“These crises do not merely adapt. They overlap and amplify one another,” Koizumi said at the Asean-Japan Defence Ministers’ Informal Meeting in Cebu.

He urged the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to protect its unity, centrality and resilience, and said the bloc must be able to overcome differences and set its priorities while acting on a common agenda with external partners.

“Unity means working together despite differences. Centrality means setting the region’s agenda and drawing external partners around it. Resilience means keeping essential functions and autonomy intact in a crisis,” Koizumi said.

The defence minister also proposed updating cooperation between Japan, Asean and partners outside the bloc in emerging security areas such as artificial intelligence technology, unmanned systems, and the protection of critical undersea infrastructure.

“When challenges change, cooperation must change with them,” he said.

‘Proactive’ Southeast Asia

Koizumi’s remarks reflect Japan’s perception of Asean as a theatre for greater strategic rivalry, as well as an anchor that enables practical cooperation across the region, observers say.

“Koizumi’s remarks show that Japan sees the regional balance shifting structurally against the status quo and fears that grey-zone coercion could escalate through miscalculation,” Sarah Soh, an associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told This Week in Asia.

“Against this backdrop, Japan sees Asean as a normative anchor, as an inclusive platform that keeps all major powers engaged, and as a partner for practical cooperation.”

While Koizumi shared Japan’s assessment of a deteriorating regional security environment, with implicit references to China, his speech “focused largely on expanding practical cooperation and building regional resilience in disasters, supply chains, and energy, alongside a reaffirmation of Asean unity and centrality”, Soh said.

“On balance, the speech strikes a measured tone and is unlikely to unsettle Asean member states.”

Satoru Nagao, a non-resident fellow at Hudson Institute, said Asean could become a theatre for a US-China power game, much like Central Europe during the US-Soviet Cold War.

“Today, Southeast Asia lies between the US and China and is made up of many small countries. This means it could become the ‘Central Europe’ between the US and China,” the Tokyo-based Nagao said, adding that the scenario highlighted the importance of Asean unity.

Don McLain Gill, an international relations lecturer at De La Salle University, agreed that it was in “the best interests of Japan to have a more resilient, aware and proactive Southeast Asia” amid the backdrop of uncertainty over Washington’s long-term strategy for the Indo-Pacific.

“For Japan, it would do its best to encourage Southeast Asia to begin thinking more proactively about its future and how its members need to work together to maintain the status quo, according to international law,” Gill said, adding that Japan could serve as an anchor and a reliable partner for the region in keeping the order intact.

Collin Koh, a senior fellow and coordinator of naval and maritime affairs projects at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies, said Koizumi’s remarks reflected Japan’s long-standing interest in Southeast Asia, adding that the rhetoric was an enduring one for Tokyo.

“It is essentially an emphasis on the interdependence across the subregions of the Indo-Pacific. And that, of course, pertains to Southeast Asia alongside Northeast Asia,” Koh said.

While Koizumi emphasised the need for Japan-Asean defence cooperation, Tokyo “would be quite cognisant of the fact that Southeast Asia itself is not a monolithic body”, Koh noted.

“Asean is far from a monolithic body with the sort of institutions that will enable much closer defence and security cooperation between Japan and Asean as an institution itself,” Koh said, noting that more concrete measures would usually happen at the bilateral and minilateral levels.

Expanding security areas

Regarding Japan’s proposal to boost cooperation with Asean and other external partners in emerging security areas such as AI, unmanned systems and sea cables, analysts warn that Asean may not be able to match Japan’s capacity.

Asean was likely to welcome the idea as it shared Japan’s concerns in these areas, but could frame the cooperation as building resilience rather than deterrence and move cautiously on involving external partners, Soh said.

“Most member states also lack the technology and experience to protect undersea cables or use AI and unmanned systems at scale. Asean is therefore likely to support Japan’s direction in principle but proceed slowly, with practical progress depending largely on Japanese support and technology,” she said.

While Japan had not developed its own capabilities well in AI and unmanned systems, it excelled in its technology for undersea cables, Nagao said.

“Japan’s concern is China’s domination in these areas because of the cost of AI and unmanned systems,” Nagao said, adding that Tokyo could leverage its goodwill in the region from having made several investments to improve Southeast Asia’s capabilities.

Koh said undersea cable infrastructure remained a vulnerability for the region and could be the most relevant area of Japan-Asean cooperation.

“In a way, Southeast Asia is a gateway and interconnection between the world’s oceans where those undersea cables pass through. So certainly it gives Asean a certain advantage purely due to geography,” Koh said.

However, individual countries’ capacities varied widely, making it difficult to establish a framework to bring member states together “largely because not all of them might be able to offer anything substantial to the table”, Koh said.

“So it could well be a pretty lopsided type of contribution where they might be sidelined for the most part,” Koh said, but remained hopeful that any initial discussions could “spawn off more substantial cooperation thereafter”.

item.title: [SCMP] Hegseth pitches new US-Asean defence framework, but doubts run deep
item.description:
What are Southeast Asian nations doing to help the United States tackle its challenges? A reporter with the American right-wing organisation Turning Point USA put the question bluntly to US President Donald Trump’s defence chief this week in the Philippines.

As US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth pitched closer naval ties and maritime security cooperation at a gathering of defence ministers from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) and other regional powers, the question injected transactional politics into what is usually the realm of diplomatic niceties.

Analysts say the Pentagon chief’s proposal is unlikely to produce a substantial Asean-wide framework, given the bloc’s long-standing refusal to choose sides and the limits of its consensus-based system.
item.content:encoded:
What are Southeast Asian nations doing to help the United States tackle its challenges? A reporter with the American right-wing organisation Turning Point USA put the question bluntly to US President Donald Trump’s defence chief this week in the Philippines.

As US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth pitched closer naval ties and maritime security cooperation at a gathering of defence ministers from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) and other regional powers, the question injected transactional politics into what is usually the realm of diplomatic niceties.

Analysts say the Pentagon chief’s proposal is unlikely to produce a substantial Asean-wide framework, given the bloc’s long-standing refusal to choose sides and the limits of its consensus-based system.

In his remarks, Hegseth urged his regional counterparts to develop a “practical” framework to deepen security cooperation between Washington and Asean.

“As we look to the future in this region, I’d like us to be even more ambitious … we propose that we work together to develop a US-Asean Framework for Defence Cooperation,” Hegseth said, without offering details.

“A practical framework that guides our cooperation over the next several years. I will note a critically important next several years,” he added, acknowledging that “we’re not going to agree on everything, nor do we need to”.

Hegseth described Washington’s approach as “strong, quiet and clear – strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics”, without explicitly mentioning Beijing or its long-standing territorial disputes with several Asean member states.

He said Washington was ready to begin work with Singapore, which is set to chair next year’s Asean meetings.

In a separate exchange on the sidelines, responding to the reporter’s question about what Asean was doing for the US, Hegseth called it a “great point” and rejected the old framing of the relationship.

“This is not an aid exercise,” he said. “This is not a foreign aid or defence aid exercise where countries come and ask for what the United States will do for them and then we do it out of the sense of international goodwill … the expectation is that allies bring what they can to the table.”

He pointed to access, basing and overflight rights across critical geography in the first island chain as the kind of contribution that matters, describing Asean’s value as lying in “mutually beneficial exchanges”.

That tension goes to the heart of Washington’s challenge with Asean: can a bloc that has long resisted choosing sides deliver the tangible returns the US is increasingly demanding?

Experts see little prospect of the proposal gaining traction at the bloc level, let alone forcing Asean to pick a side.

“There is no indication Hegseth is suggesting a mutual defence commitment of any kind, and any sort of Asean-US framework would be miles away from the defence integration and cooperation that characterises Nato,” said Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow at Defence Priorities, a Washington-based think tank.

“In any case, Asean would reject such an arrangement. Asean has always balanced and hedged between the United States and China. It rejects any sort of defence alliance and refuses to choose sides between the two powers,” she said.

Collin Koh, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, pointed to obstacles that go beyond geopolitics.

“Asean is an institution made up of 11 member states, each with its own unique national context, threat perception and priorities, as well as disparities in defence and security capacities amongst them,” he said. “Even envisaging an intra-Asean defence cooperation framework involving all 11 member states is itself fraught with challenges.”

Koh said that any cooperation beyond the “lowest common denominator” was unrealistic at the Asean level.

Without details of the proposed framework, he said realistic areas for Asean-US cooperation included “information-sharing mechanisms” to boost maritime awareness and coordinate responses to regional crises, including humanitarian help and disaster relief.

“More substantial cooperation that tangibly contributes towards building military interoperability … is likely to take place at the member states level, either bilaterally or minilaterally,” he added.

On the sidelines in Cebu, Hegseth met the defence ministers of Japan, Australia and the Philippines, which together with the US make up the informal “Squad” defence grouping focused on deterrence and operational readiness in the Indo-Pacific, with an emphasis on the South China Sea.

He also met Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. India is a member of the Quad, a strategic security dialogue that also includes the US, Australia and Japan. Quad foreign ministers are meeting in the US this week, with a leaders’ summit planned in Manila next month.

Both the Squad and the Quad are “minilateral” groups that prioritise practical maritime and security cooperation among like-minded partners, bypassing the consensus constraints of the broader Asean format.

Kavanagh noted that the US and Asean already cooperated in limited ways on defence, making the added value of Hegseth’s proposal unclear.

She pointed to the Trump administration’s preference for bilateral deals over multilateral ones, and to the practical constraints on US attention.

“The biggest constraint on any sort of deeper US-Asean cooperation is bandwidth and resources,” she said. “Can a Pentagon tied up in a war with Iran, still supporting Ukraine, and chasing drugs in Latin America afford to invest more in Southeast Asia right now? I’d bet on no.”

On China, both experts were cautious. Kavanagh said it was hard to predict Beijing’s response until more details emerged, and that she would not expect a near-term reaction.

Koh said China was “likely to view this new initiative with no small amount of wariness – on the assumption that this is part of Washington’s attempt at strategic containment”.

Beijing’s most plausible response, he added, would be to deepen bilateral ties with individual Asean members rather than offer a competing framework, though its existing relationships remain thinner than Washington’s and are complicated by South China Sea tensions.

China’s absence amplified the optics. Defence Minister Dong Jun skipped the meetings in Cebu, with Beijing sending only its Manila-based defence attache. The timing coincides with the Communist Party’s fifth plenum in Beijing, but it also follows months of escalating South China Sea tensions with the Philippines.

The US proposal lands against a backdrop of debates around enhanced defence cooperation among Asean members.

Philippine ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez recently told the South China Morning Post he hoped Asean would evolve into something “like a Nato” capable of handling its own security.

The idea was previously dismissed by his country’s defence secretary, Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, as unrealistic given the bloc’s diverging interests.

Teodoro, chairing this year’s Asean defence ministers’ meeting, welcomed continued US engagement as necessary for regional stability but stopped short of endorsing any alliance-like structure.

“We value the United States’ sustained engagement with the defence establishments of Asean, as a robust US presence is necessary for peace and stability in Southeast Asia and in the broader Indo-Pacific region,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Lula’s re-election unlock Mercosur markets for Southeast Asia?
item.description:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s re-election should provide continuity for the country’s trade push into Southeast Asia, analysts say, as Vietnam and Indonesia pursue preferential trade agreements with Mercosur, the South American bloc in which Brazil is the largest economy.

But better access to Brazil and other Mercosur markets is far from assured, with trade experts pointing to difficult negotiations over tariffs and agricultural access, as well as political differences within the bloc.

In August, Vietnam completed its first round of talks on a preferential trade agreement with Mercosur.
item.content:encoded:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s re-election should provide continuity for the country’s trade push into Southeast Asia, analysts say, as Vietnam and Indonesia pursue preferential trade agreements with Mercosur, the South American bloc in which Brazil is the largest economy.

But better access to Brazil and other Mercosur markets is far from assured, with trade experts pointing to difficult negotiations over tariffs and agricultural access, as well as political differences within the bloc.

In August, Vietnam completed its first round of talks on a preferential trade agreement with Mercosur.

Meanwhile, Indonesia proposed a narrower, preferential agreement in August this year, which Brazil said it would study. This pivot follows a lack of progress on a broader comprehensive deal that the two sides originally began negotiating in December 2021.

Brazil previously authorised its negotiators to pursue preferential deals with both nations in September last year.

“Lula’s re-election delivers immediate negotiating continuity, but it should not have much of an effect beyond that,” said Jayant Menon, a visiting senior fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

Market access would improve only if the negotiations concluded successfully, he said, while also cautioning against overstating Brazil’s potential as an alternative export market.

“While Brazil is a potential diversification market for both Vietnam and Indonesia, the reality is that Brazil currently accounts for less than 1 per cent of each country’s exports,” Menon said, and its ability to offset a major downturn in the United States, China or Europe remained limited.

Individual industries could gain substantially, however, and Menon identified electronics as a particular opportunity for Vietnam, with vegetable oils, rubber products and selected industrial goods for Indonesia.

In the first half of 2026, Brazil imported about US$2.11 billion in goods from Vietnam, a 17 per cent increase year on year, according to figures cited by Vietnam’s ambassador to Brazil Bui Van Nghi. He listed phones, computers, electronic products, machinery, garments and footwear among Vietnam’s exports to Brazil.

For Vietnam’s pangasius exports, Brazil is already a significant customer. Exports of the fish to Brazil reached US$144 million in the first nine months of this year, up 15 per cent from a year earlier, according to the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers (VASEP).

Brazil was the industry’s third-largest market, behind China and the US.

Meanwhile, 14 Vietnamese seafood businesses, including nine VASEP members, attended the Seafood Show Latin America in Sao Paulo from October 20 to 22, according to Vietnamese media. Discussions with Brazilian businesses covered topics such as tariffs, product testing and customs-clearance times.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Vietnamese seafood exporters Vinh Hoan and Navico for comment.

While Vietnamese exporters are currently testing the waters, Indonesia already has a foothold in Brazil.

Yose Rizal Damuri, executive director of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta, noted that Indonesia’s palm oil-based and natural rubber products made up over a quarter of Brazil’s imports.

Better access could deepen those sales and help diversify Indonesian exporters’ expansion into footwear, textiles and processed foods.

Brazil should be viewed as the principal market within Mercosur for Indonesian exporters, he said.

“Calling it a ‘gateway’ to Latin America’ is useful for buying support, but Indonesia should still assess each destination’s tariffs, regulations and distribution costs separately,” he said.

A narrower agreement could simplify negotiations by concentrating on selected goods, Damuri said, but the two sides would still have to agree on sensitive products and what concessions each would make in return.

According to Welber Barral, a former Brazilian foreign-trade secretary, agricultural access would be important to Mercosur, as other members like Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay are also interested in Asian markets for their agricultural commodities.

“Mercosur is not going to advance if the agricultural offer is not good,” Barral said, noting that the bloc would not sign an agreement covering only industrial goods if that left out its main agricultural interests.

The start of negotiations could itself encourage exporters to promote their products and seek distributors in a new market, but progress would also require technical agreements covering safety, health requirements and product classification, Barral said.

Alberto Maresca, a researcher at the University of Sao Paulo and fellow at UNU-CRIS, said Brazil’s recent interest in Southeast Asia was driven partly by US tariffs on Brazilian goods and concern about Brazil’s reliance on China.

Maresca identified Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore as Brazil’s main partners in Southeast Asia, citing a combination of political and commercial interests.

“In the case of Malaysia, it has to do with Lula’s personal ties with its prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim, and also a multilateral convergence of Brazil with Malaysia and Brics,” Maresca said.

He notes that Brazil has strong defence ties with Indonesia, whose armed forces operate a number of Brazilian-made equipment such as light military aircraft and rocket launcher systems. Singapore, meanwhile, has important stakes in Brazil’s domestic market, where online shopping platform Shopee is one of the most used platforms.

At the trade bloc level, Maresca expressed doubt that Lula’s election victory would quickly advance an agreement with Mercosur, even though the bloc was on a “very good trend” of finalising deals.

Mercosur recently cemented major trade deals with Singapore and the European Free Trade Association, alongside efforts to finalise a long-stalled pact with the European Union.

However, Maresca doubted the momentum would carry into the new year, pointing to political differences between the socialist-leaning Lula and Argentina’s President Javier Milei, a right-wing free-market advocate.

Maresca said Milei had been “banking on [Flavio] Bolsonaro” to win. And because of that tension, “I see it really difficult for Mercosur to unlock itself, at least in the coming year.”

Vietnam and Indonesia should continue developing commercial relations with Brazil even if a Mercosur-wide agreement proved difficult, Maresca said. But he did not expect Brazil to open sectors where domestic manufacturers faced competition from Southeast Asian imports.

For Indonesia, Damuri said a jointly agreed negotiating framework or preliminary exchanges of tariff offers would be more meaningful signs of progress over the coming year. Those steps would give exporters a clearer view of the products and trade procedures a prospective agreement might cover.

item.title: [SCMP] Asian scientists are looking to South Korea as it becomes harder to stay in the US
item.description:
As tightening US visa restrictions and geopolitics lock out Asian researchers from Western institutions, South Korea is emerging as a new academic sanctuary for top talent.

According to Yoo Ji-beom, president of Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) in Seoul, that reflects a broader trend that has seen the West giving way to Asia after decades of dominance – particularly in the field of applied technology in China, Japan and South Korea.

“Technological competition and global talent mobility are reshaping the knowledge ecosystem. Competition to attract and retain the very best researchers has become far more intense than before,” Yoo said during an interview in Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
As tightening US visa restrictions and geopolitics lock out Asian researchers from Western institutions, South Korea is emerging as a new academic sanctuary for top talent.

According to Yoo Ji-beom, president of Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) in Seoul, that reflects a broader trend that has seen the West giving way to Asia after decades of dominance – particularly in the field of applied technology in China, Japan and South Korea.

“Technological competition and global talent mobility are reshaping the knowledge ecosystem. Competition to attract and retain the very best researchers has become far more intense than before,” Yoo said during an interview in Hong Kong.

“[South Korean] students who want to stay or study in the USA have a very hard time getting a visa and they have to wait longer than before,” he said, adding that Chinese students faced similar hurdles.

“Instead of going abroad, they say ‘let’s study in our land’,” he said, noting that the popularity of K-culture in Asia, America and elsewhere was also helping to bring more students to South Korea.

SKKU – the oldest university in East Asia with 628 years of history – is capitalising on that shift.

In June, the university secured 13.5 billion won (US$10.08 million) in government funding over five years to recruit “outstanding scientists from abroad in energy, biomedicine, nanotechnology and quantum materials” through South Korea’s Brain Pool Plus programme.

Under the initiative, researchers will be employed on a tenure track and receive up to 600 million won annually in personal and research allowances.

The university said it aimed to recruit six international researchers at a time, mainly from the US and leading Asian research hubs.

SKKU said it had “already welcomed several researchers through the programme this year, with additional recruitment currently under way”.

After Washington proposed a US$100,000 fee for the H-1B visa last year, South Korean ministries were tasked with finding ways to take advantage of the tougher US immigration policy and lure scientists and engineers from abroad.

“We are working to create an environment in which they can settle in and concentrate on their research,” Yoo said, adding that South Korea should try to attract more international researchers to its science and engineering graduate programmes and support their career development.

Data from South Korea’s Ministry of Education shows that the total number of international students in higher education reached more than 307,000 this year, up 21 per cent from 2025.

Around 223,000 of them are enrolled in degree programmes – a rise of almost 25 per cent from a year ago – with Chinese students making up the largest group at nearly one-third of the total, according to a report released in August.

Asian students accounted for 92 per cent of South Korea’s international student population across both degree and non-degree programmes, such as Korean language courses.

Vietnam led with almost 100,000 students at 31.5 per cent, followed by China at 25.7 per cent, and Uzbekistan at 6.8 per cent, Nepal at 6.5 per cent and Mongolia at 5.6 per cent.

Yoo, a materials scientist, has bachelor’s and master’s degrees from Seoul National University. He completed a PhD in materials engineering at Stanford University in 1989.

Following his doctoral studies, Yoo returned to South Korea and spent five years conducting research at the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute in Daejeon before joining SKKU in 1994.

He has led research on carbon-based materials, including graphene. He served as vice-director of the SKKU Advanced Institute of Nanotechnology and as dean of the College of Engineering before beginning his four-year term as university president in 2023. He is now set to serve a second term.

Yoo described the pace of change in China’s universities and research ecosystem as “remarkable” with significant advances in almost every field of research.

“I see this growth as the result of sustained, long-term investment in research, a deep pool of young researchers and the capacity to translate research quickly into industrial application,” he said. “There is much that Korean universities can learn from this experience.

“I believe Chinese and Korean universities can be partners in a shared knowledge ecosystem – competing and cooperating at the same time, and growing together,” he added.

According to Yoo, energy materials offered the most promising avenues for joint research. He listed as examples next-generation solar cells and batteries, environmental materials for carbon neutrality, nanomedicine and biomaterials, and fundamental nanoscience such as two-dimensional materials.

“These fields have a large basic-research component, and they benefit greatly when researchers bring complementary strengths together,” he said.

While US-China tech decoupling has rattled global industries such as semiconductors and rechargeable batteries, Yoo said universities should remain neutral and prioritise open collaboration built on trust, transparency and shared challenges such as climate, energy and health.

“Over the past several years, even as geopolitical tensions have risen, SKKU’s international joint research and people-to-people exchanges with the United States, China and many other countries have expanded,” he said.

“Nature Index data show that research collaboration between Korea and China grew by more than 80 per cent in 2024, while Korea-US collaboration reached its highest level in a decade that same year.

“To me, this suggests that scientific cooperation need not be a matter of choosing one partner over another.”

Yoo said SKKU was focused on developing joint research partnerships and exchanges across Hong Kong, mainland China, the US, Japan, Europe and Southeast Asia.

In the Greater Bay Area, the university has agreements with institutions such as City University of Hong Kong, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou.

It also has long-standing partnerships with Peking University, Tsinghua University, Fudan University and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, including a regional governance forum run by its think tank with Chinese partners for the past 20 years.

He said universities were about academic work, not politics. “Instead of deep tech or hi-tech [we need to] focus on fundamental science and try to find new phenomena, new materials and new ways to do something,” Yoo said.

“Basic studies take more than 10 years, and that is one of the ways to avoid conflicts.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s battery factories could be sitting right on top of vast lithium deposits
item.description:
Lithium deposits formed by ancient volcanic activity may lie beneath parts of China’s battery manufacturing heartland, particularly along the southeastern coast, according to a new study.

In an interview with the South China Morning Post, geologist Duan Zheng said that “potential targets for clay-type lithium deposits in southeastern China overlap with lithium battery industrial clusters in East and South China”.

“Local supplies could significantly reduce transport costs and supply-chain risks,” added Duan, who is from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences’ Institute of Geology and one of the authors of the study.
item.content:encoded:
Lithium deposits formed by ancient volcanic activity may lie beneath parts of China’s battery manufacturing heartland, particularly along the southeastern coast, according to a new study.

In an interview with the South China Morning Post, geologist Duan Zheng said that “potential targets for clay-type lithium deposits in southeastern China overlap with lithium battery industrial clusters in East and South China”.

“Local supplies could significantly reduce transport costs and supply-chain risks,” added Duan, who is from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences’ Institute of Geology and one of the authors of the study.

The paper was published in September by the peer-reviewed Chinese journal East China Geology. It assessed the potential for volcanic clay-type lithium deposits in southeastern coastal China through geological comparisons with major finds in the US and Europe.

“Lithium is a critical strategic mineral, generally classified into three types: hard-rock, brine and clay,” the team wrote in the study, a collaboration with researchers from the Nanjing Centre of the China Geological Survey.

“Volcanic clay-type lithium deposits discovered in acidic volcanic regions in recent years represent an important new resource,” the paper said.

As of May 20, China had about 17,000 lithium-battery-related companies. Of these, 40 per cent were in southern China and 31.6 per cent in eastern China, together accounting for 71.6 per cent of the national total, according to several reports.

China relies mainly on imported lithium raw materials, including hard-rock lithium from Australia and resources from South America. Developing competitive domestic sources near manufacturing centres could reduce dependence on overseas producers.

“Such resources could increase the flexibility of domestic supply and strengthen China’s bargaining power, although these benefits would depend on successful exploration and commercial production,” Duan said.

According to the paper, late Mesozoic acidic volcanic rocks “are widely distributed in southeastern China, extending about 1,200km (746 miles) along the coast and roughly 500km inland, with a total area of around 150,000 sq km”.

Long-term geological surveys have identified four cycles of volcanic activity and 105 calderas in the region, which is known as the volcanic belt of southeastern China.

Calderas are large depressions that form when the ground collapses following volcanic activity. They can contain thick layers of volcanic sediments that have been altered into clay-rich deposits, creating conditions favourable for lithium accumulation.

The researchers nominated the Shirenbei Basin in Heping county, Guangdong province, as the first priority for further investigation, with clay-type lithium mineralisation identified in clay-rich layers within its volcanic rocks.

The Shouchang Basin in Zhejiang province’s Jiande city ranked second. Areas around Jinyun and Lucheng, also in Zhejiang, were considered promising, according to the researchers, because of the presence of clay minerals such as smectite and illite.

“The first step is to identify the reserves of volcanic clay-type resources in the Shirenbei Basin of Guangdong province and the Shouchang Basin of western Zhejiang province,” Duan said.

“The next step is to conduct an investigation and evaluation of the illite and montmorillonite clay layer resources in the thick continental volcanic rock area of eastern Zhejiang.”

Drilling should focus on locations where the upper sections of ring-shaped caldera faults intersected with sediments deposited in ancient caldera lakes, he added.

“The upper parts of ring-shaped caldera faults are the most favourable sites for lithium enrichment,” Duan said. “Drilling should prioritise areas where these faults intersect with caldera-lake sediments.”

The geological process begins with volcanic eruptions that produce lithium-bearing rocks and debris.

“These deposits contain lithium mainly in clay minerals formed through the weathering and alteration of volcanic debris,” the researchers wrote. “They are also modified by hydrothermal activity during the reactivation of calderas.”

Calderas create a closed hydrological system, they explained. “Rhyolitic ignimbrite and rhyolites formed during later volcanic activity continually release lithium under the influence of rainfall, allowing it to accumulate within the caldera.”

Magmatic gases and hot, mineral-rich hydrothermal fluids can also supply additional lithium or redistribute the element through surrounding rocks. Over geological time, these processes can concentrate lithium in clay minerals, particularly smectite and illite.

“The formation of major volcanic clay-type lithium deposits around the world is closely linked to acidic volcanic rocks and magmatic-hydrothermal systems,” the team wrote. “The enclosed hydrological environment created by calderas plays an important role in concentrating lithium.”

To assess the region’s potential, the researchers compared its geology with several major overseas deposits, including the McDermitt deposit – the world’s largest known volcanic clay-type lithium deposit.

Total predicted resources of the McDermitt deposit, located within a caldera spanning Oregon and Nevada in the western United States, could reach 120 million tonnes, according to the study.

The researchers also cited the Jadar deposit in western Serbia, which has identified lithium ore resources of 85.4 million tonnes at a cut-off grade of at least 1.76 per cent lithium oxide.

The study noted that estimates of US lithium resources rose from 35,000 tonnes in 2019 to 630,000 tonnes in 2020, 1 million tonnes in 2023 and 1.8 million tonnes in 2024 – a more than 50-fold increase over five years.

These figures illustrate how resource estimates can change with advances in geological knowledge and exploration. They should not, however, be confused with proven economically recoverable reserves.

China’s southeastern coastal deposits remain far less well understood. Measured lithium concentrations in the region range from several hundred parts per million to about 1,000 ppm, below the roughly 2,000 to 3,000 ppm reported for parts of McDermitt.

According to the paper, some layers in Heping contain lithium oxide concentrations of 0.1 to 0.2 per cent and are relatively thick, making them promising targets for further investigation.

The findings do not establish that southeastern China contains large deposits that can be mined commercially.

“At this stage, the findings remain exploration clues and an assessment of potential,” Duan said. “We cannot yet conclude that the deposits can be mined economically.”

Further drilling is needed to determine the size, continuity and grade of potential deposits, while processing presents another major challenge. Extraction costs and technological maturity remain significant uncertainties.

The region’s high population density and environmental restrictions could pose further obstacles to mining projects. Research into its volcanic clay-type lithium resources also remains at an early stage.

“Systematic, dedicated exploration for volcanic clay-type lithium deposits is largely absent in this region,” Duan said.

Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

item.title: [SCMP] From Hong Kong to the Olympics and beyond: swimmer Yvette Kong’s journey of resilience
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Toronto, Canada, in 1993, and moved to Hong Kong at six months old. My mother’s side of the family fled to Hong Kong from Shanghai in the 1940s; my father’s side is Hakka. My father grew up in a family that had long been in the shoe business and ran a shoe shop in Mong Kok. My parents met while studying at the University of Minnesota, in the United States. When I was little, they both worked in the shoe trade; that business went into decline after the 1997 Asian financial crisis and gradually disintegrated.

IN 1996, AT the age of three, I had a serious case of Kawasaki disease (which can cause damage to the heart and blood vessels and mostly affects children). I remember relatives arriving with lots of Sailor Moon gifts, my grandmother crying and my mother curling up on a plastic stool beside my hospital bed to sleep. A needle was stuck into my back while I screamed. Only years later did I realise it was a bone-marrow test to rule out cancer.

ALSO IN 1996, my mother enrolled me in swimming lessons, to learn a survival skill. I loved it but wasn’t really any good at first. As a child, I was very slow on land. I daydreamed at school and struggled with simple tasks such as connecting the dots on Kumon worksheets. My mother asked a doctor whether the illness had damaged my brain. Nicknames followed: “a lump of rice”, “a cloud” – I couldn’t sit still.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in Toronto, Canada, in 1993, and moved to Hong Kong at six months old. My mother’s side of the family fled to Hong Kong from Shanghai in the 1940s; my father’s side is Hakka. My father grew up in a family that had long been in the shoe business and ran a shoe shop in Mong Kok. My parents met while studying at the University of Minnesota, in the United States. When I was little, they both worked in the shoe trade; that business went into decline after the 1997 Asian financial crisis and gradually disintegrated.

IN 1996, AT the age of three, I had a serious case of Kawasaki disease (which can cause damage to the heart and blood vessels and mostly affects children). I remember relatives arriving with lots of Sailor Moon gifts, my grandmother crying and my mother curling up on a plastic stool beside my hospital bed to sleep. A needle was stuck into my back while I screamed. Only years later did I realise it was a bone-marrow test to rule out cancer.

ALSO IN 1996, my mother enrolled me in swimming lessons, to learn a survival skill. I loved it but wasn’t really any good at first. As a child, I was very slow on land. I daydreamed at school and struggled with simple tasks such as connecting the dots on Kumon worksheets. My mother asked a doctor whether the illness had damaged my brain. Nicknames followed: “a lump of rice”, “a cloud” – I couldn’t sit still.

DURING THE 2000 Summer Olympics, I sat in front of the television, hypnotised by the underwater footage and swimmers like (Ian) Thorpe, (Alexander) Popov – I announced that, one day, I would be one of them. Children don’t calculate winning odds.

WHEN I WAS seven, I joined the Good Hope School swim team as one of only two female Primary One pupils on the squad. For a girl who couldn’t organise herself on land, water became where I could be myself and feel my worth. I thought I should have been a fish.

BY THE TIME I was 10, my mother had started designing her own swimwear, based on what she had observed swimmers actually needed. She initially sold the swimsuits at my training sessions. Years later, that small poolside business grew into a shop for swimwear, in Tsim Sha Tsui, which she still operates today.

I FIRST REPRESENTED Hong Kong at age 11, at an interschool competition in Macau. At 13, I broke my first Hong Kong record – the 100-metre breaststroke, in 2006 – and everything changed. I was an up-and-coming prodigy. I set another Hong Kong record in the 200-metre breaststroke the next year. Swimming stopped being just something I loved, and turned into something everyone was invested in.

I MISSED QUALIFYING for the 2008 Olympics, in the 200-metre breaststroke, by about a second, even though a year later, I was ranked in the top 25 globally. Inexplicably, after hitting my peak, I plateaued. For the next six years, despite training harder and entering increasingly elite environments, I barely got faster.

THE NEXT OLYMPICS, in 2012, were worse: the qualifying rules changed and I landed on a wait-list. I flew to the Hong Kong team’s holding camp in Cardiff, Wales, anyway, to watch the athletes. My ego was too big at the time to let me walk away.

I WAS AT the University of California, Berkeley, in the US, from 2012 to 2015, on a sports scholarship to study cognitive science. Despite being in this elite environment, it felt like the harder I trained, the further backwards I went. By my second year at Berkeley, around 2013, I couldn’t even qualify for the NCAA (National Collegiate Athletic Association) Championships. I felt like a rock at the bottom of the pool. My body had stopped listening. I told my coaches I was quitting. I thought that would be the end of it, but memories and emotions from swimming that I had pushed down began resurfacing. I remember sitting in class and suddenly crying. I realised that emotions don’t simply disappear because you bury them.

I HAD ASSUMED that, if you did exactly what the Olympians did and had the best training, you’d go faster. What I eventually realised was that the body doesn’t respond to training in isolation. Performance is shaped by the whole person – psychology, stress, recovery, relationships, coaching and environment – and the human body isn’t a machine you can simply programme and expect an output from.

BECAUSE I WAS studying the brain anyway, I treated myself like a problem to solve. I found a book on EMDR (eye-movement desensitisation and reprocessing) therapy and thought, “Maybe I have trauma.” I found a therapist whose services I could afford and worked with her for months. Part of what I found was something simple: I’d started as a kid in la-la land who loved the water, and in the pursuit of excellence and competitions, I was lost.

AFTER I GRADUATED, I gave myself a year to swim on completely different terms. I read that the University of Edinburgh, in Scotland, turned swimmers who’d started nowhere near elite into internationally ranked breaststrokers. I cold-called and asked them to take me in. They were baffled: “You’re coming from Berkeley, where all the superhuman athletes are.” I arrived in Scotland in the summer of 2015, in flip-flops and shorts, and nearly froze. It became one of the best years of my life, mostly because my coach, Chris Jones, cared about me as a person. What I’ve carried into every workplace and classroom since is that humans are humans.

WHEN I QUALIFIED for the Rio 2016 Summer Olympics, I had already decided it would be my final try. I didn’t win a medal, but being there was more important, and the first place I went, in the Olympic Village, was the canteen. I sat watching athletes from every sport and country come and go. Every one of us had climbed a mountain to get there, I thought.

WEEKS BEFORE RIO started, I was hospitalised with a stomach bug. I thought performing at my best would take a miracle. I was anxious enough that I skipped the opening ceremony, which I now regret. When I walked out to the blocks at the start of my race, my senses seemed magnified. For a moment, it was only me and the race; the next, I was blended into the whole crowd and noise of it. I swam in that heat and went no further.

DEEP DOWN, I knew it would be my last proper race. Not to sound morbid, but it felt like the vision people describe at the end of their life – the child who wanted to be a fish, the 13-year-old breaking her first record, the girl who lost her way, the woman who found it again and even my future self, all converging at once, surrounded by everyone who had witnessed the journey.

POST-RIO, I was kind of at peace. I’d seen extraordinary athletes and how anxious and depressed they were, and I understood that achievement and well-being were not the same. It changed what success meant to me: results matter, but they are not the sole measure of life.

I JOINED MIND Hong Kong in 2017, as a founding board member. It started with just the three of us; now, there are more than 100 staff. I also gave myself a year of seriously practising martial arts and wushu, which I’d been interested in since watching Bruce Lee as a child – I’ve always been drawn to warrior-girl types such as Sailor Moon and Mulan.

THEN THE PART I never planned: I went corporate. I’d never even done an internship before, so it was a shock. I worked for half a year at Goldman Sachs, two years at McKinsey & Company and another two at Estée Lauder. I then went back to school remotely to study performance psychology at the University of Edinburgh during Covid-19. Later, I did an MBA at Tsinghua University, in Beijing, and an MSc at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in the US, where professors asked me to stay on to teach. I went from student to lecturer and built my own course on transversal design for social impact.

ALL OF THIS led to my Hong Kong-based start-up, Arelyx, founded last year. We build what I call “human-capacity intelligence” for an artificial-intelligence-shaped world, starting with education. We help schools understand and develop capacities such as resilience, ethical judgment and agency. Our first deployment began in Hong Kong this September, at Catholic Mission School.

I SPOKE ABOUT my new book, The Unmeasured Human, in August at the International Olympic Committee, in Lausanne, Switzerland, and noticed it was exactly 10 years since I had represented Hong Kong at Rio 2016. When I retired from swimming, people asked if I’d write my story. I said I was too young and there was more I needed to find out. It took a decade.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] How Hong Kong’s yuan push is becoming a challenge to the US dollar
item.description:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority.

In the first of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing and Denise Tsang examine Hong Kong’s efforts as an international financial centre to reform its market infrastructure, including building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem.

As Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, met in Washington for a historic summit last month, Hong Kong was preparing for a longer-term move: reducing reliance on the US dollar and boosting the yuan’s global use.
item.content:encoded:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority.

In the first of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing and Denise Tsang examine Hong Kong’s efforts as an international financial centre to reform its market infrastructure, including building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem.

As Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, met in Washington for a historic summit last month, Hong Kong was preparing for a longer-term move: reducing reliance on the US dollar and boosting the yuan’s global use.

While the two leaders got down to business, a mainland China-based asset management firm rolled out a suite of new renminbi products in the city to considerable fanfare. China Asset Management (Hong Kong), the city’s largest provider of listed offshore renminbi products, presented the broad range of exchange-traded funds to bankers, journalists and investors.

The company, already known for launching the world’s first offshore tokenised yuan money market fund, is not merely pursuing retail investors. It is also at the front line of a coordinated institutional push to build financial protection around Chinese capital against Western market volatility.

The firm’s CEO, Gan Tian, pointed to the recent Middle East crisis as a major “stress test” that demonstrated the Chinese currency’s resilience, noting that the renminbi remained firm even as the US dollar surged and Asian peers like the Japanese yen fell sharply.
