“On the path to yuan internationalisation, in this stress test in the first half, the People’s Bank of China has already sent a clear message to the smartest investors in the world,” Gan said.

“If de-dollarisation is a medium- to long-term trend, once you pull your money out of the US dollar, where exactly should you put it? The renminbi is the unparalleled choice.”

Driven by intensifying US-China rivalry and the strategic need to mobilise mainland capital safely abroad despite capital controls, Hong Kong is rapidly transforming its market infrastructure – building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem, developing independent gold clearing and testing alternative payment channels.

Once primarily a bridge for Western capital entering the mainland, Hong Kong is now positioning itself to support China’s financial resilience, analysts say. The aim, they add, is to establish the city as a launch pad for financial products and payment channels that rely less on traditional Western networks.

Earlier this year, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po expressed confidence that Hong Kong, currently behind New York and London in the global ranking of international financial centres, would climb to at least second place within 10 to 15 years.

In a recent interview with the South China Morning Post, Chan explained the city’s efforts on yuan internationalisation and their relevance to Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre.

Chan singled out Hong Kong’s unique role as a firewall for China’s financial security, with yuan-related products and services tested in the city.

“From China’s standpoint, to build a strong country, we need to have a strong currency. But this needs time,” Chan said.

“To strengthen the global utilisation and influence of renminbi, it is the user-case scenario, a substantive business-user case.”

‘Tremendous room for growth’

Chan said he expected global use of the yuan to rise amid geopolitical tensions.

He noted that China accounted for 14 to 15 per cent of global imports and exports combined, but only about 4 per cent of trade was invoiced in yuan last year. The ratio had grown a lot compared with a year earlier, he said.

Foreign investors have shown a strong appetite for trading in mainland stocks through cross-border schemes such as Northbound Stock Connect.

“There is tremendous room for future growth, particularly given the geopolitical context. Most countries are trying to use their own currency in terms of trading,” Chan said.

Hong Kong is the world’s biggest offshore renminbi market, with about 1.3 trillion yuan of deposits as at the end of July, according to the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau.

A high-profile move to tap international capital took place in August when China’s Ministry of Finance sold 15 billion yuan worth of sovereign bonds in Hong Kong to a strong response from institutional investors.

The sale took place just days after the city launched a long-awaited tool designed to help global investors hedge against risks in the mainland bond market.

Ho Lok-sang, adjunct professor of economics at Lingnan University, said the renminbi remained very much underutilised and did not reflect China’s economic strength, leaving huge potential for wider use.

“What we are after in the long run is that we want to build a more inclusive kind of system,” Ho said.

“At present, the current system, which is very much predominated by the US dollar, is not really an inclusive system, and especially as it has been weaponised.”

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent advocated in early September for Washington to use its financial power as a foreign policy tool to advance the interests of American allies, including ‌in financial and political situations abroad.

Meanwhile, the US Treasury Department has warned under its “Operation Economic Outcast” that entities facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risk being cut off from the US financial system, citing several Hong Kong-based companies that did business with Iran.

“China has been thinking strategically against the possibility that the US might impose different kinds of sanctions, and China is really extremely alert … strategically very, very smart,” Ho said.

Testing ground

Hard data shows the shift away from US dollar-centric systems is well under way in Hong Kong’s capital markets.

Beijing is using Hong Kong to test a China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform, mBridge, as a potential alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system. The effort has gained momentum in recent years amid heightened tensions between the world’s two largest economies and growing concerns over the reliability of the US dollar as it becomes politicised.

The project faced a setback late last month after a key participant – the Saudi Central Bank – confirmed its departure after completing what it described as “a limited proof-of-concept” trial in May last year.

Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu told the SCMP in an interview earlier this month that the Saudi departure would “not really” affect the wider experiment.

“Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said.

“So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.”

Beyond payments infrastructure, Hong Kong is also seeking to make the yuan more attractive for corporate financing.

Multinational firms need to borrow large sums of cash to run their global operations. Historically, many borrowed yen because Japan had the lowest interest rates.

But recently, the script has flipped. Japan’s 10-year sovereign bond yield rose above 3 per cent in early September, while China’s dropped below 1.7 per cent, Gan of ChinaAMC (HK) said.

Global companies were now flocking to Hong Kong to borrow yuan by issuing dim sum bonds – offshore renminbi-denominated bonds – because they offered cheaper funding, Gan said.

He noted that this rush for cheap borrowing had caused the dim sum bond market to explode to 1 trillion yuan, making it significantly larger than Hong Kong’s traditional stock IPO market.

When massive Chinese companies, such as appliance maker Midea, made profits overseas, they faced a huge problem: exchange rates were swinging wildly, Gan said.

Midea suffered a foreign exchange loss of almost 6 billion yuan in six months because the value of the currencies it was holding dropped. Normally, companies buy financial “insurance” with hedging to protect against these US dollar swings, but that insurance can cost 2.5 per cent of the hedged amount every year.

To reduce losses from volatile exchange rates, Chinese companies were simply refusing to convert their cash. Instead, they were parking their overseas profits directly into offshore yuan funds in Hong Kong, Gan said.

Liquidity boost

Chan, the finance chief, has pledged a multipronged strategy to boost yuan liquidity through an array of products. In addition to Chinese treasury bonds, he has pointed to opportunities in stock trading.

He said authorities would consider expanding the number of listed companies whose shares investors could trade using offshore yuan. At present, there are 23 such companies with renminbi business counters.

Chan said another strategy was to allow China-based investors to use renminbi to trade in Hong Kong-listed shares through the Southbound Stock Connect scheme.

“If we can achieve that, the liquidity will be quickly increased,” he said. “In summary, we want to have more product offerings.”

For Hong Kong’s manufacturers and traders, the stakes extend beyond financial markets.

Anthony Lam Sai-ho, chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong Industries, said that pricing commodities in renminbi would link finance more directly with physical supply chains, giving manufacturers a “natural hedge” against exchange rate volatility.

“If we can trade commodities in renminbi … it provides manufacturers and stakeholders with an additional method to hedge and predict procurement costs, reducing currency fluctuation,” Lam said.

He added that while markets were accustomed to US dollar pricing, importing raw materials such as rice or base metals directly in local currencies or renminbi would reduce the risk of being caught between shifting exchange rates.

“It is less about avoiding the US dollar out of fear, and more about giving the market an additional option to balance trade,” Lam added.

Commodity trading had so far started with gold but could extend to other metals, energy, grains, soft commodities and even livestock, Lam said.

Alternative clearing networks, meanwhile, are expanding their reach. China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) processed 180 trillion yuan in cross-border payments in 2025, up 373.6 times the 2015 level, according to its website.

CIPS said it provided secure, efficient, convenient and low-cost cross-border renminbi payment and settlement services for global users, offering an additional channel beyond the US-dominated financial system.

That existing US dollar-based system relies heavily on Swift, the Belgium-based Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, which connects more than 12,500 institutions across more than 220 countries and territories and enables global trade.

Dollar payments are also settled through the Clearing House Interbank Payments System (Chips), a private-sector, high-value clearing and settlement system that helps financial institutions move domestic and cross-border wire payments, according to its website.

Under Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address in September, the government has established the Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing Company and will implement targeted measures to boost the trading and settlement of gold futures contracts using the offshore renminbi.

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said market participants would have another option if access to dollar-based channels were restricted.

“A gold clearing system allows gold transactions via a local central ledger without relying on the Swift messaging network or the Chips payment system, thereby providing an alternative store of value,” Shui said.

“Unlike fiat currencies, gold is a physical commodity that inherently holds value, making it a trusted safe asset not directly tied to any jurisdiction.”

Gan of ChinaAMC (HK) said that having huge physical gold reserves in Hong Kong provided foreigners using offshore renminbi in the city with a “Plan B” if they wanted to convert or transfer those funds.

“They do not need to convert their assets into US dollars, British pounds or Japanese yen to move them globally; they can directly exchange them for physical gold in Hong Kong and have it delivered anywhere in the world,” he said.

“Therefore, gold, acting as a ‘Plan B’ and the most important collateral asset of the future, will support the development of the offshore renminbi in Hong Kong.”

The peg question

The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association warned that an overnight shift away from the US dollar was unrealistic.

“If de-dollarisation is overemphasised, international investors might interpret it as a signal of declining openness,” said the association’s chairman, Mofiz Chan.

Chan said Hong Kong had to strike a delicate balance between securing multiple sources of capital and maintaining its international free-market reputation with compliance, transparency and neutral standing.

To make this “financial armour” truly functional, the association called for specific technological and regulatory upgrades.

Gregory Yu, head of markets at Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, told the SCMP that the exchange was focused on building a more comprehensive offshore renminbi ecosystem spanning equities, fixed income, currencies and commodities, and it was actively exploring opportunities to expand the range of yuan-denominated products.

“Initiatives including the continued expansion of the LME’s warehouse network in Hong Kong strengthen the market infrastructure that supports trading, storage and delivery activities across the region,” Yu said, referring to the London Metal Exchange.

Yu added that the bourse continued to explore opportunities to enhance market efficiency through innovation, including in digital assets and tokenisation.

“Together with ongoing market infrastructure enhancements, these efforts strengthen Hong Kong’s role as the world’s leading offshore renminbi hub and reinforce its position as an international financial centre connecting China and the world,” Yu said.

But any push to reduce reliance on the US dollar runs up against a basic constraint: the Hong Kong dollar remains pegged to it.

Ho Lok-sang argued that linking exclusively to the US dollar exposed Hong Kong to extreme economic swings, recalling the 1985 “super dollar” phase, when the city lost its export competitiveness.

“It’s much, much, much better if we can peg a basket of currencies … and now devise a way to seamlessly adopt the system without any shock at all,” Ho said.

“We can continue with the linked exchange rate system, but we just link with the basket,” he added, referring to a GDP-weighted basket that would include the renminbi, euro, yen, British pound and the US, Australian and Canadian dollars.

Chan, the finance chief, along with city leader John Lee Ka-chiu have said repeatedly the government has no intention of changing the 43-year-old peg, which has been underpinning the city’s economy.

At the end of the day, the key buzzwords are hedging and strategic planning, analysts say.

And the official regulatory response has been to rapidly deepen the multi-asset ecosystem and expand mutual market access to facilitate this capital transition.

“For Hong Kong, this means strengthening its role as a resilient international financial centre while supporting the financing of Chinese technology companies and renminbi internationalisation,” Shui of the think tank said.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore tells suppliers to ‘honour commitments’ amid Indonesia’s gas cut
item.description:
Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports.

Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests.

Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports.

Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests.

Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs.

Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas demand.

About 95 per cent of Singapore’s electricity is generated using natural gas and it imports a significant amount of this gas through pipelines from Indonesia.

“The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” Wong said.

Singapore has been readying itself for such risks, the prime minister added. It has invested in liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals to import natural gas from different countries, without having to rely on pipelines, providing more options to manage any disruptions to supply.

However, Singapore must look beyond natural gas to cleaner sources of power that can provide reliable electricity around the clock, Wong added.

This is why authorities are studying the potential of nuclear energy, he said.

“Understandably, there are concerns about the safety of nuclear power in a small and densely populated country like Singapore. We take the concerns very seriously. Safety must come first,” Wong said.

“But we should not rule out an option simply because it is difficult or controversial. We must assess the risks and trade-offs carefully, engage Singaporeans, and eventually make the right decision to secure our energy future.”

From 2027, Singapore will be embarking on an assessment by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to gauge the country’s ability to make an informed decision on adopting nuclear energy.

Known as the IAEA’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review, each phase comes with key milestones that have to be reached to guide countries in their understanding of the commitments and obligations associated with developing a nuclear power programme.

Wong said: “Dealing with today’s concerns is only part of our job. We must also prepare Singapore for tomorrow – that means looking ahead, anticipating problems and acting before they become more difficult to solve.

“Consider the economy of the future. It will still be driven by ideas and talent, but computing power will become increasingly important and that requires enormous amounts of energy.”

In his speech, Wong noted that the world has become more “dangerous and troubled”, with harder challenges, but Singapore faces these difficulties from a position of strength, he added.

“We remain a trusted partner and an attractive place for businesses and investors,” the prime minister said.

In addition, Singapore is proactively strengthening partnerships across different regions of the world, with office-holders travelling more frequently to build relationships and deepen cooperation.

In the past week, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam made a state visit to Sweden, while Wong recently returned from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

“These countries are in different parts of the world, but they all see value in working closely with Singapore,” Wong said. “That reflects the trust and goodwill we have built over many years.”

Singapore is known as a reliable partner, a trusted hub and a country that delivers on its commitment, Wong said.

“This reputation is a vital asset, especially in today’s fragmented and troubled world. It helps us attract high-quality investments,” he added. “And the investments support growth, create jobs and enable incomes to rise.”

Some challenges are harder to tackle as they cross national borders – these include online scams or haze.

Singapore is grappling with its worst haze episode since 2015. It has sent notices to 10 Singapore-based firms and 10 Indonesian firms under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.

“We cannot solve these problems through our own efforts alone. We need cooperation from other countries,” Wong said.

“But that does not mean we stand by and do nothing. We are doing everything we can within our power to protect Singaporeans, strengthen our own response and work with partners to tackle these problems at source.”

Touching on governance, Wong said that the Singapore we want cannot simply be delivered by the government to Singaporeans, and has to be “built with Singaporeans”.

“That is the partnership we strive for: a PAP government that listens, acts and delivers. A people who step forward and contribute and a society where everyone looks out for one another.”

While Singaporeans have given the PAP a strong mandate to govern for another term, this mandate is not an “entitlement”, Wong said.

“It is a responsibility to deliver what we promised, tackle the difficult issues facing our country and prepare Singapore for what lies ahead. That is why we must never take the trust of Singaporeans for granted. After all, no political party has a permanent claim on that trust,” Wong said.

“Every generation of PAP leaders and activists must earn it afresh. We know what is expected of us. We must listen and deliver. We must hold ourselves to high standards and we must always put Singapore and Singaporeans first.”

Wong noted that while some sectors of Singapore’s economy are doing well, others are facing pressures.

Some workers are benefiting from new opportunities, but others are struggling to keep up. Lower-wage workers worry about keeping pace with rising costs, while Singaporeans in their 40s and 50s who lose their jobs worry about finding work again.

“We understand these concerns and we will respond to them. Our task is not just to keep the economy growing. It is to make sure that growth translates into better lives for all Singaporeans,” he said.

The government is also doing more to ease the burdens on parents and give families greater assurance, as seen by measures introduced at this year’s National Day Rally, he added.

Wong acknowledged that the government has a “full agenda”, such as continuing to tackle the cost-of-living pressures and helping Singapore secure better jobs.

Ultimately, the government will do its part, but everybody has a part to play too, the prime minister said.

“We will create opportunities and support workers through change, but workers must be prepared to learn and adapt,” Wong said.

“We will reduce the emphasis on exams and broaden education pathways, but parents must give their children space to grow at their own pace.

“We will strengthen support for families and seniors, but all of us must also look out for one another.”

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Will AI-powered open-door vending machines reshape Hong Kong’s retail landscape?
item.description:
Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan in Hong Kong.

The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the bulk of the time is spent deciding what to buy.

The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it.
item.content:encoded:
Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan in Hong Kong.

The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the bulk of the time is spent deciding what to buy.

The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it.

“I buy things basically every day … I can grab multiple items at once after just opening the door,” she said. “The open-door machines are more convenient because you do not have to wait for items to drop one by one from traditional machines that sometimes get stuck.”

Over the decades, vending machines have evolved from simple dispensers of bottled or canned drinks into smart retail points that combine digital payments and data-driven consumer insights. They now offer a low-cost retail channel for third parties such as local charities, selling products like flowers and daily necessities – from disposable underwear to sanitary towels.

These artificial intelligence-powered open-door vending machines have been growing in popularity in Shenzhen in the past couple of years, but they remain uncommon in Hong Kong.

Some operators have pledged to install more of them across the city in the coming months, with one reporting higher sales revenue during the trial stage.

IVM Technology is one of Hong Kong’s largest operators, managing about 800 AI vending machines alongside 1,500 traditional ones in Hong Kong, the firm’s founder and managing director Leo Lui told the South China Morning Post.

Hong Kong had an estimated 15,000 to 17,000 vending machines, with the number expected to increase as the lower capital costs of AI machines attract new market entrants, Lui said.

“It will not surprise me if there are 30,000 to 40,000 machines later,” he said.

Lui pointed to Hong Kong’s exorbitant logistics, labour and parking costs – such as paying HK$200 just to park a delivery van for restocking at major commercial sites – as a major bottleneck.

Unlike mainland Chinese operators who could rely on low delivery expenses to sell low-margin goods, Hong Kong vending businesses faced fixed transport costs of about HK$2 per item, forcing them to focus on higher-priced, premium inventory, Lui said.

While the new open-door models generated 20 to 30 per cent more revenue in closed environments such as offices, traditional machines still outperformed them by 30 per cent in transient public spaces like bus stops, Lui explained.

“On the streets, some consumers might find the new machines are too slow, whereas with an Octopus card on a traditional machine, the product drops in a second after a purchase is made,” he said.

While nearly 90 per cent of new vending machines deployed on the mainland were AI open-door models, Hong Kong’s adoption remained significantly slower due to distinct local economic factors, said Rex Leung, general manager of IVM Technology.

The offline nature of the Octopus card contactless payment system presented a significant hurdle for AI machines, which required post-purchase settlement after the door was closed, Leung said.

“The physical Octopus card is an offline payment method where users tap and leave immediately, which is incompatible with this machine that charges users only after they finish shopping,” Leung added.

To resolve this issue, Octopus Cards was expected to launch an integration allowing users to scan a quick response (QR) code and settle payments online via the Octopus application, Lui said.

Leung added the company aimed to evolve into a platform that allowed a wider range of organisations to sell goods in their machines.

FreshUp, another local vending machine operator with a network of more than 5,000 machines, had set up more than 500 smart coolers that allowed customers to open the door, take products and be charged automatically through visual recognition technology, said David Lam, the group’s founder and CEO.

The smart models were generating 10 to 20 per cent more revenue per transaction than traditional push-button machines because the open-door design encouraged consumers to buy multiple items at once, Lam explained.

“People might have pressed buttons for individual items in the past, but now, since they have already opened the fridge to buy a drink, they might take chocolate or potato chips if they find them interesting, increasing the overall basket value or unit items per transaction,” Lam said.

The AI models required an upfront hardware cost of HK$20,000 to HK$30,000, which was similar to the price of traditional machines, he added.

While the local smart retail sector was projected to grow steadily at an annual rate of 5 to 10 per cent, operators had to pay a recurring fixed back-end computing fee to software providers for data processing every time the cabinet door was opened, Lam said.

Beyond commercial retail, the elimination of mechanical coils and rigid size restrictions has allowed open-door cabinets to serve as low-cost “micro-retail platforms” for non-governmental organisations and local brands seeking physical exposure without traditional overheads.

The new technology provided a low-cost retail alternative for charities such as the Po Leung Kuk, which sold products made by people with disabilities, said Choi Kai-yin, a social worker and service manager at the organisation.

Listing items in physical retail stores incurred high rental and administrative costs, making it difficult for charities to generate sufficient revenue to support their disabled creators, Choi said.

“Renting a shop is [costly], as we are selling bottled drinks for about HK$10 each, and it is hard to calculate how many bottles we need to sell to cover the rent,” Choi added.

By selling bottled tea at HK$12 through vending machines, the Po Leung Kuk hoped to create a reasonable profit margin, which would directly benefit individuals with disabilities in recognition of their contributions and participation in vocational training, Choi said.

Swire Coca-Cola has been rolling out smart vending coolers on the mainland in recent years, as retail formats incorporating digital payments increase in popularity following the pandemic. Its Hong Kong bottling business has now begun introducing these coolers, which allow customers to open the door and select drinks, adapting technology and operating processes proven on the mainland.

The coolers are easy to operate: shoppers select a payment method before opening the door, choose their products and close the door. When the door is closed, the bill is settled.

“Consumers today expect to see it, want it and get it almost instantly, and Hong Kong is no exception. People want a cold drink close to where they live, work, study and play, and they want paying for it to be quick and simple,” said Hunter Jin, Greater China CEO of Swire Coca-Cola.

“Smart vending coolers meet that expectation by combining cashless payment with product-recognition technology, so the whole purchase feels seamless.”

Swire Coca-Cola has set up more than 150 coolers across sports and entertainment venues, workplaces, residential communities, educational institutions and industrial settings to reach locations unsuitable for conventional machines.

The new coolers would not completely replace the company’s network of about 6,000 conventional vending machines in Hong Kong, but would serve as a smart alternative offering a seamless digital experience, Swire Coca-Cola said.

“As Hong Kong continues to welcome major events and visitors, vending can do more than sell drinks,” Jin said. “We are exploring Hong Kong-themed vending and digital experiences at venues, transport hubs and tourist destinations that showcase local culture and add to the city’s vibrancy.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s next generation of leaders waiting in the wings for more senior roles
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the fourth part of this series, William Zheng looks at how the next generation of the party is being formed.

When China’s political elites gather behind closed doors in Beijing for the Communist Party’s fifth plenum on Monday, much of the attention will be on the quiet preparations for allocating hundreds of pivotal roles in next year’s 21st party congress.

At the heart of this transition is the rise of the party’s seventh generation – often referred to as the 7G – who were born in the late 1960s and the 1970s and whose ascent will be critical in shaping China’s political trajectory.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the fourth part of this series, William Zheng looks at how the next generation of the party is being formed.

When China’s political elites gather behind closed doors in Beijing for the Communist Party’s fifth plenum on Monday, much of the attention will be on the quiet preparations for allocating hundreds of pivotal roles in next year’s 21st party congress.

At the heart of this transition is the rise of the party’s seventh generation – often referred to as the 7G – who were born in the late 1960s and the 1970s and whose ascent will be critical in shaping China’s political trajectory.

Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at Tsinghua University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies, said the party was looking for cadres who had “absolute political loyalty, integrity, fighting spirit, technological or ‘hard science’ expertise, grass-roots experience and hardship resilience”.

“Just like their predecessors, they must demonstrate unquestioned loyalty and integrity. But given China’s technological advancement into uncharted areas, the new leaders will have to know emerging technology and hard science as China can no longer copy from others.”

However, recent patterns within the party suggest that Beijing is giving age less weight when it comes to promotions, while the far-reaching anti-corruption campaign is hitting this generation as hard as any other.

The 7G

Regardless of whether Xi Jinping, now 73, chooses to stay in charge beyond the 2032 party congress, he will still need a deep bench of loyal and talented younger officials to carry out his policies.

In recent decades, candidates for Politburo seats have usually been identified many years ahead.

Most candidates for membership of the key decision-making body in 2032 will currently be members of the party’s Central Committee or will be selected as alternate members at next year’s party congress.

Traditionally, most Central Committee members, who have a ministerial-level rank, are required to step down at the age of 65.

Meanwhile, Politburo members observe an informal rule known as “seven up, eight down”, in which those under the age of 67 may serve another five-year term, while those aged 68 or older must retire.

Xi broke these precedents for some key figures in 2022, including top diplomat Wang Yi, then aged 69, who was seen as indispensable for managing China’s foreign relations amid escalating competition with the United States.

He also kept the country’s top general Zhang Youxia, then aged 72, in place to manage the country’s military modernisation programme, but Zhang later fell from favour and was detained earlier this year on suspicion of corruption.

Roughly two-thirds of the current Central Committee will have reached the statutory retirement age by the time of the party congress in October next year.

Consequently, the seventh generation, currently about 8 per cent of the party’s central leadership body, is expected to become the biggest cohort.

Only 7G officials who are already members of the Central Committee or those who have been newly appointed as ministers and provincial leaders – who will get their Central Committee seat in 2027 – are likely candidates for leadership roles beyond 2032.

The leading candidates

Some of these contenders have already taken over top regional and ministerial roles this year.

They include Zhu Zhongming, born in April 1972, who was appointed as mayor of Shanghai late last month, a role that puts him in line to become the city’s next party chief.

Zhu, 54, is a career finance official who spent much of his working life in his native province of Zhejiang, where he worked under Premier Li Qiang while he was governor.

Other regional government chiefs of a similar age include Zhejiang governor Liu Jie, Jiangsu governor Liu Xiaotao, and Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region’s government chairman Wei Tao – all born in 1970 – as well as Shanxi governor Lu Dongliang, who was born in 1973.

Other leading candidates, including Beijing mayor Yin Yong and Hubei party secretary Guan Zhiou – who outranks the regional government chiefs – are just a few months older and also considered leading candidates to take on senior national roles.

Other contenders from that generation hold central government and party roles, including A Dong, who leads the Communist Youth League Central Committee, Zhang Chengzhong, the Minister of Emergency Management, and Cheng Fubo, the director of the state-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission.

Most of these 7G officials are full or alternate members of the Central Committee. Shanghai mayor Zhu and emergency management minister Zhang, both appointed only recently, are expected to be made full members of the Central Committee at next year’s party congress.

Xie from Tsinghua said “resilient officials”, who had cut their teeth in difficult, under-resourced environments – mirroring Xi’s own formative years – or demonstrated versatile and effective problem-solving skills would be put on a faster track to promotion, as they will have to manage more emergencies caused by extreme weather.

“The preferred style for next-generation leaders is quiet, efficient execution of central mandates rather than high-profile self-promotion or experimental local diverging policies. They must also show the ability to integrate economic development with security considerations, ensuring that local industrial policies adhere to broader central directives regarding supply-chain resilience and social stability,” Xie added.

Chinese born in the late 1960s and 1970s have often been described as “the luckiest age cohort” on social media because they were too young to experience the political turmoil of the Cultural Revolution or the physical hardship experienced by “sent-down youths” who worked as farmers in rural areas.

They also avoided the starvation endured by previous generations and grew up as the country’s economy started to boom.

An analysis published by Li Cheng, director of Hong Kong University’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World, said half of the leading 7G cadres had doctorates – making them the most highly educated cohort in party history – and often had experienced life outside the party system, including overseas study.

Li found that around one-third of them were trained in engineering, while economics and finance represented their other primary fields of study.

There was also a significant proportion that had experience of managing state assets, financial institutions or complex industrial projects, reflecting Beijing’s demand for officials capable of navigating economic headwinds and technological competition.

Yin, the mayor of Beijing, is a prominent example. He holds a master’s degree in public administration from Harvard University and previously served as vice-governor of the People’s Bank of China.

Another example is 1970-born Guo Ningning one of the few high-ranking female contenders for higher office. She was appointed party chief of Fujian’s provincial government on Saturday, paving the way for her appointment as governor.

She spent more than a decade leading operations for state banks in Hong Kong and Singapore before entering provincial governance.

Meanwhile, Hubei’s deputy party chief Zhuge Yujie, born in 1971, was named as the new party secretary of the Qinghai government, also putting him in line to become the province’s next governor.

No more fast track

However, these officials have climbed the ladder more slowly than some previous generations.

For example, the 2002 party congress saw dozens of officials in their late 30s or early 40s being given vice-ministerial posts, some of whom achieved full ministerial rank three years later, including Sun Zhengcai, who became agriculture minister at the age of 42, or Hu Chunhua, who became head of the Communist Youth League aged 43.

At the time, these promotions were seen as filling a skills gap caused by a lack of administrative skills and economic experience among older officials.

But since Xi came to power in 2012, fewer younger cadres have been given senior posts as the leadership prioritised performance and experience.

The youngest members of the Central Committee were in their mid to late 40s when they were appointed and the average age of new members of the last two Politburos – around 62 – was much higher than in the previous three, where it was well below 60.

Xi and other senior leaders have warned that fast-tracked young bureaucrats sometimes lack real-world experience.

As early as 2011, the Central Organisation Department explicitly warned of the problem caused by “three-door cadres” – a term used to mock young civil servants who moved directly from their family’s doorstep to university and then into government offices.

Xi has also introduced the concept of “letting seedlings develop firm roots”, dunmiao in Chinese, mandating that up and coming cadres spend extended periods in complex, frontline postings – such as poverty alleviation, disaster response and industrial restructuring – before being eligible for senior command.

Those who crashed out

An additional challenge for the 7G cadres is the country’s ongoing anti-corruption drive, which has already led to the downfall of some high-profile figures.

The latest case involves Beijing’s executive vice-mayor Xia Linmao, who was placed under investigation last week.

Born in 1970, Xia, who has a doctorate from Tsinghua University and held a variety of top-tier technocratic postings in the capital’s urban planning and government operations, epitomised the demographic cohort that rose swiftly through the sub-provincial ranks.

His downfall is just the latest warning that rising cadres face intense and constant scrutiny and will be judged strictly on political compliance and administrative conduct rather than their potential.

Other once-promising 7G officials who have fallen foul of the anti-corruption drive include former Urumqi party boss Yang Fasen, who was jailed for life last October for accepting more than 147 million yuan (US$20.7 million) in bribes, and Fei Gaoyun, who held a similar role in Hefei and was placed under investigation in May.

Li Yunze, the former head of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, who was celebrated as the first official born in 1970 to achieve full ministerial rank, provides another cautionary tale.

He was abruptly demoted and stripped of his seat in the national legislative body in May over disciplinary violations, underscoring that a temporary lead in the political marathon provides no immunity against tightened scrutiny.

item.title: [SCMP] Big dreams, growing pains in Indonesia: Prabowo’s turbulent 2 years in power
item.description:
When 35-year-old Bekasi resident Ika Kartika voted for Prabowo Subianto in Indonesia’s 2024 presidential election, she hoped the former general would restore a “Suharto-like” era of stability, when everyday essentials were affordable and life felt more predictable.

Growing up, she had often heard her parents reminisce about the “good old days” under the late strongman, whose rule had brought a sense of order to their lives.

Two years into his presidency, however, rising food prices have left Ika questioning whether Prabowo, who was once Suharto’s son-in-law, can deliver on that vision.
item.content:encoded:
When 35-year-old Bekasi resident Ika Kartika voted for Prabowo Subianto in Indonesia’s 2024 presidential election, she hoped the former general would restore a “Suharto-like” era of stability, when everyday essentials were affordable and life felt more predictable.

Growing up, she had often heard her parents reminisce about the “good old days” under the late strongman, whose rule had brought a sense of order to their lives.

Two years into his presidency, however, rising food prices have left Ika questioning whether Prabowo, who was once Suharto’s son-in-law, can deliver on that vision.

“I thought he would turn things around. Now I feel cheated and disappointed,” Ika said.

Her disillusionment reflects a broader loss of confidence in the 75-year-old former special forces commander – a sharp reversal from the position of strength he enjoyed after finally winning the presidency on his third attempt.

Taking office with virtually no parliamentary opposition after bringing former rival parties into a sprawling governing coalition, Prabowo rode a post-inauguration honeymoon that saw his public approval rating hit 79 per cent at the start of his term as he began implementing his blueprint to transform Southeast Asia’s largest economy and elevate its global standing.

At home, he staked his legacy on eradicating child malnutrition through his universal free nutritious meals programme – initially projected to cost 450 trillion rupiah (US$25 billion) a year at full scale – and reviving rural economies through Red and White Village Cooperatives, a state-backed network of retail and logistics hubs.

For investors, his pitch was that these and other state-led initiatives would create millions of jobs and propel annual GDP growth to 8 per cent, with sovereign wealth fund Danantara central to his plan to put state assets to work in strategic industries and accelerate development.

Abroad, he championed Global South diplomacy in the Brics bloc alongside a pledge to remain a stabilising anchor in Southeast Asia.

Yet as Prabowo marked his first 24 months in the top job on Tuesday, those lofty ambitions have collided with harsh realities on all three fronts.

An October survey by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting (SMRC) found that Prabowo’s approval rating had fallen to 44.5 per cent, below the 50 per cent mark for the first time. A separate survey by the Centre of Economic and Law Studies (Celios) found that 75 per cent of respondents felt stressed by government policies, with high prices for basic necessities and a lack of job opportunities among their chief concerns.

Simultaneously, a looming global index downgrade has triggered a bruising stock market rout, while raging forest fires have blanketed the region in toxic smog, choking neighbours Malaysia and Singapore.

In the face of those challenges, analysts say Prabowo has oscillated between reactive damage control and stubborn resolve.

Rather than fundamentally rethink his agenda, he has made adjustments, such as slashing the budget for the free meals programme but refusing to abandon it, and repeatedly reshuffling his cabinet. His government has also sent confusing signals abroad, approving foreign firefighting help to battle the haze before subsequently putting the offers on hold.

While ruling party allies defend his adjustments as “dynamic moves” to protect fiscal stability, observers argue they merely paper over the deeper structural flaws of his administration.

The question now is whether Prabowo can genuinely change course or whether the setbacks of his second year will define the rest of his term.

Prabowo himself remains publicly defiant. Brushing off economic pessimism at a nickel-processing project launch on October 8, he pointed to robust state-backed investments as proof that his administration was succeeding.

“Every month, they predict that we will collapse. But today, I have come here and I see a bright future for Indonesia,” he declared.

Fraying mandate

At the heart of the public mood shift is the troubled roll-out of the signature welfare schemes that once anchored Prabowo’s popularity. The SMRC survey showed that 61 per cent of citizens familiar with the free meals initiative were unhappy with its execution, while 71 per cent doubted the village cooperatives plan would succeed.

Saidiman Ahmad, a researcher and programme manager at SMRC, said the poll exposed a broad defection of supporters across all demographic groups, pinpointing mismanagement of the president’s flagship initiatives as the main cause of public censure.

Both the free meals initiative and village cooperatives plan “were significant factors”, Saidiman said.

Those missteps are glaring to voters like Lugas Limojoyo, 31, a resident of Purwokerto in Central Java who backed Prabowo in 2024 among the three presidential tickets.

Lugas, a former hotel chef, described the free meals programme and the cooperatives as Prabowo’s “main red flags”.

Pointing to recurring mass food-poisoning cases, he noted a lack of basic food safety protocols – an observation echoed by Indonesia’s food and drug agency, which has repeatedly cited poor sanitation and untrained staff as the primary causes behind thousands of students falling ill.

Lugas saw a similar lack of coordination in the village cooperatives initiative, noting that many state-funded warehouses “have already been built but aren’t operational, sitting there like empty husks”. Reuters has also reported concerns from analysts about the scheme’s top-down approach, the commercial viability of some locations and whether the cooperatives can respond to local needs.

Still, the programmes retain pockets of support. Anissa Fadhilah, a 29-year-old greengrocer in Surabaya, said she remained satisfied with Prabowo’s performance and would vote for him again in 2029 after her daughter received school meals and her business landed supply commissions from the scheme.

“I think [the free meals initiative] has the desired effect of lifting ordinary people economically, so I’m for it,” Anissa said.

Officials also defended the administration’s two-year track record.

Jasmine Herawan, a spokeswoman for Indonesia’s Government Communications Agency, said the administration had expanded the social safety net, with its free meals programme reaching 57 million recipients, while nearly 1.5 million people had been lifted out of extreme poverty within a year.

She also cited gains in food security, saying Indonesia produced 34.71 million tonnes of rice in 2025 without importing any that year.

On the extractive sector, Jasmine said: “We’ve also affirmed our mineral sovereignty by setting up a single-door export system for our key commodities.” The system is intended to give the government greater oversight of mineral exports and make it harder for companies to understate the value of what they sell overseas, potentially depriving the state of tax revenue.

Market reckoning

Costly spending commitments, however, have raised broader concerns about fiscal sustainability. Earlier this year, the government cut 67 trillion rupiah from the free meals programme before imposing further spending curbs across ministries in the final quarter to help keep the budget deficit within its legal ceiling of 3 per cent of GDP.

But fiscal tightening did little to reassure investors. On October 16, index provider MSCI warned that Indonesia could be downgraded from “emerging” to “stand-alone” market status over concerns about opaque corporate ownership and trading manipulation, triggering a bruising sell-off in Indonesian assets. The Jakarta Composite Index plunged 11.6 per cent and the rupiah fell to 18,050 per US dollar.

Despite emergency regulatory fines against market manipulators and bourse officials pledging swift governance reforms during a meeting with MSCI on Monday, the benchmark index hit a six-year low this week, as investors continued to digest the warning and the risk of billions of dollars in passive capital outflows.

Siwage Dharma Negara, co-coordinator of the Indonesia Studies programme at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said regional investors continued to view Prabowo’s economic policy as unpredictable.

“He will not give up his populist programmes, like the free meals and rural cooperatives, but it is not clear what the economic benefit for the country will be,” Siwage said.

Siwage noted that the recent fiscal correction was too small to satisfy investors, many of whom viewed the free meals as a waste of state resources that should be redirected towards education, health or struggling regional governments.

“Prabowo fundamentally does not trust anyone else to advise him on economic direction,” Siwage said, warning that such moves were creating a poor investment climate. “If we want to restore market confidence, the most urgent fix is reducing this state intervention in the economy.”

Inside Prabowo’s ruling Gerindra party, lawmakers reject assertions that the administration’s economic agenda is faltering. Gerindra spokesman Sugiat Santoso dismissed Celios’ two-year study as “over the top” and “deliberately dramatised” to create mass panic.

Defending the village cooperatives as a path to financial independence for disadvantaged communities and the free meals as an ongoing investment in future generations, Sugiat added, “The president is definitely not here to please analysts, but to bring about real changes for the welfare of the people.”

Musical chairs

Unwilling to abandon his core populist pledges, Prabowo has instead turned to frequent personnel changes to tighten his grip on the bureaucracy – reshuffling his cabinet or installing new officials three times in the first two weeks of October alone, bringing his total number of cabinet shake-ups to eight in two years.

Arya Fernandes, head of politics and social change at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies Indonesia, said these shake-ups stemmed from the president’s underlying political vulnerability – specifically Gerindra’s lack of parliamentary dominance and the lingering influence of his predecessor, Joko Widodo.

This has forced Prabowo to consolidate power by accommodating a wide political spectrum, Arya noted. But the high cost of maintaining that stability – through an oversized cabinet and increased military budgets – has driven up fiscal pressure and forced the central government to slash local funding.

“In sum, Prabowo has secured elite support and lost mass support,” he said.

Yoes C. Kenawas, a researcher at Lembaga Survei Indonesia, said this dynamic reflected a leader whose authoritarian instincts make him insecure about elite loyalty.

“He remains deeply paranoid about elite betrayal and being backstabbed by coalition partners,” Yoes said. “Even with an 80 per cent parliamentary majority, he does not feel secure.”

Siwage said swapping out officials would not solve the administration’s deeper flaws: “We have seen many cabinet reshuffles so far, and he will likely continue shuffling officials, thinking a new person will fix the problem. But the real issue is that the entire system of governance is currently ineffective at implementing sound economic policy.”

Fanning flames

Nowhere has that administrative strain spilled beyond Indonesia’s borders more visibly than in the transboundary haze crisis.

Since August, severe forest and peatland fires across Sumatra and Kalimantan have sent thick smoke across the region, forcing school closures in Malaysia, prompting diplomatic protests and leading Singapore’s prime minister to warn of action against errant companies.

Siwage linked the resurgence of the fires directly to Prabowo’s domestic fiscal squeeze, which he said left local governments “without enough operational funds to fight the fires”.

For months, Jakarta resisted regional offers of firefighting help, while public remarks by officials only inflamed tensions – most notably when the newly appointed communications agency head suggested neighbours should remember Indonesia’s forests “send oxygen” when there is no haze.

Rifki Dermawan, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Andalas in West Sumatra, says the episode highlights a stark contrast: while Prabowo frequently travels globally, “Asean does not seem to be a priority”.

Pointing to the president’s failure to apologise or engage with regional counterparts over the pollution, Rifki said it suggested the bloc “might not be among Prabowo’s interests”. He attributed Jakarta’s reluctance to accept outside help to Prabowo’s suspicion of foreign involvement and repeated rhetoric blaming “foreign agents”.

A diplomatic thaw seemingly arrived on October 15 when Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir announced Prabowo had approved regional firefighting help. But the administration later abruptly backtracked when security chief Dudung Abdurachman put the offers on hold, declaring Indonesia was “still capable” of managing the blazes.

Prabowo then railed against “countries that like to insult” his nation over the wildfires, amid growing public anger and calls for Indonesia to be treated as an “outcast” in the region.

“Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” Prabowo said on Wednesday.

⁠⁠Prabowo also told his cabinet ‌on Wednesday that MSCI was trying ⁠to “scare us”, adding ‌that Indonesia was “not afraid” ‌and would not ⁠buckle, Reuters reported.

Despite plunging approval ratings, a market sell-off and diplomatic fires, Yoes warned Prabowo might not feel compelled to change course because the pain of his second-year slump had not hit his immediate political centre.

“The crisis is fragmented,” Yoes said. “The toxic haze chokes Sumatra and Kalimantan, but it does not blanket Jakarta or Java.”

Because the distress was clustered outside the capital, it looked manageable on paper, he added, “but underneath the surface, this is a crisis in the making”.

Defiance or adaptation

Analysts say moving beyond short-term diplomatic firefighting to rebuild his popular mandate and calm financial markets over the remaining three years of his term could depend on Prabowo’s willingness to look outside his inner circle.

So far, however, the president has framed mounting resistance not as a symptom of policy missteps but as a manufactured campaign by entrenched elites bankrolling paid protesters and online influencers – known locally as “buzzers”.

“We have no doubts. Even if they have hundreds of trillions of rupiah, they pay buzzers, they pay for algorithms, they attack us on social media, and they finance demonstrations, we are not afraid. We stand with the people, we are ready to die for the people,” Prabowo said during a fiery speech on October 6.

That defiant posture worries observers who believe Prabowo must adapt his approach to meet the challenges he is facing.

SMRC’s Saidiman argued that reversing the polling slide would require structural reform – starting with shrinking the cabinet, pulling back from the ongoing militarisation of the civilian sphere and conducting a “radical review of the administration’s costly yet ineffective populist programmes”.

“The president needs to step up and enact fundamental changes to how he governs the nation,” Saidiman said, adding Prabowo “should let opposition forces fulfil their function as a democracy should”.

Siwage warned that without an effective parliamentary opposition to check the president’s instincts, financial market tremors could eventually spiral into a wider political reckoning.

“Prabowo currently controls most of the government coalition and the parliament. With essentially no opposition, why would he change course when nobody dares to oppose his policies?” he said.

Outside Jakarta’s corridors of power, voters who helped put Prabowo in the presidential palace say he still has a window to turn things around – if he starts listening to ordinary Indonesians.

In Central Java, Lugas urged the president to break out of his palace echo chamber.

“My suggestion for Prabowo is to cross-check the reports he gets from those closest to him, because obviously he is only being fed information on the good things,” he said.

And in Bekasi, despite feeling let down by rising living costs, Ika said she was not ready to give up on Prabowo’s presidency just yet.

“Maybe these are growing pains for us,” she said. “I’m still optimistic about Prabowo’s leadership and I pray he won’t prove me wrong.”

item.title: [SCMP] JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong redefines luxury dining with zero-waste culinary innovation
item.description:
For Tony Wong Chi-chuen, the executive chef of JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, waste is never the conclusion of an ingredient’s story. Lemon ends can be used to perfume seafood, shrimp shells to deepen the nuance of a broth and fishbones to build a base for pasta dough. In Wong’s kitchen, food waste is simply ingredients waiting for a second life.

“Discarding something is easy,” says Wong. “[Reusing] is not about saving cost; saving is about reinvesting in more quality ingredients.”

In person, he doesn’t mince his words. As the conversation turns to his craft, Wong – who has 38 years of experience in the industry – becomes animated, revealing a passion honed over decades, rooted in a lesson learned long before he entered a professional kitchen.
item.content:encoded:
For Tony Wong Chi-chuen, the executive chef of JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, waste is never the conclusion of an ingredient’s story. Lemon ends can be used to perfume seafood, shrimp shells to deepen the nuance of a broth and fishbones to build a base for pasta dough. In Wong’s kitchen, food waste is simply ingredients waiting for a second life.

“Discarding something is easy,” says Wong. “[Reusing] is not about saving cost; saving is about reinvesting in more quality ingredients.”

In person, he doesn’t mince his words. As the conversation turns to his craft, Wong – who has 38 years of experience in the industry – becomes animated, revealing a passion honed over decades, rooted in a lesson learned long before he entered a professional kitchen.

His parents used to run a dai pai dong-style stall behind the Yau Ma Tei Police Station, peddling steaming bowls of fish-ball noodles, before it closed more than 40 years ago. From the age of 12, Wong would help out after school. He watched his parents work hard, stretch ingredients and make full use of what they had.

He recalls that “they didn’t throw anything away”: fishbones were simmered into broth for the noodles – an ingrained reflex that later inspired his fishbone fettuccine at JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, showing how every ingredient could be made to work harder. Wong came to understand that saving on food waste only mattered if it was turned into something better eventually.

“When I was 18, I realised being thrifty is not enough,” he says. “You have to use what you save and make it into something good for customers.” His philosophy – waste not, but elevate – became the bedrock of his kitchen. It is an exercise not in austerity, but in wringing maximum quality and flavour out of scraps.

Wong joined JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong in 1990, a year after its opening. He started as a senior cook at the former Marriott Cafe, now JW Cafe, and steadily moved up the ranks: sous chef in 2003, executive sous chef in 2009 and, finally, executive chef in 2018.

As a young cook, he noticed how quickly bins filled up. Celery ends, carrot peels, onion trimmings and other offcuts were tossed aside because only the neatest parts were used. When he became sous chef, he began making changes: a bucket near a chopping board was added to hold bones, end cuts and trimmings to be reused.

Now, the system has become part of kitchen culture. Watermelon rind is blended into a light breakfast drink, valued in traditional Chinese medicine for its refreshing sweetness and cooling effects; leftover pieces from Peking ducks are shredded into a braised rice-vermicelli dish.

What it has done for food-waste numbers is significant – the hotel repurposes around 8.2 tonnes of watermelon rind a year, along with 900kg of lemon peel, more than 3.6 tonnes of fishbones and 3.65 tonnes of shrimp heads and shells, says Wong. At its core, however, his philosophy remains simple: an ingredient should have as many “lives” as possible before it leaves the kitchen.

“I see an ingredient and think, ‘How can it be used again?’”

Tony Wong

“I see an ingredient and think, ‘How can it be used again?’”

Across JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong’s eight dining venues and multiple event spaces, Wong’s strategy goes beyond creating isolated “green” dishes – it is about building a circular kitchen system. His approach aligns with Marriott’s Serve 360 sustainability and social-impact platform, which is guided by the belief of “doing good in every direction”.

Furthermore, the culinary initiatives sit within the property’s broader push towards responsible luxury – a commitment that has won prestigious recognition, recently from the US Green Building Council for sustainable building operations and maintenance, and the International WELL Building Institute for health and wellness, ensuring that guest well-being and environmental stewardship are both fully considered.

In a five-star hotel, sustainability has to meet the expectations of luxury dining. Wong does not see a contradiction. He believes that responsible cooking should make food better, not lesser, and the clearest expression of this thinking is Fish Bar’s lobster fishbone fettuccine, one of the restaurant’s signature dishes. Instead of treating grouper bones as waste, Wong’s team dries and pulverises them into a fine powder, then blends the meal with gluten-free flour to make pasta. No mere sustainability gimmick, the bones add calcium and deepen the pasta’s umami, turning scrap into part of the dish’s flavour structure.

If anything, Wong says, zero-waste practices allow him to be more generous. Financial savings from careful portioning and cross-kitchen reuse are channelled back into premium buffet offerings, such as abalone, fish maw, sea cucumber, lobster and crab.

High-quality offcuts receive similar care: Australian Wagyu trimmings are crafted into burger patties, while at the hotel’s Michelin-star Man Ho Chinese Restaurant, prime cuts of Iberico pork are reserved for char siu and flavourful remnants are minced for xiaolongbao fillings at The Lounge.

For banquets and functions, Wong’s team makes enough food for no more than 10 per cent above the expected number of guests. At the buffet, dishes are prepared in smaller, more frequently replenished batches, ensuring that food does not sit for long periods. It is a more labour-intensive practice, but one that benefits the environment and creates a better experience for diners. “Other places refill food maybe twice; we do it 20 times,” says Wong.

Luxury diners used to fixate on origin – lobsters from France, tomatoes from Italy, sea urchin from Japan – but these priorities have shifted. “I think guests mainly care about the taste, quality and freshness of the ingredients – these are the three things they focus on now and they care less about where they come from,” says Wong.

For him, this change has widened the meaning of luxury. Premium dining is no longer defined only by provenance or price, but by how thoughtfully an ingredient is sourced, handled and cooked. If a dish tastes good and aligns with sustainable values, guests will often see it as something better.

JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong prioritises local sourcing where possible, which helps reduce transport time, spoilage and carbon emissions. Suppliers are screened for certifications – including from organisations such as the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) and Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) – and traceability. Purchasing decisions made by the procurement team are guided in part by monthly WWF recommendations of vetted seafood suppliers and sources, says Wong. Endangered species, such as bluefin tuna and shark, are off the menu, replaced by alternatives like yellowtail and vegetarian shark’s fin – a plant-based ingredient that replicates the texture of the original.

At Fish Bar, renovated in 2024, sustainability is built into the space as well as the dining programme. An open design allows for natural ventilation, reducing reliance on air conditioning. Uniforms were designed in partnership with the Caritas Bianchi College of Careers and incorporate coffee-ground materials. Bottled water has been replaced with a filtered system.

Meanwhile, JW Garden grows herbs such as rosemary, basil and perilla, which are used in drinks, dishes, amenities and even canned beverages that extend the farm-to-table idea into a “farm-to-home” experience. Edible surplus, such as croissants and muffins, is donated to organisations serving people in need, while food waste that cannot be reused is sent to recycling partners for renewable energy or composting. JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong also works with The Nature Conservancy, turning discarded oyster shells into reef substrate for local marine restoration.

From Wong’s point of view, these hotel-wide initiatives connect back to the same principle: resources should circulate, not dissipate. His message for the next generation is clear: cooking well is no longer enough, because a chef must also think about impact.

His 180-strong team, many of whom have worked with him for decades, now closely follow his doctrine.

It has created a virtuous cycle: the kitchen grows increasingly efficient as reuse practices are streamlined; diners enjoy fresher, higher-quality food; staff develop discipline and pride – all while protecting the environment. Wong shares of his team that “they feel this is a good habit; they feel like they can be good people”.

Some might label the rethinking of food waste as accumulating good karma, but in hospitality terms, it’s simply good business.

item.title: [SCMP] Vietnam’s 2045 vision faces a reality check as capital squeeze tests growth ambitions
item.description:
Since coming to power in August 2024, General Secretary To Lam has emphasised his ambition to turn Vietnam into a high-income country by 2045. Towards this goal, a National Assembly resolution in April set a target of average annual growth of 10 per cent through 2030, with infrastructure building expected to serve as a major growth engine.

However, Vietnam is struggling to mobilise sufficient capital to finance this ambitious agenda because of both domestic and external constraints. Hanoi therefore faces a choice: align its growth targets with the capital it can raise at a reasonable cost or accept considerably greater economic risks.

The projects illustrate the scale of the challenge. The North–South high-speed railway is projected to cost US$67 billion, while the two Ninh Thuan nuclear power plants, with a combined capacity of 4,000 megawatts, are expected to cost at least US$22 billion. Financing Vietnam’s high-growth plans for 2026–2030 is estimated to require about US$297 billion annually, or 40 per cent of nominal GDP.
item.content:encoded:
Since coming to power in August 2024, General Secretary To Lam has emphasised his ambition to turn Vietnam into a high-income country by 2045. Towards this goal, a National Assembly resolution in April set a target of average annual growth of 10 per cent through 2030, with infrastructure building expected to serve as a major growth engine.

However, Vietnam is struggling to mobilise sufficient capital to finance this ambitious agenda because of both domestic and external constraints. Hanoi therefore faces a choice: align its growth targets with the capital it can raise at a reasonable cost or accept considerably greater economic risks.

The projects illustrate the scale of the challenge. The North–South high-speed railway is projected to cost US$67 billion, while the two Ninh Thuan nuclear power plants, with a combined capacity of 4,000 megawatts, are expected to cost at least US$22 billion. Financing Vietnam’s high-growth plans for 2026–2030 is estimated to require about US$297 billion annually, or 40 per cent of nominal GDP.

Domestic banks carry most of this burden. Bank lending accounts for about 83 per cent of Vietnam’s financing mix, compared with 13 per cent for bonds and 4 per cent for equity. By late June, outstanding credit reached 19,970 trillion Vietnamese dong (US$760 billion), up 18.1 per cent year on year. Credit expanded by 7.41 per cent in the first half, while deposits grew by only 5.02 per cent, pushing the loan-to-deposit ratio to about 112 per cent.

Banks have responded by competing more aggressively for funding. Posted six- to 12-month deposit rates are generally 5.0 per cent to 6.5 per cent, in line with the State Bank of Vietnam’s efforts to keep rates low. In practice, however, depositors are reportedly offered effective yields of 8.5 per cent to 11.0 per cent through private negotiations.

Scarce credit is also distributed unevenly. In June, 18 major projects requiring 752 trillion dong were exempted from standard credit-growth limits. Developers include large and well-connected conglomerates like Vingroup, Sun Group and Masterise. By contrast, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which account for 98 per cent of Vietnamese firms, receive only about 20 per cent of bank credit. They face lending rates of 10 per cent to 12 per cent, while 93.5 per cent of loans require collateral. Yet SMEs account for most employment and household incomes.

The strain is already visible: new business registrations fell 13.9 per cent year on year in July, while completed dissolutions rose by 270 per cent. This writer’s recent field trip to Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City revealed that many SMEs are struggling because they cannot access the credit needed to sustain or expand operations. This is happening despite stellar headline GDP growth of 9 per cent in the first nine months of 2026.

High interest rates have brought the property market close to a standstill. Average home-loan rates have reached 14 per cent to 16 per cent, while the number of residential property transactions nationwide fell by 36 per cent year on year in the first half. This has cooled speculation and reduced the risk of a property bubble.

However, the high rates have also created new vulnerabilities. Developers depend heavily on property sales for cash flow, while their average bond issuance rate has risen to 11.4 per cent, and their debt-to-equity ratio has climbed to 74 per cent, against an average of 54 per cent during 2022 to 2025. Disrupted cash flows increase the risk that repayment difficulties will translate into higher bank bad debt. As China’s experience illustrates, a prolonged property slowdown can also weigh on household confidence, consumption, public finance and economic performance.

The logical response is to look abroad, but external options remain limited. The international financial centres in Da Nang and Ho Chi Minh City, launched in January and February, have issued certificates to only a few dozen investors, while credit-rating requirements exclude some major foreign banks. Sovereign bond issuance is constrained by Vietnam’s credit rating, which is one notch below investment grade from S&P and Fitch and two from Moody’s.

The government aims to achieve investment-grade status by 2030, which analysts estimate could cut borrowing costs by as much as 1.5 percentage points. But that benefit would come too late for many projects beginning now.

International capital markets are also becoming less welcoming to Vietnamese firms and banks. The US 10-year Treasury yield is about 5 per cent, while the Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent in September. Surging global demand for capital, particularly to finance AI and related technologies, is intensifying competition for funding. Meanwhile, geopolitical pressures, including the US-led war against Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, are pushing up the risk premium that emerging markets like Vietnam must pay.

Looking ahead

There are three key implications here.

First, Vietnam may need to align its growth ambitions with what it can finance at a reasonable cost, to ease funding pressures and put expansion on a more sustainable footing.

Second, if Hanoi maintains its targets while domestic interest rates remain high, the wider economy will bear the strain, with SMEs likely to feel it first. High borrowing costs could produce more closures and discourage private investment, leaving the economy more fragile even as infrastructure spending sustains headline GDP growth.

Third, Vietnam will increasingly need international funding, creating opportunities for foreign banks and other credit institutions. But greater reliance on debt carries risks. Much public infrastructure does not generate direct returns sufficient to service the borrowing used to fund it. In an environment of prolonged high interest rates, excessive debt-financed investment could weaken the repayment capacity of both the government and Vietnamese enterprises.

Vietnam can still build the roads, railways, airports and energy infrastructure it needs, but not necessarily at the pace envisaged. Ambition must be matched by affordable capital, and the two are increasingly moving apart. A more calibrated growth target would reduce financing pressures and the risk of a costlier debt adjustment later.

Le Hong Hiep is a Senior Fellow and Coordinator of the Vietnam Studies Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published by ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s 700-year-old oyster industry goes hi-tech with ‘super’ specimen
item.description:
Out on Deep Bay, between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, the first thing you notice is what doesn’t seem to belong there.

Many of the oyster-farming rafts here are old. Weathered wood, greyed by salt and sun – the kind that has floated in these waters for generations. A few look abandoned, but this is inevitably the appearance a 700-year-old industry takes on when it is running out of time.

And then, there are the newcomers – bobbing buoyantly in a bright, unmistakable shade of blue – made of fibreglass. Pacing back and forth on one in a pink shirt and dark trousers is Professor Thiyagarajan Vengatesen, a marine biologist from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) who is better known as Professor Rajan.
item.content:encoded:
Out on Deep Bay, between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, the first thing you notice is what doesn’t seem to belong there.

Many of the oyster-farming rafts here are old. Weathered wood, greyed by salt and sun – the kind that has floated in these waters for generations. A few look abandoned, but this is inevitably the appearance a 700-year-old industry takes on when it is running out of time.

And then, there are the newcomers – bobbing buoyantly in a bright, unmistakable shade of blue – made of fibreglass. Pacing back and forth on one in a pink shirt and dark trousers is Professor Thiyagarajan Vengatesen, a marine biologist from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) who is better known as Professor Rajan.

Born in India’s Tamil Nadu state, Vengatesen came to Hong Kong in 2001 to take up seven years of advanced research into larval biology at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. His interests lay in how oyster larvae were struggling with environmental adaptation and building their shells at a time of increased ocean acidification.

Vengatesen’s mentor at the time predicted that oysters would become vulnerable to climate change, but the gravity of the situation only sank in when he witnessed it first-hand. After Vengatesen joined HKU, in 2008, a colleague connected him with an oyster expert, who took him to Zhanjiang, in Guangdong province, in 2009, and showed him an industry suffering without scientific involvement. Vengatesen became one of the first scientists in the region to study how climate change would affect oyster farming, but meeting the growers in Zhanjiang – seeing how their livelihoods depended on a species they could not protect – convinced him this was worth a life’s work.

Little did he know he would spend the next decade and counting looking for a solution to save Hong Kong’s oysters.
