item.title: [SCMP] TV showman Robert Chua spells out his vision for his vast collection of Chinese antiquities
item.description:
Robert Chua Wah-peng does not have the air of a stereotypical collector.

He does not demand of you the donning of cotton gloves or scrubbing of fingernails before touching his Chinese antiquities; he excitedly invites you to pick up vases and vessels with your bare hands; he encourages you to engage with his acquisitions up close. Most of them are not sequestered away behind glass or acrylic.

He also does not have an exact number for how large his collection is.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Chua Wah-peng does not have the air of a stereotypical collector.

He does not demand of you the donning of cotton gloves or scrubbing of fingernails before touching his Chinese antiquities; he excitedly invites you to pick up vases and vessels with your bare hands; he encourages you to engage with his acquisitions up close. Most of them are not sequestered away behind glass or acrylic.

He also does not have an exact number for how large his collection is.

“Could be hundreds of thousands of pieces,” he muses when asked.

Originally from Singapore, Chua began collecting in 1967 – the year he arrived in Hong Kong – but it was not until his first visit to mainland China, in 1979, that he got serious about his hobby. He became a regular presence at the antiques dealers’ shops on Hong Kong’s Hollywood Road, sweeping through new shipments twice a week for decades, like clockwork, buying entire lots – everything from late-Qing ceramics bearing illustrated foo dogs in bright orange and terracotta “stickmen” from the Han period to wooden mooncake moulds and snuff bottles.

In his home in Kowloon, he has a room dedicated to blue-and-white porcelain from the Ming and Qing dynasties to the Republic era, rows of Chinese wedding cabinets heaving with tableware, wardrobes bursting with vibrant stoneware and jars, a corridor with more than 180 horse sculptures, shelves groaning beneath fossilised dinosaur eggs and Neolithic pottery, and drawers holding delicate jade accessories and brass buttons. Neolithic, Warring States, Han, Sui, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming, Qing – Chua’s collection reads like a chronicle. Inching along narrow pathways cleared between stacks for necessity’s sake, he is talking a mile a minute, propelled by obvious fervour, sharing historical facts, stories about how he obtained an artefact, the technique used to make it.

Chua is an oddity among his peers in the collecting community in that his incentive to collect really isn’t that deep. “Honestly, I don’t know,” he shrugs. “I just love beautiful things. Never do I buy anything and at any moment say, ‘I bought this for HK$1,000. One day, maybe it will fetch me HK$5,000.’ Never. I buy for the beauty. And if I see something that is lovely, I’ll buy 30 of them, to share with people.”

Among Chua’s extensive accumulation, one theme stands out, not only in quantity but also in peculiarity: his collection of ancient Chinese mingqi – “spirit objects”, traditionally placed in tombs as funerary items to comfort the deceased in the afterlife. As far as the eye can see, there are small-scale models of dwellings, animals, furniture and carriages, as well as figures of guardians and attendants.

For visitors familiar with Chinese customs, it might come as a shock to see Chua living among mingqi. Despite their exquisite craftsmanship and three-colour sancai glaze, keeping burial goods intended for the dead in one’s home is thought to invite misfortune and disruptive yin energy into the household.

Chua is aware of the taboo, but it doesn’t faze him. “I am a bit Western in that sense,” he says. “Western collectors don’t mind antiques like these, but Chinese collectors are too superstitious to want them, so that made it easier for me to acquire them; the demand was lower and they were not difficult to source.

I have thousands of happy spirits at home. I’m not worried about anything – there’s so much company. It’s always a party

Robert Chua

“But I’m happy. I have thousands of happy spirits at home. I’m not worried about anything – there’s so much company. It’s always a party,” he laughs.

Indeed, Chua has a penchant for entertaining and hosting. His calendar is ordinarily filled with visits, events, meetings, lunches and dinners, both personal and professional. He likes to receive guests in the sunroom. He has a talent for driving conversations, and his candour and quick wit work in tandem to put people at ease.

To understand and appreciate Chua’s gravitational pull towards people and telling stories, taking a gander at his own history pulls back the curtains.

Chua, 80, made his name in television broadcasting. His first job, as a property assistant at ADS Channel 7 in Adelaide, Australia, in 1964, sparked an enduring fascination with the industry. After rotating through several positions at the Australian network, he returned to Singapore two years later, to produce for Radio Television Singapore, gaining experience in light entertainment.

It wouldn’t be long before another door opened for Chua: he was offered the role of senior production executive at Hong Kong’s TVB in 1967, to help set up its first colour-television station. At just 21 years old, he created Enjoy Yourself Tonight, which became the city’s longest-running live variety programme, airing more than 6,610 episodes between 1967 and 1994 on the TVB Jade channel.

Colin Bednall, the then-general manager of TVB, “trusted me to do the job. Had I failed, he would have lost his job for sure. But luckily, everything went so well. I am grateful to him”, Chua says of the opportunity extended to him despite his age.

As someone who avowedly attributes his life’s trajectory to an improbable series of events and a chain of people betting on him against all odds, Chua has held up his end of the bargain to deliver on those instincts and that faith in his potential.

Enjoy Yourself Tonight garnered him acclaim, promotions and opportunities. Chua rose through the ranks to serve as the special assistant to the managing director and also brought the Miss Hong Kong Pageant to the local network in 1973, before leaving TVB to start his own production house. Back then, freelance television facilities were few and far between, due to the high upfront costs of launching one. Coupled with its founder’s established reputation, Robert Chua Production House (RCP) readily landed work with broadcasters, agencies and corporate clients to do commercials, shows, documentaries and the like.

Chua expanded his business to the mainland in 1979, brokering deals on behalf of foreign advertisers looking to gain a foothold in the market.

Over a decades-long career in television, Chua put his mark on numerous other ventures, but his success and tenacious pursuit of achieving “firsts” did not come without challenges. In March 1995, after more than three months of experimental screenings, his Chinese-language China Entertainment Television Broadcast (CETV) channel began airing around Asia, showing original productions, films, soap operas, children’s series and more through 24 hours of daily programming. CETV reached millions of households across the region over the 21 years it was in operation, but it also proved to be one of the most difficult periods of Chua’s life.

Already burdened by the stress of keeping the station financially afloat, in January 1999, he suffered from a build-up of excess blood fluid in his brain, which required urgent surgery. While recuperating at home – his first time off since his marriage, in 1974, to his former assistant at TVB, Peggy Jen Ping-ping – and spending more time among his collection, by then already formidable, Chua began to view his antiques in a different light. Damaged and incomplete pieces caught his attention in particular, planting a seed for a new artistic vision: to flip the script on the notion that, in their marred condition, these objects were useless or to be discarded, and revive them through novel methods.

The resulting “Antique Arts” is part of Chua’s mission to find new meaning for his pieces. “An antique does not lose its soul because it is broken,” he explains, and neither should they be valued only for what they once were. A shattered vessel or a shard of porcelain is not just “a remnant of the past. It is a survivor. It carries memory, human touch, craftsmanship, cultural identity and the passage of time”.

Rather than restoring them to their original state, Chua believes that transforming them into new artworks allows them to keep existing through a modern narrative. Combining periods, dynasties, shapes, textures, mediums and contexts, his “Antique Arts” tell a fresh story, simultaneously embodying a metaphor for Chua’s own journey of recovery. (He would go on to have a second brain surgery, in 2008, informing his decision to take a step back from his company.)

Where collectors, dealers and auction houses see broken antiquities as defective, Chua thinks of them as a continuation. “Antique Arts” is his attempt to symbolically collaborate with the “many hands” of bygone makers, resulting in a creative dialogue across time. A Song dynasty pot fragment is paired with Neolithic earthenware to depict the pouring of tea, bridging thousands of years; the remaining handle of an ancient jug is juxtaposed with a modern ink painting to “complete the gaps” of the one-time vessel, leading to an abstract installation.

Chua’s personal relationship with the material feeds into his creation process, too. Anonymous objects they are not. He has lived with them, studied them and cared for them across decades, forming an intimate connection with the pieces.

From a slim case, he pulls out slender sticks of ivory, their tips wrapped in thread, ending in thin brushes of fine hair. Qiancao – cricket ticklers – are tools used in cricket combat, to goad the insects into fighting each other for sport.

“When I have an antique, like this one, I wonder who it belonged to. I imagine what their lives were like. Everything I look at, everything I touch, I feel someone in my mind – the people who used these objects, these pieces that lived in their homes. Frankly, that’s better to me than something that’s brand-new.” He continues, “How much is the value of a piece? It’s not so much about the actual monetary value, but how much it really means to you. ‘Expensive’ is in the mind of the person.

“For most collectors, when something breaks, it’s gone forever. But for me, if something breaks somehow, my consolation is that I can give it a new life. What I have, what’s broken, I try to put them together anyway. I never break anything on purpose. Sometimes, it just happens. But I wait for the right moment. I find the right pieces that will come together, and if they don’t, I won’t rush it.”

As he left broadcasting behind, the “right pieces” ended up falling into place, anyway. Chua’s affinity for entertainment, connecting with an audience and shaping narratives continued to find ways to manifest through different avenues.

In 2013, Chua followed his entrepreneurial nose and snapped up the Asia-Pacific franchising rights to Tim Ho Wan, often hailed as the cheapest Michelin-star restaurant in the world, launching it in Singapore with his brother, Harry Chua Wah-eng. He credits “luck and fate” as the reason for their winning bid – at the time, neither sibling had any experience in the food and beverage industry to speak of – but it was, once again, trust that paved the way to the next chapter.

“At TVB, [Bednall] shouldn’t have given me Enjoy Yourself Tonight, and likewise with Tim Ho Wan, they shouldn’t have given it to me with all the food and beverage professionals out there, but they did,” he told the South China Morning Post in 2024.

Tim Ho Wan co-founder Mak Kwai-pui was a fan of Enjoy Yourself Tonight, and Chua’s unconventional thinking – unhampered by orthodox restaurant strategies – allowed him to be bold and brave. When Tim Ho Wan arrived in Singapore, Chua positioned the brand as an elevated dining experience, growing its footprint to more than 40 outposts. Kam’s Roast (known in Hong Kong as Kam’s Roast Goose) followed in 2016.

“Entertainment and food are the same to me,” he explains. “It’s a people’s business. I look at food as my programmes and I look at my chef as my director.”

Four years later, he founded Joy Luck Teahouse, a chain of food kiosks specialising in Hong Kong-style cha chaan teng snacks, and in 2021, he launched Sinstant, a gourmet line of ready-to-eat and -cook Asian meals designed for home consumption.

At 80, most people would slow down. But Chua, being the “ideas guy”, has not stopped thinking about the future. As he considers his collection, and the richness it holds, there is but one thing left to do with it: share it with the world.

He has laid out the blueprint for his vision, combining his passion for food and Chinese antiques: an all-day restaurant-cum-museum, where the cuisine echoes a rotating curation of pieces from his personal Aladdin’s cave. Imagined as a “cultural-dining landmark”, Treasure of China is designed as an immersive destination to close the distance between heritage, gastronomy and storytelling. Guests will indulge in refined dishes, surrounded by centuries-old artefacts, with restaurant staff providing the backgrounds behind each object to engage visitors.

“Many restaurants, hotels and clubs have their own collection, but the art is just part of the furniture. It’s not interactive. It’s not engaging. It doesn’t change,” says Chua. “Here, the artwork is part of the meal. Whatever you see and touch has a story.”

Chinese history and culture shape each pillar of the museum-restaurant, down to the beverage programme, which will exclusively feature Chinese wines, baijiu, huangjiu and teas. Chua’s “Antique Arts” creations are also planned to be part of the display, and select works – both ancient and “new” – will be made available for purchase, with a percentage of the proceeds donated to charities.

Regional Chinese flavours, ranging from Cantonese and Sichuan to Jiangsu, Fujian and more, will make up the concept’s culinary foundations. But something that is, perhaps, unexpected is that Chua intends to place the experience in the “affordable premium” bracket, offering Michelin-level dining at accessible prices, making good on his ambition to embrace and give back to the wider community.

“Bringing art to a greater audience and developing a concept that not only preserves history, but presents it as a new experience that people can engage with, breaks down barriers,” says Chua. “Antiques are precious because they are records of history, but that doesn’t mean you can’t engage with them on an interpersonal level, because that’s what really creates a connection for people to appreciate them.”

With more than 200 seats envisioned in the estimated 7,000 sq ft floor plan, interactive elements – such as hands-on “touchable history” encounters to hold fossilised dinosaur eggs – and aesthetic spatial design engineered for the social-media generation, Chua plans to appeal to residents and tourists alike.

Treasure of China feels like a natural next step for Chua, whose joy in amassing antiques is matched only by the unadulterated delight he expresses when sharing their stories. On our tour of his “home museum”, through rows of gleaming porcelain and stoic figurines, it is his enthusiasm that leaves the biggest impression.

But this project is not Chua’s alone to bring to fruition. Adviser Jacco Klip, a Dutch F&B professional with nearly 40 years of experience in opening and managing restaurants, provides guidance on the charitable arm of the business. Meanwhile, Choi Biu, a veteran of Hong Kong’s dining scene and long-time member of the Shun Tak Fraternal Association and local Shunde community, and Lawrence Chong, a property-development consultant who has held positions at Sino Land and Galaxy Entertainment Group, serve as co-founder and special adviser to Chua, respectively.

Chua’s concept is still in its early stages, and there’s a lot of work ahead. His collection needs to be catalogued, the search for a suitable venue is ongoing and most of the items he owns hold taboo connotations within Chinese cultural norms, raising questions about how guests will perceive the curated works and whether superstitions around their provenance will win out against curiosity. Not to mention, there are like-minded backers to find and convince.

None of these hurdles seem to be stopping the lifelong pioneer from forging ahead to secure interest and investors in Treasure of China. He has already mapped out a multi-stream revenue model, which includes brand collaborations, merchandising and licensing – a “gastro-tainment” approach, so to speak.

“We’re looking for people with passion,” Chua says. “When I do any business, profit is not my No 1 priority. You must make sure you do a good job. If you think profit comes first, you’ll never be successful, because you’re trying to compromise. I want the partners to feel proud of how they are contributing to society.”

Whether the museum-restaurant sets its roots down in Hong Kong or Macau is still to be determined, but Chua believes that the objective of his cultural destination – to entertain, educate and connect – aligns with either city’s broader tourism goals.

“Over the years, I have always believed in creating ‘firsts’ that change how people think and experience things”

Robert Chua

Whatever shape his new project takes, Chua’s mission has not changed. From “Antique Arts” to Treasure of China, giving the pieces in his collection a new voice remains central to his pursuits, as a poignant reminder that history can be palpably felt, reimagined and revived. “Over the years, I have always believed in creating ‘firsts’ that change how people think and experience things,” he says.

“With art, if it’s something you like, you enjoy, you appreciate, it doesn’t have to be that profound, right? I look at these objects, and some of them look so rough. But to me, they are beautiful because they hold so many stories and years of life.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
item.description:
Indonesia officially barred under-16s from using “high-risk” social media earlier this year. But that hasn’t stopped the son of one Jakarta-based writer from using it.

Aged 14, he already had accounts on Instagram and TikTok – among the platforms Jakarta said children would be banned from using – as well as popular video game Minecraft and gaming platform Roblox. To register, he simply lied about his age.

“He can access everything,” Inne Abidin said of her son. “His friends use everything too.”
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia officially barred under-16s from using “high-risk” social media earlier this year. But that hasn’t stopped the son of one Jakarta-based writer from using it.

Aged 14, he already had accounts on Instagram and TikTok – among the platforms Jakarta said children would be banned from using – as well as popular video game Minecraft and gaming platform Roblox. To register, he simply lied about his age.

“He can access everything,” Inne Abidin said of her son. “His friends use everything too.”

Since March, Indonesia has had some of Southeast Asia’s strictest rules governing children’s social media use.

Yet like elsewhere in the region, such restrictions are only as effective as the systems Big Tech platforms put in place to identify underage users – and keep them out.

From Malaysia to Vietnam, the Philippines and Singapore, governments that once merely urged platforms to protect children are now imposing rules designed to force social media companies to take responsibility.

Patchy compliance

Indonesia’s child protection regulations have already had an effect on how social media companies operate.

In April, Meta Platforms raised the minimum age for a Facebook, Instagram or Threads account from 13 to 16 in Indonesia, with YouTube following suit later that month. Both said they would begin a phased deactivation of accounts belonging to underage users.

TikTok, which was the first platform to comply with the new rules, raised its minimum platform age to 16 on March 28. By October, it had deactivated 9 million underage accounts, Indonesia’s digital affairs minister announced on Wednesday.

And online gaming platform Roblox now scans Indonesian users’ faces to estimate their age, restricts some communication features for children and has added age-based account limitations.

Yet youngsters seemingly still find ways to skirt the rules. To combat this, Indonesia’s government has given tech companies until the end of the year to complete comprehensive self-assessments detailing how their algorithms, age-verification and ad-targeting systems protect children.

If the platforms fail to comply, the Communications and Digital Affairs Ministry has finalised a sanctions mechanism that – once codified into law – would allow Indonesia to levy fines of up to 6 per cent of tech firms’ global revenue. Applied to Meta’s reported revenue for 2025, that would amount to roughly US$12 billion.

Such a fine would not be without precedent. In August, Meta agreed to pay a coalition of US states up to US$18 billion to settle lawsuits alleging Facebook and Instagram were deliberately designed to make children addicted and caused them harm.

The settlement also forced sweeping changes to how teens experience the platforms, including daily usage limits, overnight usage blocks and strengthened age-verification controls.

Meta has reportedly migrated some 22.5 million Indonesian platform users across to these “teen accounts”, but for the country’s government this does not go far enough.

“While we see this as progress, we still do not consider Instagram and Facebook teen accounts to be low-risk,” Communication and Digital Affairs Minister Meutya Hafid told reporters in Jakarta on Wednesday. “They remain categorised as high-risk.”

Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost

Unggul Sagena, digital rights advocate

For Southeast Asia, the unavoidable question now being asked is whether governments can turn the threat of penalties into real change.

“In my view, the level of cooperation comes down to a few factors: how valuable the market is, how credible the government’s enforcement is, whether the rule threatens the platform’s global business model, how closely it aligns with obligations they already meet elsewhere and whether it carries legitimacy,” said Unggul Sagena, head of internet access at the Southeast Asia Freedom of Expression Network, an Indonesian digital rights organisation that advocates for internet freedom and user safety.

As the region’s largest economy, the sheer size of Indonesia’s consumer market – as well as its risk-based approach to online child protection – lent its arguments and regulations weight that smaller countries lacked, Unggul said.

“Global platforms are complying,” he said. “Even if not yet fully.”

Part of the reason for the changes is the legal machinery Indonesia already has in place, including a regulation passed in 2020 that obliges platforms to act on government takedown orders within tight deadlines, as short as four hours in urgent cases.

“The government has also taken the issue directly to headquarters,” Unggul said, noting that the communications minister met representatives from Meta’s global public policy and safety leadership team in New York last month to push for faster deactivation of underage accounts.

“Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost,” he added.

Still, Indonesia’s proposed fine framework has yet to be legally codified and many question marks remain over how it will ultimately be implemented.

Unresolved issues include how to collect fines from companies with no local assets, how to accurately verify global revenue “and what due process exists when the same ministry writes the rules, judges compliance and imposes the sanction”, Unggul said.

Blocking sites, meanwhile, “hurts Indonesian users more than the companies”, he said. “And the government can order [content] removals, but it still has little visibility into how the platforms are actually designed.”

The threat of high fines could push platforms to invest more in safety-by-design and high-privacy defaults for children, said Indriyatno Banyumurti, executive director of ICT Watch, an Indonesian civil society organisation focused on digital literacy.

But he warned that legal clarity and consistent enforcement were key, stressing that child safety “should not depend solely on voluntary corporate commitments”.

Indriyatno said much would depend on how violations were defined, how compliance was monitored, how evidence was assessed and whether sanctions could be applied fairly and consistently.

Regional rules

Indonesia’s social media ban may have been Southeast Asia’s first, but it is far from alone in trying to make Big Tech take responsibility for children’s safety online.

In Malaysia, rules in force since June now bar under-16s from opening or maintaining social media accounts and require platforms to verify users’ ages. Companies that fail to comply face fines of up to 10 million ringgit (US$2.5 million), with further penalties for ignoring regulatory directives.

Vietnam is considering a draft decree that would limit under-16s to a view-only mode of social media, preventing them from posting content, commenting, sharing or reacting to other posts. Accounts would have to be registered using a parent or guardian’s details under the proposed rules, with platforms compelled to block age-inappropriate material and place caps on children’s online gaming time.

The Philippines’ approach has been more piecemeal. It already legally forces internet providers to block child sexual abuse material or face heavy penalties and has used regulatory pressure to squeeze direct concessions from platforms. Lawmakers are also considering introducing age limits and other measures.

In August, Meta and Roblox agreed to strengthen age checks, parental controls and content takedowns following talks with Philippine authorities over child safety and online radicalisation. A spate of school shootings this year also spurred officials in Manila to order Reddit and Discord to appoint local representatives to coordinate on online threats. Discord was briefly blocked before agreeing to cooperate.

Singapore requires social media giants to shield users, including children, from harmful material under its Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act that came into effect in 2023, with non-compliance carrying a financial penalty of up to S$1 million (US$781,500).

App stores have been legally required to verify the ages of users who want to download age-restricted material in the city state since April this year. And an Online Safety Commission, launched in June under legislation passed last year, has the power to order the immediate removal of harmful content and restrict offending accounts.

While these efforts have helped effect some change, analysts say the results have been uneven.

“Platforms do respond, but market size is a factor they consider,” said regional tech policy adviser Paco Pangalangan, a technology and human rights fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School in the US. “A large market might get more attention, while a smaller one might get a slower, more minimal version. Whether there’s a law matters too.”

By his count, most of the big social media companies do not even have in-country representatives in five of Asean’s 11 member states.

“So there’s often no real channel for regulators or civil society to raise problems,” Pangalangan said.

Strength in numbers

Individual governments, especially those that represent sizeable markets with credible enforcement mechanisms, may be able to force social media platforms to comply with their rules.

But global technology companies can also opt to deal with countries one by one, which analysts and advocates say makes it harder for smaller markets to exert sustained pressure. One solution could be to present a more united front.

“A regional coalition can push Big Tech to create child-friendly ecosystems in ways no single country can,” Unggul said. “Individually, each Asean country is a market platforms can afford to deprioritise. Together, the region is not.”

Pangalangan said that, taken as a whole, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations could leverage the region’s more than 400 million social media users to strengthen its hand in negotiations..

“Collectively, we have a market that platforms can’t afford to simply deprioritise,” he said.

“If we can agree on common standards, including requirements around how platforms are designed, there’s less room for platforms to play one country off against another or just wait things out.”

Allan Cabanlong, Asean regional director for cybersecurity and cloud services provider CyberCX’s regional cyber advisers programme and a former assistant secretary at the Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology, agreed that collective action could hand regional governments greater bargaining power.

“A broom with one strand cannot sweep,” he said. “We have hundreds of millions of users in Asean. If the Philippines were to stand alone, it would not be listened to.”

As this year’s Asean chair, the Philippines could push the protection of children online higher up the regional agenda, Cabanlong said, while the bloc could also work to strengthen its existing mechanisms for digital regulation.

Asean would not be starting from scratch. Its declaration on the protection of children from online exploitation and abuse, adopted in 2019, and associated regional plans of action already recognise online harm to children as a cross-bogrder issue.

Other frameworks on personal data protection – and a declaration on safe and responsible social media use, adopted last October – widen that scope to include online radicalisation and AI-related risks.

But few observers expect a single, regional law on children’s social media use to be the end result.

“Asean does not necessarily have to start by creating one identical social media law for all member states,” said Ysrael Diloy, executive director of Stairway Foundation, a non-profit children’s rights organisation in the Philippines.

“Given differences in national legal systems, regulatory structures and capacities, that may not be the most realistic starting point.”

Indriyatno agreed that a more realistic approach would be for Asean to agree on common expectations for factors such as risk assessments, minimum standards of platform accountability, privacy defaults for children and cooperation on cross-border cases.

“Regulators could also develop more compatible requirements for platform transparency and information sharing,” he said.

Alejandro Reyes, chief strategic officer of non-profit organisation AI Safety Asia, said national regulators would also need to share information and cooperate more closely.

“If Singapore identifies a serious failure in a platform’s child-safety systems, its counterparts in Malaysia, the Philippines and elsewhere should have access to those findings,” he said.

“Joint investigations, shared technical expertise and coordinated enforcement would make it harder for companies to exploit differences between national regulatory regimes.”

Such a baseline would not demand identical laws, but it would provide common ground in dealing with companies that straddle borders.

It would also carry risks. “The concern here is that child protection is part of a much broader framework of government control over online content and expression,” Reyes said, urging caution given the differences in countries’ legal systems, political priorities and enforcement capacity.

Other issues, according to Unggul, include the fact that Asean members currently compete for technology investment, have very different track records when it comes to free expression and make decisions as a bloc by consensus.

“Collective leverage only works if it is credible and rights-based, and that is where civil society across the region must make sure the coalition strengthens accountability rather than state control over content,” he said.

“Child safety must not become cover for censorship. Bargaining power comes not only from penalties but from legitimacy.”

Limits of laws

Governments can restrict access, require age verification and impose penalties on platforms, but they cannot regulate the behaviour of children and families, online child safety experts say.

Fandy Zulmi, programme manager at the Centre for Child Study and Protection in Indonesia, pointed to recent Communications Ministry data showing that three out of five Indonesian children had falsified their age to access restricted platforms.

Without stronger digital literacy, parental involvement and robust reporting mechanisms, Indonesia’s social media ban for children might simply move the risks “somewhere else”, he said.

“It is still too early to conclude that the policy has effectively deterred children from going online,” Fandy said.

Indonesia’s implementation challenge begins with the fact that there are between 60 million and 80 million children in the country whose circumstances differ enormously, according to Diena Haryana, founder of the Sejiwa Foundation, a Jakarta-based child welfare organisation.

“Where they live, what education their parents have, what digital parenting awareness the parents have, whether the parents themselves have digital skills – all of that varies massively, especially between somewhere like Jakarta and rural areas,” she said.

Some parents used social media platforms to keep children occupied while they worked, Diena said, while others were more aware of the risks involved with giving their children unfettered access.

“We all need to work much harder to make sure children understand what the regulation is, why it exists and how implementation should actually work,” she said.

But ultimately, it is the platforms themselves that bear the brunt of the responsibility for child safety, according to Pangalangan.

“They already know where many of the harms are,” he said. “They don’t need a law to fix things they control in their own products.”

item.title: [SCMP] Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
item.description:
When the time came to renew his certificate of entitlement (COE), Andrew Tan hit the brakes on coughing up an eye-watering S$112,000 (US$87,400) to keep his car on Singapore’s roads for another 10 years.

Instead, the 49-year-old business consultant decided in May to go without a car for the first time in two decades.

High COE prices, rising running costs and the hassle of parking and congestion are prompting more Singaporeans to reconsider car ownership, as the land-scarce city state expands public transport, cycling infrastructure and other alternatives in a push for a more “car-lite” society.
item.content:encoded:
When the time came to renew his certificate of entitlement (COE), Andrew Tan hit the brakes on coughing up an eye-watering S$112,000 (US$87,400) to keep his car on Singapore’s roads for another 10 years.

Instead, the 49-year-old business consultant decided in May to go without a car for the first time in two decades.

High COE prices, rising running costs and the hassle of parking and congestion are prompting more Singaporeans to reconsider car ownership, as the land-scarce city state expands public transport, cycling infrastructure and other alternatives in a push for a more “car-lite” society.

Quarterly figures released by the government’s Land Transport Authority in July showed there were 516,237 privately owned cars in Singapore, the lowest number since 2019, even as the share of rental, ride-hailing and corporate cars had increased. Privately owned cars still accounted for 79 per cent of all those on the roads, however.

When Tan bought his first car in May 2006, he said the COE cost S$10,000. A decade later it had climbed to S$50,000 and renewing again this summer would have cost more than double that amount.

Other reasons to give up driving included rising road tax, fuel, maintenance and insurance costs, he said, as well as the city state’s congestion-charging system, known as electronic road pricing (ERP).

An automated system that charges drivers a fee for using busy roads during peak hours, ERP dates back to 1998, though there were other paper-based systems in place beforehand.

At the start of last month, ERP charges returned to the Orchard Road shopping district for the first time since the start of the pandemic in 2020.

Singapore has been actively encouraging people to walk, cycle and use more public transport under the Land Transport Authority’s “Move Lite” campaign, first launched in 2022.

In its early days, the campaign mostly focused on the positives of public transport and not owning a car, but the strategy has since moved towards spotlighting the downsides of driving such as being stuck in traffic and wasting time hunting for parking.

Still, its main aim was to promote more sustainable ways of travelling, not deter people from driving, through its use of “relatable, everyday scenarios”, a spokesman for the authority said.

“The campaign seeks to help commuters make informed travel choices while raising awareness of the increasingly convenient and accessible alternatives to driving,” he said, adding that planning and managing Singapore’s transport network meant balancing the needs of different road users while making the best use of limited land.

To achieve this, the spokesman said Singapore was investing in public transport and “active mobility” infrastructure while managing vehicle ownership and road usage to keep transport efficient and sustainable.

“Our objective is not to prioritise one group of commuters over another, but to provide Singaporeans with more mobility options that are safe, reliable and sustainable for different journeys and needs.”

Singapore only has 744.3 sq km (287.4 square miles) of land and roads take up about 12 per cent of it, which is why authorities have been working to make walking, cycling and public transport more accessible and convenient.

The COE system, launched in May 1990, controls how many vehicles are allowed on the roads by requiring motorists to bid for a certificate in online open auctions. Each COE confers the right to own a vehicle for 10 years.

Singapore has maintained a zero-growth policy for private cars and motorcycles since February 2018 and the Land Transport Authority aims to keep this cap in place until January 31, 2028, while allowing for a small expansion of commercial vehicle and bus fleets.

With the cost of living on the rise, Tan said owning a car was a poor coping strategy for uncertain times, especially considering he had to “set aside contingency funds for young children and aged parents as well”.

Rising costs have also prompted other car owners to think twice about renewing their COEs.

Retired engineer Ricky Quek, 63, recently decided to stop driving after 28 years, citing high COE and petrol prices. Renewing his COE would have cost him S$130,000, he said.

“Public transport is reasonably cheap and no hassle compared to owning a car,” Quek said. “Having a car is definitely convenient but drives up the expenses.”

Small annoyances

Mounting expenses are only part of the picture, however. Other factors discouraging driving include efforts to lower speed limits with stricter enforcement and penalties, and extensive road works linked to major construction projects.

Work on a new multilayered expressway known as the North-South Corridor, the multimodal Changi Northern Corridor project near the airport and a new subway called the Cross Island Line is affecting a number of major arterial roads and highways.

Tech entrepreneur Davidson Chua, 27, says he has noticed more of these roadworks recently, especially during the off-peak times when he likes to commute.

“I do often feel a small annoyance when I am expecting less traffic but end up [encountering] lane closures because of road works or pruning,” said the self-proclaimed motoring enthusiast, adding that he typically preferred covered parking spaces though those could be harder to come by.

Chua said he would only drive two or three days some weeks, “because I don’t see a point in driving down to areas like the CBD [central business district]. It costs more time and money.”

His car is now on its second 10-year COE cycle, with the next renewal due in three years’ time.

“I would love to renew,” he said. “But the COE price will definitely play a huge role in the decision-making process.”

Gopinath Menon, a former chief transport engineer at the Land Transport Authority who led the ERP’s roll-out, told This Week in Asia that measures to limit car ownership had been a part of Singapore’s overall transport strategy since the mid-1970s.

“Realising that the small island cannot keep building more roads to tackle traffic congestion, the strategy called for reasonable demand management for private vehicle travel and for public transport to be the main mode of travel,” said Menon, who is now an independent transport engineering consultant.

Higher parking charges were first to be introduced, alongside an analogue predecessor to the ERP known as the Area Licensing Scheme in 1975. The COE bidding framework followed in 1990, with ERP being rolled out later that same decade.

“Higher driving costs have pushed more people to switch from cars to vastly improved public transport and other public modes such as private-hire vehicles and active mobility,” Menon said, referring to walking and cycling. “This is called the push-pull strategy.”

Speed bumps on the road to a “car-lite” concept included “ambition and attitudes towards car ownership”, he said.

But infrastructure can help lead the way. Menon pointed to the increasing number of pedestrianised zones and bus lanes as ways to reclaim road space for non-car traffic.

Some districts and towns are also car-lite by design, with amenities placed close together, public transport prioritised and access to cycle paths and footpaths improved.

Given the high costs of car ownership, Singapore’s government needs to make the case that cars are a luxury, not a necessity, for the vast majority of citizens, according to public policy expert Terence Ho, an adjunct associate professor in practice at the National University of Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

“There will naturally be some unhappiness about the high COE and ERP charges, particularly when certain roads are still congested at peak hours despite the charges,” Ho said. “But by and large, the vehicle control measures have been effective.”

The number of private cars, excluding private-hire vehicles, had grown just 1 per cent over the past five years, he said, while the share of resident households owning a car had fallen from as high as 42 per cent in 2012/13 to 36 per cent in 2023.

This was despite the fact that many households included young children or elderly family members, Ho said.

For Derek Wong, 35, a car is a non-negotiable for ferrying around his two young children and ageing parents. He bought a second-hand Honda Freed in December, with a COE that expires in September 2035.

“I just felt we had to bite the bullet and this will probably be our last car since we won’t need it when the children are older,” said Wong, a writer whose children are aged two and seven.

“The benefits of the convenience still outweigh the drawbacks. It is a hefty investment but given the time it saves, we feel it is worth it.”

Whether COE subsidies should be granted to large families or to those with elderly members, young children or people with disabilities has repeatedly been raised in parliament.

In a reply on the government portal AskGov in November, the Transport Ministry said the difficulty lay in deciding which groups should receive preferential treatment. A COE subsidy for families would have to be substantial, it said, and lower-income families unable to own a car would be unlikely to benefit.

“COE revenues go towards funding public transport,” the ministry said, adding that its approach was to provide high-quality public transport, complemented by taxis and private-hire cars.

On the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), Singapore’s main underground and elevated railway system, reliability hit a record in August, the Land Transport Authority said in a report released last month. The network’s mean kilometres between failures, a measure of the average distance a train travels before a delay of more than five minutes, rose to 2.88 million km (1.79 million miles) from 2.37 million km in July.

About seven in 10 resident households are already within a 10-minute walk from an MRT station and the government aims to raise that proportion to 80 per cent by the 2030s.

Yet the overall decline in private car ownership had as much to do with the cap on total vehicle numbers as improving public transport links, said Walter Theseira, an associate professor of economics at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

This restriction tended to push car usage towards private-hire models whereby higher utilisation rates made the expensive COE premiums easier to justify, Theseira said.

“The high willingness to pay for COEs suggests that the underlying private demand for cars continues to be strong,” he said.

“The policy objective can’t be to help Singaporeans achieve car ownership ambitions, as it’s a zero-sum game, but … to help Singaporeans stop needing a car.”

Alternative paths

For those ready to ditch the car, Singapore’s expanding cycling network offers a ready alternative. The city state currently has more than 730km (454 miles) of cycling paths and dedicated traffic-free green corridors known as “park connectors”, with work under way to expand the network to about 1,300km by 2030.

Bicycles have been allowed to share pavements with pedestrians since around 2010, according to Menon, with many walkways later widened to ease congestion and improve safety.

Even so, he said cycling was still mainly used for recreation, running errands and so-called first- and last-mile trips to railway stations and bus interchanges. It was unlikely to become the No 1 choice for most commuters given the high quality of public transport, Menon said.

Theseira agreed, pointing to Singapore’s hot climate and the relatively long distance of an average commute as limiting factors – though he saw potential in electric bikes and other motorised devices.

“In many places, very quickly, when people get access to electrified modes of cycling, they usually take that up,” he said, while noting the city state’s current restrictions on such devices, imposed for pedestrian safety, and lack of suitable infrastructure.

Jason Slaughter, an Amsterdam-based content creator who runs the YouTube channel Not Just Bikes, published a video late last month arguing that rules forcing riders to frequently slow down, give way to cars or dismount and push would limit the take-up of cycling in Singapore.

He also critiqued the city state’s cycling infrastructure, highlighting what he called “questionable choices” such as 90-degree turns and lanes that end abruptly, adding he suspected it was “designed by people who never ride a bicycle”.

His video, titled “Cycling Made Difficult (but it’s getting better!)”, had been watched almost half a million times as of Friday.

For Tan, who now relies on public transport and bicycle paths to get around after giving up on car ownership, the trade-offs are worth it.

“I grew up without a car, so I do not have much difficulty adjusting,” he said. “For my Japanese wife, my two young kids and business needs, the adjustments are not as easy. Yet for the amount saved, it’s worth the inconvenience.”

item.title: [SCMP] Pacing problem: can AI fears overcome US-China race dynamics and force a slowdown?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.

On Wednesday, Amodei pushed further for a slowdown when he addressed the UN Security Council by video link, warning that mismanaged AI posed an existential threat to humanity and urging nations to unite on global safety standards.

These public statements come ahead of a highly anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met in New York City on the weekend to discuss AI safety, among other issues.

Yet despite converging on the language of restraint, Silicon Valley’s AI leaders remain locked in a high-stakes and costly tech race against each other – and with China – with no clear winner in sight.

These dynamics, both domestically between industry players and globally between the world’s two AI superpowers, make it highly unlikely that a slowdown will happen any time soon, analysts told the South China Morning Post.

“Even the US companies themselves cannot agree on that,” said Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California San Diego and an expert on Chinese elite politics. “So certainly the US and China will not agree on that.”

It has been four years since Washington imposed wide-ranging controls on the export of advanced semiconductor technology to China, citing national security concerns. Yet Chinese AI models from the likes of DeepSeek and Moonshot AI continue to be competitive with their US counterparts in price and capability.

This, in turn, threatens the trillion-dollar valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic as they head towards initial public offerings, as well as challenging US claims of global AI leadership – an explicit priority of US President Donald Trump, who outright dismissed the calls for a slow down in AI development.

“AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a hoax,” he wrote on social media last week, raising questions about whether the world can pace AI without the support of one of its most powerful leaders.

The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share

Oskar Galeev, Concordia AI

What is driving calls to slow down?

There have long been concerns about the existential risks of AI. Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, winners of the Turing Award computer science prize and widely regarded as the “Godfathers” of AI, have both warned that the technology could eventually displace all humans, with Hinton saying earlier this month that a 10 per cent chance of AI killing all humans within a decade was not an “unreasonable” estimate.

While such concerns are legitimate, what sets apart the recent statements by industry leaders such as Amodei and Altman was that their AI safety proposals also served commercial and geopolitical ends, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

Sun pointed to Amodei’s recent essay “We Must Pace the Frontier”, in which the Anthropic founder warned that a swarm of AI agents could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, potentially causing “hundreds of billions of dollars in damage”.

While the essay laid out why Amodei believes pacing is needed, it also devoted a large part to advocating for tighter restrictions on China’s AI industry. These included US semiconductor chip export controls and a “crackdown on unauthorised distillation by companies” in “autocratic” China.

“Amodei explicitly connects pacing with preserving a US lead over China,” Sun said. That made it “difficult” for Chinese policymakers to view the move as “politically neutral”, the Tsinghua fellow added, even if Amodei acknowledged that “[global] pacing will require cooperation with China”.

Reaction in China to Amodei’s essay was dismissive, with many accusing the tech CEO of using the guise of AI safety to shape the rules governing the sector and to entrench Anthropic’s position as an industry leader.

Last week, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, People’s Daily, published a commentary accusing the US of seeking to monopolise frontier AI development, while a DeepSeek engineer invoked Nazi Germany in a blog post that criticised OpenAI and Anthropic for their latest pacing calls.

China was likely to draw a sharp distinction between AI safety and efforts it viewed as “AI containment”, according to Wei Sun, principal analyst for AI at Counterpoint Research. Beijing has recently unveiled new AI initiatives that call for greater AI safety measures and international cooperation on AI governance, including a new “AI Safety Governance Framework” standards document for the industry released last week.

Oskar Galeev, a researcher at Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI, said the Chinese government had demonstrated that it increasingly cared about AI safety. But it would still require the US to deal with it on an “equal footing”, he said, rather than as a subordinate being dictated to by a stronger power.

“The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share,” he said.

Existential risks, practical realities

Geopolitics aside, even getting the US to pace its own industry would be a challenge, according to UC San Diego’s Shih. While the Anthropic and OpenAI founders have raised alarms about the existential risks of AI, they have also been rebuffed by fellow industry titans including Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who dismissed such worries as “complete nonsense” at an event last week.

Huang dismissed such “doomerism” while on a New York Times podcast on Wednesday , arguing that fearmongering only slowed down industry adoption.

There are questions over how a pacing mechanism would be enforced given high levels of mistrust between US AI companies.

As Karen Hao chronicled in her award-winning 2025 book Empire of AI, Altman and Musk helped found OpenAI in 2015 because they did not trust Google to develop AI safely. Six years later, Amodei and other former OpenAI executives and researchers left to start Anthropic after losing trust in Altman to develop AI safely.

Musk, founder of Grok model developer SpaceXAI – formerly xAI – took Altman to court earlier this year after having long accused the OpenAI CEO of prioritising profits over AI safety.

Qian Zilan, a research scholar at the independent AI governance think tank GovAI, said US AI leaders claimed that they wanted to build safe AI but did not trust others to do the same. This created pressure to continue building powerful AI systems, driven by fears that slowing down would cede ground to a rival who would deploy a system with far fewer safeguards.

Further intensifying these dynamics are the massive investments being made by US and Chinese companies in underlying AI infrastructure, such as chips and data centres, with the pace of spending not slowing down.

According to a Morgan Stanley report published earlier this month, capital expenditure by Chinese AI hyperscalers was forecast to jump 121 per cent year on year in 2026 to 995 billion yuan (US$142 billion), outpacing the 41 per cent growth among US peers.

China has long been a laggard in terms of AI investment, but recent successes, including DeepSeek’s breakthrough moment in January 2025 and growing policy support from Beijing, have spiked investment levels.

Still, even as the gap narrowed, China was set to spend only around 17 per cent as much as the US on AI infrastructure over the five years to 2030, Morgan Stanley estimated. Given that China’s AI spending was a much smaller share of its economy than the US, it would not likely slow down its investment momentum, Lu Ting, managing director and chief China economist at Nomura Securities, said at a Fortune event in Guangzhou last week.

“I think the key question in China is whether it can obtain chips, how many chips it can get, and how many Nvidia chips it can buy,” he said.

With China not showing signs of slowing down, the US want to maintain its pace over fears of China fully catching up, said Shan Hui, chief China economist at Goldman Sachs, at the same event. “The next 12 to 18 months will not slow down, and may even accelerate, especially in terms of AI infrastructure,” she said.

Adding to investor frenzy is the rush from both leading American and Chinese AI companies to go public. Despite its high-profile safety warnings, Anthropic itself was still expected to go public later this year, with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, Axios reported earlier this month, citing multiple sources.

In China, Kimi developer Moonshot AI has reportedly been valued at US$50 billion in an ongoing funding round and confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, people with knowledge of the matter told SCMP earlier this month.

Meanwhile, GLM developer Z.ai, which is listed in Hong Kong, announced plans earlier this month to raise an additional US$5 billion through a combination of new shares and convertible bonds, just two months after raising US$4 billion in a share placement.

According to Tsinghua’s Sun, the new influx of capital and unprecedented investor interest made a collective slowdown difficult. “If one frontier company deliberately slows the development of its most capable models while its competitors continue to move ahead, it risks losing market share, capital, talent and technological leadership,” he said, adding that this also applies to countries.

Genuine safety fears

While there were legitimate concerns about the feasibility of pacing AI development, recent incidents involving AI agents demonstrating unprecedented cyber hacking capabilities had “captured the attention of both policymakers and the public”, said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent months released details about how their models hacked into other companies’ internal systems through “agentic swarms” that went undetected for weeks.

Besides industry warnings, calls for greater safeguards have also intensified among US and European politicians after former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from his role at Anthropic earlier this month and accused the companies of “gambling with our lives” with their plans to accelerate AI development.

Central to their plans was recursive self-improvement (RSI), Coxon warned, which involved automating the AI research and development process itself with the use of AI – a controversial practice that some experts say could lead to humans losing control of AI entirely.

Still, both American and Chinese AI industry leaders have in recent months described RSI as imminent. Given the AI hacking incidents, calls for restraint from industry should not be dismissed as “regulatory theatre,” said Counterpoint Research’s Sun, as the arguments for AI safety had become “much more concrete.”

According to Singer, AI’s growing threat to both US and Chinese interests and humanity as a whole could ultimately be what overrides geopolitical and commercial incentives to continue racing ahead.

“At this stage, voluntary pacing isn’t just feasible, it’s pragmatic [in] the face of serious risks,” Singer said. “Regardless of whether a model is developed in San Francisco or Shanghai, they can create risks that transcend borders.”

Even in its attacks on Amodei and Washington’s hawkish tech policy towards China, the People’s Daily commentary nonetheless called on Washington to work with Beijing to “manage risks through dialogue and communication” and “promote AI to benefit mankind”.

Wang Shengyu, a research assistant at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, said China’s dominant national security apparatus may be more sympathetic to calls for a slow down given the risks of AI expanding from cyberattacks to bioweapon development.

Last week, China’s top intelligence official Chen Yixin called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the emerging technology in an article published in a journal run by the country’s Cyberspace Administration.

“Once the benefits and risks of frontier AI become concrete enough to create real policy trade-offs, the final judgment is likely to rest with President Xi [whether to slow down AI development]”, Wang said.

As the Xi-Trump meeting nears, experts cautioned against expecting a sweeping agreement on AI, saying any breakthrough would focus on narrower areas where US and Chinese interests overlapped.

A good deliverable from the summit would be for the two sides to agree to have more AI dialogue in future, while finding out what the common concerns over AI risks were, said Tsinghua’s Sun.

There are early signs that this may be possible. Following Sunday’s meeting, US Treasury Secretary Bessent said that the US and China had discussed a “US-China AI dialogue” mechanism and further meetings to discuss AI-related issues.

He added that the US side would “want a shared vision of common goals and threats” with China, including a proposed “notification mechanism” between the two countries.

“Just like any cross-border activity, moving from opaque to more transparency between the No 1 and No 2 AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent said.

item.title: [SCMP] As the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
item.description:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.
item.content:encoded:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.

Under contracts signed by non-Chinese entities, models have been trained on cutting-edge Nvidia processors housed thousands of miles, away outside the reach of US authorities, he said.

That critical lifeline could be on the verge of collapsing.

Washington is reportedly moving to expand its tech blockade from physical hardware to cloud networks. As the US Congress weighs legislation to restrict foreign remote access and executive agencies review cloud-leasing loopholes, China’s AI sector faces its most severe choke point since the chip bans began.

The impending US crackdown threatens to reshape the global AI ecosystem, challenging Southeast Asia’s data centre boom, squeezing Nvidia’s international revenues and forcing Beijing into an acceleration of its domestic chip push.

The cloud escape hatch

Developing AI infrastructure across borders has long been common practice among Chinese developers looking to bypass hardware bans while avoiding US regulatory hurdles, according to observers.

“For a long time, Chinese AI companies have circumvented chip export bans by leasing overseas data centres,” said Arisa Liu, chief director and research fellow at Taiwan Industry Economics Services, a unit of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research. “[This] has indeed contributed a significant amount of overseas market demand to Nvidia.”

To make good use of these remote servers, some Chinese teams have taken extraordinary measures to overcome technical bottlenecks. Chinese engineers personally carried hard drives storing 80 terabytes of data from Beijing to Malaysia to train an AI model at a local data centre, saving months of digital transfer time, The Wall Street Journal reported last year.

Driven by the global AI boom, demand for high-performance computing power has sent global cloud rental rates soaring.

Leading AI infrastructure provider Nebius Group raised rental prices on certain Nvidia chips by roughly 30 per cent in June, with a further 21 per cent increase to come into effect on October 1. Hyperscaler rates for Nvidia’s A100 processors rose to US$3.75 per hour in late August, up from US$3.71 a month earlier, according to tracking firm Silicon Data.

To maintain secrecy and navigate cross-border payments, some Chinese teams have even executed cloud-leasing transactions via blockchain-based smart contracts and paid in cryptocurrency to keep both parties hidden behind anonymous digital wallets, the Journal reported in 2024.

However, the regulatory net in Washington is rapidly closing.

The administration of US President Donald Trump was reviewing remote access arrangements and was working on policies to curb it, according to reports by Bloomberg and The Information. In January, the US House passed the Remote Access Security Act, which, if signed into law, would expand American export controls to remote cloud computing access.

“If the US passes and implements relevant legislation that extends restrictions from physical chips to cloud leasing, Nvidia’s overall sales growth momentum will inevitably be curtailed to some extent,” Liu said.

Legal experts noted that current compliance remained a grey area. Currently, there are “no regulations or similar provisions in place to restrict or prohibit” such remote access, said Hong Jiayang, managing partner of US law firm Joint-Win Partners.

The only measure that came close to banning the practice was the “AI Diffusion Rule”, said Hong, who focuses on trade compliance. The regulation, which requires US cloud service providers to exercise caution when providing cloud services for Chinese AI models, was introduced by the Biden administration in January 2025 but rescinded by the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) after Trump came to power.

The Remote Access Security Act “was introduced for a similar purpose”, Hong said. However, once it goes into effect, “the businesses of cloud service giants such as Oracle and Amazon.com will be significantly impacted, which is bound to provoke a strong backlash”.

Even if the US did not enact legislation to regulate cloud services, the BIS could “theoretically impose penalties on data centres and even model developers that use illegally smuggled chips” on the grounds of “General Prohibition 10”, which penalises transactions conducted with knowledge that a violation has occurred, Hong explained.

“Hi-tech companies should avoid becoming entangled in such legal liabilities at all times,” he added.

Southeast Asia’s data centre boom

If Washington closes the cloud computing loophole, the immediate shock waves will hit Southeast Asia, one of the world’s fastest-growing data centre hubs.

Local data centre capacity in the region was projected to expand at 35 per cent each year from 2023 through 2028, outpacing the global average of 15 per cent, according to market intelligence platform Speeda.

Chinese tech giants, including Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – Tencent Holdings and TikTok owner ByteDance, have spent years building out regional infrastructure to serve the Chinese market.

Asian hyperscalers preferred the region for several reasons, including “competitive development costs across construction, equipment and human capital; and lower operating costs”, according to Vivian Wong, lead analyst for APAC at DC Byte, a market consultancy in the data centre industry.

If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market

Alex Cordovil, Dell’Oro Group

“If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market … Southeast Asia is the natural first step for that expansion, given proximity, existing business ties, land and power availability,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group, a market research firm in the telecommunications, security and data centre industries.

Beyond local demands, the region has attracted international workloads, “including from Chinese internet and cloud companies”, Cordovil said. “Export controls are part of that picture: certain accelerator architectures are only available outside mainland China, so workloads that depend on them naturally gravitate to locations where that supply is accessible.”

The region also offers competitive energy economics.

In Southeast Asia, electricity prices average US$118 per megawatt hour (MWh), with the lowest in Indonesia at US$60 per MWh, according to Wood Mackenzie, a consultancy focusing on the energy, chemicals, renewables, metals and mining.

While higher than China’s average industrial rates - between 600 yuan (US$89) and 700 yuan per MWh, and half that in energy-rich regions like Inner Mongolia and Guizhou – Southeast Asia remains cheaper than US hubs like northern Virginia and Silicon Valley, where prices range between US$70 and US$120 per MWh. In comparison, European centres like Germany and Ireland see prices ranging between €150 (US$174) and €250 per MWh, according to state-backed media China Energy News.

Should remote access become a constraint for certain customers in Southeast Asia, it would “likely create a transient imbalance between supply and demand in the region”, he said, adding that the imbalance was expected to be “short lived” as demand was deep.

Wong held a similar view, saying that “any released capacity is likely to be taken up relatively quickly by other customers”.

The domestic bottleneck

For Chinese AI firms, losing overseas cloud access will lay bare a troubling reality: despite heavy state investment, domestic hardware is not yet fully equipped to handle frontier model training at scale.

Despite China’s push for self-sufficiency in chips, the country’s most advanced AI models are still being trained on Nvidia chips, the SCMP previously reported.

The AI development life cycle involves training and inference – the use of a trained model to generate new content. Systems such as DeepSeek-V4 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3 have been successfully adapted to Chinese hardware for inference work only.

For now, the most advanced Nvidia chips remain unavailable in China, including the B200, B300, H100 and H800. Chinese firms either use Nvidia chips they have in inventory or gain access through cloud computing.

The H200, the latest of Nvidia’s Hopper-series chips but a generation behind the Blackwell family, was approved for import by both Washington and Beijing but is only available in small quantities.

ByteDance and Tencent Holdings each received about 10,000 H200s and a few other Chinese customers obtained shipments of a similar size, the Financial Times reported in August.

“There is a massive gap between this quantity and the actual demand of such top-tier tech giants, which often consume tens of thousands or even over 100,000 advanced [graphics processing units],” said Liu of the Taiwan institution.

Nvidia in late August reported that shipments of H200s to China accounted for less than 1 per cent of its US$89 billion data-centre revenue in the quarter that ended July 26. However, it said it did not expect any data-centre computing revenue from China in the following quarter.

Liu added that even though Nvidia’s income might be temporarily curtailed if the US imposed the ban on remote access, “this shortfall may be partially offset by massive orders from other international tech giants” given strong AI demand globally.

Accelerating self-reliance

If the US bans Chinese companies from renting Nvidia-powered data centres overseas, it may lead to higher domestic rental rates, the Shenzhen-based data centre broker noted. For now, rates for B300 chips outside China are two to three times higher than local prices, not including differences in electricity costs.

Even if there were no restriction on renting overseas data centres, replacing Nvidia with domestic chips was “the main trend”, said a semiconductor designer at one of China’s biggest chipmakers, who requested anonymity.

“Who knows if Nvidia processors have back doors,” the person said. Nvidia has repeatedly said that there are no back doors, kill switches or spyware in its products.

Some Chinese teams have started using local chips for AI training. In June, Meituan released LongCat-2.0, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that it said was fully trained and run on a 50,000-card domestic computing power cluster, without naming the supplier.

Huawei Technologies’ rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun expected a major domestic shift towards its AI computing infrastructure for model training next year.

The semiconductor design engineer said the best domestic AI chip currently was the Ascend 950 from Huawei Technologies, not only for its performance but for the whole ecosystem from architecture to networks. Huawei announced last week that the next-generation Ascend 960DT, designed for model training, will be ready in the first quarter of 2027, nine months ahead of schedule.

However, transferring training workloads from Nvidia to domestic chips is a steep engineering bottleneck. The hurdles included the software ecosystem, as Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) platform has long been the industry standard for AI development, the SCMP reported in August.

Migrating existing workflows to Huawei’s Ascend chips could add at least 50 per cent to training time and cost, according to researcher James Wang.

Still, China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade. The supply of advanced-node wafers made using 7-nanometre processes and below was projected to grow at 46 per cent annually between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a recent report.

That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035 from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank.

As Washington moves to extend its tech blockade from hardware shipments to virtual server networks, Chinese AI developers may soon lose their refuge in the cloud. What remains to be seen is whether the squeeze will stall China’s frontier AI ambitions or simply accelerate its push towards technological self-sufficiency.

item.title: [SCMP] China has gained pace in the space race by recovering rockets – but can it relaunch one?
item.description:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead.

US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components.

Despite a succession of breakthroughs in booster-recovery efforts in recent months, both on land and at sea, China has yet to reuse one – a stark contrast laying bare the gap between Beijing’s space ambitions and the challenges that remain.
item.content:encoded:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead.

US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components.

Despite a succession of breakthroughs in booster-recovery efforts in recent months, both on land and at sea, China has yet to reuse one – a stark contrast laying bare the gap between Beijing’s space ambitions and the challenges that remain.

Last month, Chinese private aerospace company LandSpace landed the booster of its Zhuque-3 rocket on deployable landing legs at a site in the northwestern province of Gansu, marking the country’s first successful ground-based controlled recovery using landing legs, an approach that closely resembles that of SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

The significance of landing a launched rocket goes beyond the spectacle of bringing a booster back intact, according to industry experts.

Rocket reuse was “essential for achieving low-cost, frequent and sustainable [launches] … and providing new opportunities for large-scale commercial space exploration”, a team from three major Chinese aerospace research institutions said in a paper published in March.

LandSpace said the first stage represented “about 70 per cent” of a rocket’s cost, with reuse able to spread that expense over multiple missions, underscoring the cost advantages of reusing first-stage boosters.
