“These are not symbolic things; they are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do, serious partners train together, learn together, plan together, and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict,” he said.

Hegseth’s comments come as the Philippines, a close US ally, has been embroiled in simmering maritime tensions with Beijing over disputed waters in the South China Sea.

‘Not a military alliance’

Although Hegseth has yet to provide further details, analysts say the proposed framework is likely to focus on a limited set of defence cooperation priorities rather than cover a comprehensive range of security issues.

“First, Hegseth’s own emphasis was narrow, [specifically mentioning] maritime domain awareness and naval interoperability,” Keith Mahoney, president of defence intelligence at the Studebaker Defence Group, told This Week in Asia.

Mahoney said the ADMM-Plus mechanism was consultative and did not typically work on build-up pacts.

According to Mahoney, the Philippines, as Washington’s sole Asean treaty ally, is likely to play a central role in this framework, and is the one country Hegseth singled out at the Shangri-La Dialogue.

Hegseth had praised Manila’s shift to external defence, its interoperability work, and the 12 per cent defence-spending increase under President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr.

Mahoney pointed to the 10-year Framework for the US–India Major Defence Partnership, which he described as a “direction-setting” document, as a likely template for how cooperation would work out between Washington and Asean.

However, he said Manila was unlikely to achieve consensus within the bloc, as its maritime disputes with China “make it the most exposed member, and several neighbours will keep their distance precisely to avoid being drafted into that front”.

Rommel Jude Ong, a retired rear admiral of the Philippine Navy and a professor at the Ateneo School of Government, expressed doubt that the framework would materialise because the US had little economic leverage against Asean.

“Perhaps if it is addressed bilaterally, some countries would be amenable to its request. Moreover, Asean is not a military alliance, despite the ADMM-Plus mechanism,” he said.

Ong pointed out that the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak’s State of Southeast Asia survey this year showed that the region largely preferred China if forced to align itself with either Beijing or Washington, adding that most countries “are more inclined to collaborate economically with China”.

Observers also note the “poor timing” in proposing such a framework, especially when America’s partners have been questioning its commitment to those partnerships.

“How can he demand from Asean when most of its naval resources have been shifted to the Middle East?” Ong said. “Obviously its role as security guarantor has been diminished. If their objective is to create a burden-sharing set-up, that would be a game killer.”

Chester Cabalza, president and founder of the Manila-based think tank International Development and Security Cooperation, said the framework offering “comes at a time when there is a fractured world. Some of the nations in the region tend to question American policies and leadership”.

Cabalza told This Week in Asia that most Southeast Asian nations “will call for strategic autonomy and hedging, and [will not just be] passive pieces on a global chessboard”.

Washington must demonstrate its sincerity to Southeast Asia, including “low-hanging fruit” in trust-building measures such as real-time maritime domain awareness, and logistics and supply chain interoperability, to avoid the trap of empty diplomatic rhetoric, Cabalza said.

He called the next few years a “critical stress test for Asean centrality”, and said Washington’s proposal could only succeed if “the US recognises the role of the middle powers in Southeast Asia as complementary and not a competitor to US military might in the region that elevates collective strategic culture”.

Joanne Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, noted that many of the areas Hegseth mentioned on Wednesday were already covered under existing Asean-US cooperation.

“The question, therefore, is what additional value this framework can bring,” Lin said, suggesting that it could provide a more structured and longer-term approach to defence cooperation.

The move also appeared to demonstrate Washington’s continued commitment to Southeast Asia’s security and strengthen the defence capabilities of some of its regional partners, in line with the Trump administration’s emphasis on burden-sharing, Lin said.

“However, the extent of cooperation will likely vary across Asean members, given their different security relationships with Washington.”

As Asean is not a military alliance, it would be difficult to expect the bloc to collectively undertake the kind of burden-sharing commitments that Washington sought from its treaty allies, Lin added.

The main challenge, Lin noted, would be ensuring that the framework remained inclusive “and is not perceived as an arrangement directed against China”.

Asean would also prefer to see such cooperation embedded within the existing ADMM-Plus framework and complement bloc-led mechanisms, she added.

The framework would likely be a more “focused cooperative arrangement” beyond the US’ current bilaterally ties with Asean members, said Muhammad Faizal Abdul Rahman, a research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

Chief among the US goals were to soothe doubts about its reliability as a defence partner and hold on power as China rises and the Middle East conflict persists, he said.

But it remains to be seen how this proposal turns into an actual framework.

“Although Singapore is a close US defence partner, as the 2027 Asean chair, it would have to consider the different strategic interests of other Asean members and ensure Asean maintains its autonomy and neutrality as major powers compete to pull the grouping to their side,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] US warns China is expanding its space toolkit with spaceplane and energy weapons
item.description:
A rare satellite image of China’s secretive spaceplane has appeared in a new US intelligence report that warned Beijing was expanding its ability to track American forces and could deploy space-based directed-energy weapons by the late 2020s.

The US Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA) report published on Sunday included an image of the reusable spacecraft, credited to satellite imagery firm Maxar in 2024, showing its shuttle-like design and apparent solar arrays.

A spaceplane is a spacecraft designed to operate in orbit and return to Earth through the atmosphere, much like the US Space Shuttle, although China’s secretive vehicle is believed to be uncrewed and more closely resembles the smaller American X-37B.
item.content:encoded:
A rare satellite image of China’s secretive spaceplane has appeared in a new US intelligence report that warned Beijing was expanding its ability to track American forces and could deploy space-based directed-energy weapons by the late 2020s.

The US Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA) report published on Sunday included an image of the reusable spacecraft, credited to satellite imagery firm Maxar in 2024, showing its shuttle-like design and apparent solar arrays.

A spaceplane is a spacecraft designed to operate in orbit and return to Earth through the atmosphere, much like the US Space Shuttle, although China’s secretive vehicle is believed to be uncrewed and more closely resembles the smaller American X-37B.

The DIA said Chinese spaceplane missions had involved manoeuvring close to a companion satellite and releasing an object in orbit, adding that the vehicles were more manoeuvrable than traditional satellites.

The report also marks the first time that the agency has given a potential timeline for China’s development of space-based directed-energy weapons in its “Challenges to Security in Space” series of reports.

The DIA did not specify whether the weapons would use lasers or high-power microwaves, both of which direct electromagnetic energy at targets and can potentially interfere with or damage satellites.

To date, no Chinese spacecraft has been publicly identified as carrying an operational directed-energy weapon.

The report said that, by the late 2020s, China might also field more powerful ground-based directed-energy systems capable of affecting satellites beyond low Earth orbit.

The DIA said the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) “probably” viewed attacking satellites as a way of deterring or preventing foreign intervention in a regional conflict. It also cited Chinese defence academics who suggested that reconnaissance, communications, navigation and early-warning satellites could be targeted to “blind and deafen the enemy”.

“The US will be far more dependent on space than the PLA” in a potential conflict, Brendan Mulvaney, director of the China Aerospace Studies Institute, told the South China Morning Post in August. Disrupting those satellites could therefore disproportionately affect US forces, potentially weakening their ability to intervene in a regional conflict, such as one over Taiwan.

But how soon China could deploy such weapons remains uncertain. The DIA report does not disclose what evidence underpins its forecast, and analysts differ over when the systems could become operational.

Namrata Goswami, a space security professor at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies, argued that Beijing could achieve an operational capability even sooner, citing China’s reusable spacecraft, orbital manoeuvres and long-standing directed-energy research as evidence of its progress.

Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation, took a more cautious view.

“I would be very surprised if China fielded space-based laser weapons by the late 2020s,” she said.

An April report from the foundation cited major obstacles, including the weapons’ weight, power requirements and difficulties tracking targets.

If those hurdles were cleared, such weapons could interfere with or damage satellites without generating debris, Samson said, reducing the danger to China’s own spacecraft. Lasers “could interfere with optical sensors”, impeding US and allied satellites monitoring a potential Taiwan conflict, she said.

While the foundation’s report cited US Space Force officials as saying China already had space-based directed-energy weapons, Samson said the foundation’s own view was that Beijing was “thought to have at least one space-based jammer”.

But disrupting an opponent’s satellites may be only one element of the PLA’s ambitions in space. The DIA said the PLA’s objectives included “space dominance”, which it defined as “the ability to control the space-enabled information sphere and deny its adversaries their own space-based information gathering and communications capabilities”.

China’s number of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance satellites has more than tripled since 2018 to over 510 as of July, the DIA said. The network was designed to improve worldwide surveillance and “enable long-range strikes”, and could support the tracking and targeting of US and allied forces.

The DIA said China’s low Earth orbit satellites could capture an image of a location within 30 minutes or less, while geosynchronous satellites, which remain positioned over the same region of the planet, could provide “persistent coverage with no latency”.

That expanding network could improve the PLA’s ability to monitor military bases, logistics hubs and ships, according to Garrett Hinck, a researcher at Columbia University. China’s geosynchronous sensors, including Ludi Tance-4 and Yaogan-41, could alert higher-resolution satellites in lower orbits to investigate potential targets, he said.

But seeing a target is not the same as hitting it. Hinck said the DIA’s 30-minute figure would likely hold only “under ideal conditions – daytime, no cloud cover, no jamming”, while deception tactics could further hinder tracking. A carrier “would move between the time that a firing solution could be created and a missile is launched”, he said. “True ‘persistence’ would mean no gaps in coverage.”

Hinck said there was some evidence that China was developing networks linking sensors with weapons in what one Chinese analysis called a “space-air-sea dynamic kill web”, although he would not say China had shown such a capability operationally.

Goswami also cautioned that China could not yet detect aircraft carriers in real time, saying there was “still a lag”, reducing the military effectiveness of its satellite network.

Meanwhile, China’s foreign ministry reiterated Beijing’s opposition to the weaponisation of space in an October 23 policy document. Washington, for its part, made “space superiority” a priority in a December 2025 executive order issued by US President Donald Trump. US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink acknowledged in September that his country already possessed on-orbit space-control weapons but did not identify them.

“There is always going to be a contest between ‘hiders’ and ‘finders’ and reliability is a spectrum,” Hinck said. “China’s capabilities are certainly improving, and the United States will seek to develop ways to negate those.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s ties with Serbia face scrutiny, not severance, after historic Vucic loss
item.description:
Massive crowds, fireworks and dancing have filled the streets across Belgrade since Serbia’s nationalist strongman Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Sunday’s parliamentary election after 14 years in power.

The political shift could cool diplomatic ties between Beijing and Belgrade and invite sharper scrutiny of Chinese investments in Serbia, but was unlikely to upend a relationship built on years of cooperation, analysts argued.

Vucic conceded the defeat of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party to a grass-roots movement called Student List about an hour and a half after polls closed, setting off waves of celebrations around the country.
item.content:encoded:
Massive crowds, fireworks and dancing have filled the streets across Belgrade since Serbia’s nationalist strongman Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Sunday’s parliamentary election after 14 years in power.

The political shift could cool diplomatic ties between Beijing and Belgrade and invite sharper scrutiny of Chinese investments in Serbia, but was unlikely to upend a relationship built on years of cooperation, analysts argued.

Vucic conceded the defeat of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party to a grass-roots movement called Student List about an hour and a half after polls closed, setting off waves of celebrations around the country.

The student-led movement, which started in 2024, consists largely of people outside the country’s established political parties, including university professors, doctors, farmers and cultural figures.

It built its mandate around tackling domestic challenges, prioritising institutional transparency and fighting corruption, departing little from Vucic’s party on issues such as ties with Russia and the European Union, or the status of Kosovo, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008.

Vucic had been an “ironclad friend” to China, making his first state visit to Beijing in May and signing more than 20 deals covering cooperation in politics, trade, tech, education and cultural exchanges.

Four months later in September, Vucic stepped down from the term-limited role as president to lead his party and run for prime minister, a post he had hoped to reclaim in Sunday’s vote.

Cui Hongjian, director of European Union studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said the fall of Vucic did not guarantee a clean break from the past. It remained to be seen whether Serbia’s political landscape would enter an era of stability or remain locked in a protracted tug of war.

He added that Vucic’s party still stood as Serbia’s second-largest political power and there remained a “real question mark” over whether the anti-Vucic forces could form an effective governing coalition.

Both the motivation and leeway for the incoming government to drastically shift its China policy remain limited. Serbia’s room for manoeuvre in its great-power balancing act has narrowed sharply in the wake of the war in Ukraine, according to Cui.

While the West has long viewed Serbia under Vucic as a close partner of Moscow, Belgrade insists it remains committed to joining the EU, even as it has refused to join European sanctions against Russia.

Cui said the incoming government faced a “tough situation where their choices are quite limited”.

“Over the years, China and Serbia have forged deeply intertwined economic interests and a solid foundation of cooperation … Given the tangible benefits these ties deliver, is there any real incentive for the incoming government to disrupt a China policy – and a bilateral architecture – that has served the country so well?” he said.

Cui’s view was echoed by Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy education at King’s College London, who noted that geopolitical alignment and great-power influence had played a smaller role than in any Serbian election in decades.

Sunday’s vote was primarily fought over domestic issues, making foreign policy the area “least susceptible to change”, according to Vuksanovic.

The China-Serbia partnership “has considerable potential to endure, as the new government in Belgrade will recognise China’s growing geopolitical weight and remain attracted by the economic opportunities it offers”, he said.

“The major challenge for Serbia, as for many other countries, will be navigating Sino-American rivalry, but that is a longer-term challenge.”

Stefan Vladisavljev, a visiting fellow with the China Observers in Central and Eastern Europe, cautioned that the student movement’s push for greater oversight of public contracts could bring heightened scrutiny to Chinese investments in the country.

The movement’s 11-point election manifesto called explicitly for full transparency in public procurement and auditing of state projects.

“While [Student List] is not saying that they will stop cooperating with China, it might be that the new rules and standards that will be set by the new government serve as a sort of deterrence to new projects between the two sides,” Vladisavljev said.

He said the student-led movement also pushed for stricter labour and environmental regulations – areas where Chinese operations in Serbia have faced frequent controversy – and would be more rigorous in setting rules and standards.

It was the 2024 collapse of a concrete canopy at a renovated railway station – a flagship project of China’s Belt and Road Initiative in Europe – that ultimately led to the formation of Student List.

The collapse, in the northern city of Novi Sad, killed 16 people and fuelled two years of nationwide protests that culminated in the movement’s election victory on Sunday.

Both Vucic and Beijing said the collapse had nothing to do with work done by Chinese companies. However, there were also allegations that two contractors were involved in inflating invoices on the project last year.

In May, Beijing’s embassy in Belgrade dismissed allegations that Vucic had promised that the Chinese consortium renovating the Novi Sad railway station would be shielded from accountability over the deadly incident.

Vuksanovic in London predicted that the new Serbian government would still “preside over a middle-income economy that needs investment and infrastructure development”.

“It may seek to renegotiate some existing contracts with Chinese partners to ensure greater compliance with environmental standards, stronger labour protections and increased transparency,” he said.

“Chinese investments may therefore face greater scrutiny but the new government is unlikely to push them out.”

China is Serbia’s second-largest individual trading partner and a top source of foreign direct investment, while Belgrade is a cornerstone of Beijing’s European strategy.

Serbia was the first country in Europe to join China’s initiative to build a “community with a shared future for mankind”, which aims to redefine the norms of international cooperation around principles such as mutual respect, sovereignty and non-interference.

According to Cui in Beijing, China is observing to what extent the movement can become a governing party capable of leading Serbia, as well as whether its scrutiny of the Vucic administration spills over into foreign policy or remains confined to domestic issues.

He predicted some initial turbulence in bilateral ties while the new government seeks to set itself apart from its predecessor.

“In the short term, the political dimension of China-Serbia’s ‘ironclad’ ties could experience a noticeable cooling, or even turn frosty – which is, frankly, an unavoidable reality,” he said.

“While the practical foundation based on shared interests might stay the same, the emotional bonds and political trust could be put to the test.”

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s haze crisis becomes rallying point for student anger at Prabowo
item.description:
Yosafat Menteng travelled from Kalimantan on Indonesia’s Borneo island with five fellow students to join Wednesday’s protest in Jakarta against the government’s handling of forest fires that have blanketed parts of Indonesia and neighbouring countries in toxic haze.

Back home in Palangka Raya, one of the worst-affected cities by the haze, he heads the students’ council at the University of Palangkaraya’s Faculty of Social and Political Sciences.

“We in Kalimantan strongly urge the government to declare the forest fires happening in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua a national disaster,” he said.
item.content:encoded:
Yosafat Menteng travelled from Kalimantan on Indonesia’s Borneo island with five fellow students to join Wednesday’s protest in Jakarta against the government’s handling of forest fires that have blanketed parts of Indonesia and neighbouring countries in toxic haze.

Back home in Palangka Raya, one of the worst-affected cities by the haze, he heads the students’ council at the University of Palangkaraya’s Faculty of Social and Political Sciences.

“We in Kalimantan strongly urge the government to declare the forest fires happening in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua a national disaster,” he said.

The protests, taking place in several spots around the capital, have been organised by student leaders from the University of Indonesia along with a coalition of student organisations from universities across the country and civil society groups.

Hundreds of security personnel were deployed in Jakarta ahead of the demonstrations, with a heavy police and military presence and armoured vehicles visible in busy parts of the capital.

The rally is a follow-up to a demonstration on October 20 and is timed to coincide with Youth Pledge Day, a national commemoration of a 1928 declaration that helped lay the foundations for Indonesia’s independence movement.

Organisers have framed the protest around five broad demands: declaring the fires a national disaster and holding responsible companies to account; redirecting public spending towards people’s needs; reducing education costs; tackling corruption and abuse of power; and protecting civil liberties and human rights.

Prabowo’s administration has so far resisted calls to designate the fires a national disaster, arguing it can handle the crisis without outside assistance.

“We continue to monitor [the forest and land fires] and their impact vigorously, evaluating our response to it,” Kurnia Ramadhana, deputy head of media relations at the National Communications Agency (Bakom), told This Week In Asia on Wednesday.

Critics say the reluctance may reflect concerns about the financial burden of a national disaster designation and greater scrutiny it could bring to the government’s response.

Yosafat said he would like to invite central government officials to spend time working from disaster zones. “It will help them understand the scale and severity of the destruction involved and their consequences for human lives.”

Syahganda Nainggolan, head of Indonesia’s Government Communication Agency, struck a conciliatory tone in response to Wednesday’s protests, saying the government respected students’ right to demonstrate and urging them to hold their rallies “in an orderly, safe and peaceful manner”.

“The government will continue to be open to public input, and this interaction is a positive space that needs to be safeguarded together,” he said in a statement, adding that security forces should adopt a “persuasive and humane approach”.

The students at Wednesday’s protest were also pressing the government to reconsider its spending priorities, including some of Prabowo’s signature welfare programmes.

“We also call for the immediate termination of white-elephant programmes such as the Free Meals and the Red and White Cooperative and channel the funds into free education instead,” Yosafat said.

Prabowo’s free nutritious meals programme aims to provide food to 83 million schoolchildren and pregnant women but has faced mounting criticism over its cost, logistical failures and food-poisoning incidents, with at least 57,000 cases reported.

His Red and White Cooperative initiative aims to establish 80,000 village cooperatives, with 240 trillion rupiah (about US$13 billion) in state-bank loans earmarked for building stores and related facilities. The government will repay the loans, raising concerns among analysts about pressure on public finances and the risk of bad debts.

“Today’s public pressure goes beyond the forest fires alone,” said Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies Indonesia. He said the protests reflected accumulated frustration with government policies “that are out of step with public sentiment and common sense”.

“Calls for the government to act swiftly to tackle the forest fires and declare a national disaster have been voiced by the public for some time,” Nicky noted. “Unfortunately, the government appears to have lacked focus, allowing the crisis to drag on without a dedicated response, firm law enforcement or an evaluation of the officials responsible.”

Rifki Dermawan, a lecturer in international relations at Andalas University, also noted that Wednesday’s rally was far from the first attempt to pressure the government over the fires. Criticism had also flooded social media, while Malaysian civil society groups had raised concerns at Indonesia’s embassy in Kuala Lumpur, he said.

“Unfortunately, no meaningful action has been taken,” Rifki said, adding that preventing the fires from recurring would require systemic change.

Whether the protests could translate into policy changes would depend partly on the authorities’ handling of the demonstrations, said Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political analyst at Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency.

He warned that a crackdown on protesters could lead to further backlash, referring to the death in August last year of a 21-year-old motorcycle taxi driver who was killed after an armoured police vehicle ran him over during a demonstration in Jakarta, triggering outrage and demands for police accountability.

Wasisto said another incident like that “would lead to broader political liability for Prabowo”.

He also argued that if public anger were to escalate into riots, it could “trigger negative sentiment among economic actors, which could lead to real policy changes”.

On top of the domestic outcry, Prabowo’s government is also facing pressure from neighbouring countries affected by the haze, amid criticism of Jakarta’s reluctance to seek further foreign firefighting assistance while insisting it could contain the fires itself.

On Tuesday, Indonesia and Singapore agreed to establish a joint task force to coordinate investigations into companies linked to forest and land fires. The initiative is intended to strengthen information sharing, financial intelligence and cross-border evidence gathering, with the possibility of recovering assets where appropriate.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said Singapore had offered to share data on companies linked to the fires, while Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said the two countries would coordinate their actions closely.

Wasisto described the task force as a “stepping stone” for both countries, particularly Indonesia, to address neighbouring countries’ concerns. But he said it was “still too early” to conclude that Jakarta’s approach had fundamentally changed, as the government’s commitment to follow-through remained uncertain.

“The protests may attract regional attention to Jakarta’s responses and, again, to Jakarta’s approach to regional cooperation, depending on whether national elites lower their nationalistic tone to achieve common ground,” he added.

Rifki said the agreement could “help ease tensions between Indonesia and Singapore”, particularly after Indonesia cut gas exports to the city state.

“However, it also indicates that current frameworks in Asean to deal with transboundary haze, such as the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, are not working effectively,” he said.

Fahrizal was sceptical that public pressure alone would change Prabowo’s position, given the emphasis on political, national and economic sovereignty within the ruling circle.

“This closed-off stance risks making regional cooperation more difficult,” he said, arguing that governments should open channels of communication to find common ground in tackling the haze.

The call for a stronger response to the haze comes amid reports of its severe health impact on the country. Indonesia’s Health Ministry has reported more than 333,000 cases of acute respiratory illness across seven affected provinces since mid-August.

Katherine Hasan, a researcher and analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, welcomed the students’ action.

“The escalating air pollution from blazing forest and land fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra, alongside chronic pollution across Java, must serve as a wake-up call for all,” she said.

Clean air was a fundamental human right and the government had a duty to protect it, she added. Through the student protests, “we have a crucial window and opportunity right now to put citizens’ rights and public health back at the top of the national agenda – without compromise”.

Additional reporting by Reuters

item.title: [SCMP] EU plans high-level China currency talks as fears of new trade shock mount
item.description:
After convincing China to accept a cap on its hybrid car exports, a stream of top-level European finance and banking officials will descend on the Chinese capital in the coming months on a far trickier mission: persuading Beijing to stop holding down its currency to help save the bloc’s struggling industry.

In the week of November 23, top European Union economy officials led by director general Maarten Verwey will sit down in Beijing for a “macroeconomic dialogue” with their Chinese counterparts.

Plans are in the works, meanwhile, for a heavyweight trio – from the European Central Bank, Eurogroup and European Commission – to follow them there around the turn of the year, though no final date has been set, according to multiple people familiar with the planning.
item.content:encoded:
After convincing China to accept a cap on its hybrid car exports, a stream of top-level European finance and banking officials will descend on the Chinese capital in the coming months on a far trickier mission: persuading Beijing to stop holding down its currency to help save the bloc’s struggling industry.

In the week of November 23, top European Union economy officials led by director general Maarten Verwey will sit down in Beijing for a “macroeconomic dialogue” with their Chinese counterparts.

Plans are in the works, meanwhile, for a heavyweight trio – from the European Central Bank, Eurogroup and European Commission – to follow them there around the turn of the year, though no final date has been set, according to multiple people familiar with the planning.

This would be the first formal meeting in over a decade for a revived format with People’s Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng and Finance Minister Lan Foan. The talks were kick-started on the margins of global financial meetings in Bangkok earlier this month.

The European delegation – comprising the three institutions responsible for managing the euro zone’s monetary policy and coordinating its economic policies – will likely be led by ECB President Christine Lagarde, along with EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis and Kyriakos Pierrakakis, president of the Eurogroup, a coalition of euro-using EU members.

It comes amid frenzied political interest in Europe about the perceived undervaluation of the Chinese yuan, which EU leaders say is making the country’s products cheaper for European buyers, contributing heavily to what is now commonly described as a “China shock 2.0” to European industry.

The Chinese currency is not freely floated, meaning its value is not entirely determined by market forces. For decades, this has led trading partners to suspect it is undervalued in order to boost the country’s exports, a vital engine for economic growth.

Estimates on the currency’s comparative valuation vary wildly. The International Monetary Fund suggested this year that it could be up to 21 per cent undervalued, while researchers at the Centre for European Reform put that figure at closer to 30 per cent.

Research by Chinese think tank CF40 also suggests the yuan has considerable room to strengthen in the coming years, based on its analysis of Chinese and American prices.

BusinessEurope, Brussels’ umbrella corporate lobby group, said last week that China “actively restrains the appreciation of the renminbi that a surplus of this size would normally trigger, keeping exports artificially competitive”. This factor “compounds direct state support”, the chamber said.

But both publicly and behind closed doors, Beijing has pushed back, pointing to official data showing that the yuan has strengthened by almost 10 per cent against the euro in 2026.

“Global imbalances cannot be resolved through exchange rate adjustments,” Pan said in an official PBOC account of the October 16 meeting, insisting there was “no straightforward relationship between exchange rate and current account”.

While the yuan has made gains in 2026, “any appreciation has really vanished in real terms” due to flat inflation and years of falling producer prices in China, which have run counter to rising prices elsewhere in the world, said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief Asia-Pacific economist at French bank Natixis.

Pan and Lan came to Bangkok extremely well-prepared, according to people familiar with the discussions. The PBOC governor is well-liked in EU circles and seen as a pragmatic operator. In recent weeks, he has met a flurry of senior European officials, including governors of the central banks of France and Sweden, as well as Emmanuel Bonne, French President Emmanuel Macron’s diplomatic adviser.

Nonetheless, in Bangkok Pan politely drew on a long paper published a week earlier by the PBOC that said the Chinese central bank did not agree with analysis that the yuan was manipulated to boost exports.

“China has no need or intent to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation,” said the paper, published on October 8.

The European side, meanwhile, broached the topic carefully, lest it appeared that they were ganging up on China along with the United States. The delicate issue was couched in the diplomatic language of “global imbalances”, with acknowledgement that China’s underconsumption was an issue when placed alongside European underinvestment and American overspend.

There was an effort not to appear confrontational – instead officials highlighted how the parties could work together to address these imbalances, with currency being one area to tackle. Ideally, the Europeans would like a glimpse of Beijing’s internal financial numbers to make fresh assessments on the yuan, even if that is seen as unlikely.

The dialogue “is aimed at enabling discussions on all relevant economic policies in a holistic manner, including global imbalances and their deep causes and the need for an orderly rebalancing in the interest of both sides and the global economy”, an ECB spokesperson said.

The Bangkok talks, then, did not achieve a breakthrough, but were seen as the gateway to technical discussions on the topic, in which technocrats will engage on the numbers, rather than getting bogged down in political bickering.

In Europe, however, the issue has boiled over into messy, mainstream political discourse. German media reports suggest that Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s dramatic pivot on China policy this month came directly from research linking an undervalued yuan to his country’s industry woes.

“Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response,” Merz said at an event in Berlin last week.

In June, he pointed to the Plaza Accord as a model for today’s issues with manipulated currencies, referring to a 1985 pact that saw the US pressure Japan into accepting a sharp rise in the yen to curb its trade surplus.

Merz’s comments were anathema to Beijing’s official organs. In China, the accord is popularly seen to have crippled Japan’s export prowess, contributing to decades of perceived economic stagnation.

“China will not accept using exchange rates as a pretext for oppression, nor will it return to the old era of great powers coordinating the fate of a few countries. Today’s China is not the Japan of the past,” fumed Global Times, a tabloid under the official mouthpiece People’s Daily, in the days after Merz spoke.

European analysts believe, however, that allowing the yuan to strengthen would be a salve to Europe’s struggling manufacturing heartlands and help avert a potential broader trade war.

“If it’s a sizeable revaluation, of course it will [move the needle],” said Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform and co-author of a paper that reportedly helped convince Merz of the need to change tack on China.

“Most models would suggest that a 10 per cent real effective exchange rate change shifts real net exports by 1.5 per cent of GDP on average,” he said.

“Beijing faces a real choice here: either revalue the currency to lower pressure from trading partners ranging from the EU to India or accept that said partners will ratchet up the trade ramparts.”

Garcia-Herrero from Natixis said expectations were being managed as to how much ground Beijing would give on this front, since “Chinese companies’ profits are small” and an appreciation “would only reduce them further”.

The economist suspects that for China, currency talks with Europe may have a different objective. The country is on a drive to globalise its currency and the buy-in of the EU would be a big help.

“I think renminbi internationalisation is also very important, and I do think China wants some support,” Garcia-Herrero said. “I think they want to exchange with the Europeans on a multipolar world of currencies.”

But she doubted whether Europe alone could convince Beijing to change course on currency intervention, saying such a mission would be “doomed” without US support. “This not something we can achieve without the dollar.”

item.title: [SCMP] The West’s double standard on global unrest
item.description:
In the early days of the student protests in France, mainstream Western media took the protesters’ claims about poor school facilities and declining resources at face value. Only when the violence spread across the country, and to some of its European neighbours, did people begin to ask whether deeper causes were at play.

Leftists blame social problems, from the cost-of-living pressures linked to the war in Ukraine to rising unemployment, especially among the young. Right-wing critics blame Islamists, antifascists, radical environmentalists and, of course, immigrants.

A Financial Times report said: “EU regulators are examining possible foreign interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and outbursts of violence and looting in other European countries. According to security officials, pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos. Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, experts said.”
item.content:encoded:
In the early days of the student protests in France, mainstream Western media took the protesters’ claims about poor school facilities and declining resources at face value. Only when the violence spread across the country, and to some of its European neighbours, did people begin to ask whether deeper causes were at play.

Leftists blame social problems, from the cost-of-living pressures linked to the war in Ukraine to rising unemployment, especially among the young. Right-wing critics blame Islamists, antifascists, radical environmentalists and, of course, immigrants.

A Financial Times report said: “EU regulators are examining possible foreign interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and outbursts of violence and looting in other European countries. According to security officials, pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos. Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, experts said.”

As I follow the unrest unfolding in Europe, I find it uncanny how closely it parallels the 2019 anti-government riots in Hong Kong. Such mass disturbances almost always have many causes, including underlying social malaise and long-standing grievances. There is no single causal factor, only, perhaps, a single trigger.

In Hong Kong, the trigger was a proposed extradition bill. The protests then broadened into demands for immediate democratic transition. I, and many others, have extensively documented foreign government and semi-government involvement. The players included the US Congress, the US National Endowment for Democracy, the National Democratic Institute for International Affairs, the US Agency for Global Media and the Open Technology Fund.

In fact, we didn’t have to dig much. They were rather proud of their handiwork, with some testifying in Congress that they could not continue because of funding cuts by the first Trump administration.

To this day, many Western media outlets still claim it was all a fight for democracy, later suppressed by the national security law.

I don’t deny that democratic demands played a significant role in the 2019 riots. But they were not the sole or even the underlying cause, just as poor facilities alone cannot explain the social breakdown we are witnessing in France, even though they first led high school students into the streets.

Yet mainstream Western media instinctively reach for mono-causal explanations, usually a struggle for democracy, however they define it, when mass unrest breaks out in non-Western countries. Only when similar breakdowns happen in allied or friendly countries do they allow for nuance and deeper social analysis.

One reason is, of course, simple ignorance of those other societies. “Democracy” is the one-size-fits-all explanation when you need to write a column about an unfriendly country you know nothing about.

I recently watched an amusing French TV news programme in which the moderator asked professional pundits to name two other living Chinese persons besides Xi Jinping, and they all had difficulty doing so. It was reminiscent of George W. Bush, while running for president, being embarrassingly unable to identify foreign leaders.

Ukraine was similar to Hong Kong in this respect. The so-called Maidan revolution of 2014 is seen in the West, especially now, as a democratic revolution. Never mind that the governments that followed were as corrupt as the pro-Moscow one before. The rest of the world mostly sees it as a coup, or is at least neutral about it.

At the very least, it triggered the Russian aggression that has continued ever since. Many Ukrainians may now be rethinking the wisdom of poking the bear and – for heaven’s sake – of trying to join Nato.

A recorded telephone conversation between Victoria Nuland, then US assistant secretary of state, and Geoffrey Pyatt, then US ambassador to Ukraine, was leaked in February 2014. They discussed political strategy, which leaders to support and the composition of a post-Yanukovych government amid the Euromaidan protests. In the leak, she famously said, “F*** the EU”, signalling a readiness to act unilaterally.

Indeed, American scholars such as John Mearsheimer and Jeffrey Sachs have argued that the 2014 uprising was a coup. Of course, everyone knows there were many causes. But everyone has an ideological axe to grind.

I, for one, would argue that the world would be more peaceful today without the 2014 coup. But to each their own.

While ignorance and strategic opportunism helped explain how social unrest is portrayed differently in mainstream Western media, the biggest motivation is probably ideological.

What happened to Hong Kong now seems almost comical, though quite tragic for the Hongkongers who left

Between 2010 and 2020, data-tracking projects recorded nearly 7,000 protests across 153 countries, at least 900 of them major, each involving more than 10,000 participants.

Naturally, Western pundits and politicians, especially those in Washington, would focus on those affecting antagonistic China and Russia. Exploiting internal opposition and unrest in unfriendly countries has long been Washington’s default playbook, followed sometimes, but not always, by its Western counterparts.

But it is short-sighted. An unstable Hong Kong or China would be terrible for the world economy and, by extension, for the US. A successor state to the current Putin regime – should it collapse from losing the war in Ukraine – would probably be neither pro-Western nor democratic, but even more bent on revanchism.

What happened to Hong Kong now seems almost comical, though quite tragic for the Hongkongers who left. Several Western governments bought into their own propaganda and, from 2020, offered them exits, as if they were fleeing persecution like Ukrainians and Yemenis. Many have had difficulty adjusting to their new lives; some have returned to Hong Kong.

Those same Western countries are now beset by anti-migrant populism, resulting in a brutal migrant crackdown, as in the US, or the rollback of easy access in the migrant application process, as in Canada and Australia.

Meanwhile, some Hong Kong and mainland officials remain under US sanctions. Perhaps Beijing should sanction some top officials in Washington and Paris for their own brutal domestic police and military crackdowns.

Of course, China has never been so petty and ridiculous.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s humanoid robots hunt for work in South Korea as Seoul bets on physical AI
item.description:
This article was first published by The Korea Times in a partnership with the South China Morning Post.

Chinese humanoid robot makers are accelerating efforts to gain a foothold in South Korea, moving beyond dance performances and showroom displays to factory trials and commercial deployments, as Seoul ramps up investment in physical artificial intelligence.

A growing number of Chinese robotics companies – including Hong Kong-listed UBTech Robotics, start-up Anyverse Dynamics, Shanghai-based AgiBot and leading robot maker Unitree Robotics – have flexed their muscles or announced projects in South Korea this year.
item.content:encoded:
This article was first published by The Korea Times in a partnership with the South China Morning Post.

Chinese humanoid robot makers are accelerating efforts to gain a foothold in South Korea, moving beyond dance performances and showroom displays to factory trials and commercial deployments, as Seoul ramps up investment in physical artificial intelligence.

A growing number of Chinese robotics companies – including Hong Kong-listed UBTech Robotics, start-up Anyverse Dynamics, Shanghai-based AgiBot and leading robot maker Unitree Robotics – have flexed their muscles or announced projects in South Korea this year.

“China’s new generation of robot companies has global DNA and naturally looks overseas, and South Korea is one of the most important markets in the Asia-Pacific region,” said Ethan Qi, an associate director covering robotics at Counterpoint Research. The lack of locally built humanoid robots available at scale had created an opening for Chinese suppliers, he added.

Commercial foothold

Representatives of Galaxy Robot Park, a robot-themed entertainment venue in Seoul, agreed to buy UBTech’s lifelike U1 model after seeing its debut in Shenzhen in June, according to Sean Qin, overseas head of the company’s commercial robots division.

The robot, designed with a female appearance and standing 1.68 metres tall, cost around 170,000 yuan (US$25,000) and was delivered to the park last month, Qin said. UBTech entered the South Korean market as early as 2019 and had since sold more than 10,000 robots to dozens of corporate and government customers, he added.

In July, UBTech, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, also announced plans to trial humanoid robots on a South Korean automotive parts production line with local partner Duksan JM Robotics and parts maker Ajin Industrial. Several UBTech models were undergoing on-site operational tests in the country, Qin said, without providing details.

“As a manufacturing powerhouse, South Korea already makes extensive use of robotic arms, autonomous mobile robots and other conventional systems,” he said. “The next step is to help workers become more productive in tasks that demand greater flexibility. That makes Korea a key market for UBTech and for humanoids more broadly.”

Zhang Yufeng, founder and CEO of Anyverse Dynamics, who previously worked with SK Telecom and Hyundai Motor, said South Korea was “one of our most important overseas markets”.

The Beijing-based start-up teamed up with South Korean coffee chain Hollys at the World Robot Conference in Beijing in August to test robots that serve drinks, clear tables and reset seats. The robots were currently undergoing trial operations at a cafe in Beijing, Zhang said.

South Korea ranked as China’s third-largest export market by value for “intelligent bionic robots” in the first nine months of 2026, behind the United States and Japan, according to Chinese customs data. Exports to South Korea totalled US$19.99 million, or 9.7 per cent of the US$206.95 million China shipped globally. China exported 16,559 robots to 108 countries and regions under the customs category, introduced this year, which covers humanoids and robot dogs.

Eight of China’s 10 top-selling humanoid robot makers had been testing the waters in South Korea through product certification, trademark filings and sales channels, according to a report by industry research platform Labsdeep that was cited by Electronic Times this month.

“We plan to begin trials in Korean cafes and other commercial service settings in the fourth quarter, before expanding into manufacturing,” Zhang said, noting that the company had been working on product certification for the market.

Seoul’s stringent Korea Certification requirements prompted UBTech to adapt its communications modules and radio frequency settings for local use, Qin said.

Factories as main testing ground

China’s robotics boom has spawned a wave of unicorn firms over the past two years, some of which have already begun shipping products at scale, backed by an extensive supply chain at home. Their push to find commercial applications to justify the investment and hype surrounding humanoid robots coincides with South Korea’s drive to deploy physical AI across its industrial base.

Seoul is prioritising the technology to strengthen manufacturing as its working-age population shrinks and potential economic growth slows. The government has proposed 3.1 trillion won (US$2.3 billion) in physical AI funding for 2027, more than triple this year’s level.

The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources’ Manufacturing AI Transformation programme, dubbed M.AX, supports AI adoption and factory trials involving robots, including humanoids, with a target of 500 AI factories by 2030. The ministry has budgeted 1.1 trillion won for AI transformation this year.

Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said in August that the government would support factories operated by AI and robots, helping South Korea become “a global leader in manufacturing AI transformation by 2030”.

South Korea’s industrial heavyweights are also moving quickly.

LG Electronics is building its Data Factory in Seoul to train robots for industrial and household applications, while testing robots on its own production lines. Samsung Electronics established its Robotics eXperience division in July, targeting manufacturing before expanding into homes and retail. A bipedal robot designed to operate round the clock in manufacturing and logistics could debut at the CES annual consumer electronics trade show in Las Vegas in January 2027, JoongAng Ilbo reported on Tuesday.

Hyundai Motor Group has begun training Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoids at its factory campus in the US state of Georgia, ahead of a planned 2028 deployment in manufacturing. Doosan Robotics has unveiled AI-powered sanding and palletising systems and is developing robot-control software, with support from Nvidia.

South Korea’s start-up ecosystem is also drawing fresh capital. AI and robotics accounted for 45 per cent of third-quarter investments tracked by The VC, a local start-up and venture capital investment database platform. Within physical AI, funding is flowing to robot makers as well as start-ups developing foundational models for robots and supplying training data.

The country offered a broad range of potential deployment sites in carmaking, shipbuilding and semiconductor manufacturing, Counterpoint’s Qi said. But gaining access was difficult for Chinese suppliers because they needed local customers willing to participate in proof-of-concept trials.

Partners and rivals

The growing presence of Chinese firms has stirred political debate. At a parliamentary audit on October 6, lawmaker Lee Jeong-heon of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea brought robots from China’s Unitree and AgiBot to challenge the government over South Korea’s competitiveness in physical AI.

Lawmaker Ahn Cheol-soo of the main opposition People Power Party questioned whether the robots had undergone security checks and accused the National Assembly of providing a stage for Chinese technology.

Deputy Prime Minister Bae Kyung-hoon, who is also the Science and Information and Communications Technology minister, urged South Korea to ramp up physical AI investment and development, pointing to China’s growing deployment of humanoids.

“China is also deploying more humanoid robots in the field and collecting data,” he said during a Physical AI Tech Week round table in Seoul on October 13, according to news outlet MoneyToday.

Bae questioned whether Korea’s plans were bold enough and called for higher targets to avoid regretting insufficient investment in the future. Companies also needed to shoulder greater responsibility because the government could not support every initiative, he said.

Park Young-hoon, head of the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency’s Shenzhen office, said he also saw room for cooperation.

“Companies need to explore new business opportunities using Shenzhen’s local supply chains and innovation capabilities while competing with Chinese technology companies,” he told local media outlet Newspim in October.

Anyverse Dynamics’ Zhang said he saw the two countries’ industrial strengths as “highly complementary”. South Korea combined global leadership in advanced manufacturing with a capacity for AI innovation, while China offered a comprehensive supply chain, a deep pool of engineering and AI talent, and rapid product iteration, he said.

For UBTech’s Qin, policies favouring domestic companies have not deterred Korean customers from considering Chinese suppliers. “The Korean customers we have dealt with are open to working with Chinese robot makers,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s private firms are fighting for profits. Are regulations adding to the burden?
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the second part of this series, Emma Ma speaks to businesspeople as they adapt to stepped up regulatory enforcement and deal with other economic issues the government has pledged to solve.

Six years after China Evergrande Group started to show signs of insolvency – the beginning of a downward spiral that would eventually lead to the property developer’s bankruptcy and its founder sentenced to life in prison – Zhu Yinfen is still waiting to recover money the company owes to her Shanghai firm.

“Evergrande still owes us 500,000 yuan (US$74,885),” Zhu said, adding that the worst problem was not the unpaid debt, but the many other clients who routinely failed to settle their bills on time.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the second part of this series, Emma Ma speaks to businesspeople as they adapt to stepped up regulatory enforcement and deal with other economic issues the government has pledged to solve.

Six years after China Evergrande Group started to show signs of insolvency – the beginning of a downward spiral that would eventually lead to the property developer’s bankruptcy and its founder sentenced to life in prison – Zhu Yinfen is still waiting to recover money the company owes to her Shanghai firm.

“Evergrande still owes us 500,000 yuan (US$74,885),” Zhu said, adding that the worst problem was not the unpaid debt, but the many other clients who routinely failed to settle their bills on time.

“I was quite anxious at first, but I’ve grown accustomed to it. Payment delays are rampant in the construction sector,” said Zhu, whose company supplies water-purification equipment for construction projects.

While government data shows China’s private sector accounts for about 80 per cent of urban employment and 90 per cent of new jobs, its performance has become increasingly uneven.

Though emerging industries such as technology and advanced manufacturing benefit from government support and attract investment, firms in traditional industries, including construction and manufacturing, have borne the brunt of an economic slowdown.

Delayed payments rank among the biggest concerns of Chinese entrepreneurs. At the same time, compliance costs are rising rapidly as tax authorities step up enforcement of rules and scrutinise the collection of social insurance premiums.

Some local governments simply cite audits as excuses. We have a project in a small city ... payments for it have been held up for a decade

Wang Xianhui, Shanghai

“Dented by weaker profit expectations and faltering investment confidence, private‑sector enterprises have stepped up deleveraging,” wrote Zhang Xiaojing, a researcher at Beijing-based National Institution for Finance and Development, in a July note.

The government has not ignored these issues. President Xi Jinping personally pledged to address arrears owed to private companies in a high-profile address to the country’s leading entrepreneurs in February 2025.

The central government has since rolled out measures designed to help businesses weather the storm. But some businesspeople said that while the policies appeared promising in theory, they remained challenging in practice.

Now, attention is turning to the fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s Central Committee, to be held from Monday to Wednesday. The committee will focus on “strictly governing the party,” including measures to enforce party discipline and combat corruption.

Xi has repeatedly said such efforts are needed to ensure Beijing’s policies, including those intended to benefit the private sector, are properly implemented.

Payment delays evolve

Wang Xianhui runs a medium-sized firm on the outskirts of Shanghai. It mainly works with local governments and major state-owned construction enterprises.

According to him, a 12‑month payment cycle is considered normal for the sector, yet delays stretching beyond that time frame can also occur. Before 2020, he said, receipt of payments typically took only three to six months.

“Some local governments simply cite audits as excuses. We have a project in a small city in [central China’s] Hubei province, and payments for it have been held up for a decade,” Wang added.

With the property market yet to recover from a prolonged slowdown catalysed by Evergrande’s default, the construction sector remains the epicentre of overdue payments. In the years since the slump, the problem has only evolved, industry insiders said.

Over the past two years, Zhu said she has watched the situation shift from payment delays to debt settlement via unsold flats.

“One of my clients is a major Shanghai-based developer. Starting in 2024, they began settling out contract obligations with unsold apartments in the suburban areas,” Zhu said.

She added that the properties were part of the developer’s unsold inventory, and the firm offset her construction payment at the original sales price – far higher than current market rates.

“Housing prices have kept falling over recent years. Local authorities set pricing for new apartments, and it is common for new-home prices to stand well above resale values – a 10 per cent to 20 per cent premium is typical in Shanghai,” Zhu said.

That means if Zhu took ownership of these flats and tried to sell them, she would incur losses. On top of that, her firm would also be required to cover transaction-related taxes.

“And it is not a choice between cash or property – it is either accept the apartment, or keep waiting,” she said. “It’s not limited to just one developer.”

According to China’s National Bureau of Statistics, total accounts receivable of China’s industrial enterprises above a designated size hit 29.48 trillion yuan (US$3.9 trillion) by the end of August, up 9 per cent year on year and outpacing the 6.6 per cent growth in revenue.

To address the issue, Beijing has reiterated that state-owned enterprises (SOEs) must settle payments in cash. At a mid-September press conference, an official with the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission said cash payments to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) “must be enforced as a hard rule”.

The government has also set up a website where SMEs can report delayed payments. Still, some private business owners said that while the initiative was well-intentioned, it lacked practical effectiveness.

“I can sense the government’s resolve to fix these issues through the website. But we would only file a complaint there if we no longer wanted to do business with those SOEs,” Wang said.

“Besides, our firm is a lower-tier contractor. That means even if we chose to submit a complaint via the website, we lack many key contracts and supporting documentation. The reality is far too complicated.”

Problems with delayed payments are not unique to China, however. In Europe, business-to-business transactions generally face a 60-day deadline for fulfilment. Late payments carry statutory interest set at least 8 percentage points above the European Central Bank’s reference rate.

Zhang Lin, deputy director at the research centre of Shanghai-based Far East Credit Rating, wrote in a May column for financial media outlet Caixin that Beijing could draw on Europe’s measures to impose tangible financial costs for payment delays.

“What awaits settlement is not merely individual invoices, but better liquidity and stronger confidence across the economy,” he said.

I’ve heard of several larger firms getting calls from the tax authorities recently

Richard Zhu, Shanghai

Paying in full

This summer, Shanghai entrepreneur Richard Zhu began ensuring full social security payments are made for his employees, a process he jokingly described as “window dressing”. He heads a medical-device contract manufacturer generating 20 million yuan in annual revenue.

Previously, his company had been remitting most social security contributions at the statutory minimum – more than 7,500 yuan a month for Shanghai as of this year – even though over half of his staff earned higher salaries.

At his firm, he said, workers in their 20s were willing to accept lower insurance premiums to boost their take-home cash. For his older, core employees, he has always made full social security contributions, he added, as they were mature enough to understand the value of social security benefits.

The informal practice is widespread among China’s SMEs as they deal with heavy operational burdens.

Combined employer and employee social insurance contributions in China can reach as high as 38 per cent of an individual’s wage, a higher share than in some developed economies, including the US at 15.3 per cent and Japan at 30 per cent.

Social security premiums have emerged as a significant source of public revenue. According to figures from the Ministry of Finance, national social insurance premiums hit 9.12 trillion yuan in value in 2025, outstripping the 6.89 trillion yuan in proceeds from value-added tax.

“I’ve heard of several larger firms getting calls from the tax authorities recently. Officials flagged mismatches between their social-security contribution bases and actual payroll, ordering them to get their social-security contributions into line with regulations,” Richard Zhu said.

Even though he has not received any notification from the local tax authority, he said he proceeded with the adjustments as a precautionary step – though he remains worried that non-compliance might derail his company’s partnerships with large pharmaceutical firms.

A professor with close ties to the State Taxation Administration, who requested anonymity over the sensitivity of the matter, said that enforcement has ramped up this year, and that provincial governments have established specific performance targets stipulating what proportion of local enterprises should achieve social security compliance.

After the change – made without reducing the pay of younger staff members to compensate – the combined outlay for social security contributions and the mandatory housing fund at Richard Zhu’s firm has surged to nearly 40 per cent of the expanding wage base, eating into the company’s profit margin.

He and others in the private sector are asking a similar question: why step up enforcement of premium collection when the economy is losing momentum?

“As China’s population is ageing at an accelerating pace, rigid expenditure pressures on the pension fund have risen steeply,” said Tony Peng, an independent researcher who has studied the domestic social security system for more than 10 years. “The domestic pension fund is confronted with heightened real-world pressures to balance its current-year revenues and outlays.”

Those pressures compound as local governments’ fiscal positions grow strained with less revenue from land sales, he added. In the past, fiscal resources have served as a backstop for social insurance accounts whenever premium collections came up short.

The fallout

Peng said he believed tightening enforcement was still the correct policy direction. However, he added, “with weak domestic demand and extremely thin profit margins among private firms, a tighter enforcement ramp‑up would exacerbate their difficulties and could trigger wage cuts or lay-offs.”

The repercussions already appear to be manifesting in the job market, insiders said.

Confronted with narrowing profit margins, Richard Zhu opted for the simplest solution – scaling back new hiring. This summer, he slashed his recruitment quota, dropping from eight positions for engineers and office-based staff to two.

Research from 2025 by Ye Jingjing, a professor at Zhongnan University of Economics and Law in Hubei province, found that heavier social security contributions led to a decline in new job postings.

Beginning in 2019, China’s tax authorities took over collection of social insurance premiums, an institutional shift that triggered an earlier round of tighter regulatory enforcement.

Ye’s research showed that average new job listings on one major domestic online recruitment platform dropped by 7.2 per cent in the post-2019 period relative to the 2017-19 baseline. At the same time, total social security contributions from surveyed companies climbed by 16.22 per cent.

“Conditions differ from one firm to another. Labour-intensive enterprises that carry relatively high wage-to-cost ratios are more vulnerable to changes in the social security contribution base,” Ye said.

Peng, the independent researcher, suggested that authorities carefully consider the pace of implementation and design of transitional arrangements.

He proposed that local governments provide rebates or interest subsidies for those firms that remit full social-security contributions and have avoided staff lay-offs. This kind of “targeted compensatory support” would help incentivise some enterprises to abide by the law more willingly, he said.

Richard Zhu, meanwhile, said he was choosing to stay positive.

“Having spent 23 years in this business, I’ve learned it’s all about cycles. There have been ups and downs. Perhaps in another five years, all these problems will be absorbed during an economic upturn.”

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Incisive’ final report on Tai Po blaze singles out 4 government bodies
item.description:
An independent committee investigating Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades has submitted its findings to the government, with a source saying the “incisive” report has singled out four government bodies for accountability.

It is understood that the 12-chapter report found that among the four government bodies named, the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit should bear the greatest responsibility for a lack of oversight of renovation work at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate, which contributed to the heavy death toll from the inferno.

But the insider said on Thursday that the report did not name any bureau secretaries in connection with the blaze that broke out at the Tai Po estate on November 26 last year, killing 168 people.
item.content:encoded:
An independent committee investigating Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades has submitted its findings to the government, with a source saying the “incisive” report has singled out four government bodies for accountability.

It is understood that the 12-chapter report found that among the four government bodies named, the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit should bear the greatest responsibility for a lack of oversight of renovation work at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate, which contributed to the heavy death toll from the inferno.

But the insider said on Thursday that the report did not name any bureau secretaries in connection with the blaze that broke out at the Tai Po estate on November 26 last year, killing 168 people.

The judge-led panel submitted its final report to Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu after holding 30 public sessions and hearing from 80 witnesses, including residents, firefighters, government officials and experts.

“With the evidence and materials received as the factual framework, the committee has completed its inquiry work on the matters set out in its terms of reference, and prepared the report accordingly,” the committee said.

The panel, ordered by Lee, ceased operating following the submission of the report, its website showed.

Lee thanked the committee members for their efforts, saying the panel had provided a comprehensive review of the causes of the fire and recommendations on large-scale building maintenance and renovation projects.

“The government will make comprehensive reforms in areas including the supervision of building maintenance works, building management and the regulation of fire service installations,” he said.

“We will carefully study the committee’s report, actively follow up on its recommendations and shortly announce plans for comprehensive reforms and pursuing accountability.”

The government said it would seek legal advice on how best to publish the report at the “earliest possible juncture” without prejudicing court proceedings. Charges have been laid against seven individuals and two companies for their alleged roles in the tragedy.

A redacted version of the report could be made public next week at the earliest.

The source told the South China Morning Post that the report contained 12 chapters detailing the committee’s findings on the causes of the fire.

He described the report as “incisive”, refuting speculation the tone was mild, but without providing additional details.

The report singled out four government bodies for accountability – the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department, the Labour Department and the Independent Checking Unit – as well as some civil servants named during the hearings, the insider said.

The Labour Department was deemed to carry a smaller share of responsibility for failing to act promptly on residents’ complaints about workers smoking at the site.

The source added that the report also included recommendations on construction material standards and measures to combat bid-rigging.

The blaze engulfed seven of the estate’s eight blocks and became Hong Kong’s deadliest fire since 1948.

The committee’s lead counsel, Victor Dawes, identified six “human failures” that led to the tragedy. These included the use of non-fire-retardant scaffolding mesh, the widespread installation of combustible polyfoam boards over windows, the deactivation of the fire alarm system and the suspension of the fire hosepipe reel system.

The other failures involved temporary openings in emergency staircases, where fire-rated windows had been replaced with movable boards, and workers’ smoking habits.

At the final hearing, the committee’s legal team presented a 627-page closing statement, blaming the “litany of failures” for the disaster.

The statement said the government bore “unshirkable responsibility” for the tragedy and singled out the four government bodies.

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said it was premature to pre-empt the government’s response as the report had not yet been made public.

However, he called on the administration to gauge public sentiment before taking any follow-up actions, adding that he expected Beijing and the government would act to strengthen support for the revamped political system under the “patriots administering Hong Kong” principle.

“I believe the central government and the chief executive will consider the matter from the perspectives of the government’s credibility, governance effectiveness, political stability and the unity of the governing team,” Lau said.

“It has to assure the public that the government is accountable and handles the matter in a fair and impartial manner.”

Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing said the public expected not only civil servants but also ministers to be held accountable. But he noted that with a government transition next July, the administration might decide against a cabinet reshuffle so close to the end of its term.

Lo also suggested that the government publish a report outlining its reform measures to deepen public understanding of its follow-up actions.

The committee counsel’s closing remarks criticised the Fire Services Department for failing to detect that the fire alarm system had been deactivated at the estate and for avoiding its statutory duties.

Following the blaze, the department stepped up inspections of fire services installations and put forward legislative proposals to strengthen regulation of such equipment.

During a check of 1,500 old buildings across Hong Kong, the department found 64 of them had not carried out annual inspections, with malfunctioning fire alarm systems found in 13.

The department extended the checks in April, aiming to inspect 5,000 blocks in two years.

Among its legislative recommendations, the department has proposed amending the Fire Services Ordinance so contractors and technicians would be legally required to obtain prior approval before shutting down fire safety equipment.

Lawmaker Peter Shiu Ka-fai, chairman of the Legislative Council’s security panel, declined to comment on the accountability of the department, arguing that the full picture would only be available after the report was released.

He expressed confidence in the department for “discharging its duty with integrity”.

“The Wang Fuk Court fire was an occasion to remind us that some regulations will have to be updated,” he said. “Many lawmakers agreed that doing so would enhance public safety. I believe when these amendments are submitted for vetting, they will be passed.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will China travel hurt US students’ careers? FBI battles fears as talent pipeline stalls
item.description:
An American student considering studying in China attended a briefing with a senior FBI official at a Washington think tank last month to address her concerns about whether such an experience could jeopardise her prospects for a career in the federal government.

The official’s message: travelling to China would not automatically disqualify her.

She welcomed the clarification but said she wasn’t “completely reassured”.
item.content:encoded:
An American student considering studying in China attended a briefing with a senior FBI official at a Washington think tank last month to address her concerns about whether such an experience could jeopardise her prospects for a career in the federal government.

The official’s message: travelling to China would not automatically disqualify her.

She welcomed the clarification but said she wasn’t “completely reassured”.

“I’m still wondering if it’s a good idea to go,” said the student, who requested to remain anonymous because of the issue’s sensitivity.

Her hesitation illustrates a dilemma for Washington: the US needs more Americans with first-hand knowledge of China to navigate the growing US-China rivalry, but students and educators say fears about future security clearances are discouraging some young Americans from gaining that experience.
