She was among a group of students and professors who attended the special briefing with Joshua Obstfeld, a senior executive in the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, organised by the US-China Education Trust.

“Definitely do keep records of where you are going and what you are doing and who you are interacting with, so that you can then report it to us,” Obstfeld told his audience.

With Washington and Beijing locked in an increasingly securitised geopolitical competition, the US is struggling to maintain its China expertise and cultivate the next generation of specialists.

This is happening amid declining numbers of American students studying in the country, cuts to federal funding for related programmes and US efforts to sever research ties between universities in both countries.

“The United States is facing a genuine policy paradox,” said Denis Simon, a professor at Schwarzman College at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

He said the US wants “more Americans who understand China”, yet the “increasingly securitised atmosphere” could discourage “precisely the kinds of educational and professional experiences necessary to develop that expertise”.

“Students pick up on the geopolitical climate, and when they hear that time in China might count against them, many just don’t go,” said Rosie Levine, executive director of the US-China Education Trust, who moderated the discussion with the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) official.

“Many students now believe time in China could be treated as a liability rather than an asset.”

During the discussion with the students, Obstfeld stressed that the FBI expects prospective candidates with experience in China to be “open and honest” about their interactions while in the country.

“Are you a trustworthy person? Are you somebody that we can rely on and depend on as part of our mission to protect the American people?” he asked rhetorically.

The official said the FBI valued experience and expertise gained abroad but cautioned students to be mindful of personal and professional relationships that could expose them to foreign influence.

“Who do you have in your life that could influence you? And I’m not trying to suggest that any of this is fair,” he said. “That’s not really what this is about. This is about protecting national security.”

He also distinguished between developing contacts overseas and being approached to establish clandestine ties, urging students to report any such attempts.

“If anybody asks you to enter a covert relationship, those are the types of things that are definitely concerning to us. So report it.”

However, the student said she was not “convinced” that, if she decided to go to China, she would be “completely aware of what is going on” around her all of the time.

“The FBI couldn’t say you’ll definitely get a security clearance, and when you do go to China, you’re more at risk of meeting people who might lead you to have a greater chance of getting disqualified, and this could be totally out of your control,” she added.

The FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division did not respond to a request for comment.

Dennis Wilder, a former senior US intelligence official and a professor at Georgetown University, concurred that “American students are very worried” that “travel to China will either extend the security clearance process indefinitely or even make it impossible to get a clearance”.

“Such a perception is difficult to verify because there are many possible reasons why an individual is denied a clearance,” he said.

Wilder advised students to go to China only on “programmes sponsored by reputable US academic institutions where there are US citizens who can vouch for their activities” in the country.

“They should not, under any circumstances, take Chinese government or university funding,” he added.

Simon from Tsinghua University emphasised that “responsibility for managing national security risks should not be placed entirely on individual students”.

“The US government should provide clear, consistent and accessible guidance about what is expected of students before, during and after their visits to China,” he said.

Simon added that while the FBI’s advice was “fundamentally sensible” and students should be transparent about their activities, he would be concerned if such guidance “inadvertently creates the impression that travelling to China is inherently suspicious”.

“There is a danger that students will interpret the FBI’s guidance as suggesting that virtually every interaction with a Chinese academic, university official, government representative or business-person could eventually become a potential security problem,” he warned.

“We should not create a situation in which young Americans conclude that the safest career decision is to avoid China altogether.”

The number of American students studying long-term in China has fallen from about 11,000 in 2019 to fewer than 2,000 currently, according to research by the US-China Education Trust.

Conversely, more than 265,000 Chinese students enrolled in US universities during the 2024-25 academic year.

“Fewer Americans studying in China today means fewer people with the language skills, cultural fluency and on-the-ground understanding the United States will need to manage the relationship,” Levine said.

However, the situation has also been compounded by China’s pandemic-era visa restrictions, tighter controls on Western researchers and heightened risks of detention and arrests.

Last week, the US State Department added a “wrongful detention” warning to its travel advisory for China, alerting Americans to the risk of being detained arbitrarily under Chinese law.

“The [department] has determined that Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China,” the State Department told the SCMP.

US media reports linked the advisory to the detention in China of two US scholars, Chen Youlin and Min Zin, both of whom the US government has designated as wrongfully detained.

“China is creating this problem,” Wilder said.

“Heightened security concerns about studying or doing research in China are very real as the recent case of a US professor in Southwest China demonstrates,” Wilder added, citing Min Zin’s detention in June in the country’s Yunnan province.

The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that the country’s judiciary handles cases in accordance with the law.

During the discussion, the FBI official noted that while credible risks exist, most visits to China take place without incident.

“There are millions of people who go to China every year, every month, and everything, and nothing happens,” the FBI official said.

Beyond the sharp decline in student numbers, the Trump administration has halted or disrupted several federal programmes designed to help build China expertise.

The State Department’s Critical Language Scholarship experienced funding interruptions, while the National Resource Centres and Foreign Language and Area Studies Fellowships, which provided millions of dollars in grants, tuition help and stipends to university students nationwide, lost federal funding.

Washington is also accelerating efforts to sever academic ties with Beijing, with growing scrutiny of research partnerships between universities in the two countries.

The Pentagon’s push for greater oversight has resulted in more than 80 termination-related actions at 30 American colleges, prompting some institutions to scale back collaboration with Chinese counterparts.

Simon argued that “academic suspicion” is hurting the professional networks that make international research productive.

“The United States risks weakening its own scientific competitiveness,” he said, stressing that collaboration benefits both countries.

“The decline in educational engagement could create a dangerous knowledge gap in Washington,” he warned, noting that the strategic rivalry made deeper expertise essential.

“Yet we risk producing a generation of American policymakers who know more about China as a strategic adversary than as a country.”

item.title: [SCMP] 5 things to watch out for in 2027 US defence bill aimed at countering China
item.description:
The 2027 US defence bill, covering more than US$1 trillion in proposed defence spending, will be one of the most closely watched pieces of legislation when Congress returns after the midterm elections, with efforts to counter China running through nearly every corner of the text.

The US House of Representatives passed its version of the bill, known as the National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA), in July. The bill faces a tougher path in the US Senate, where a July procedural vote to begin consideration failed after Democrats objected to US President Donald Trump’s military actions involving Iran.

Whatever happens to the bill, competition with China looms large across the legislation. Provisions targeting “foreign adversaries” and “entities of concern” would curb Pentagon purchases of Chinese-made technology and materials, while restricting the use of defence funds to buy certain used foreign-built vessels.
item.content:encoded:
The 2027 US defence bill, covering more than US$1 trillion in proposed defence spending, will be one of the most closely watched pieces of legislation when Congress returns after the midterm elections, with efforts to counter China running through nearly every corner of the text.

The US House of Representatives passed its version of the bill, known as the National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA), in July. The bill faces a tougher path in the US Senate, where a July procedural vote to begin consideration failed after Democrats objected to US President Donald Trump’s military actions involving Iran.

Whatever happens to the bill, competition with China looms large across the legislation. Provisions targeting “foreign adversaries” and “entities of concern” would curb Pentagon purchases of Chinese-made technology and materials, while restricting the use of defence funds to buy certain used foreign-built vessels.

Other measures would bolster Taiwan’s defences and expand security cooperation with US allies along the first island chain, require a strategy for responding to crises in the South China Sea, and increase scrutiny of AI chips and sensitive research-related information.

The measures could shape the Indo-Pacific security balance and US-China relations well into next year.

Lawmakers must pass the bill before the US Congress adjourns at the end of the year and reconcile differences between the two versions before sending it to Trump for his signature, amid uncertainty over the election results and a shifting geopolitical environment.

Here are five of the most notable and provocative provisions to watch, all likely to draw opposition from Beijing.

1. Support for Taiwan

Despite Trump’s recent remarks describing arms sales to Taiwan as “negotiating chips” to Beijing, the versions of the bill under discussion in both chambers would keep money flowing to Taiwan’s defence.

The House version would authorise up to US$1 billion for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative – a US defence assistance programme – maintaining the previous financial year’s level, and create a US-Taiwan partnership on defence industrial priorities.

It would also establish a joint programme to develop and test drones and counter-drone systems, and require a plan for Taiwan’s navy to take part in the Rim of the Pacific Exercise by 2028 – a clause that was dropped in last year’s final compromise bill.

Further House provisions call for an annual report on Taiwan’s capabilities and a strategy to support its cyber defence through Five Eyes coordination.

The Senate version would authorise arms transfers to Taiwan from the US War Reserve Stockpile. It would also rename the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative the “First Island Chain Security Cooperation Initiative”.

The Chinese embassy in Washington has told the South China Morning Post that it “strongly deplores and firmly opposes” Taiwan-related provisions in the bill that “grossly interfere” in China’s internal affairs, and that any attempt to arm Taiwan will face “grave consequences”.

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with the mainland, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force and is committed to supplying the island with defensive weapons.

2. Planning for a South China Sea crisis

The Senate version focuses far more on the first island chain, the arc of islands from Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines to Borneo that encloses the South China Sea.

It would require the Pentagon to draft a crisis-management strategy for the sea within a year, identify likely flashpoints short of war, and outline phased responses coordinated with partners.

The stated aim is to “deny the aim of the People’s Republic of China and deter further [PRC] provocation or actions that expand the crisis.” It would also order facilities planning for rotating US forces in the Philippines, which has clashed with Chinese vessels, and seek a report on Japan’s counterstrike capabilities.

The House version did not mention the South China Sea or the first island chain.

3. Countering China’s shipbuilding dominance

China’s dominance in shipbuilding has helped it build the world’s largest navy by number of vessels, according to the Pentagon.

The Trump administration has been attempting to increase cooperation with allies with shipbuilding capacities, such as South Korea and Japan, to help revitalise depleted US naval shipbuilding capabilities.

However, the House and Senate versions take contrasting approaches to foreign shipyard involvement in US Navy shipbuilding.

The House version prohibits using any funds to contract for or procure battle force or combat ships in a foreign shipyard, completely barring overseas construction for the combat fleet.

The Senate version amends the current law by allowing the Pentagon to procure up to two bulk fuel vessels and two strategic sealift/auxiliary non-combat ships from treaty-ally shipyards.

4. Tightening of tech restrictions

Both bills would prohibit the Pentagon from using Chinese-manufactured optical fibre and restrict purchases of certain used vessels built in China.

The House would also bar the procurement and use of humanoid robotic systems produced, developed or controlled by foreign adversaries, and restrict purchases of photovoltaic cells, modules and inverters from foreign entities of concern.

The Senate would prohibit acquisitions of modems, routers and televisions involving entities owned or controlled by China. It would also require an annual assessment of how certain advanced AI chips contribute to China’s military capabilities.

Tougher chip export controls, including the AI OVERWATCH Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act, could be added before final passage. Zack Cooper, a China expert and senior fellow of the American Enterprise Institute, said the three measures were “perhaps the most important portions related to China right now”.

Beijing has condemned plans, warning chip curbs would cause “arbitrary disruption and damage” to global supply chains.

5. Reducing reliance on China for critical minerals

Responding to China’s global dominance in critical mineral supplies that are essential for advanced military technology, the Senate bill would prohibit the Pentagon from buying certain minerals from non-allied nations and set up a pilot programme to restart antimony and copper production in the US.

It also orders an assessment of the Pentagon’s phosphate supply chain, including its dependence on China.

The House bill is broader. It would cap the share of metals the Pentagon can source from abroad and set up tiered sourcing restrictions for critical minerals from China and North Korea.

It would also ban silicon-carbide semiconductors made in China and order studies on reliance on Chinese processing and on aluminium and synthetic diamond supplies.

One report would examine whether US scrap exports are feeding rare-earth refining and magnet production in China. Another study would assess whether combatant commands should be able to buy critical minerals on their own.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Indian-American support for Trump is slipping before midterms
item.description:
Immigration restrictions, rising living costs and strains in US-India relations are testing support for President Donald Trump among some Indian-Americans who backed the Republican Party in 2024, analysts say, ahead of November’s midterm elections.

A survey released in August by AAPI Data and Asian and Pacific Islander American Vote found that 66 per cent of Indian-American respondents favoured Democratic candidates for the US House of Representatives, compared with 18 per cent for Republicans. For the Senate, 66 per cent preferred Democrats and 22 per cent Republicans.

The findings follow a reported rise in support for Trump among Indian-American voters between the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections. A pre-election survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in October 2024 found that 32 per cent of registered Indian-American voters intended to vote for Trump that year, up from 22 per cent in 2020.
item.content:encoded:
Immigration restrictions, rising living costs and strains in US-India relations are testing support for President Donald Trump among some Indian-Americans who backed the Republican Party in 2024, analysts say, ahead of November’s midterm elections.

A survey released in August by AAPI Data and Asian and Pacific Islander American Vote found that 66 per cent of Indian-American respondents favoured Democratic candidates for the US House of Representatives, compared with 18 per cent for Republicans. For the Senate, 66 per cent preferred Democrats and 22 per cent Republicans.

The findings follow a reported rise in support for Trump among Indian-American voters between the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections. A pre-election survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in October 2024 found that 32 per cent of registered Indian-American voters intended to vote for Trump that year, up from 22 per cent in 2020.

The endowment’s surveys also showed that the share identifying as Democrats fell from 56 per cent in 2020 to 47 per cent in 2024, before edging down to 46 per cent in its February 2026 survey. Republican identification stood at 19 per cent in 2026, while 29 per cent identified as independents.

The US midterm elections on November 3 will determine the balance of power in Congress and shape legislative priorities and oversight of the president, potentially constraining Trump’s ability to advance his agenda.

Analysts point to a number of reasons why Indian-Americans appear to be moving further from Trump and the Republicans ahead of next week’s vote.

“Sections of Indian-Americans will gravitate towards the Democrats, especially those who were persuaded by Trump to vote for the Republican Party. This is because of deportations, visa curbs and price rises,” said Vivek Mishra, deputy director of strategic studies at the Observer Research Foundation.

The Trump administration has introduced major restrictions on visas and stepped up immigration enforcement, affecting Indian professionals and graduate students, including through a steep increase in visa fees.

Indian-Americans had also been stung by rising living costs since the US-Iran war started in late February, Mishra said.

Inflation was 3 per cent when Trump took office last year and reached 3.7 per cent last month.

Rising costs for food, fuel and other essentials are expected to influence Indian-American voters, alongside immigration restrictions and US-India relations, potentially benefiting Democrats in some closely contested races, according to Mayilvaganan Muthumariappan, US-based founder and director of the Centre for Human Security and International Affairs.

Indian-Americans are widely regarded as an economically successful and influential community in the United States, although they account for less than 1.5 per cent of American voters.

Clinching votes

The Indian-American community is concentrated in states including California, New Jersey, New York, Texas, Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan and Pennsylvania, several of which have competitive electoral contests

“While Indian-American voters are unlikely to decide the overall outcome of the 2026 midterms on their own, their voting patterns may be important in races with narrow margins,” Muthumariappan said. “They could greatly influence the voting results [and] in a way the control of Congress.”

However, he said their voting support could diverge.

“While some may lean towards Democrats due to dissatisfaction with Trump, others – especially independents and moderates – are expected to consider economic conditions and policy priorities when deciding,” he said, adding that these issues would count more than any traditional choice.

Monish Tourangbam, a fellow at the New Delhi-based Chintan Research Foundation’s Centre for Geopolitics and Strategic Studies, said the Indian-American community was leaning towards Democrats, although a section of them would be distinctly independent in their choices.

“They may vote for a third party that is neither Republican nor Democrat or not vote at all,” he said.

With Trump’s approval rating hovering near record lows, that had created an opportunity for Democrats, but the party would need to outline robust policies to win back Indian-American voters, he said.

Yashwant Deshmukh, founder of opinion and exit poll survey firm C-Voter, said parts of Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement and the wider right-wing political ecosystem had increasingly engaged in anti-Indian racism and xenophobia.

A recent example came in September, when Bo French, the Republican nominee for the Texas Railroad Commission, posted a photograph of South Asian students celebrating a University of Texas at Austin football victory, claiming it showed how many Americans had been “displaced by foreigners”.

The post drew widespread criticism, including from Republicans such as Senator John Cornyn, who condemned French’s remarks as racist. French defended his comments, arguing that universities should prioritise Americans over foreign students and workers.

“That is making Indians a bit apprehensive,” Deshmukh said. “It is taking away a lot of goodwill Republican lawmakers had generated because of their pro-business policies.”

While some pro-business Republicans favour attracting technology talent, populist and “America First” factions have repeatedly targeted the H-1B visa and green card programmes, which provide routes for skilled workers to enter the US and for eligible immigrants to obtain permanent residence.

Deshmukh said Maga campaigns whipping up public sentiment against highly qualified Indian-American professionals, including doctors and finance and software specialists, were irrational.

“We are seeing very sustained and racist campaigns against Indian immigrants suggesting that they are taking away jobs which appeal to middle- and low-skilled workers,” he said. “They are not stealing your jobs. They are highly qualified.”

He said the pro-Trump sentiment that had emerged a couple of years ago was over.

Priyajit Debsarkar, a London-based political commentator, said Indian-Americans felt let down by the Trump administration, which they had assumed would largely target illegal immigrants rather than professionals such as technology workers.

Trump’s public support for Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had also led some Indian-Americans to believe his policies would favour closer engagement with Delhi, Debsarkar said, but subsequent developments had challenged those expectations.

“There has instead been bizarre oscillations in trade policies,” Debsarkar said, highlighting how Trump’s administration had moved from proposing 100 per cent tariffs on Indian goods, partly in response to India’s purchases of Russian oil, to subsequently changing course.

He also said Trump’s outreach to Pakistan had rankled some Indian-Americans, given Delhi’s concerns about Islamabad’s alleged support for cross-border militancy and Trump’s claims to have mediated during a five-day India-Pakistan war last year, which India disputed.

The biggest change under the current US administration was the shift in sentiment towards Indian immigrants, Debsarkar said.

“I think the notion among the Indian diaspora that the US is tolerant and inclusive has changed,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Can India turn wartime ammo sales into lasting European defence ties?
item.description:
India has emerged as a major exporter of ammunition and other weapons to Europe since the outbreak of the Ukraine-Russia war, but analysts caution that New Delhi has yet to secure a lasting foothold in Europe’s defence market.

Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh cited a Bloomberg report last Friday stating that India had become the third-largest arms exporter to Europe under the “ReArm Europe” initiative – also known as Readiness 2030 – largely because of ammunition demand.

Bloomberg, citing Trade Data Monitor data sourced from India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, reported that Indian arms manufacturers had exported about US$872 million worth of ammunition, including artillery shells, mortar shells, propellant and explosives, to European countries since the Ukraine war began.
item.content:encoded:
India has emerged as a major exporter of ammunition and other weapons to Europe since the outbreak of the Ukraine-Russia war, but analysts caution that New Delhi has yet to secure a lasting foothold in Europe’s defence market.

Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh cited a Bloomberg report last Friday stating that India had become the third-largest arms exporter to Europe under the “ReArm Europe” initiative – also known as Readiness 2030 – largely because of ammunition demand.

Bloomberg, citing Trade Data Monitor data sourced from India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, reported that Indian arms manufacturers had exported about US$872 million worth of ammunition, including artillery shells, mortar shells, propellant and explosives, to European countries since the Ukraine war began.

This marked a 1,600 per cent increase from the US$49.2 million exported to Europe in the four years leading up to February 2022. Most of these exports reportedly went to countries that have been major arms suppliers to Ukraine, although the nations were not named.

The South Asian nation ranked as the second-largest supplier of shells, mortars, propellants and explosives to Europe over the four years since 2022, rising from 28th place in the preceding four years, the import and export statistics from tracking platform Trade Data Monitor showed.

Singh said Delhi was now looking to expand its presence in Europe’s defence procurement programmes through joint ventures with European companies, while encouraging European partners to establish ventures in India to tap into its domestic market.

Lasting foothold?

Europe’s rearmament drive offered India a way into a market dominated by established suppliers, but securing a lasting position would require more than filling ammunition shortages, said Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at the Indic Researchers Forum, a Delhi-based security think tank.

“The real opportunity is to turn wartime orders into long-term industrial partnerships, trusted supply chains and technology collaboration,” he said. “India’s success will ultimately depend on whether it remains a reliable supplier when the urgency of war subsides.”

Balakrishnan said that “India can compete selectively” to become a serious defence supplier to Europe, noting that its advantage lay in combining competitive costs with scalable production, proven systems and selective technology partnerships.

The next step would be to move towards co-developing platforms and becoming a long-term partner in Europe’s defence industrial base, he said.

The United States and South Korea remain Europe’s top two non-European arms suppliers. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, South Korea accounted for 8.6 per cent of European Nato members’ arms imports between 2021 and 2025, reaching US$11.03 billion last year to cement its position as their second-largest supplier after the US. Poland alone sourced 47 per cent of its arms imports from South Korea over that period.

Last year, European countries spent US$38.6 billion under the US Foreign Military Sales programme – which facilitates the purchase of American arms and other military equipment by foreign governments – representing 37 per cent of total US defence exports in 2025, according to the EU Institute for Security Studies. This marked a sharp decline from 2024, however, when European procurement stood at US$76.7 billion.

Rajiv Kumar Narang, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analysis in Delhi, urged India’s defence sector to capitalise on the opportunity afforded by Europe’s rearmament and work closely with European partners to identify their requirements.

“India and Europe should have mutual acceptance of defence equipment standards and certifications for ease of export,” Narang said. “India should also continue to make investments in core technologies and pursue a spiral development approach for building world-class defence systems.”

South Korea serves as a template for India, analysts say, having expanded its footprint in Europe beyond ammunition to encompass major weapons systems, such as K9 self-propelled howitzers, K2 Black Panther main battle tanks and Chunmoo multiple-rocket launchers.

Antoine Levesques, senior fellow for South and Central Asian defence at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said India’s defence industrial base was seeking to reposition itself as more than just a buyer or licence assembler.

“It [India] wants to become, as a higher aspiration, a co-developer with European defence primes or at least a major contributor to their supply chains present and future,” he said, adding that increased exports and a strategic normalisation of the country’s status as a trusted defence partner would help in this regard.

“But this will take time due to significant political-strategic, technological, capacity or funding gaps, in a wider context of rapidly evolving global economic and diplomatic patterns creating new push and pull factors on either side of India’s ties to Europe.”

Still, Levesques pointed to “steady progress” in India-EU ties, suggesting cooperation had surpassed the baseline of “civilian or potentially dual-use, trusted de-risked critical supply chains”.

He added that a drop in talent emigrating to the US in recent years meant more Indian engineers and technical specialists were now working for domestic companies, including established defence firms.

“The value proposition India is bringing to Europe’s defence recapitalisation is therefore slowly but truly changing,” Levesques said.

Romania, Slovenia and the Czech Republic were among the top European buyers of Indian arms and ammunition in 2025, taking in a combined US$288.6 million worth of exports, according to the World Bank’s World Integrated Trade Solution data platform.

India’s emergence as a leading arms supplier to Europe is more than a short-term windfall arising from the Ukraine war, according to Ambika Vishwanath, co-founder and director of the Kubernein Initiative think tank and a Maitri research fellow at La Trobe Asia.

“The EU is realising that a more self-sufficient and diversified Europe is a smarter move forward,” Vishwanath said. “The new EU Readiness 2030 road map reflects this well through more structural defence expansion. This is not only in weapons or manufacturing but also in partners and technology.”

India had yet to reach a point where it could act as a comprehensive defence partner for Europe, she said, pointing to challenges such as interoperability, standards and capabilities.

“[But] we are seeing an upwards trend, and by entering the supply chain space along with small parts manufacturing, we have a good chance for a more lasting foothold” and gain more flexibility against future geopolitical risks and shocks, Vishwanath said.

item.title: [SCMP] The ‘Queen of the Chinese’ and a forgotten history on the US-Mexico border
item.description:
At Texas’ dusty Concordia Cemetery, grass grows over graves in a 140-year-old Chinese burial ground. Some headstones have been stolen or vandalised; others have been marked by flat concrete slabs etched with names in Chinese and English. The slabs were harder to steal than traditional headstones. Still other graves have no visible markers.

“I don’t think many people go out there,” says Linda Chew, a retired judge in El Paso, the state’s sixth-largest city.

Yet interest in the history of the Chinese community in the Lone Star State is growing. “There’s a real resurrection in understanding the influence of the Chinese in Texas,” Chew adds.
item.content:encoded:
At Texas’ dusty Concordia Cemetery, grass grows over graves in a 140-year-old Chinese burial ground. Some headstones have been stolen or vandalised; others have been marked by flat concrete slabs etched with names in Chinese and English. The slabs were harder to steal than traditional headstones. Still other graves have no visible markers.

“I don’t think many people go out there,” says Linda Chew, a retired judge in El Paso, the state’s sixth-largest city.

Yet interest in the history of the Chinese community in the Lone Star State is growing. “There’s a real resurrection in understanding the influence of the Chinese in Texas,” Chew adds.

This is the story of one family.

But it represents a much larger Chinese immigrant community in Texas that worked on the railroad, lived alongside cowboys, and established laundries, grocery stores and restaurants, contributing to the rich cultural tapestry of the US-Mexico borderlands.

Researchers and community members are now working to document and reawaken the history of Chinese in Texas that, like the cemetery, has faded and grown scruffy over time.

They’re also drawing lessons from that extended history of prejudice and exclusion to counter efforts by today’s lawmakers to restrict property, education and voting rights.

“We are using history and what happened a hundred years ago to reflect what’s going on right now,” said artist June Xu, who seeks to draw the parallels in her work.

“People take civil rights for granted because they don’t know how hard that fight was.”

Building a life on the US-Mexico border despite sweeping restrictions on Chinese citizenship

In the early 20th century, Linda’s grandparents built their lives and businesses on the US-Mexico border during the era of sweeping restrictions on Chinese immigration and citizenship.

Her grandmother, Herlinda, became known as the “Queen of the Chinese”, as showcased in a 1919 El Paso Times article.

“The Chinese woman is a queen so far as the Chinese population of Juarez is concerned,” the article reads. The same piece also claimed she once taught at a Presbyterian mission in Hong Kong.

“She was a powerhouse,” Linda says, before pointing to a photograph of her grandmother, Herlinda Wong Chew, whose likeness appears on a bright pink mural in Austin, the state capital, celebrating a woman whose family helped shape Texas history.

The painting was commissioned as part of a project to honour influential Asian-Americans, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders.

Herlinda was born around 1894 in Guadalajara, Mexico, according to her family, to a Mexican mother and a Chinese father. She married Antonio Yee Chew, a Chinese immigrant who had moved to Mexico for work.

Herlinda was self-taught and “really brilliant”, her granddaughter Linda says. Herlinda’s Chinese name was Wong Sun Far and Antonio’s was Yee Wing Chew.

During the turbulent Mexican Revolution, Herlinda and Antonio temporarily escaped to El Paso. Linda says Herlinda built a rapport with border agents, helping bring 250 people to the US from the Chinese community across the border to temporary safety during the Third Battle of Ciudad Juarez in 1919.

When Herlinda and Antonio returned to Mexico, they continued to operate their grocery business in Juarez before deciding to move to the US, perhaps for its economic and educational opportunities, Linda says.

One big problem: the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 – the first major US law to restrict immigration based on race and nationality – barred Chinese labourers from entering the US and prevented Chinese immigrants from becoming naturalised citizens.

Undeterred, however, Herlinda researched American immigration law and realised that Chinese merchants could legally move to the US if they met certain strict requirements and had documentation, a provision also open to diplomats, teachers, students and tourists.

In 1922, Herlinda and Antonio settled in El Paso using this exemption, where they established more grocery stores.

Four of their children were born in Mexico and four in the US. In classic immigrant fashion, their eight children, including Linda’s father, Wellington Yee Chew, worked in their shops.

But Herlinda was careful to keep their other tradition alive.

“She made sure that they really understood their Mexican culture and their Chinese culture,” Linda adds.

Drawing on what she had learned, Herlinda became a de facto immigration specialist in El Paso, working directly with the railways and steamship lines to help Chinese people travel to the US or back to China.

Linda believes Herlinda would have become an immigration lawyer, if that had been possible at the time.

In 1943, the Chinese Exclusion Act was repealed when China and the US allied during World War II. While this restored eligibility for naturalisation, strict Chinese immigration quotas remained. But Herlinda and Antonio both died in 1939 and never became US citizens.

Generations of Chews help keep proud legal legacy alive

Generations of Chews have picked up Herlinda’s legal legacy. Wellington became an immigration lawyer and criminal defence lawyer in El Paso and was reportedly the first Chinese-American lawyer licensed by the State Bar of Texas.

“He was so proud of my grandmother and his parents, and the established community they created here in El Paso,” Linda says.

In addition, Linda became a judge, as did her sister Patricia, who serves on El Paso’s County Probate Court No 1. And her brother David became chief justice of the Texas Eighth Court of Appeals.

Many of the details of Herlinda and Antonio’s story are difficult to trace, a pattern seen with Chinese history more broadly, particularly among other families that left few written records, something historian Anna Fahy is working to remedy.

Concordia, a one-time ranch framed by the Franklin Mountains, gradually became a burial ground in the late 1800s. It now houses some 60,000 graves in a patchwork layout across 52 acres (21 hectares).

Its plots were sold over the years to church groups, the military and different organisations for burial grounds. The Chinese were one of these groups.

Among those buried there are the notable outlaw John Wesley Hardin and the lawman who gunned him down, as well as two Chinese men who built the rock wall around Concordia’s Chinese section and were later buried within its confines.

Entering the gates of the Chinese section, Fahy points out Chinese inscriptions on one side and English on the other. The Chinese community has always owned its plots outright within Concordia, she says. “The only Chinese cemetery in the state of Texas. Period,” Fahy adds.

Into the mid-1920s, El Paso had the largest Chinese community in Texas. Janine Young of the El Paso County Historical Society attributes this to the arrival of the Southern Pacific Railroad in 1881, just before the Exclusion Act.

While the Chew family built a generational legacy, far less is known about the Chinese railroad workers, many illiterate, who left faint footprints.

“They were such anonymous workers,” Young adds. “Most of them died without families here and if they had families, they would have stayed back in China.”

Most of the laundries in El Paso were initially owned and operated by Chinese, who developed their own business practices, Young says.

A newspaper from the time details how Chinese laundry owners kept notes to help them remember their non-Chinese customers.

“They have all these different descriptions about people,” says Fahy, citing an example as: “short woman who sneezes a lot”.

Almost all early Chinese immigrants in the area were men, Young adds, which was not strictly because of the types of work available. The Page Act of 1875, which treated Chinese women as potential sex workers, made it harder for them to enter the US, tearing apart families.

Nowadays, Chinese communities remain an established part of Texas, with sizeable populations in San Antonio, Houston, Austin and Dallas.

According to US Census data, Texas has the third-largest ethnically Chinese population of any state, at around 275,000, behind California and New York.

In 2025, Xu, the artist, launched an exhibit in Austin as part of the Asian-American Art & Culture Initiative that featured Herlinda.

Titled “Root Unveiled: Chinese-American History, 1783-1946” and curated by Xuhua Zhan, it aims to preserve “fading stories”. The Houston-based artist plans to bring it to her hometown early next year.

For Xu, the history of Chinese immigrants in the state has renewed relevance as lawmakers introduce new restrictions affecting foreign nationals, with parallels between historical discrimination and policies such as Texas Senate Bill 17, passed in 2025.

That law restricts certain individuals and entities linked to China, Russia, Iran and North Korea from acquiring interests in Texas real estate.

While supporters frame it as a national security measure, opponents see it aimed at the Chinese, in particular, given the minuscule investment by nationals from the other countries.

US citizens and lawful permanent residents are exempt. The law also provides a limited exception for a residential property used as a homestead by lawful US residents.

Documentary to explore historical legal issues over the years

Xu is producing a documentary called “Under Her Name” that explores links between historical restrictions such as the Chinese Exclusion Act and contemporary legislation governing foreign land ownership.

Xu hopes to bridge the gap between the long history of Chinese-Americans in the US and public understanding of their place in the country.

“People who arrived in the last 30 years often don’t know how long Chinese-Americans have been rooted here,” she says.

As Linda recounts her family history, she reflects on the debt owed to her ancestors and so many others in the community.

“This country was built on their backs,” she says. “On the backs of Chinese and on the backs of Mexicans.”

item.title: [SCMP] German leader’s China visit latest sign of foreign diplomacy pivot beyond Beijing
item.description:
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has begun his state visit to China in the eastern province of Anhui, spotlighting a growing trend among visiting foreign leaders to look well beyond Beijing.

Steinmeier arrived in the provincial capital Hefei early on Tuesday to begin a five-day state visit, marking his first trip to China in nearly eight years and confirming an exclusive report by the South China Morning Post earlier this month.

When foreign dignitaries bypass Beijing for provincial hubs, it is a deliberate diplomatic move, with itineraries carefully curated to project a commitment to deeper ties. Regional stops offer a direct window into China’s industrial landscape while opening doors for cooperation in trade, hi-tech manufacturing, tourism and clean energy.
item.content:encoded:
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has begun his state visit to China in the eastern province of Anhui, spotlighting a growing trend among visiting foreign leaders to look well beyond Beijing.

Steinmeier arrived in the provincial capital Hefei early on Tuesday to begin a five-day state visit, marking his first trip to China in nearly eight years and confirming an exclusive report by the South China Morning Post earlier this month.

When foreign dignitaries bypass Beijing for provincial hubs, it is a deliberate diplomatic move, with itineraries carefully curated to project a commitment to deeper ties. Regional stops offer a direct window into China’s industrial landscape while opening doors for cooperation in trade, hi-tech manufacturing, tourism and clean energy.

According to his office, Steinmeier’s itinerary in Anhui includes a visit to German carmaker Volkswagen’s innovation hub in Hefei, alongside cultural exchange sites. He will then travel to Beijing, where he will meet top leaders including President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang before concluding his visit.

His office said the trip aimed to address “Germany’s multifaceted and complex relations with China and the challenges they face”, while his time in Anhui would highlight “the China of the turn of the century around 1900 and the significance of this era in the history of German-Chinese relations”.

Choosing Anhui underscores Berlin’s push for dialogue even as bilateral ties sour over mounting trade friction, driven by German anxiety that fierce Chinese competition could hollow out its manufacturing heartland.

In early October, Germany and France co-signed a proposal calling for a new trade mechanism to bar European Union market access to countries that cause market distortion – a measure widely seen as aimed at China.

Steinmeier’s first stop in Hefei was the former residence of Li Hongzhang – a Chinese statesman of the late Qing dynasty who pioneered China’s early modernisation.

Li met former German chancellor Otto von Bismarck in 1896, a historic encounter in which the Qing envoy sought a blueprint for China’s industrialisation while observing first-hand the rise of a modern industrial power.

Moving from history to sustainability and innovation, Steinmeier toured Luogang Central Park, a sustainable urban development project built on the site of Hefei’s former international airport.

His schedule in Hefei also featured a visit to the research and development centre of the Volkswagen Group China Technology Company.

Hefei has transformed into a hi-tech hub backed by heavy investment in emerging industries, including artificial intelligence, semiconductors and new energy vehicles.

Steinmeier’s presence in the city underscores Berlin’s recognition of China’s vast consumer market and integrated supply chains, as well as its desire to sustain practical cooperation in trade, technology and innovation despite broader geopolitical headwinds.

Before heading to Beijing, Steinmeier will also visit the historic village of Hongcun and Mount Huangshan – sites that the German presidency noted as uniting “nature, architecture and philosophy”.

In the capital, Steinmeier is due to tour the Institute of Atmospheric Physics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences to examine climate cooperation, followed by an address at Peking University. Xi is later expected to welcome him with full military honours.

Regional engagement by visiting leaders extends well beyond Anhui, with Shanghai – China’s financial capital – remaining one of the most sought-after stops.

The city hosted both South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer in January alone, before a visit in August by King Abdullah II of Jordan further cemented its status as an entry point into China’s technology and consumer markets.

Just south of Shanghai, Hangzhou has similarly emerged as an essential diplomatic stop. Once celebrated primarily for the classic scenery of West Lake, the Zhejiang provincial capital has evolved into an innovation powerhouse, drawing foreign heads of state with itineraries anchored in robotics, e-commerce and advanced manufacturing.

In February, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz led a high-powered business delegation to the city, visiting Siemens Energy and humanoid robotics maker Unitree to assess the rapid pace of Chinese technological commercialisation

Over May and June, the city hosted Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif for a bilateral business conference, as well as Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith for a tour of tech giant Alibaba – owner of the SCMP – and quadruped robot pioneer Deep Robotics.

Chengdu, the capital of southwestern Sichuan province, has also emerged as a popular destination. It drew at least four world leaders in the second half of 2025 alone, among them French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish King Felipe VI.

In July last year, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese wrapped up his visit to China in Chengdu, where he toured the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.

The following September, Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari also visited Chengdu, where he toured the advanced manufacturing complex of the state-owned aerospace and defence giant Aviation Industry Corporation of China.

Chengdu is one of China’s major aviation industry hubs, closely associated with the development and manufacture of civil aircraft and fighter jets including the J-10 and J-20.

Guangzhou, the capital of southern China’s Guangdong province, hosted Italian President Sergio Mattarella in November 2024, when he praised the metropolis as a vital historic bridge for East-West exchange, according to local authorities.

Long a “gathering point for Western envoys, missionaries and merchants travelling to China”, as China’s State Council Information Office describes it, the city remains a major hub for China’s foreign trade. The China Import and Export Fair, or Canton Fair, was established in Guangzhou in 1957 and has built trade links with more than 229 countries and regions, according to the fair’s website.

Papua New Guinean Prime Minister James Marape visited Guangzhou in April to promote economic cooperation and trade ties.

Xiongan New Area, a state-level mega city project about 100km (62 miles) from Beijing and held up as “a strategy crucial for a millennium to come” has emerged as yet another fixture on foreign itineraries. It has hosted delegations from at least 82 countries and regions since 2025 alongside high-profile leaders such as Vietnamese President To Lam.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Singapore’s PAP internal vote is the wrong place to look for signs of leadership renewal
item.description:
Singapore’s ruling People’s Action Party (PAP) has retained its core executive team in what is seen as a cautious approach despite pledges of renewal, with observers pointing to ministerial promotions as a better indication of leadership plans.

The PAP emerged from an internal election on Sunday with an unchanged slate for the Central Executive Committee (CEC), its highest decision-making body, as rising ministers Jeffrey Siow and Jasmin Lau failed to secure seats, though four remaining co-opted positions could yet provide an opening for fresh faces.

Sunday’s vote – the first since PAP’s massive victory at the 2025 general election – saw some 2,000 cadres return Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and senior ministers Lee Hsien Loong and K. Shanmugam to the apex of the party’s power structure.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s ruling People’s Action Party (PAP) has retained its core executive team in what is seen as a cautious approach despite pledges of renewal, with observers pointing to ministerial promotions as a better indication of leadership plans.

The PAP emerged from an internal election on Sunday with an unchanged slate for the Central Executive Committee (CEC), its highest decision-making body, as rising ministers Jeffrey Siow and Jasmin Lau failed to secure seats, though four remaining co-opted positions could yet provide an opening for fresh faces.

Sunday’s vote – the first since PAP’s massive victory at the 2025 general election – saw some 2,000 cadres return Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and senior ministers Lee Hsien Loong and K. Shanmugam to the apex of the party’s power structure.

Ministers Desmond Lee, Chan Chun Sing, Masagos Zulkifli, Grace Fu, Chee Hong Tat, Edwin Tong, Indranee Rajah, Ong Ye Kung and Vivian Balakrishnan rounded up the 12, which did not feature any newcomers.

Out of 19 candidates, seven were marked on the ballot paper for cadres to consider – inclusive of Wong, Lee Hsien Loong and Shanmugam, the others were Chan, Desmond Lee, Fu and Masagos.

Transport minister Siow and acting manpower minister Lau – both first-term MPs – were among the 19 nominated but not voted in.

Internal elections at the PAP, which has been in power since 1959, are designed to ensure top leaders are picked only by the most senior rank-and-file members, known as cadres.

There are 12 elected seats in the party’s CEC, which can co-opt up to six more members into the committee – two of these will be cadres with the 13th and 14th highest number of votes, and the remaining four are chosen by the new CEC.

Energy and Industry Minister Tan See Leng and acting minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs Zaqy Mohamad were co-opted into the committee with the 13th and 14th highest vote counts on Sunday.

Promotions a ‘better indication’

Nydia Ngiow, managing director at strategic advisory firm BowerGroupAsia, said the internal poll did not throw up surprises and closely mirrored its 2024 precedent, reflecting stability and policy continuity.

“The co-opting process lets the leadership maintain flexibility on who it ultimately brings in,” Ngiow said. “How the four remaining slots are filled in the coming weeks will signal the pace of renewal.”

Mustafa Izzuddin, a senior international affairs analyst at Solaris Strategies Singapore, described Sunday’s election as “non-pivotal” and said the current CEC “only partially reflected” the party’s future.

“We may however see changes in 2028, which is around the midway [point] of the current term in office, with the general election slated to take place in 2030,” he said.

While the CEC was a reflection of party leadership at the particular point of time, it was not necessarily indicative of who would rise to the highest level of government or take the helm, said independent political observer Felix Tan.

“I would be cautious about reading too much into current CEC results as an indication of PAP’s longer succession plans,” he said. “Political trajectories can change considerably over time.”

Felix Tan noted that the PAP “is voting for that status quo for now, and seeing what the new faces can contribute in the coming year because the CEC will be refreshed again”. He predicted Siow and Lau “will be co-opted, as members who have no important role to play yet and more like accepted members, but it’s still a good start somewhere”.

In July, Siow was made a full minister 14 months after taking office, and Lau rose to acting minister after being appointed minister of state following the 2025 election.

“The promotions tend to be a better indication of how political office holders are regarded,” Ngiow said, pointing to how Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong assumed the No 2 position in 2024 even after stepping down from the committee in 2022.

Of the 32 new PAP candidates fielded in 2025, five – including Lau – have been made ministers of state. Like Siow, Minister for Culture, Community and Youth David Neo also became a full minister in July, 14 months after taking office.

It marked the biggest number of new faces taking political office since 2001, when then prime minister Goh Chok Tong similarly inducted seven new MPs, including Balakrishnan and Tharman Shanmugaratnam – now Singapore’s foreign minister and president respectively.

Six new faces took office in 2020 and five each were inducted after elections in 2015, 2011 and 2006.

On Sunday’s internal vote, Walid Jumblatt Abdullah, a political scientist at Nanyang Technological University, said the marked names on the ballot sheet for cadres were a common practice indicating office holders singled out by the party for cadres to consider.

“It was a curious choice to have Masagos instead of Zaqy Mohamad as the Malay representative in the seven when the latter is the current acting minister in charge of Muslim affairs,” he said on social media.

“Perhaps, like Lau, Siow and David Neo, the party feels Zaqy and the newer ministers have to earn their stripes first.”

Shots fired

In his speech before the vote on Sunday, Wong took aim at the city state’s main opposition party for its policy positions.

The Workers’ Party (WP) was “not always consistent or coherent” when taking policy positions, which seemed to “shift with the political winds”, the prime minister said.

“The opposition has taken different positions at different times, depending on the concerns of the day or what they believe will be popular,” he said, citing issues such as public housing supply and foreign worker intake as areas the opposition had shifted its stances on.

“But these positions do not always add up to a coherent approach that takes account of the trade-offs or the longer-term consequences, and this is part of opposition politics.”

Hours after Wong delivered his address, WP MP Jamus Lim posted a rebuttal on social media, calling the prime minister’s remarks “an incredible double standard”.

The ruling party was known for “massive U-turns in policy”, Lim pointed out, including on issues such as minimum wages and the colonial-era Section 377A law that criminalised sex acts between consenting men.

Lim described Wong’s views as “disappointing”.

“It belies a lack of understanding of how Singaporeans would like to see their political leaders tackle constructive challenges to the policy choices of the ruling party,” Lim said.

“Adjusting one’s position is a mark of wisdom and maturity, not opportunism … It is this sort of back-and-forth debate that refines policy, and keeps it relevant.”

During the conference in 2024, Wong said opposition parties had tried to exploit cost-of-living concerns to turn public sentiment against the PAP, despite not having good solutions themselves, but did not name the WP explicitly.

Observers said PAP’s criticism of the WP for inconsistent policy positions could be expected more frequently in the future as the opposition gained ground.

Such exchanges had increased over the years with the WP’s growing influence, Felix Tan said. “You can’t dismiss the fact that during last year’s general election itself there was already a significant shift towards the WP, as seen by some constituencies which were very close.”

While the PAP increased its vote share to 65.57 per cent in 2025, the WP repeated its 2020 feat of winning more votes than the PAP in the constituencies it retained. The WP held onto its 10 seats in parliament after narrow losses in group representation constituencies like Tampines and Punggol.

Ngiow said the consistency charge had resurfaced time and again. “Parties can revise their positions, but with information so easily accessible, both parties will increasingly need to show how the pieces add up when those positions change.”

item.title: [SCMP] Air Force crash revives debate on Philippine military’s modernisation limits
item.description:
The collision of two Philippine Air Force training aircraft that killed four pilots has raised questions about whether the service’s training, maintenance and safety systems can keep pace with Manila’s ambitions to acquire more advanced combat aircraft.

The crash, which occurred during a fly-by rehearsal at Fernando Air Base in Lipa City, Batangas province, south of Manila, on Friday has renewed calls for a comprehensive review of the Air Force’s ageing fleet, pilot instruction, maintenance practices and operational safety.

The air force temporarily grounded all SF-260 aircraft as a precautionary safety measure.
item.content:encoded:
The collision of two Philippine Air Force training aircraft that killed four pilots has raised questions about whether the service’s training, maintenance and safety systems can keep pace with Manila’s ambitions to acquire more advanced combat aircraft.

The crash, which occurred during a fly-by rehearsal at Fernando Air Base in Lipa City, Batangas province, south of Manila, on Friday has renewed calls for a comprehensive review of the Air Force’s ageing fleet, pilot instruction, maintenance practices and operational safety.

The air force temporarily grounded all SF-260 aircraft as a precautionary safety measure.

Defence chief Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, acting on an order from President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, called for an investigation into the incident, noting that it was the third such occurrence since 2023 and raising the possibility of a systemic problem.

Teodoro said investigators would examine maintenance records, preserve salvageable aircraft parts, review the pilots’ past performance and conduct toxicology testing if samples remained available.

It was the latest in a series of fatal accidents involving that aircraft type. An SF-260 crash in Benguet killed two pilots in May, while another in Bataan left two aviators dead in 2023.

Widening gap

The accidents have highlighted what experts describe as a widening gap between the Philippines’ ambitions to modernise its air force and its capacity to sustain that transformation over the long term.

Since launching its military modernisation programme in 2013, Manila has sought to rebuild capabilities eroded by years of underinvestment, acquiring more advanced aircraft, helicopters, transport planes and air-defence systems.

In 2024, Marcos approved a revised phase of the programme, known as Re-Horizon 3, which envisaged about US$35 billion in spending over the following decade.

The effort includes plans to acquire more advanced fighter jets, with South Korea’s KF-21 among the candidates, although no contract has been signed. Marcos has presented the wider push as part of a drive towards a more self-reliant defence posture and reduced dependence on foreign suppliers.

But acquiring new aircraft is only part of the challenge. The air force must also ensure it could train pilots and maintain its fleet as it took on more sophisticated capabilities, said Justin Kyle Malarayap, a defence analyst and visiting assistant professor at Arellano University in Manila.

That meant upgrading pilot training alongside the fleet, as the service did when it introduced the F-5A/B jets, Malarayap said. “This would be the case should the Philippines acquire the KF-21, F-16 C/D Block 72, or Gripen, as most of their packages already include pilot retraining and maintenance pipelines.”

However, the SF-260 “has been pushed beyond its limit”, Malarayap said, noting that variants of the aircraft had been used for counter-insurgency missions that were beyond its primary role as a trainer.

Budget constraints repeatedly forced the air force to use aircraft for missions beyond their intended roles, which accelerated wear and tear, increased maintenance demands and reduced the number of aircraft available for operations, he said.

Competing demands on the defence budget also delayed purchases of newer aircraft and constrained pilot training, Malarayap added.

Arnaud Leveau, a geopolitics professor at Paris Dauphine University, said the Philippines’ training infrastructure remained relatively limited compared with that of some Southeast Asian neighbours, particularly in bridging basic flying and advanced jet operations.

Indonesia and Thailand, for example, invested in more diversified training systems, including modern turboprop and advanced jet trainers, he said.

“These provide a more progressive pathway towards operating modern combat aircraft. The Philippines has made progress in rebuilding its air combat capabilities, but its training system needs to catch up with its procurement ambitions,” he said.

Leveau cautioned against permanently grounding the SF-260 fleet before investigators established the causes of the latest accidents.

“That would risk confusing the age of an aircraft design with its actual airworthiness. However, this is an appropriate moment to review the long-term future of the fleet and consider a phased replacement programme,” he said.

The ongoing investigation is examining whether shortcomings in training or flight planning contributed to the latest crash.

Speaking to reporters a day after the accident, Teodoro said investigators would examine administrative procedures, flight planning, and the training, attitude and aptitude of student and instructor pilots.

Budget constraints and institutional reform

Malarayap said the Philippines’ phased military modernisation programme had limited the air force’s ability to respond to emerging needs, including the purchase of advanced fighters and the support systems required to operate them.

Allocating funds through a rigid pipeline could restrict spending on urgent capabilities, while proposals from Sweden, the United States and South Korea had faced delays partly because packages including logistics support could exceed the air force’s budget, Malarayap said.

While the three fatal accidents involving the same aircraft family over a relatively short period warranted closer scrutiny, Leveau cautioned against assuming a common cause.

“We need to be careful. The latest accident appears to have involved a mid-air collision, which is not necessarily related to the age or mechanical condition of the aircraft. Different accidents can have very different causes,” he said.

“What matters is whether the [air force] has the institutional capacity to identify weaknesses, learn from previous incidents and introduce effective corrective measures. There is a distinction between an individual accident and a systemic problem.”

As the Philippines acquired more sophisticated aircraft, it also had an opportunity to overhaul pilot training, Leveau said. That should include modern training platforms, flight simulators, stronger maintenance support and a more structured progression from basic flying to advanced combat operations.

To support those changes, Manila could build on its defence ties with South Korea while expanding cooperation with European countries in pilot training, aviation safety, maintenance standards and simulation technology, Leveau said.

He pointed to France’s experience in integrating military pilot training, operational preparation and technical support, which could benefit the Philippines without requiring it to purchase French combat aircraft.

Leveau stressed that such cooperation should form part of a broader institutional effort.

“For me, the broader issue is one of institutional maturity. As an air force becomes more technologically sophisticated, its procedures, safety standards and organisational culture must evolve accordingly,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s new estimate on Greenland ice loss speed is 55% lower than America’s
item.description:
Chinese researchers have created a new model to convert satellite surface elevation data for the Greenland Ice Sheet into a detailed estimate of how much ice it has lost in recent decades.

Using satellite altimetry data covering 2002 to 2023, they found that the ice sheet lost an average of about 120 gigatonnes (264.5 trillion lbs) of mass per year.

This figure is considerably lower than the widely cited figure reached by Nasa, which previously estimated Greenland’s annual loss to be nearly 270 gigatonnes using satellite gravity data.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese researchers have created a new model to convert satellite surface elevation data for the Greenland Ice Sheet into a detailed estimate of how much ice it has lost in recent decades.

Using satellite altimetry data covering 2002 to 2023, they found that the ice sheet lost an average of about 120 gigatonnes (264.5 trillion lbs) of mass per year.

This figure is considerably lower than the widely cited figure reached by Nasa, which previously estimated Greenland’s annual loss to be nearly 270 gigatonnes using satellite gravity data.

The new figure is also lower than the Chinese team’s own estimate derived from the same data used by the US space agency.

The lower number does not suggest Greenland’s melting is less severe than previously thought. Rather, the researchers said their study sought to refine elevation monitoring to provide a high-resolution map of exactly where the loss was happening.

“A comparison between different satellite technologies reveals that satellite altimetry offers a significant advantage in spatial resolution over satellite gravimetry, enabling the identification of ice-flow channels in local glaciers,” the team said in a paper published in the Chinese-language Journal of Marine Information Technology and Application on October 19.

Gravity-based data can offer a full picture of how much mass has been lost. Altimetry, or elevation data, can provide a more zoomed-in 1.9km (1.2-mile) resolution, but it needs to be converted into mass using density.

The researchers from China’s Jiangsu Ocean University developed a dynamic conversion model that was able to identify glaciers experiencing the most rapid loss. This could help reduce uncertainties in estimates of ice sheet dynamics across space and time.

The Greenland Ice Sheet covers about 80 per cent of the territory’s total land area and is the second-largest ice sheet in the world.

The sheet stretches across 1.7 million sq km (656,300 square miles) and contains about 2.9 million cubic km (696,000 cubic miles) of ice, according to the US National Snow and Ice Data Centre (NSIDC).

Since the mid-1990s, the sheet has been losing mass “in earnest”, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

This affects not only sea levels but also ocean circulation and properties, nutrient and sediment flux, as well as local ecosystems, contributing as feedback to future melting, NOAA said.

The sheet’s maximum elevation reaches 3,673 metres (12,050 feet), and the sheet’s average thickness is about 1,800 metres. The sheet’s ablation or melting period typically occurs from May to August, according to the Chinese team.

“Accurately estimating the spatiotemporal characteristics of the mass change of the Greenland Ice Sheet is of great scientific significance for understanding the complex feedback relationship between the polar ice sheet and the global climate system,” the team wrote.

Precisely determining ice mass changes and where they are happening is also important for predicting future evolution and impact on sea level rise, they added.

One of the primary methods to monitor long-term ice mass changes in the polar ice sheets is satellite gravimetry, which maps changes in the Earth’s gravitational field and can be used to determine mass loss.

“Satellite gravimetry allows for the direct monitoring of relative changes in the total mass of an ice sheet, yet its spatial resolution is insufficient to capture fine-scale, localised variations,” the team said.

Another method is satellite altimetry, which uses lasers or radar to track changes in the Earth’s surface elevation. This method offers the best resolution, but converting the data into mass can lead to estimation errors.

Over the past few decades, satellites equipped with radar altimeters have been launched to track ice sheet elevation and monitor the ice sheets.

In 2002, Nasa and the German Aerospace Centre launched two satellites as part of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (Grace), which orbited until 2017, collecting data on the Earth’s gravity field. Its successor, Grace-Fo, was launched in 2018.

Using data from Grace, Nasa estimated that Greenland lost 264 gigatonnes of ice per year between 2002 and 2025.

According to the Chinese team, although there had been previous studies using altimetry data, these often focused on using the data to downscale or correct gravimetric results.

There was a lack of systematic comparison between mass changes obtained from both methods, they said.

In their paper, the team proposed a way to estimate mass changes using satellite altimetry data with the help of a climate model called Mar, allowing them to build a dynamic snow and ice density model.

They evaluated mass changes from 2002 to 2023 using Mar to process surface elevation measurements.

These measurements were derived from NSIDC’s multi-source satellite altimetry data, which incorporates measurements from Nasa’s ICESat.

The researchers then compared this to the results from Grace-derived satellite-based mass concentration gravity data released by the University of Texas at Austin.

The Chinese team found that the Greenland Ice Sheet “was in a state of continuous mass loss” between 2002 and 2023, with an annual loss of nearly 120 gigatonnes based on altimetry data. The melting rate of the ice sheet accelerated significantly after 2010.

This meant a total loss of about 2,248 gigatonnes, contributing about 6.26mm (0.25 inch) to global sea level rise.

Using the gravity-based data, the team estimated a total mass loss of about 2,830 gigatonnes over the same 22-year period.

Thinning was most pronounced in the northwestern and southeastern parts of the ice sheet where the ice transitions into the ocean.

They found that significant mass loss signals were seen in the coastal Jakobshavn, Helheim, Kangerlussuaq and 79N glaciers.

In the hardest-hit basins, the altimetry data showed significantly less mass loss than the gravity measurements. This discrepancy suggests that melting may be occurring at the base of the ice sheet, or that ice and snow density was underestimated.

According to the Chinese team, future research would seek to further refine density estimates by incorporating on-site density observations.

“This integrated approach is intended to improve the accuracy of mass change estimates derived from satellite altimetry, provide more reliable data for analysing long-term trends in ice sheet mass and reduce uncertainties regarding the contribution of polar ice sheets to future sea-level rise projections,” they said.

item.title: [SCMP] Weapon or armour? The contentious debate over China’s open-weight AI
item.description:
Are China’s increasingly powerful open-weight AI models a cybersecurity threat, or could restricting them ultimately make the internet less secure?

The dilemma has become a growing concern as Chinese developers including DeepSeek, Z.ai and Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – continue to challenge their American rivals by releasing models that anyone can download, modify and deploy.

The growing impact of advanced AI on global cybersecurity has also forced governments and cybersecurity agencies across the world to scramble to shore up their digital defences, with this week’s uncovering of critical vulnerabilities in the internet programming language PHP just the latest example.
item.content:encoded:
Are China’s increasingly powerful open-weight AI models a cybersecurity threat, or could restricting them ultimately make the internet less secure?

The dilemma has become a growing concern as Chinese developers including DeepSeek, Z.ai and Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – continue to challenge their American rivals by releasing models that anyone can download, modify and deploy.

The growing impact of advanced AI on global cybersecurity has also forced governments and cybersecurity agencies across the world to scramble to shore up their digital defences, with this week’s uncovering of critical vulnerabilities in the internet programming language PHP just the latest example.

Critics warn that open-weight models allow malicious actors to easily strip away safety protections and use advanced AI to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. But other researchers argue that the same technology could help proliferate the cyber defence capabilities of AI systems more widely to counter emerging threats.

The debate has intensified following a report by US artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic that found Z.ai’s open-weight GLM-5.3 model had crossed critical thresholds for conducting sophisticated cyberattacks, similar to its own Claude models, while lacking the very safeguards that are possible due to Claude models being closed-source.

Yet researchers remain divided over whether the technical risks associated with open-weight AI translate into greater real-world harm, and whether the distinction between open and closed models is the right way to assess their dangers.

“Open models present different governance challenges than closed models, but that does not necessarily make them more dangerous,” said Kristy Loke, a fellow at MATS Research focusing on China’s AI innovation and governance strategies.

Open-weight models inherently have a larger attack surface for misuse

Edward Yee, AI safety researcher

The risks of openness

At the heart of the debate is a fundamental difference in how developers control their technology.

Closed models are typically accessed through application programming interfaces, or APIs, allowing developers to monitor suspicious activity, restrict requests and revoke access when necessary.

Open-weight models, by contrast, allow users to download the underlying parameters and run the systems independently, but they also mean malicious actors can remove safeguards designed to prevent harmful activities.

Edward Yee, researcher and chief growth officer at US-based AI safety organisation Far.AI, said open-weight structures create a significant security disadvantage. “Open-weight models inherently have a larger attack surface for misuse,” Yee said.

While closed models can rely on multiple layers of protection such as external monitoring systems, open-weight models depend primarily on safeguards embedded in the models themselves, which can often be removed through techniques such as “abliteration” – a technique that involves editing a model’s internal weight matrices to bypass its refusal mechanisms.

As open-weight models are widely released, their model weights cannot effectively be recalled, even if developers subsequently discover dangerous capabilities. Attackers could therefore gain unrestricted access to models without the protections their original developers deployed, Yee said.

The implications could become more serious as open-weight models approach the capabilities of the most advanced closed systems. While evidence of widespread harm remains limited, Yee said the lack of comprehensive data should not be mistaken for proof of safety, particularly because open models can be deployed on private servers, without knowledge of the authorities or the model developers themselves, making them difficult to monitor.

The most serious concerns relate to misuse of AI systems by non-state actors, with both Washington and Beijing expressing willingness to jointly combat such risks in recent weeks. On Thursday, Tech Against Terrorism – a counterterrorism non-profit organisation backed by the United Nations – released its latest findings showing that closed models “do far better” than open models at refusing to help terrorists with planning an attack, while “abliterated” open models comply easily.

Where is the evidence?
