Still, the ability to remove safeguards in open-weight models on paper does not necessarily translate into greater real-world harm, researchers cautioned.

“Real-world harm is no longer theoretical, but so far the evidence doesn’t show that releasing the weights is what makes the difference,” said Oskar Galeev, a researcher at Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI.

Galeev said attackers tend to use whichever AI systems best suit their needs, turning to proprietary models for their capabilities and open-weight alternatives when they are cheaper or less restrictive.

“Attackers tend to shop around. They don’t care much about the theoretical distinction between closed and open-weight,” he said.

Even when open-weight models are used in cyberattacks, malicious actors may access them through commercial AI platforms without downloading their weights or removing safeguards. This makes it difficult to establish whether the availability of model weights contributed to an attack, Galeev added.

“For now, open and closed models fail in different ways, so neither is safe by default,” Galeev said.

“The right question is not whether a model is open or closed, but what extra risk a specific model release adds,” he added.

Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher and author of the AI 2027 forecasting project, said a model’s capabilities mattered more than whether its weights were publicly available.

“I would not say that open-weights models are inherently more dangerous,” he said. “All models are dangerous in proportion to how capable they are.”

Loke warned that closed models could pose greater risks as frontier AI developers pursued techniques such as recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems progressively improve their own capabilities, making human oversight more difficult.

A weapon for attackers – and defenders

Complicating the debate is the dual-use nature of AI’s cybersecurity capabilities.

The same technology that helps attackers discover software vulnerabilities can also help security researchers identify and fix weaknesses before they are exploited.

Open-weight models offer defenders several advantages. They can be deployed on local servers, adapted to specialised tasks and used to analyse sensitive systems without sending confidential information to external providers.

Clement Neo, founder of NEO Research, a Singapore-based frontier AI safety evaluation group, warned that banning open-weight models could backfire on safety.

Blanket restrictions on open models would likely hurt defenders more than attackers

Clement Neo, founder of NEO Research

“Open-weight models are a major asset for cybersecurity,” he said. “Blanket restrictions on open models would likely hurt defenders more than attackers.”

In a high-profile cyber hacking incident in July involving OpenAI’s GPT models, researchers at the affected company Hugging Face turned to a Chinese open-weight model – Z.ai’s GLM 5.2 – to investigate the breach after safeguards on closed US models refused to assist due to the companies’ built-in safeguards.

Researchers cited the incident as an example of how open models could benefit defenders when proprietary systems struggle to distinguish legitimate security research from malicious activity.

Open-weight models could also be particularly valuable to smaller organisations that lack the resources to purchase expensive proprietary tools or develop their own AI systems, according to Joshua Saxe, co-founder of US start-up Abundant Security and former tech lead in AI security at Facebook owner Meta Platforms.

Such models could allow companies to deploy affordable defensive systems across their software and infrastructure, identifying vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them.

“There’s also an institutional asymmetry: criminals don’t have procurement departments, compliance committees, or lengthy AI governance processes. Defenders do,” Saxe said.

“We’re in an adoption race as much as a capability race. Restrictions that slow defenders more than attackers could leave us less secure,” he added.

Kokotajlo, the former OpenAI researcher, said the benefits of open-weight AI models had so far outweighed their costs.

Open-weight’s transparency made it harder for developers to embed hidden agendas in the technology than in proprietary systems, whose inner workings were less accessible to outside scrutiny, he said.

While open-weight models provide “real benefits” to defenders, Yee said the benefits should still be weighed against the risks.

For some developers in China, running open-weight models locally has proven essential for security investigations.

When investigating suspicious application server activity, Shenzhen-based independent AI engineer Wen Sheng found cloud-based AI services accessed via an API unhelpful.

“The hosted model refused to analyse logs containing attack commands,” Wen said, without specifying which model. Switching to Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 model on his own server allowed his team to “reconstruct the sequence of events without uploading logs or internal credentials”, making it a boost for privacy as well.

While running the open-weight model on his own server required managing hardware, permissions and updates internally, Wen noted the added control made the effort worthwhile.

“Using a closed model is like renting a house: the provider holds the keys, sets the price and can lock you out,” said Shawn Lin, who leads a data annotation team at a major Chinese technology company in Shenzhen.

“When we run an open-weight model on our own infrastructure, we can keep sensitive data in-house and decide how the system is used,” Lin said.

“The practical question is who can access our data, what gets logged and whether we can keep using a model version that works for our workflow.”

Beyond the open-versus-closed divide

The debate carries particular significance for the China-US AI race, where China’s open-weight releases have become a central strategy for competing with better-funded American rivals.

Contrary to suggestions that China’s open-weight approach comes at the expense of safety, Chinese researchers and developers have been taking steps to address its risks, researchers said.

China’s national information security standardisation body, TC260, has begun drafting a security standard for open-weight AI models, recognising that safeguards can be removed once models are released.

Chinese AI companies are also developing their own approaches to managing these risks. Z.ai has worked with Concordia AI on a safety framework addressing the specific challenges of open-weight releases.

The framework distinguishes between dangerous capabilities that warrant restrictions regardless of whether a model is open or closed, and additional risks arising specifically from making model weights publicly available.

“While critics of open models are afraid of the democratisation of advanced cyber capabilities, many in China believe that this democratisation is precisely what is needed,” said Concordia’s Galeev. China supports open models precisely because it recognises that they empower cybersecurity defence, he added.

The challenge is finding ways to preserve those benefits as open-weight models become increasingly capable, researchers said.

Galeev said models should be evaluated after their safeguards have been removed, rather than relying solely on safety tests conducted under normal operating conditions. Developers could also consider staged releases, initially providing access through controlled interfaces or to trusted researchers before making the weights more widely available.

Yee of FAR.AI questioned whether the defensive benefits actually require unrestricted public release, or if providing access to trusted researchers and defenders under controlled conditions would suffice. Open-weight models currently take an extreme approach – offering “near-zero safeguards” and “maximum access for both defensive use but also offensive abuse,” he said.

Saxe, the former AI security tech lead at Meta, said the industry should focus more on restricting malicious users than the models themselves.

Stronger coordination among AI service providers to identify abusive users, share intelligence and terminate accounts, alongside measures to monitor access to advanced computing infrastructure, could help curb misuse without limiting legitimate access, he said.

“The goal should be to restrict attackers, not models, wherever possible,” Saxe said.

“AI gives us an extraordinary opportunity to find and repair vulnerabilities across the world’s enormous software infrastructure. We should be hardening as much of it as possible, as quickly as possible.”

Additional reporting by Minxiao Chang

item.title: [SCMP] China is moving past a GDP-first mindset. Can local officials get with the programme?
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the first part of this series, Frank Chen and Alice Li track the ways top-level policy decisions flow down to local officials – and the challenges those officials face in balancing a wide set of priorities.

When many took time off to enjoy China’s National Day holiday earlier this month, stories from media outlets in the eastern province of Jiangsu showed the region’s Communist Party chief, Xin Changxing, hard at work.

He started the day by conducting a safety inspection at a metro station, then visited local shops to see how sales were faring over the holiday. Later, he observed a fire drill before spending the rest of the day checking in on crowd control measures at major tourist hotspots.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the first part of this series, Frank Chen and Alice Li track the ways top-level policy decisions flow down to local officials – and the challenges those officials face in balancing a wide set of priorities.

When many took time off to enjoy China’s National Day holiday earlier this month, stories from media outlets in the eastern province of Jiangsu showed the region’s Communist Party chief, Xin Changxing, hard at work.

He started the day by conducting a safety inspection at a metro station, then visited local shops to see how sales were faring over the holiday. Later, he observed a fire drill before spending the rest of the day checking in on crowd control measures at major tourist hotspots.

As China’s economy continues its transition to an era of lower absolute growth figures but greater sophistication, Beijing has expanded its to-do lists for local officials like Xin who are on the front lines of implementing policy.

Once tasked almost solely with stimulating economic growth, these political cadres are now juggling a set of increasingly complex – and sometimes competing – priorities.

To name a few, officials are taking steps to fight corruption, maintain national security, improve public safety, reduce debt, create jobs, nurture China’s home-grown tech and keep the economy growing.

But under the weight of weak domestic consumption and a tepid property market, gross domestic product figures have been fluctuating. Earlier this year, Beijing said it would aim for 4.5 to 5.0 per cent GDP growth for 2026 – the lowest target since 1991.

Caution wins over initiative ... A mistake could cost them more than doing nothing

Alfredo Montufar-Helu, Ankura

While concerns grew about meeting that benchmark after a 4.3 per cent growth rate was reported in the second quarter, a 4.5 per cent rate recorded in the third quarter suggests the lower end of that range remains in sight, pushing the rate up to 4.6 per cent for the first nine months of the year.

All eyes are now on the fifth plenum of the party’s Central Committee, to be held from October 26 to 29. The meeting comes roughly one year before the party’s twice-a-decade national congress, a session expected to feature an extensive personnel reshuffle, including the formation of a new decision-making Politburo.

The plenum is an occasion for Beijing to clarify its policy goals. But analysts said the focus of this edition of the high-stakes gathering might be on the party’s self-improvement and strengthened rule.

Some observers expressed worries that Beijing’s shifting, sometimes contrasting priorities could divert local officials’ attention away from growth.

Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China managing director at consulting firm Ankura, said while economic development still mattered, Beijing’s definition of it had changed.

“Growth [is] increasingly judged by its contribution to security and tech self-reliance,” he said.

Local officials, typically risk-averse, would be paying close attention to the party’s signals, Montufar-Helu added.

“Caution wins over initiative,” he said. “A mistake could cost them more than doing nothing.”

Broadening priorities

While the policy juggling act expected of local officials is not a new phenomenon, analysts said more targets are being set.

“Every day, they might have different orders cascade down to them,” said Zhu Jiangnan, an associate professor of politics at the University of Hong Kong. “So what are the real priorities? Those emphasised more by the topmost leaders would become the ones to work on.”

But what localities are told to prioritise today is drastically different from the growth-centric mandate handed down decades ago.

Then, the binding principle was “economic construction”, shaped by China’s paramount leader Deng Xiaoping after he came to power at the end of the 1970s. Successive leaders such as Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao largely adhered to a similar policy.

But Xi Jinping, Communist Party general secretary since 2012 and president since 2013, has broadened what Beijing viewed as critical, analysts said.

First, there was his instruction to “coordinate economic development and security”, enshrined into the party constitution at its 20th national congress in 2022.

At the previous congress in 2017, he coined the term “high-quality development”, introducing another overarching principle to inform decision-making and indicate growth was no longer the only benchmark at play in policy work.

China’s intensifying rivalry with the US has also prompted Beijing to make self-reliance in tech another high-level mandate as it seeks to break the West’s chokehold on advanced products and components, with localities urged to coalesce their resources in this effort.

After Xi visited Shanghai twice this year – trips that were centred around tech – the city’s government gazetted two documents to supercharge basic research and innovation and promote the use of artificial intelligence, observers noted.

To help cadres at all levels tackle the new priorities, Beijing has been pushing to install a “correct” understanding of what constitutes good performance among officials since February, eyeing a strong start to its 15th five-year plan.

The move was seen as a pivot away from focusing on raw GDP growth and “at-all-costs” development as the sole criterion for promotion, placing the debt, fraud and vanity projects that sometimes resulted from this mindset in the crosshairs.

“Nowadays, the focus is on politics and party doctrine,” said the head of a government agency in Zhejiang province who declined to be named. The official, who oversees financing for small and medium-sized enterprises, said she and her colleagues were beginning to make decisions with more caution, weighing the political dimension alongside the economic realm.

“We study political theories and top leaders’ directives and apply them to our work,” she added.

Growth not out of focus

However, this shift in perspective has not left the problems plaguing the economy without a response. When momentum appeared to be waning in the second quarter despite a strong start to the year, Beijing held a succession of meetings, seminars and inspections dedicated to diagnosing and tackling the most pressing issues.

Larry Hu Weijun, chief China economist at Macquarie, said Beijing tended to take a dynamic and adaptable approach.

“Having multiple goals doesn’t mean growth is not important,” he said. “Rather, the importance of growth diminishes once the target is within reach, but rises sharply when the target is under threat.”

Recent actions bear this logic out. Last month, policymakers unveiled a series of measures in quick succession to resuscitate the economy: cutting policy interest rates, offering mortgage interest subsidies for homebuyers and unlocking 550 billion yuan (US$82.18 billion) in local debt quotas to boost investment.

At a meeting of the party’s Politburo in July, Beijing pledged to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending, promptly roll out incremental policies and speed up the transition of growth models for the remainder of the year amid rising volatility in global markets and the second-quarter GDP downturn.

Among these efforts, top economic planner the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Finance and the People’s Bank of China have set up a 100 billion yuan fiscal-financial coordination fund to boost domestic demand.

Policymakers have resisted letting loose a stimulus “flood”, saying their intent has been to focus on countercyclical adjustments and the precise targeting of priority areas, including private and small-scale enterprises, domestic demand and the green energy transition.

Putting officials on notice

However, local officials are frequently reminded on what their priorities are – and how they must deliver. Beijing is unafraid to name and shame as it admonishes deviations in the understanding and implementation of its directives.

One area that has been given extra attention in recent years is public safety, particularly in the wake of several natural disasters. Central authorities have stepped up scrutiny of local governments this year over safety issues and tightened accountability.

Since September, over 400 officials across four regions – Hainan and Jiangsu provinces, as well as the Guangxi Zhuang and Xinjiang Uygur autonomous regions – have been held responsible for safety risks and lapses in local oversight following evaluations by central government inspectors.

Beijing has also taken a closer interest in localities that have been instructed to fire up their economic engines, examining the results of their efforts in detail and doling out penalties for ill-fated or extravagant projects.

In June, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection – the party’s chief anti-corruption organ – named and shamed officials in Jiangxi, Sichuan and Hebei provinces, as well as the Guangxi and Inner Mongolia autonomous regions, for chasing development that increased debt risks and using public funds for projects that did not return a profit.

Businesses get reality check

As local officials work to navigate Beijing’s shifting requirements, they may in turn alter their practices as they deal with businesses, particularly the private and foreign firms operating in the country.

While some firms have acknowledged the need to curb debt and move away from a GDP-first mindset, others have voiced concerns about mixed, even conflicting signals and structural mismatches in policy implementation.

The American Chamber of Commerce in China flagged some of these issues in its annual white paper.

“Central directives prioritising hi-tech self-reliance and domestic national security controls often clash directly with local-level efforts to rebuild foreign business confidence and revive consumer spending,” the chamber wrote in April.

The business advocacy body called on policymakers to create a “proportionate, predictable balance” between national security and economic openness, warning sudden shifts or conflicting signals could lead multinationals to defer long-term investments.

A heavier focus on national security and public safety has been cited by some business figures as complicating their operating environment.

One common complaint, for instance, centres on frequent safety inspections and red tape disrupting firms’ normal operations and adding to their costs. A report published last year in an online content platform run by the Chongqing municipal committee of the Chinese Communist Party noted that some companies were subjected to four or five safety inspections in a single week.

Ankura’s Montufar-Helu said Beijing’s increasing emphasis on security and party discipline has made local officials more risk-averse as they choose which projects and businesses to support with incentives.

“Local governments will steer resources towards the sectors Beijing has flagged as strategic and away from anything that looks risky … Officials will be slower to back projects that could draw scrutiny, including those involving foreign and private companies,” he warned.

“For them, getting things done with local authorities is likely to be harder.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why are Turkey, Pakistan, Qatar and Indonesia joining forces?
item.description:
A decision by Turkey, Pakistan, Qatar and Indonesia to jointly develop and produce weapons systems marks a major push to reduce reliance on Western armaments that come with political strings attached, observers say.

Following the signing of the Badr memorandum of understanding in Doha on Wednesday, the four governments separately said they would work towards integrating their defence industries and supply chains to meet military needs.

“By leveraging the capabilities of each country in the field of military production, cooperation and integration will be achieved, defence industry capacities will be developed, and the needs of allied and friendly nations can thus be met,” Turkey’s Ministry of Defence said.
item.content:encoded:
A decision by Turkey, Pakistan, Qatar and Indonesia to jointly develop and produce weapons systems marks a major push to reduce reliance on Western armaments that come with political strings attached, observers say.

Following the signing of the Badr memorandum of understanding in Doha on Wednesday, the four governments separately said they would work towards integrating their defence industries and supply chains to meet military needs.

“By leveraging the capabilities of each country in the field of military production, cooperation and integration will be achieved, defence industry capacities will be developed, and the needs of allied and friendly nations can thus be met,” Turkey’s Ministry of Defence said.

Nato member Turkey, which has the most prolific defence industry of the new grouping, is slated to host most of the production facilities. But Western technology would remain indispensable – especially for advanced propulsion, avionics, sensors and certain electronic components, analysts said.

Access to these technologies is frequently subject to export controls and political restrictions – and the Badr pact is partly “to escape precisely this vulnerability”, according to Andreas Krieg, a former British defence ministry adviser to Qatar’s armed forces.

He described the new pact as an attempt to reduce dependency on Western suppliers of sophisticated equipment for maintenance, ammunition, technology – and “ultimately political decisions about how and when those systems can be used”. The Iran war had “exposed the limitations” of a regional security system reliant on external suppliers.

“Badr is an attempt to reduce that dependence by pooling industrial capabilities, rather than simply pooling military forces,” said Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London.

The Badr MOU is the second such step taken recently by Muslim-majority states in response to the chaos from the US-Israel conflict with Iran and its regional militia allies. Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan formed the Mecca Defence Alliance in early August.

“[Mecca] offers a political promise of deterrence, while [Badr] could eventually help supply the means to sustain it,” Krieg said.

Badr was as much an exercise in building strategic relationships as it was an industrial agreement, he added. Joint factories, shared intellectual property and integrated supply chains “can bind countries together more durably than declarations of strategic friendship”.

‘Statement of desire’

Viewed together, the overlapping agreements could be seen as an emerging strategic challenge by countries viewed as hostile to the Badr signatories, analysts said.

Former senior Pentagon official Dave Des Roches said the Badr MOU was politically significant because it represented a “statement of desire” by the four countries to acquire advanced military capability for defence.

For Qatar, “of course, right now the main issue is Iran”, which has repeatedly targeted its energy infrastructure and shipping in response to the war launched by Israel and the US on February 28, said Des Roches, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, a think tank based in Washington and Doha.

Tensions between Turkey and Israel over Syria have been rising since Islamist rebels seized power from Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024. Des Roches saw the possibility of “limited clashes” between the two in Syria because Ankara viewed the country as a “client state and spirit influence”, while Tel Aviv thought of President Ahmed Sharaa’s regime as a “serious defence vulnerability”.

Indonesia differs in that it faces no imminent threat, being far from the Middle East and not a party to the South China Sea dispute. Its prime objective is strategic autonomy.

On the other hand, Pakistan has fought several wars with India over the last 80 years, most recently a short air conflict in May 2025.

The nuclear-armed rivalry between Pakistan and India was “the wild card”, Des Roches said, because the ruling Hindu nationalist government in New Delhi could potentially view Badr as evidence that Indonesia, the world’s most populous Muslim-majority country, had been “enlisted as a military ally or partner” of Islamabad.

Similarly, Krieg said Tehran would see Badr as an increasingly interconnected defence-industrial network emerging around it, even though its individual members have different threat perceptions.

While Qatar was not joining an anti-Iranian military alliance and remained committed to dialogue with Tehran, Doha “increasingly recognises that diplomacy must be supported by credible deterrence” – particularly through the ability to deny an adversary the military advantages of attacking the country.

“This creates an additional deterrent, but also the risk that Iran interprets greater Gulf military cooperation as a form of strategic encirclement,” Krieg said.

Military balance

Israel’s greatest concern would be Turkey’s growing ability to organise defence-industrial relationships beyond Nato while for India, the principal issue would be Pakistan’s ability to diversify its military-industrial partnerships beyond China, Krieg said.

Turkish technology, Qatari investment and access to additional industrial partners could gradually improve Pakistan’s technological capabilities and reduce some of its supply vulnerabilities. “That is consequential for the long-term military balance with India,” Krieg said.

Both analysts were sceptical, though, that the Badr MOU could have an immediate impact on the military capabilities of all four nations. “It would take a very long time indeed,” Des Roches said.

There was obvious scope for Turkey to develop unmanned aerial systems and naval ships for its partners, while Pakistan’s defence industry could provide basic military materials like Nato-standard artillery ammunition – “but it’s hard to see how they would acquire, for example, the sort of air defence network that they need from this alliance”, Des Roches said.

He saw the agreement as “making sense in the abstract but not … in real life” because of issues such as transfer of technology restrictions placed on Turkey by its Nato suppliers.

Badr risked becoming “another ambitious memorandum that generates committees and announcements without creating a functioning industrial ecosystem”, Krieg said.

Its credibility would depend on whether the partners commit real funding, allocate production responsibilities and agree on intellectual property and export rights.

Badr’s success should be measured “not by the number of agreements signed”, but by whether it produces equipment that member states can manufacture, maintain and replenish “without constantly turning to outside suppliers”, Krieg said.

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia’s housing paradox: too many homes, too few buyers
item.description:
In parts of Southeast Asia, unsold homes are piling up as developers struggle to clear housing stock – yet young buyers hoping to land their first property still cannot find an affordable home.

The paradox reflects a growing mismatch between the homes being built and what aspiring buyers can afford, according to analysts, who point to speculative investment, financing hurdles and poor locations as factors leaving properties empty even amid demand for affordable housing.

In Vietnam, the problem centres on what developers have built and the returns they expect, according to Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. His research examines how the country’s increasing reliance on land to finance growth can favour property investment over the housing needs of new urban families.
item.content:encoded:
In parts of Southeast Asia, unsold homes are piling up as developers struggle to clear housing stock – yet young buyers hoping to land their first property still cannot find an affordable home.

The paradox reflects a growing mismatch between the homes being built and what aspiring buyers can afford, according to analysts, who point to speculative investment, financing hurdles and poor locations as factors leaving properties empty even amid demand for affordable housing.

In Vietnam, the problem centres on what developers have built and the returns they expect, according to Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. His research examines how the country’s increasing reliance on land to finance growth can favour property investment over the housing needs of new urban families.

The pressures take a different form in the Philippines, where investment-led condominium projects and low initial payment plans have left some buyers unable to complete their purchases.

In Malaysia, meanwhile, a substantial share of completed unsold homes falls within the price range conventionally described as “affordable”, raising a different question: why do these properties not meet the needs of the people who could buy them?

Competing interests

According to Vietnam’s construction ministry, the country’s reported property inventory reached about 51,950 units and land plots in the third quarter of 2026. This number covered 27 of 34 provincial-level localities and included housing and land, not just completed empty flats.

Meanwhile, flats priced at 70 million dong to 100 million dong (US$2,707 to US$3,867) per square metre accounted for about 48 per cent of third-quarter launches, according to the Vietnam Association of Realtors. Another 23 per cent cost between 100 million dong and 200 million dong.

Giang said local governments’ pursuit of land revenue and developers’ expectations of rising prices helped explain the imbalance. Higher land costs encouraged more expensive projects to recover the investment.

“During a boom, serving ordinary buyers becomes less attractive than betting on further appreciation,” he said.

A paper Giang published in August put land-related revenue at 575.5 trillion dong in 2025, or 21.7 per cent of state revenue. However, linking public finances and bank lending to property values left both vulnerable to falling prices, he warned.

“Cheaper land could improve affordability, but it would also weaken public revenues and the financing of infrastructure. The state therefore has competing objectives: affordable homes and valuable land.”

Sharp price falls would also hurt developers and banks holding property-backed loans. Developers able to refinance or hold inventory faced less pressure to discount, Giang said.

“These pressures can delay a correction, although they cannot prevent one indefinitely.”

His paper cited China as a warning about dependence on property-linked revenues and called for more transparent land allocation and investment of land-value gains in compensation and affordable housing.

For buyers, the shortage of homes within the reach of ordinary incomes made deposits and repayments daunting.

“Mortgage-rate uncertainty adds another barrier, because a buyer who can afford the introductory rate may struggle when it resets. Easier loan approval alone cannot fix that,” Giang said.

Low entry

In the Philippines, the gap between entering the property market and sustaining home ownership is evident in the way some condominiums are sold, according to Joey Roi Bondoc, research director at Colliers Philippines.

Developers marketed instalments as little more than a buyer’s monthly “Starbucks budget”, Bondoc said, meaning buyers could spread a small down payment across several years while the building was under construction.

For example, Bondoc calculated that the 10 per cent down payment on a 7-million peso (US$109,560) flat could be spread over 60 months. But once the unit was completed, the buyer would need to finance the much larger outstanding balance through a bank loan.

Monthly payments could then triple or quadruple, he said, with some buyers unable to afford the difference or obtain loan approval.

The problem was compounded by the influx, then retreat, of Philippine offshore gaming operators (Pogos), whose workers had supplied rental demand during the condominium boom. Investors had expected that income to help cover their payments, Bondoc said.

Bondoc noted that speculative demand peaked between 2017 and 2019, when developers were completing almost 14,000 condominium units annually. From 2027 to 2029, he said he expected annual completions to range around 6,000 in response to weaker market conditions.

Yet the unsold stock does not necessarily offer an accessible alternative for homebuyers.

Colliers’ data shows that more than 40 per cent of Metro Manila’s 32,600 unsold units fall within the company’s “lower-mid” price segment of between 3.6 million and 7 million pesos. But this is a market category, not a guarantee of affordability for an early-career worker.

Bondoc estimated that buyers considering homes in that segment should earn at least 70,000 pesos a month. That figure, however, is about 2.4 times more than the average monthly wage in Metro Manila of 29,310 pesos, according to the 2024 national wage survey.

For some workers, even renting near employment centres remains too expensive. Bondoc described employees commuting from Cavite, Bulacan and Laguna to Metro Manila, with journeys taking an hour or two because they could not afford accommodation nearer their jobs.

Market mismatch

Malaysia shows that unsold housing is not confined to expensive properties.

Recent data from Malaysia’s National Property Information Centre revealed that 33,094 completed residential units remained unsold in the first half of 2026, of which 37.3 per cent (12,340 units) were priced at 300,000 ringgit (US$73,400) or below.

Siva Shanker of Rahim & Co Chestertons, a property consultancy, said unsold homes could reflect the wrong product, location, price, or a combination of all three. In his experience, location was often the main problem.

Lower-priced homes built far from workplaces and schools could force households into unmanageable commutes, he said. “The person or household would rather not buy, they would just rent something nearby.”

For younger buyers, Siva identified a separate obstacle: raising the cash needed even when monthly repayments appeared manageable.

Using a hypothetical 500,000 ringgit home financed with an 80 per cent loan, he said a buyer would need 100,000 ringgit for the deposit alone, before other upfront expenses such as conveyancing fees and stamp duty. Not to mention potentially another five-figure sum for home renovations.

“They may be able to afford the repayment” but lack the down payment, he said. Potential buyers might also postpone ownership to save for the down payment, only to find prices had increased.

“They end up chasing forever,” he said.

In Malaysia’s recent Budget 2027 reading, the government announced measures to help first-time buyers, such as 20 billion ringgit in financing guarantees through the state-managed Housing Credit Guarantee Scheme targeting up to 80,000 first-timers, particularly the self-employed without fixed incomes.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim also proposed full stamp duty exemptions on transfer documents and loan agreements for first homes costing up to 500,000 ringgit, covering purchase agreements signed between January 2027 and December 2030.

Similarly in Vietnam, the construction ministry proposed in April to promote lower-cost commercial housing and accelerate a 145 trillion dong credit programme for social and worker housing, including support for buyers under 35.

But financing support alone would not resolve the price-income gap, Giang said.

“Even a sizeable discount on an expensive flat can’t help much for young first-home buyers.”

item.title: [SCMP] Climate damage to Philippine ports could cost US$70b a year by 2100
item.description:
The Philippines faces the highest climate-driven port damage costs in Southeast Asia, with annual losses projected to hit US$70.2 billion by 2100, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has warned.

Analysts say the damage could cripple supply chains, drive up food prices and threaten livelihoods, urging Manila to adopt a more coordinated approach to flood protection rather than simply strengthening port infrastructure.

In its latest report titled “Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026: Coastal Risks on the Rise – Actions for a Resilient Future”, the ADB said the Philippines could sustain US$20.6 billion in port damage under a moderate-emissions scenario, in which sea levels were projected to rise by 50cm to 80cm.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines faces the highest climate-driven port damage costs in Southeast Asia, with annual losses projected to hit US$70.2 billion by 2100, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has warned.

Analysts say the damage could cripple supply chains, drive up food prices and threaten livelihoods, urging Manila to adopt a more coordinated approach to flood protection rather than simply strengthening port infrastructure.

In its latest report titled “Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026: Coastal Risks on the Rise – Actions for a Resilient Future”, the ADB said the Philippines could sustain US$20.6 billion in port damage under a moderate-emissions scenario, in which sea levels were projected to rise by 50cm to 80cm.

A high-emissions scenario where sea levels could rise up to 1 metre could see annual port damages climb to US$70.2 billion by 2100.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the Philippines only trails China, with projected annual losses ranging from US$82.2 billion to US$332 billion, while India’s projections are from US$70 billion to US$254 billion, which would be expected to include the cost of repairing damaged port infrastructure and losses from maritime trade disruption.

Port damage can disrupt operations, delay shipments and interrupt supply chains that businesses and communities rely on for essential goods.

“Because these networks link farms to markets, fishers to buyers, and households to health services and food supplies, their disruption cascades directly into livelihoods, nutrition, and well-being,” said the report, released last Wednesday.

“The extent of exposed infrastructure is likely to increase as urban development increasingly puts these built assets in harm’s way.”

In September, the Philippine Ports Authority (PPA), the agency tasked with regulating and managing the country’s seaports, said that it had embarked on efforts to strengthen its infrastructure, including climate- and disaster-resilient measures, to ensure business continuity and that ports could withstand typhoons and earthquakes and continue moving essential items in times of emergencies.

“We continue to conduct drills, test different scenarios, strengthen coordination, and improve our infrastructure so that when a disaster comes, our ports can continue serving as safe and reliable lifelines for the country,” PPA general manager Jay Santiago said in a statement.

This Week in Asia has reached out to the authority for comments on the ADB report.

Manuel Jose Camagay, a transport, urban and logistics specialist, said the Philippines bore higher logistics costs than its neighbours in mainland Southeast Asia.

“Ports are gateways to supply chains and natural disasters play the crucial villainous role of disrupting the normal flow of goods and people across the country,” he said.

Ven Paolo Valenzuela, a research fellow at Singapore Management University’s College of Integrative Studies, said that when ports failed in an archipelagic country, the whole economy would stumble.

“We’re very dependent on ports. Your food prices spike, your supply chain is severely disrupted, and post-typhoon relief cannot access devastated islands or coastal communities,” Valenzuela said.

He echoed the report’s implications, adding that port damage created a compounding effect, from physical destruction to longer operational downtime.

Valenzuela added that sea level rise was not the sole factor that could devastate ports, though it amplified other hazards such as coastal flooding from storm surges, powerful winds from intensifying tropical cyclones and coastal erosion in port areas.

“Because of that, the disruption ripples across industries’ supply chains. You cannot move goods from Luzon to Visayas without going through a port,” he said, calling the problem a “big gap”.

More than 20 typhoons hit the Philippines each year, affecting ports that dot its coasts.

Typhoon Haiyan in 2013 showed “how storm surges can wipe out ports and the communities around them”, Valenzuela said.

Camagay said that port damage was tantamount to trade and economic loss due to shipment delays and disruptions of basic commodities, losses of raw materials and equipment to continue operations, higher cost of goods and forgone income when deadlines were not met.

He also called ports “employment magnets” given their appeal to flocks of migrant workers living in urban areas around these ports.

Such communities were directly affected by port damage and coastal flooding, Valenzuela said, adding that Metro Manila’s main port complex, which handled the bulk of the country’s international and domestic container throughput, was vulnerable to storm surges, coastal flooding and knock-on effects of groundwater extraction.

Other coastal hubs such as Iloilo, Cebu, Batangas, Subic, Davao and Cagayan de Oro were seeing rapid urbanisation in flood-prone zones that outpaced the building of drainage and other protective infrastructure, he said.

Beyond port infrastructure

Valenzuela said the Philippines lacked the means to protect its ports against climate change.

“Technically, we know how to elevate and climate-proof ports – my own research in Japan proves it can be done sequentially without halting trade,” he said.

“It’s easy to defend the port itself, but if the surrounding infrastructure isn’t planned as a system, it doesn’t matter how nice your defences are.”

Valenzuela said that raising a port to address sea level rise would be “pointless” if drainage systems from the land were blocked and if the challenges of land sinking were not addressed.

As for seismic risks, the Philippines cannot afford to ignore them, as it is a country prone to earthquakes, according to Valenzuela.

Meanwhile, the Philippines could look to Indonesia and Singapore to learn how these countries had progressively upgraded their port facilities to mitigate climate impact without causing disruptions to cargo operations, he said.

Indonesia had deployed floating piers, pontoons and logistics bases that could adjust to rising water levels, Valenzuela said.

Singapore had been protecting its ports as part of its national efforts against rising sea levels, anchored by a multibillion-dollar coastal and flood protection fund, he added.

Camagay said that at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations level, the bloc could also do its part to mitigate climate damage such as through its proposed adoption of green shipping operations, he added.

“The goal is to reduce, if not eliminate, the carbon footprint not only from the sea vessels but also from the cargo, the packaging and the use of plastics and anything that impacts the environment.”

item.title: [SCMP] Can Hong Kong deliver in trying to build its yuan credentials?
item.description:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority.

In the first of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing and Denise Tsang examine Hong Kong’s efforts as an international financial centre to reform its market infrastructure, including building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem.

As Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, met in Washington for a historic summit last month, Hong Kong was preparing for a longer-term move: reducing reliance on the US dollar and boosting the yuan’s global use.
item.content:encoded:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority.

In the first of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing and Denise Tsang examine Hong Kong’s efforts as an international financial centre to reform its market infrastructure, including building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem.

As Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, met in Washington for a historic summit last month, Hong Kong was preparing for a longer-term move: reducing reliance on the US dollar and boosting the yuan’s global use.

While the two leaders got down to business, a mainland China-based asset management firm rolled out a suite of new renminbi products in the city to considerable fanfare. China Asset Management (Hong Kong), the city’s largest provider of listed offshore renminbi products, presented the broad range of exchange-traded funds to bankers, journalists and investors.

The company, already known for launching the world’s first offshore tokenised yuan money market fund, is not merely pursuing retail investors. It is also at the front line of a coordinated institutional push to build financial protection around Chinese capital against Western market volatility.

The firm’s CEO, Gan Tian, pointed to the recent Middle East crisis as a major “stress test” that demonstrated the Chinese currency’s resilience, noting that the renminbi remained firm even as the US dollar surged and Asian peers like the Japanese yen fell sharply.

“On the path to yuan internationalisation, in this stress test in the first half, the People’s Bank of China has already sent a clear message to the smartest investors in the world,” Gan said.

“If de-dollarisation is a medium- to long-term trend, once you pull your money out of the US dollar, where exactly should you put it? The renminbi is the unparalleled choice.”

Driven by intensifying US-China rivalry and the strategic need to mobilise mainland capital safely abroad despite capital controls, Hong Kong is rapidly transforming its market infrastructure – building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem, developing independent gold clearing and testing alternative payment channels.

Once primarily a bridge for Western capital entering the mainland, Hong Kong is now positioning itself to support China’s financial resilience, analysts say. The aim, they add, is to establish the city as a launch pad for financial products and payment channels that rely less on traditional Western networks.

Earlier this year, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po expressed confidence that Hong Kong, currently behind New York and London in the global ranking of international financial centres, would climb to at least second place within 10 to 15 years.

In a recent interview with the South China Morning Post, Chan explained the city’s efforts on yuan internationalisation and their relevance to Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre.

Chan singled out Hong Kong’s unique role as a firewall for China’s financial security, with yuan-related products and services tested in the city.

“From China’s standpoint, to build a strong country, we need to have a strong currency. But this needs time,” Chan said.

“To strengthen the global utilisation and influence of renminbi, it is the user-case scenario, a substantive business-user case.”

‘Tremendous room for growth’

Chan said he expected global use of the yuan to rise amid geopolitical tensions.

He noted that China accounted for 14 to 15 per cent of global imports and exports combined, but only about 4 per cent of trade was invoiced in yuan last year. The ratio had grown a lot compared with a year earlier, he said.

Foreign investors have shown a strong appetite for trading in mainland stocks through cross-border schemes such as Northbound Stock Connect.

“There is tremendous room for future growth, particularly given the geopolitical context. Most countries are trying to use their own currency in terms of trading,” Chan said.

Hong Kong is the world’s biggest offshore renminbi market, with about 1.3 trillion yuan of deposits as at the end of July, according to the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau.

A high-profile move to tap international capital took place in August when China’s Ministry of Finance sold 15 billion yuan worth of sovereign bonds in Hong Kong to a strong response from institutional investors.

The sale took place just days after the city launched a long-awaited tool designed to help global investors hedge against risks in the mainland bond market.

Ho Lok-sang, adjunct professor of economics at Lingnan University, said the renminbi remained very much underutilised and did not reflect China’s economic strength, leaving huge potential for wider use.

“What we are after in the long run is that we want to build a more inclusive kind of system,” Ho said.

“At present, the current system, which is very much predominated by the US dollar, is not really an inclusive system, and especially as it has been weaponised.”

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent advocated in early September for Washington to use its financial power as a foreign policy tool to advance the interests of American allies, including ‌in financial and political situations abroad.

Meanwhile, the US Treasury Department has warned under its “Operation Economic Outcast” that entities facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risk being cut off from the US financial system, citing several Hong Kong-based companies that did business with Iran.

“China has been thinking strategically against the possibility that the US might impose different kinds of sanctions, and China is really extremely alert … strategically very, very smart,” Ho said.

Testing ground

Hard data shows the shift away from US dollar-centric systems is well under way in Hong Kong’s capital markets.

Beijing is using Hong Kong to test a China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform, mBridge, as a potential alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system. The effort has gained momentum in recent years amid heightened tensions between the world’s two largest economies and growing concerns over the reliability of the US dollar as it becomes politicised.

The project faced a setback late last month after a key participant – the Saudi Central Bank – confirmed its departure after completing what it described as “a limited proof-of-concept” trial in May last year.

Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu told the SCMP in an interview earlier this month that the Saudi departure would “not really” affect the wider experiment.

“Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said.

“So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.”

Beyond payments infrastructure, Hong Kong is also seeking to make the yuan more attractive for corporate financing.

Multinational firms need to borrow large sums of cash to run their global operations. Historically, many borrowed yen because Japan had the lowest interest rates.

But recently, the script has flipped. Japan’s 10-year sovereign bond yield rose above 3 per cent in early September, while China’s dropped below 1.7 per cent, Gan of ChinaAMC (HK) said.

Global companies were now flocking to Hong Kong to borrow yuan by issuing dim sum bonds – offshore renminbi-denominated bonds – because they offered cheaper funding, Gan said.

He noted that this rush for cheap borrowing had caused the dim sum bond market to explode to 1 trillion yuan, making it significantly larger than Hong Kong’s traditional stock IPO market.

When massive Chinese companies, such as appliance maker Midea, made profits overseas, they faced a huge problem: exchange rates were swinging wildly, Gan said.

Midea suffered a foreign exchange loss of almost 6 billion yuan in six months because the value of the currencies it was holding dropped. Normally, companies buy financial “insurance” with hedging to protect against these US dollar swings, but that insurance can cost 2.5 per cent of the hedged amount every year.

To reduce losses from volatile exchange rates, Chinese companies were simply refusing to convert their cash. Instead, they were parking their overseas profits directly into offshore yuan funds in Hong Kong, Gan said.

Liquidity boost

Chan, the finance chief, has pledged a multipronged strategy to boost yuan liquidity through an array of products. In addition to Chinese treasury bonds, he has pointed to opportunities in stock trading.

He said authorities would consider expanding the number of listed companies whose shares investors could trade using offshore yuan. At present, there are 23 such companies with renminbi business counters.

Chan said another strategy was to allow China-based investors to use renminbi to trade in Hong Kong-listed shares through the Southbound Stock Connect scheme.

“If we can achieve that, the liquidity will be quickly increased,” he said. “In summary, we want to have more product offerings.”

For Hong Kong’s manufacturers and traders, the stakes extend beyond financial markets.

Anthony Lam Sai-ho, chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong Industries, said that pricing commodities in renminbi would link finance more directly with physical supply chains, giving manufacturers a “natural hedge” against exchange rate volatility.

“If we can trade commodities in renminbi … it provides manufacturers and stakeholders with an additional method to hedge and predict procurement costs, reducing currency fluctuation,” Lam said.

He added that while markets were accustomed to US dollar pricing, importing raw materials such as rice or base metals directly in local currencies or renminbi would reduce the risk of being caught between shifting exchange rates.

“It is less about avoiding the US dollar out of fear, and more about giving the market an additional option to balance trade,” Lam added.

Commodity trading had so far started with gold but could extend to other metals, energy, grains, soft commodities and even livestock, Lam said.

Alternative clearing networks, meanwhile, are expanding their reach. China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) processed 180 trillion yuan in cross-border payments in 2025, up 373.6 times the 2015 level, according to its website.

CIPS said it provided secure, efficient, convenient and low-cost cross-border renminbi payment and settlement services for global users, offering an additional channel beyond the US-dominated financial system.

That existing US dollar-based system relies heavily on Swift, the Belgium-based Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, which connects more than 12,500 institutions across more than 220 countries and territories and enables global trade.

Dollar payments are also settled through the Clearing House Interbank Payments System (Chips), a private-sector, high-value clearing and settlement system that helps financial institutions move domestic and cross-border wire payments, according to its website.

Under Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address in September, the government has established the Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing Company and will implement targeted measures to boost the trading and settlement of gold futures contracts using the offshore renminbi.

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said market participants would have another option if access to dollar-based channels were restricted.

“A gold clearing system allows gold transactions via a local central ledger without relying on the Swift messaging network or the Chips payment system, thereby providing an alternative store of value,” Shui said.

“Unlike fiat currencies, gold is a physical commodity that inherently holds value, making it a trusted safe asset not directly tied to any jurisdiction.”

Gan of ChinaAMC (HK) said that having huge physical gold reserves in Hong Kong provided foreigners using offshore renminbi in the city with a “Plan B” if they wanted to convert or transfer those funds.

“They do not need to convert their assets into US dollars, British pounds or Japanese yen to move them globally; they can directly exchange them for physical gold in Hong Kong and have it delivered anywhere in the world,” he said.

“Therefore, gold, acting as a ‘Plan B’ and the most important collateral asset of the future, will support the development of the offshore renminbi in Hong Kong.”

The peg question

The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association warned that an overnight shift away from the US dollar was unrealistic.

“If de-dollarisation is overemphasised, international investors might interpret it as a signal of declining openness,” said the association’s chairman, Mofiz Chan.

Chan said Hong Kong had to strike a delicate balance between securing multiple sources of capital and maintaining its international free-market reputation with compliance, transparency and neutral standing.

To make this “financial armour” truly functional, the association called for specific technological and regulatory upgrades.

Gregory Yu, head of markets at Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, told the SCMP that the exchange was focused on building a more comprehensive offshore renminbi ecosystem spanning equities, fixed income, currencies and commodities, and it was actively exploring opportunities to expand the range of yuan-denominated products.

“Initiatives including the continued expansion of the LME’s warehouse network in Hong Kong strengthen the market infrastructure that supports trading, storage and delivery activities across the region,” Yu said, referring to the London Metal Exchange.

Yu added that the bourse continued to explore opportunities to enhance market efficiency through innovation, including in digital assets and tokenisation.

“Together with ongoing market infrastructure enhancements, these efforts strengthen Hong Kong’s role as the world’s leading offshore renminbi hub and reinforce its position as an international financial centre connecting China and the world,” Yu said.

But any push to reduce reliance on the US dollar runs up against a basic constraint: the Hong Kong dollar remains pegged to it.

Ho Lok-sang argued that linking exclusively to the US dollar exposed Hong Kong to extreme economic swings, recalling the 1985 “super dollar” phase, when the city lost its export competitiveness.

“It’s much, much, much better if we can peg a basket of currencies … and now devise a way to seamlessly adopt the system without any shock at all,” Ho said.

“We can continue with the linked exchange rate system, but we just link with the basket,” he added, referring to a GDP-weighted basket that would include the renminbi, euro, yen, British pound and the US, Australian and Canadian dollars.

Chan, the finance chief, along with city leader John Lee Ka-chiu have said repeatedly the government has no intention of changing the 43-year-old peg, which has been underpinning the city’s economy.

At the end of the day, the key buzzwords are hedging and strategic planning, analysts say.

And the official regulatory response has been to rapidly deepen the multi-asset ecosystem and expand mutual market access to facilitate this capital transition.

“For Hong Kong, this means strengthening its role as a resilient international financial centre while supporting the financing of Chinese technology companies and renminbi internationalisation,” Shui of the think tank said.

item.title: [SCMP] Lula pulls off Brazil’s first-ever run-off comeback to beat Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro
item.description:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won re-election on Sunday in a dramatic comeback after trailing in the first round, extending the rule of a government that has overseen record Chinese investment.

The Superior Electoral Court said Lula had 51.8 per cent of valid votes against 48.2 per cent for right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. No candidate who trailed after the first round had won a run-off since Brazil adopted the system in 1989.

Addressing reporters and allies at a hotel in Sao Paulo, Lula said: “This election was one in which we had to defeat interference coming from outside, through digital platforms, and we are going to have to regulate them”.
item.content:encoded:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won re-election on Sunday in a dramatic comeback after trailing in the first round, extending the rule of a government that has overseen record Chinese investment.

The Superior Electoral Court said Lula had 51.8 per cent of valid votes against 48.2 per cent for right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. No candidate who trailed after the first round had won a run-off since Brazil adopted the system in 1989.

Addressing reporters and allies at a hotel in Sao Paulo, Lula said: “This election was one in which we had to defeat interference coming from outside, through digital platforms, and we are going to have to regulate them”.

“This country does not accept being anyone’s backyard,” he added.

He also vowed to lead an energy and AI revolution in South America’s biggest economy.

“We have to take advantage of the energy potential of a country that perhaps has the greatest renewable energy capacity, to bring here the data centres needed to keep our data in Brazil as well,” Lula promised.

But the outcome could still be contested after a Supreme Court justice ordered polls to stay open for two more hours, minutes after voting officially ended at 5pm. No court had extended voting in Brazil before.

The order came from Justice Cristiano Zanin, who was Lula’s lawyer before joining the court in 2023. He acted on a complaint from Lula’s campaign that cities in Bahia state run by allies of Flavio Bolsonaro had kept buses in depots and that poorer voters could not reach the polls.

Flavio Bolsonaro’s lawyers had separately asked the electoral court to extend voting in 17 flooded municipalities in three states.

Many stations had already shut their machines when Zanin’s order arrived, and the system does not allow a closed machine to be reopened. The electoral court then told regional courts that only stations still open should keep receiving voters until 7pm, and Zanin narrowed his order to match.

Flavio Bolsonaro refused to acknowledge defeat in a speech to reporters at his campaign headquarters in Brasilia on Sunday night, about 90 minutes after the result was confirmed.

“It is impossible to recognise the results of the elections in the context in which these things happened. We are going to use our legal team, we are going to ask for these elections to be annulled,” he said.

Some voters were sent home at 5pm while others cast ballots until 7pm, and either campaign could cite that to seek an annulment. Any such request would go to the electoral court, chaired by Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed by former president Jair Bolsonaro, the senator’s father.

The result keeps Latin America’s largest economy – and Beijing’s biggest destination for Chinese capital – out of the group of Trump-aligned governments that now includes Argentina, Chile and Colombia, frustrating Washington’s bid to curb Beijing’s presence in the hemisphere.

Talks with the US over tariffs and critical minerals would resume with a government that has offered American companies access to its rare earths but without preferential treatment.

Lula’s programme also commits Brazil to a regional strategy for mapping and processing critical minerals, and to pressing ahead with a Brics agenda that Trump has threatened to punish with extra tariffs. Brics is a grouping of Global South economies formed to increase global economic cooperation and counter Western dominance.

While Washington offered no immediate comment, leaders across Latin America swiftly congratulated Lula, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hailed his victory as a win for democracy.

Lula, who at 80 is Brazil’s oldest-ever sitting president, will begin his fourth term in January, more than two decades after he first took office.

He governed from 2003 to 2010 and returned in 2023 after narrowly beating the elder Bolsonaro, who is now serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting to overturn that defeat.

Flavio Bolsonaro built a campaign around ties to the Trump administration, which received him in the Oval Office in May. Flavio Bolsonaro pledged to join a US-led security alliance in the Americas and offered Brazil’s rare earths to Washington as an alternative to Chinese supply.

For most of this year, Lula had looked like the favourite, and pollster Quaest gave him a seven-point lead over the senator in a run-off in January.

Six of the seven pollsters that published surveys on the eve of the first round still had him ahead, yet he finished 2.2 million votes behind.

Most run-off polls showed Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly ahead or tied within the margin of error. Lula’s team tried to deepen voters’ resistance to his rival and to bring first-round abstainers back to the polls.

Lula’s political attacks focused on Jair Bolsonaro’s handling of the Covid-19 pandemic and on Flavio Bolsonaro’s dealings with Daniel Vorcaro, a banker who is now in jail.

The senator had asked that banker for US$24 million to fund a biopic of his father, months before the central bank shut down the financial institution for suspected fraud.

Flavio Bolsonaro responded by raising a police investigation into Lula’s son Fabio Luis.

A Supreme Court justice authorised the inquiry in July to examine whether he lobbied officials for a company linked to a scheme that allegedly skimmed money from pensioners’ benefits, and Lula said in a televised debate this month that the fraud had begun under Jair Bolsonaro’s government.

Sovereignty and Washington

Lula has tried to keep a working relationship with Trump, whom he met at the White House in May for about three hours as Brazil sought to head off a new round of tariffs.

Washington imposed duties of up to 50 per cent on Brazilian goods last year in protest at Jair Bolsonaro’s trial.

During the meeting, Lula told the US president that Brazil’s critical minerals were open to any country willing to process them locally. “Americans, Chinese, Germans, Japanese, French, whoever wants to participate with us to help us mine, separate and produce the wealth that these rare earths offer us, they are invited,” he said afterwards.

The talks did not stop Washington from imposing a 25 per cent tariff on most Brazilian goods in July, and Lula blamed the Bolsonaro family. The senator’s brother Eduardo had spent last year lobbying Washington for sanctions against Brazilian officials over their father’s trial.

Lula made sovereignty the centre of his campaign, and in a television broadcast in September he said those willing to hand Brazil’s rare earth reserves to other countries were “the real traitors of the homeland”.

Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China.

“There are people abroad keeping an eye on them and people here ready to hand everything over on a platter,” Lula said.

“This time we will not export rocks only to buy back technology.”

Two weeks later, he signed a law creating a national policy for critical minerals, including rare earths.

In the final week of the campaign, he accused the US government of meddling on Flavio Bolsonaro’s behalf, and his campaign asked the electoral court to disqualify the senator over claims that Meta Platforms had boosted him online.

Ties with Beijing

Lula travelled to Beijing in April 2023 on a trip his government described as an effort to restart ties that had cooled under Jair Bolsonaro.

In Shanghai, he toured Huawei Technologies’ research centre and called for an alternative to the US dollar in trade between the two countries.

President Xi Jinping returned the visit with a state trip to Brasilia in November 2024, when the two governments signed 37 agreements and raised their relationship to a “community with a shared future”.

Brazil stopped short of joining the Belt and Road Initiative, China’s global infrastructure strategy, and chose instead to link it to its own investment programmes.

Lula was back in Beijing in May last year for a summit with Latin American leaders and came home with 27 billion reais (US$4.7 billion) in investment pledges from companies such as Great Wall Motor and Meituan.

Chinese companies put more money into Brazil than into any other country last year, with a record US$6.1 billion spread across 52 projects, according to the Brazil-China Business Council.

Bilateral trade then hit a record US$143 billion in the first nine months of this year as oil sales surged after the war in Iran disrupted Gulf supply, and Brazil’s treasury is now preparing to issue its first yuan bonds in China with a view to borrowing there regularly.

China takes over the chair of Brics next year, and Lula’s government programme promises closer ties with the bloc of emerging economies. Flavio Bolsonaro had said he might pull Brazil out of the grouping, which Washington has worked to undermine.

Less than two weeks after Washington announced its tariffs, Xi told Lula in a phone call that China supported Brazil in “safeguarding sovereignty and independence, opposing external interference”.

The hour-long call was their second this year, and the two leaders agreed to speed up talks on a trade deal between China and the South American trade bloc Mercosur without providing details.

item.title: [SCMP] Eye on China: Japan reopens taboo debate over nuclear-powered submarines
item.description:
With China flexing its naval power across the Pacific and bilateral tensions running high, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is weighing a move long viewed as taboo – nuclear-powered submarines for the Maritime Self-Defence Force fleet.

“We will seriously consider [the possibility] in a concrete and realistic manner,” Takaichi told the Japanese parliament on October 14.

Yet with Tokyo set to revise its core security documents by year’s end, the proposal is dividing the ruling coalition.
item.content:encoded:
With China flexing its naval power across the Pacific and bilateral tensions running high, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is weighing a move long viewed as taboo – nuclear-powered submarines for the Maritime Self-Defence Force fleet.

“We will seriously consider [the possibility] in a concrete and realistic manner,” Takaichi told the Japanese parliament on October 14.

Yet with Tokyo set to revise its core security documents by year’s end, the proposal is dividing the ruling coalition.

The Japan Innovation Party – the junior coalition partner – wants nuclear propulsion introduced quickly, while some lawmakers from Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party are asking whether the military benefits justify the high costs and legal hurdles.

At issue is whether Japan needs nuclear-powered submarines when it already operates an advanced conventional submarine fleet and is developing uncrewed maritime capabilities.

Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told parliament last December that Japan’s pacifist constitution did not prohibit nuclear propulsion for military vessels.

But the country’s Atomic Energy Basic Act restricts nuclear energy to peaceful purposes. Successive governments have interpreted this as ruling out military nuclear propulsion, a position Takaichi’s cabinet reaffirmed later that month.

Beijing has criticised the controversial proposal, with Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning on October 16 accusing Tokyo of seeking to gradually loosen its nuclear restrictions and linking the proposal to the wider debate over Japan’s nuclear policies.

Such moves threatened regional peace and stability, Mao warned.

The debate comes amid growing concern in Tokyo about the People’s Liberation Army’s expanding operations in the western Pacific.

On October 16, Koizumi said China’s military operations were expanding while Japan’s Pacific intelligence-gathering and surveillance capabilities remained limited, making stronger defences urgent.

The defences include underwater assets. Japan’s conventional submarines are particularly well-suited to defending the maritime chokepoints around its southwestern islands, where operating quietly at low speeds makes them effective in ambushes.

Nuclear-powered submarines could also defend these chokepoints, but their advantage lies in speed and range.

Conventional submarines can only travel at high speeds underwater for a limited time before their batteries need recharging. Nuclear-powered boats can sustain high underwater speeds over much longer distances.

That could help Japan reach Chinese naval forces in the western Pacific with greater speed, shift between patrol areas or interception points as they change course, and retreat more quickly from dangerous waters after an attack.

Such mobility and endurance would be costly.

Eric Heginbotham, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology security scholar, told The Japan Times in January that nuclear-powered submarines could cost roughly two to three times as much to buy and four times as much to operate as conventional boats, depending on design.

A June study by Hudson Institute researcher Masashi Murano and four colleagues estimated that, for similar expenditure, Japan could acquire and maintain six nuclear-powered attack submarines (SSNs) or 10 large conventional missile submarines, supplementing a baseline fleet of 22 conventional boats.

The researchers also estimated that an average of one or two nuclear-powered boats would be deployed at any given time, compared with three of the large conventional missile submarines.

They concluded that conventional missile submarines combined with underwater drones would be likely to offer Japan better value for conventional warfare.

In an interview, Murano said: “Nuclear propulsion extends a submarine’s reach, but a single boat on station cannot search blindly for Chinese SSNs across the vast Pacific.”

While nuclear propulsion becomes more valuable further from home, he questioned whether Japan should prioritise such missions, noting that “distant open-ocean operations are where the US Navy is strongest”.

Despite its sophisticated submarine-building industry and civilian nuclear expertise, Japan would need entirely new military infrastructure for nuclear-powered submarines.

Defence Minister Koizumi highlighted the financial and technical demands of nuclear propulsion on October 9, noting that nuclear reactors were expensive, required larger submarine hulls and demanded specialist expertise for their operation and maintenance.

He said nuclear-powered submarines were generally considered noisier than conventional boats, although their acoustic performance was improving.

Another pivotal question is how Japan would obtain naval reactor technology.

Tokyo would have to develop its own propulsion system or get help from countries such as the United States or France, with the choice affecting submarine design, construction costs and long-term dependence on foreign suppliers.

American nuclear-powered submarines use highly enriched uranium, which Japan cannot currently produce, while French designs use low-enriched uranium that is closer to the fuel used in civilian reactors.

Japan would also need specialised shipyards, maintenance facilities, nuclear-safety systems and trained naval reactor personnel.

A US Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarine requires about 140 crew members – roughly twice the complement of a Taigei-class boat.

Additional personnel would be needed for maintenance, technical support and nuclear safety, placing further pressure on Japan’s already overstretched military.

The transition would take considerable time as well.

Murano estimated that even if development began now, Japan would need “a decade or more” to field its first nuclear-powered submarine – “realistically not before the late 2030s and more likely the 2040s”.

Establishing a sustainable operational fleet would therefore take even longer.

That raises an immediate question for Tokyo: whether investing billions in nuclear-powered submarines would deliver greater military value than expanding its existing conventional submarine force and further developing its uncrewed maritime capabilities.

Christopher Hughes, a professor of international politics and Japanese studies at the University of Warwick, questioned whether countering the PLA Navy was necessarily the “prime function” of Japan’s interest in nuclear-powered submarines.

Tokyo might instead be seeking a more survivable conventional counterstrike capability, he suggested.

But this would not necessarily require nuclear propulsion. Japan is studying how to integrate vertical missile-launch systems into future submarines.
