Jeffrey Hornung, Japan lead for the think tank Rand Corporation, said that if he were a Japanese lawmaker, he would seek an assessment of whether nuclear-powered submarines would close “an important gap” in Japan’s capabilities.

If conventional submarines, underwater drones and advanced mines could meet those needs, that should give policymakers “reason for pause” before rushing into acquisition, he said.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korean CEO’s 4-year jail term over plant fire that killed 23 spurs anger
item.description:
“How can South Korea’s law be this weak? Twenty-three people died!”

Those were the words of Chinese mother Li Shun-ji after South Korea’s Supreme Court upheld a reduced four-year prison sentence for Aricell CEO Park Soon-kwan over a 2024 factory fire that killed 23 workers, including Li’s then 24-year-old daughter, Yan Jing-jing.

The blaze at the lithium battery manufacturer’s factory in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi province, killed 17 Chinese nationals, one Laotian national and five South Koreans, injuring nine others. About 35,000 lithium batteries exploded in a chain reaction, with defective products and rushed operations to meet military supply deadlines reportedly contributing to the tragedy.
item.content:encoded:
“How can South Korea’s law be this weak? Twenty-three people died!”

Those were the words of Chinese mother Li Shun-ji after South Korea’s Supreme Court upheld a reduced four-year prison sentence for Aricell CEO Park Soon-kwan over a 2024 factory fire that killed 23 workers, including Li’s then 24-year-old daughter, Yan Jing-jing.

The blaze at the lithium battery manufacturer’s factory in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi province, killed 17 Chinese nationals, one Laotian national and five South Koreans, injuring nine others. About 35,000 lithium batteries exploded in a chain reaction, with defective products and rushed operations to meet military supply deadlines reportedly contributing to the tragedy.

“Are you making this decision because we are foreigners?” Li, 56, said through tears after last Tuesday’s ruling.

Under South Korea’s Serious Accidents Punishment Act (SAPA) – introduced in 2022 to strengthen corporate accountability for fatal workplace accidents – Aricell was found to have sent 53 unskilled workers to work on the batteries, neglected safety training and failed to secure evacuation routes.

Last year, a district court sentenced Park and his son, the factory’s managing director, to 15 years in prison each, marking the harshest sentences ever handed down to company executives under SAPA.

The appeal court later cleared both men of a key charge relating to the failure to install an emergency exit on an upper floor, reducing Park’s prison sentence to four years and his son’s to seven. The Supreme Court last week upheld the sentence for Park’s son.

Aricell was also fined 800 million won (US$604,000).

In its ruling, the appeal court had said safety regulations did not require exits on every floor and were applicable on a building-by-building basis. It also considered Aricell’s settlements with bereaved families.

The Supreme Court’s judgment last week has drawn criticism from the victims’ families and labour activists, who argue that it exposes a judicial system too lenient towards corporate offences.

‘Is this real?’

“When the court ruling ended in just 10 seconds, my heart started pounding so hard that my mind went completely blank,” said Li, referring to the time between the court convening and announcing its verdict.

“I kept asking the person next to me: ‘Is this real? Is this really happening?’”

Yan had been working at Aricell for only two months. She had trained as a teacher in China but left everything behind in the summer of 2024 to join her family, who were planning to apply for permanent residency in South Korea.

She took a job at the factory to help support them and received a pay rise after just two months.

“She was happily telling me that her managers seemed to have a good impression of her,” Li said. “But not long afterwards, the accident happened.”

Li arrived in South Korea in 2002 and later opened a Chinese restaurant in Siheung with her husband. However, after the pandemic forced its closure, she joined an insurance company while he returned to factory work.

The ruling prompted criticism from civic groups, including the National Council of Churches in Korea, with legislators highlighting shortcomings in government workplace inspections.

Li has also faced abuse online, including comments telling her family to return to China.

“If it were up to me, I wouldn’t want to continue living here,” she said. “After living here for more than 20 years, I have only just realised how much discrimination there is against foreigners like us.”

A survey by the Seoul-based East Asia Institute think tank released last year found that more than 70 per cent of South Koreans in their twenties and thirties held unfavourable views of China.

Still, Li has decided to stay in South Korea for the sake of her other daughter, 17, who arrived as a toddler, speaks only Korean and attends high school in Siheung.

“After seeing how worried she was about me, I decided I couldn’t go on living like a dead person,” Li said, recalling the two years of her anguish following Yan’s death. “I started going out into the streets to protest and fight for justice.”

Persistent workplace dangers

South Korea has reported other deadly industrial accidents in recent months.

In March, 14 people died in a fire at an auto parts factory operated by Anjeon Industrial, also in Daejeon. The company’s CEO was among 13 people referred to prosecutors on charges including professional negligence resulting in death and injury.

Then in June, five people died in an explosion at Hanwha Aerospace’s factory in Daejeon. A special inspection by the Ministry of Employment and Labour found 473 violations, 189 of which were referred for legal action.

Overall, workplace deaths have been declining in South Korea, though fatalities in the manufacturing sector have risen. According to the labour ministry, 366 people died in workplace accidents subject to official investigation between January and September – down 20 per cent from 457 during the same period last year – while manufacturing deaths increased from 119 to 132.

Jeon Soo-kyong, a coordinator at the labour rights group Solidarity for Worker’s Health, said unsafe conditions disproportionately affected people in precarious employment.

“Many of the workers dying in industrial accidents in South Korea today are migrant workers, as in the Aricell case, or Korean workers on non-regular contracts,” she said.

“There are subtle forms of discrimination in the workplace. A non-regular worker may be left to work alone without adequate safety measures, while a permanent employee has a colleague to help with the same task.”

Jeon said such practices reflected an entrenched management culture that prioritised cost-cutting. She also pointed to South Korea’s history of treating labour activism as a threat.

“Campaigns by workers to address industrial accidents have also been stigmatised by society, particularly by the prosecution and the government,” she said.

Cases under SAPA have placed corporate accountability under greater scrutiny in recent years.

In February, a district court acquitted the construction materials giant Sampyo Group and its chairman over a 2022 quarry landslide that killed three workers, prompting widespread public outrage.

Choi Cheong-hak, a law professor at the Korea National Open University, attributed the courts’ hesitancy to hand down severe punishments to “a widely shared belief that these people play an important role in society”.

Despite 167 first-instance verdicts being delivered under SAPA, only three corporate executives had received final prison sentences, he said, adding: “This is an extremely small rate”.

Vow to keep fighting

Shin Ha-na, the lawyer representing the bereaved Aricell families, said she would challenge last week’s ruling, arguing that it effectively gave the company a free pass.

“Safety laws are not being properly enforced in practice and rulings like this narrow what those laws are meant to achieve,” she said. “Our priority is to ensure that existing laws are properly implemented and enforced.”

Her team is preparing to file a complaint against the ruling with the Constitutional Court within the 30-day deadline.

For Li, the fight is not over as she is seeking to recover her daughter’s remains.

Of the 23 people killed in the fire, only one body was found intact. The bereaved families continue to push for a thorough search to recover any further remains, hoping to hold a joint funeral afterwards. Hwaseong city officials have discussed plans for a memorial park.

“All the families want this case to end,” Li said. “But what we want most of all is for our loved ones to finally have a proper resting place.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why cloud computing pioneer Wang Jian thinks space is the next AI frontier
item.description:
Long before artificial intelligence became the next big thing in the tech industry, Wang Jian was crafting the foundational infrastructure that would eventually power it. In 2008, he joined Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – as chief architect and founded Alibaba Cloud in 2009, convincing the company’s leadership to invest heavily in building a cloud computing infrastructure from scratch.

Today, Wang’s purview has expanded considerably. As an academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering and the director of Zhejiang Lab, a research institution backed by the Zhejiang provincial government, his focus has turned to a new frontier: space computing.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Long before artificial intelligence became the next big thing in the tech industry, Wang Jian was crafting the foundational infrastructure that would eventually power it. In 2008, he joined Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – as chief architect and founded Alibaba Cloud in 2009, convincing the company’s leadership to invest heavily in building a cloud computing infrastructure from scratch.

Today, Wang’s purview has expanded considerably. As an academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering and the director of Zhejiang Lab, a research institution backed by the Zhejiang provincial government, his focus has turned to a new frontier: space computing.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The current excitement over AI models is not the first wave of enthusiasm you’ve observed. How has this been different?

The pace of this wave of AI development has clearly exceeded my expectations.

AI has been developing for nearly 40 years, if we start from the 1980s, and I have lived through more than one developmental cycle.

In the 1980s, Japan launched its ambitious Fifth Generation Computer Systems initiative. People thought it would bring sweeping changes, but it ultimately fell short of expectations.

Over the past decade, China has had its own wave of enthusiasm around the “four AI tigers”: SenseTime, Megvii, CloudWalk and Yitu, with their focus on computer vision technology. That, too, did not deliver what many had expected.

The current wave is different. Its progress has exceeded expectations, and its impact extends far beyond AI itself. AI is no longer just an industry; it is a variable that will affect almost everything, as we are already seeing in how it assists mathematics research.

To understand this wave, we need to look at how the roles of data, models and computing power have changed over time. We often discuss all three together without making it clear that their importance shifts in different phases of AI development.

The AlexNet model in the 2012 ImageNet competition showed the importance of data. The introduction of the Transformer architecture in 2017 showed the importance of model design. And Nvidia’s rise over the past few years reflects the significant role that computing power has played more recently.

My view is that data will become more important again over the next three to five years, perhaps longer. Internet text is depleting fast for AI training, while vast amounts of scientific data remain under-explored.

I also think we need to reconsider what we mean by “artificial intelligence”. Much of the discussion today treats it as artificial human intelligence. I think that is the wrong way to frame it. I think when we talk about AI, we’re actually talking about machine intelligence.

Machine intelligence and human intelligence have overlapping capabilities, but they need not develop along the same path. If we constantly measure machines against human intelligence, we risk starting from a mistaken premise. Changing that perspective could change how we think about many questions in AI.

I use AI tools intensively, but I still create all my own presentation decks

You predicted that 90 per cent of AI applications and technologies will disappear within the next decade. Which AI tools are truly useful, and which ones are just there to address “pseudo-demands”?

I made that prediction against a very specific backdrop. At that time, everyone was just building extensions on top of ChatGPT and other GPTs. Even OpenAI wants to turn ChatGPT into a platform for developers to build applications on top of it.

If you look at it today, a chat tool itself is a very small application. If you view AI so narrowly that you only derive applications from a chat platform, you are only capturing a very small fraction of what AI can do for the world. If we calculate by token volume today, the vast majority are already being used elsewhere; they are not on those initial ChatGPT-based applications.

I believe AI will be able to do lots of things for us. As its capabilities expand, applications built around a chatbot platform to perform a few limited functions may struggle to be sustained.

In AI applications, at least two areas deserve particular attention. The first is coding. I prefer to describe it as “coding” rather than “writing software”.

Coding used to be seen as a specialised skill belonging to software engineers. Now, anyone with an idea could turn that idea into something tangible with the help of AI coding tools. This explains why I believe AI coding opens up a wide range of use scenarios and will create value far beyond the traditional software industry.

The second area is scientific research. Computers were widely used in research from their earliest days, and AI could now further change research practices.

In the past, people might ask how much training someone needed to become a scientist, or whether someone who had not attended a leading institution such as MIT was qualified to conduct research.

AI could lower these barriers and unlock potential that previously went unrecognised. That is what I consider a seismic change: people who cannot code may be able to build software, and people without traditional research training may be able to contribute to scientific discoveries.

Journalists also have to confront these changes. I do not believe good journalists will be easily replaced by AI, but repetitive work that lacks independent thinking or creativity could certainly be replaced. I use AI tools intensively, but I still create all my own presentation decks.

The AI race between the United States and China has intensified, with a tendency towards decoupling at both the model and computing levels. How do you picture the future of China’s AI industry against this backdrop?

I am very optimistic about China’s AI development over the long term, while recognising that there are challenges in the short term.

Unlike many other technologies, AI will affect all of society and is difficult to confine to one place. It is inherently global. I agree with China’s view that AI should be a global public good.

It is already too late to “decouple” China and the US in AI models and compute.

For one thing, China’s open models are approaching the capabilities of leading US proprietary models in certain areas. Disruptive breakthroughs may still emerge, and it is difficult at this stage to say who has an absolute lead.

For another, China’s domestically developed computing chips have already reached a certain level of capability.

In an open market, Chinese computing hardware would struggle to compete with US products on price-performance and technological sophistication. But the US has disrupted that open market.

Under the current conditions, China’s computing hardware has to be sufficient for itself, and it is basically sufficient. US restrictions may therefore not be a catastrophic problem; instead, the restrictions helped accelerate the development of China’s chip capabilities.

China’s leading AI companies have been sticking to open-source or open-weight models, while closed-source remains the dominant format in the US. Why has there been such a divergence, and which approach will win?

We cannot simply apply the experience of traditional software – open-source versus closed-source – when it comes to AI.

Traditional open-source software offers an alternative in a market where commercial software has been relatively mature. AI is different: open and closed approaches have emerged side by side while the industry itself is still taking shape.

There is also a worldwide debate over whether some models described as “open-source” actually qualify, since they release only their weights. Applying the traditional software definition of “open-source” may not accurately describe what a model “opens”.

I prefer the term “open-resource” to describe model openness.

Training each model requires substantial resources, including computing power and electricity. Some countries, even if they have the money, may not have access to sufficient electricity, computing capacity or talent.

Making a model open shares the benefits of those resources, allowing people who cannot afford to make the same investment themselves to use the resulting capabilities.

Open and closed models are not in a zero-sum contest, nor must one eliminate the other. Competition between them can help both advance.

A company that operates efficiently and has a viable business model can also grow while making its models openly available. Valuation considerations and business conditions may differ between China and the US, so openness may affect their companies’ valuations differently. DeepSeek, for example, has maintained a high valuation despite making its models openly available.

AI tokenises data. Are token prices low enough to maintain market demand while covering the computing cost? Will they drop further as technology develops? How will the token industry appear in the US and China given the gap in resource costs?

A key step in AI advancement is whether token prices can fall further. This is closely tied to the importance of data represented as tokens.

As I have said before, we should think about data in terms of tokens, and share and use data through tokens.

The cost of tokens reflects several factors: computing power, electricity, models and crucially, the value of the underlying data. It should not be understood simply as how much electricity or computing capacity has been consumed to generate the tokens.

Over time, electricity and computing expenses should account for a smaller share of token costs, while the value attributed to data should account for a larger share. I believe tokens will become increasingly affordable while still commanding a reasonable price that reflects the value of the data behind them.

China and the US may gradually diverge in their approach to tokens and their underlying business ecosystems.

If we look only at electricity and computing costs, their understanding of token value is likely to converge. Although these costs vary between locations, industrial production and circulation tend to keep them within a certain comparable range over time.

I am reluctant to call China’s electricity abundance an ‘advantage’. Having the wiggle room is one thing, whether it could be put to good use is another

The real difference lies in the value of data. One important contribution of this wave of AI development is that it has shown us how significant data is as a factor of production.

Tokens should be cheap, but they are not yet cheap enough. Model training is generally expensive, and those costs must, in principle, eventually be spread across each token.

Token prices in China are relatively low for several reasons. The average cost of computing resources used to train models is lower. China’s electricity supply and renewable energy development also provide wiggle room, particularly when it comes to supporting concentrated model training. Compared with the US, China has less reason to worry about electricity constraints.

I am reluctant to call China’s electricity abundance an “advantage”. Having the wiggle room is one thing, whether it could be put to good use is another.

When it comes to AI and computing, semiconductors are always a focus. As the US retains tight control over chip exports to China, especially the most advanced units, home-made hardware has achieved breakthroughs in recent years. How do you evaluate the actual progress of the domestic chip sector?

We should not view China’s domestically developed chips narrowly as a response to the US refusing to sell advanced chips to China. Instead, we should also ask how chips made in China can serve users around the world.

I believe Nvidia deserves tribute. Without Nvidia, we might all still be exploring in the dark. It initially developed chips for gaming rather than AI. But through its sustained investment in computing power, it was well positioned when the AI industry emerged and helped explore a path for the entire industry.

Today, once we know the chips are serving AI, the difficulty actually drops a lot. AI chips can be categorised into two types of demand: training and inference.

We know that chips need to support model training and inference, and we can design and optimise them around clearly defined requirements. Their design requirements differ, allowing developers to make more targeted trade-offs between performance, efficiency and application needs.

New entrants no longer have to begin by figuring out what their chips could be used for. Nvidia undertook that exploration for the industry, lowering the barriers for those that followed.

Chinese chip developers know which requirements they are designing for and understand how training and inference work. That allows them to optimise chips effectively for tasks such as inference. I am fully confident in China’s ability to develop inference chips.

It is difficult to say what chips will look like in 10 or 20 years, because we do not know what AI will look like then. We must all continue to innovate and face the next set of challenges together.

I do not believe the concept of “overtaking on a bend” actually exists. Today, the US and China can jointly solve the challenges we are facing as humanity.

You founded Alibaba Cloud in 2009, when most people considered cloud computing an unattainable concept. What prompted you to stick to this decision?

Looking back at the industrial revolutions, it was the steam engine that set change in motion, and electricity that amplified its impact. The information technology revolution followed a similar pattern. If computing had remained confined to mainframes, it would have been like the industrial revolution stopping at the steam engine: its impact would never have become so widespread.

Cloud computing is a revolution in how computing power is delivered, much like the transition from steam power to electricity.

Once you truly believe in that direction, you have the motivation to persevere. I once thought that if I didn’t finish the work myself, others could have carried it forward. I was fortunate enough to see the cloud computing sector thrive.

The mobile internet’s explosive growth gave us tremendous support. Without it, cloud computing might have faltered. Then AI emerged, making the cloud’s importance even clearer. Nvidia’s massive chip sales to cloud providers are one example.

I have always believed that cloud computing is an enduring business, not something ephemeral.

Building cloud computing, like developing AI, requires wholehearted conviction. If there is even the slightest weakness in that conviction – something that may not yet amount to doubt – difficulties can overwhelm you. It is like a crack in an aircraft’s surface that gradually widens under pressure.

An employee once told me that he worked hard, frequently stayed late and was willing to be “the last to leave” the company. My response was that being “the last to leave” is completely different from being “the last man standing”. The former ultimately leaves; the latter remains through the hardest times.

Another colleague who later left to start an AI company described the feeling perfectly. He said he felt like a group of us were holding hands trying to hug a massive tree, but we had no idea how thick the tree actually was, or when our hands would finally meet. The uncertainty was beyond imagination.

US hyperscalers have long maintained higher margins than their Chinese peers. Does this mean China’s cloud industry is smaller? How can China’s cloud computing market become bigger?

China’s cloud computing market is no smaller than that of the US, and it has technological capabilities, but the industry as a whole remains underdeveloped.

The US has Amazon, Microsoft and Google, as well as Oracle, which is increasingly focused on its cloud business. China has relatively fewer companies with comparable scale and cloud capabilities, with Alibaba Cloud being the most prominent.

I would like to see two more companies similar to Alibaba Cloud emerge, giving China at least three significant cloud providers operating at scale. That would help the industry flourish, strengthen economies of scale and create fuller competition. Alibaba Cloud has played a leading role, but one company cannot drive innovation across the entire market alone.

Competition does not have to mean suppliers continually undercutting one another on price. There are two kinds of competition. Destructive competition can ruin a market. Healthy competition encourages companies to improve their operations and efficiency, giving customers better prices and services while allowing providers to earn reasonable profits. Low prices don’t necessarily come at the expense of suppliers’ profitability.

Fuller competition can also spur creativity across companies. When others continually push you to improve, efficiency, service quality and profit margins can rise together.

Furthermore, in Chinese Premier [Li Qiang]’s government work report this year, the term “public cloud” was heavily emphasised. This was the first time it was used in such a report. In China, we used to constantly debate “public cloud” versus “private cloud”, which is not really helpful to industry development. It is a matter of public service versus proprietary networks. Computing must become a public service. No public service can exist if costs remain high, so it must scale to become cost-effective.

You have served as the director of Zhejiang Lab since 2023. The research institute focuses on AI and computing, including space computing. What drove you to pivot towards space computing?

The rationale is very simple: the problems facing Earth – climate change, extreme weather, geological disasters like landslides – can no longer be solved by only looking at them from the ground. You have to go to space to see the whole picture. Going into space is not just about exploring space itself, it is also about solving problems on Earth.

Short-term weather forecasting for aviation, for example, requires observations made by satellites in space to see the full picture.

When observations are made and data is collected in space, we also need to consider where the computing should take place. If a satellite collects data, sends it back to Earth for processing and then delivers the results to those who need them, that can delay time-sensitive work. It is like having to bring surgical instruments from a distant location when an operation is already needed.

Putting computing power in space would allow data generated there to be processed promptly. AI has made this need more urgent: there is already an abundance of data in space, but what once was missing was the ability to analyse and use it in the right place. Now with AI, we are able to process all this data, hence the urgency to build space computing facilities.

There is a substantial gap between satellite observations and the use of the resulting data. AI could help process and use more of it.

Cameras and other observation payloads on some remote-sensing satellites sit idle roughly 90 per cent of the time because they cannot continuously collect and transmit everything. Meanwhile, roughly 90 per cent of data collected in space is lost because bandwidth is insufficient to transmit it back to Earth.

Cloud computing mainly addresses computing needs on Earth. Space computing has its own requirements and development logic. It should not be understood simply as moving terrestrial data centres into orbit or finding another location to address electricity constraints on Earth.

We have to be very clear about how our approach differs from Elon Musk’s. Space computing is not simply moving ground-based data centres up to space. If Musk says he wants to put a data centre in space, today he is the only one who can do it because he is the only one with that kind of launch capacity.

We are not doing that. We are solving the fundamental issue of processing space-native data directly in space.

The first questions are how data generated in space should be processed and how it can be turned into timely, usable results. I have also discussed this in Geneva. “Putting computing power in space” and “sending data centres into space” may sound similar, but the approach is different.

Sending data centres into space may seem like a daunting task. But space computing involves much more than that, because processing space data requires an entire value chain, with opportunities for a wide range of participants.

item.title: [SCMP] Why foreign companies are still betting on Hong Kong’s culinary reputation
item.description:
Despite a downturn in Hong Kong’s food and beverage sector, foreign enterprises are still betting on the city as a fine-dining destination, with a South Korean hydroponic ginseng grower and a 123-year-old Japanese confectioner choosing it for their first overseas ventures.

Jack Kwon, founder and CEO of Seoul-based Biofx, signed a deal with Hong Kong hydroponics firm Farm66 last Thursday to grow Korean gourmet ginseng in the city and sell it to local consumers and restaurants.

The deal marks the first time the Korean company has expanded hydroponically grown ginseng operations overseas.
item.content:encoded:
Despite a downturn in Hong Kong’s food and beverage sector, foreign enterprises are still betting on the city as a fine-dining destination, with a South Korean hydroponic ginseng grower and a 123-year-old Japanese confectioner choosing it for their first overseas ventures.

Jack Kwon, founder and CEO of Seoul-based Biofx, signed a deal with Hong Kong hydroponics firm Farm66 last Thursday to grow Korean gourmet ginseng in the city and sell it to local consumers and restaurants.

The deal marks the first time the Korean company has expanded hydroponically grown ginseng operations overseas.

Hydroponics is an indoor cultivation technique in which plants are grown not in soil but in mineral- and nutrient-infused water under LED lights, typically using a method that allows crops to be planted vertically on shelves to optimise space.

“We had several choices: Japan, Singapore, Vietnam and so on, but we made the decision to go to Hong Kong because Hong Kong is the number one fine dining market in Asia,” Kwon told the South China Morning Post.

The group also hopes to use Hong Kong as a springboard to other markets in the region, such as Singapore, Vietnam and Japan, he said.

He added that the process of opening a company in the city for his international ambitions was also the most flexible and that he had strong relationships with an accounting firm in Hong Kong, which provided support.

Kwon said all of the ginseng plant, including the stems and leaves, could be turned into products, unlike traditional ginseng harvested just for the roots. He aimed to bring that expertise, as well as marketing materials, to a Hong Kong urban farm.

Kwon said he had used ChatGPT in August last year to find Farm66 for his first overseas venture. The company will provide infrastructure and technologies for his operation in Hong Kong.

Gordon Tam Chi-ho, founder and CEO of Farm66, said his firm was currently looking for a site to house a container farm for hydroponic ginseng, and was confident that it could secure a place within a year.

“We learned a lot from them because from their research, the leaves are higher in nutrients and could also become products,” Tam said.

The leaves could be harvested every two months and used to make pesto, served in salads or brewed as tea, he added.

Victoria Wang, the farm’s chief information officer, said Farm66 used cameras linked to artificial intelligence and real-time data analytics, allowing Kwon to keep a close eye on the plants in Hong Kong while he was in Seoul.

Wang added that manipulating the LED lights could also help grow more, larger leaves, with adjustments done electronically.

Bringing in foreign capital has been a top priority for Hong Kong. The city’s investment promotion arm, InvestHK, has helped set up or expand 516 overseas and mainland Chinese companies in the city in the first eight months of the year, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah told the SCMP in an interview earlier this month. He believed they tapped the Hong Kong market because the city was “stable, safe and free”.

The investment came despite restaurant receipts and purchases remaining flat, with 0.8 per cent growth in value offset by a 0.1 per cent reduction in volume in the first six months of this year, compared with the same period last year.

Another newcomer to Hong Kong is Okaman Honpo, a 123-year-old producer of wagashi, or Japanese confectionery, from Tokushima.

The company recently launched its first overseas outlet in Hong Kong in collaboration with local brand Master Gift, owned by 78-year-old Hong Kong chef Wan Tat-kong, who has lived and worked in Japan for more than 30 years and whose food has received accolades there.

Kenji Okada, the 79-year-old fourth-generation owner of Okaman Honpo, said he had not thought about expanding the company beyond Japan but decided to do so after being persuaded by Wan, a friend.

The pair jointly developed wagashi that combined Chinese and Japanese influences for the Hong Kong market, in a project initially planned to run for five years.

“There is a limit to the [amount of] ingredients we have, such as sugar from cane, because we grow them on our farm, and cannot scale too much. So the company will focus on its Hong Kong business first,” Okada said through an interpreter.

Okada said he would have retired had it not been for Wan’s proposal to collaborate. But now he hopes that whoever takes over the family business will continue with the joint venture.

Wan said he would visit Okada’s workshop in Japan three to four times a year to jointly produce the wagashi, which would be delivered to Hong Kong at a more affordable price than what was currently available on the market.

“This is also a form of people-to-people cultural exchange between two countries,” Wan said.

Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, noted that both businesses had partnered with Hong Kong firms to enter the market, adding that such synergy benefited both local and overseas enterprises.

“If the economy were great, perhaps they [foreign businesses] could just set up here on their own. In reality, it’s not as easy to do so, so this allows them to share risks and achieve a win-win scenario,” Ng said.

These collaborations demonstrate that businesses are exploring new growth avenues, from creating tailored products to reach customers more effectively to offering fresh dining choices, according to Ng.

Ng also pointed out that the target market segment for both the Japanese and Korean businesses, though smaller, appeared to be more premium and niche, which could present unique opportunities in Hong Kong.

Another factor prompting Korean and Japanese businesses to venture overseas is weakness in their domestic markets, even as specific sectors – such as semiconductors in South Korea and tourism in Japan – continue to perform well.

As a result, many enterprises were looking to export products to sustain growth, and Hong Kong presented targeted opportunities for those seeking expansion, Ng said.

Vera Yuen Wing-han, a lecturer in economics at the University of Hong Kong, noted that despite shifting consumption patterns, with many local residents heading across the border to mainland China for food and entertainment, the city still retained strong spending power.

“If there are special enough offerings, Hongkongers are willing to pay a premium,” Yuen said. “If it’s a concept backed by good promotion, a rich story, quality, and unique selling points, it can become very popular.”

She pointed out that Hongkongers’ penchant for all things Japanese and Korean significantly boosted market receptivity for products from the two countries while frequent cultural exchanges and tourism further facilitated business collaborations.

“It’s more special when these are brands from overseas, not affordable products or those that you could secure from the mainland, as many people already have access to those by spending time across the border,” Yuen said.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
item.description:
While walking alongside Victoria Harbour or riding the Star Ferry, luck might have allowed you a glimpse of Way Foong motoring by. Its old-fashioned appearance is a sign that the boat is obviously from an era long past but, because it is not a traditional junk, you may not have realised you were looking at an authentic piece of Hong Kong history: a wooden motoryacht constructed locally almost 100 years ago.

Commissioned by the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (now HSBC) – “Way Foong” being a transliteration of the bank’s name in Cantonese – and built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, the vessel was used by the bank as a ferry, a tugboat and a pleasure craft for employees for more than seven decades before passing into private ownership. In the late 2010s, it was acquired by a patron of the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF) – an organisation officially founded earlier this year by individuals passionate about preserving the city’s maritime legacy.

When hired for parties or other events, Way Foong can often be seen cruising side by side with Java, another 1930s-era wooden vessel built by the same shipyard. Java entered service in 1935 and served for decades in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1. It transported VIPs and port officials, conducted anti-piracy patrols, towed and positioned mooring buoys and even corralled the odd swimming water buffalo. Its Burmese-teak construction, with deck planks measuring almost 4.5cm thick, earned the boat a reputation for being “almost unsinkable” and invulnerable to typhoons.
item.content:encoded:
While walking alongside Victoria Harbour or riding the Star Ferry, luck might have allowed you a glimpse of Way Foong motoring by. Its old-fashioned appearance is a sign that the boat is obviously from an era long past but, because it is not a traditional junk, you may not have realised you were looking at an authentic piece of Hong Kong history: a wooden motoryacht constructed locally almost 100 years ago.

Commissioned by the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (now HSBC) – “Way Foong” being a transliteration of the bank’s name in Cantonese – and built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, the vessel was used by the bank as a ferry, a tugboat and a pleasure craft for employees for more than seven decades before passing into private ownership. In the late 2010s, it was acquired by a patron of the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF) – an organisation officially founded earlier this year by individuals passionate about preserving the city’s maritime legacy.

When hired for parties or other events, Way Foong can often be seen cruising side by side with Java, another 1930s-era wooden vessel built by the same shipyard. Java entered service in 1935 and served for decades in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1. It transported VIPs and port officials, conducted anti-piracy patrols, towed and positioned mooring buoys and even corralled the odd swimming water buffalo. Its Burmese-teak construction, with deck planks measuring almost 4.5cm thick, earned the boat a reputation for being “almost unsinkable” and invulnerable to typhoons.

Way Foong and Java are two of five vessels now owned and maintained by the HKHVF. “By restoring and preserving such examples of the world-class craftsmanship that Hong Kong shipyards were capable of, we aim not only to encourage Hongkongers to discover the city’s commercial, governmental and recreational maritime heritage, but also to nurture the region’s next generation of boaters and ocean-lovers,” says CEO Philip Giannecchini.

Java, the first vessel in the collection, was found by chance. One of the avid sailors who would later establish the HKHVF noticed Java moored in Tai Tam Harbour, on the south side of Hong Kong Island, when taking out his own boat, and wanted to learn more about the 56-foot wooden launch. He ended up meeting the then-owner, and bought Java in the early 2000s. At the time, the rationale behind the purchase was simply to have such a historical pleasure craft in one’s possession. Eventually, the desire to safeguard Hong Kong’s maritime history took hold, setting in motion other acquisitions and the founding of the HKHVF.

A years-long search for extant, pre-50s boats built in the city followed. Nine, in various states of repair, have been identified by the organisation’s historians – some now in the HKHVF collection, others happily and privately owned, and one, Mon Lei, whose whereabouts are unknown.

Given Hong Kong’s coastal geography, boats have, and will always be, an integral part of the city. Yet, while today’s harbours and inlets are teeming with craft of various shapes and sizes, most are built elsewhere, the city’s shipbuilding days having long passed.

However, in the early 20th century, two giants of the industry, the Taikoo Dockyard and the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, were firmly in their prime, and a number of small and medium-sized shipbuilders, such as Hung Hom’s Hop Kee Shipyard, Ah King Slipway and Cheoy Lee Shipyard, also produced wooden vessels for global clients.

Teresa Mak Hiu-see, one of the in-house researchers at the HKHVF, notes that “the 30s were one of the high points in Hong Kong’s shipbuilding tradition for all types of vessels, from cargo liners to pleasure craft, and the industry steamed ahead until Japan invaded Hong Kong in December 1941. Until the end of World War II, all dockyards were under Japanese control”.

Rare survivors such as Way Foong and Java escaped the scrapyard, but many other Hong Kong-built vessels from the 20s and 40s were not so lucky. Says Mak, “With the 40s being a time of war and post-war recovery, that might be a factor in the small number of surviving pleasure craft from that decade.”

In 1972, the Taikoo Dockyard and the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company were merged to form the Hongkong United Dockyards. In 1980, the Whampoa site was shut down and the land was redeveloped into the Whampoa Garden housing estate, now easily identified by its superyacht-shaped shopping centre, a 110-metre-long concrete landmark “moored” amid the residential blocks.

When the Cheoy Lee Shipyard at Penny’s Bay was reclaimed by the Hong Kong government in 1999 to provide a location for Hong Kong Disneyland, it signalled the end of an era: shipbuilding operations in the city were coming to an end. But the final straw came when Ah King’s Causeway Bay shipyard closed, in 2002.

With shipbuilding essentially a thing of the past, the preservation of Hong Kong-made boats has become ever more important, Giannecchini explains, as these examples are “more than just beautiful old vessels – they tell the story of Hong Kong’s craftsmanship, ingenuity and connection to the sea, and that’s a story we want future generations to be able to experience”.

James Barker, captain of the HKHVF fleet, who coordinates the repairs, maintenance and operation of the boats and can often be seen piloting them, adds, “Caring for nearly century-old boats is not easy. Every project you take on turns out to be much larger, more complicated and more expensive than you first envision. For example, the Gardner engine on Way Foong needed to be replaced, but that [British] company went out of business in the 90s, so we had to source everything we needed from other places.”

It is not just hardware that is difficult to secure. Experts who have the technical knowledge to carry out such repairs are dwindling in number as well, he says. “Everyone who used to do these specialised jobs has either retired or passed away. In the absence of all other options, we are forced to research, plan and take on the task ourselves,” says Barker.

“We recently had to pull the propeller shaft from So Fong and replace the rotten timber around the stern, which meant drilling a new hole through the replacement wood,” he continues. “We’re looking at the bones of these boats, not just making sure they look beautiful on the surface. Significant work is needed to ensure these vessels can last for another 100 years.”

As Giannecchini notes, preservation in its finest form means not only maintaining the physical aspect, but also the histories of these vessels. In an effort to share the stories behind the fleet, the HKHVF website has detailed introductions to each boat.

Some have lived lives rich with adventure and drama. Way Foong transported gold and silver bullion to and from ships anchored in Victoria Harbour, as well as chests of banknotes to HSBC branches on Hong Kong’s outlying islands. It was even used for “burning picnics”: junior staff from the bank’s note-cancellation department would burn sacks of old bills in the boiler room, back when Way Foong had its original steam engine, converting the to-be-disposed-of cash into fuel.

According to one account, Way Foong was taken up the Pearl River at the outbreak of World War II and scuppered to prevent it from falling into Japanese hands. After the war, its skipper reportedly returned to the bank to ask for his job back. He was told that it was his if he could find the missing launch. He did – Way Foong was recovered in 1945 and returned to service after a major refit.

Another HKHVF vessel, Tai Mo Shan, served as a film prop in Mamma Mia! (2008), appearing as the sailing boat that transports the three male co-leads – Pierce Brosnan, Colin Firth and Stellan Skarsgård – to the fictional Greek island of Kalokairi, where the wedding in the plot takes place. Tai Mo Shan had been domiciled in Athens at the time of filming and a broker linked the producers to its owner. While the boat was not in great condition, this suited the filmmakers, who wanted to show the fictional owner, played by Skarsgård, as a “scruffy” character; they even exaggerated its run-down look to drive the point home.

Tai Mo Shan was undergoing restoration work at a shipyard in Greece when the HKHVF became aware of it, in the summer of 2025, through a yacht broker’s flier. Arrangements were made to buy the boat, and it was delivered in October 2025.

Tai Mo Shan was built by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, in 1933, and left the city on a 16,000-plus-mile transpacific and then transatlantic voyage to Dartmouth, in Britain, which, by some accounts, included an attempt to spy on Japanese naval installations in the Kuril Islands.

Another vessel, Typhoon, was discovered by the HKHVF through research on Facebook. Built in 1934 at the Hop Kee Shipyard to a design by Harold S. Rouse, for the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, the boat enjoyed a successful racing career up until the relocation of its owner, back to his native Britain. Typhoon was in Scotland when it was acquired, also in 2025.

Late last year, Tracy Van Buskirk, a retired banker who enjoys exploring coastal Maine, in the United States, aboard a 30-foot retrofitted lobster boat, shared her recollections with the HKHVF after having googled the name “So Fong” out of curiosity and found out that the schooner, on which she had sailed in the 70s, from Stamford, Connecticut, to Singapore, was still afloat.

So Fong, a gaff-rigged schooner measuring 82 feet, was built on an Ah King slipway, on commission for American yachtsman A. Thornton Baker. It took around 250 artisans more than seven months to complete the boat. Following its launch in March 1937, So Fong sailed for about 30,000 miles, travelling through the Philippines, the South Seas, the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean and the South Atlantic before reaching San Juan, Puerto Rico, in April 1938. During World War II, the US Coast Guard requisitioned So Fong, according to a commemorative plaque aboard the vessel. After the war, it returned to the Pacific and was used for racing.

Van Buskirk recalls that, at the age of 21, in 1978, she had recently graduated from university after spending a year studying Mandarin in Taiwan.

“I had every intention of returning to Asia, but decided to spend the summer in my hometown of Fairfield to get a job. By early October, I had started planning my flights back to Taipei. One weekend, my mother invited me to go sailing with a family friend, on his 28-foot sloop. He asked me about my plans and volunteered that his son had been hired as first mate for a delivery job of a large schooner that was scheduled to leave Stamford soon and sail to Singapore. William Mathers, the new owner, had bought So Fong earlier that year and hired the captain, Don Kuhn, to take her on this 14,000-mile journey.

“I was intrigued and immediately drove to the Stamford Yacht Club to introduce myself and see about a berth. Kuhn was busy with last-minute arrangements but took a moment for a brief interview. After determining that I was healthy, held a current passport and had some savings, he said I was hired. We left two days later [on October 18, 1978].”

Van Buskirk and So Fong would reach Singapore on March 21 of the following year.

In 1984, Vietnamese authorities seized the vessel in the Pacific Ocean, on suspicion that its sophisticated navigation equipment was being used for espionage, and its owner was placed in solitary confinement. He was released the following year, having paid his way to freedom, but So Fong remained confiscated.

It would spend the next few years abandoned at anchor until yacht enthusiast Robert Verschoyle located the vessel in 1989.

Following an intensive 11-month restoration in Ho Chi Minh City, Verschoyle executed a nighttime escape with So Fong in the early 90s. Under cover of darkness, he smuggled the boat out, and the vessel eventually reappeared in Hong Kong in 1993. After a few decades, during which the boat passed through private hands, Giannecchini was alerted to So Fong’s existence in February 2025, by a friend who had read about it in an article about vintage sailing vessels available for charter in Spain. So Fong finally returned home last October, after being acquired by the HKHVF.

Earlier this year, the HKHVF learned of another Hong Kong-built wooden yacht from the 30s that was still sailing in local waters. Ariki III was constructed in 1939 at the Ah King shipyard, to a design by American naval architect Ralph E. Winslow. Completed just before the outbreak of World War II, she was meant to be shipped to the US, but those plans were foiled by the Japanese occupation of Hong Kong. After years of neglect, she sank in 1946.

New Zealander Hector Forsyth raised the boat, restored it and named it after the Maori word for “leader”. Ariki III became part of the city’s sailing scene, eventually coming into the ownership of long-time sailor Graeme Large, who restored it anew, together with Stanley-based wooden-boat specialist Fan Kwei-sum.

Current owner Peter Lau Man-pong, a businessman and the chairman of the Hong Kong Arts Centre, developed a passion for the sea at an early age, having grown up sailing in the waters around Hong Kong with his father.

“My father was the founding chairman of the Hong Kong Sea Cadet Corps. Now, as its deputy chairman, I also have a deep connection with the sea and related youth activities,” says Lau.

He believes that the HKHVF’s mission to educate the public about Hong Kong’s maritime heritage is important; the team “has a noble vision and noble hearts, in addition to their love of boats”.

Although he used to paddle his wooden kayak from Hong Kong to Macau for leisure, “unfortunately, I am getting old and don’t have the time nor energy to take my boats out as much as I used to. As the HKHVF continues to mature, I am planning on gifting them Ariki III, but the details are still being worked out”.

As its collection grows, the HKHVF has begun making its vessels accessible to the public, through collaborations with people and organisations involved in history, conservation and education, such as the Hong Kong Maritime Museum and the Royal Geographical Society. Additionally, the vessels can be chartered for business and recreational use.

As early as next year, the HKHVF plans to open a small museum at its floating headquarters – a structure made of two connected industrial barges, in the Kwun Tong Typhoon Shelter – to provide a permanent home for its fleet.

“Our vision is to keep researching Hong Kong’s maritime history, preserve significant vessels whenever we have the opportunity and find new ways to share their stories,” says Giannecchini. “We don’t want these boats sitting in a museum as artefacts. We want them to remain active, accessible and connected to the people of Hong Kong.”

As Way Foong and its restored kin continue to glide through Hong Kong’s waters, they do much more than offer a glimpse of a bygone era – they keep part of the city’s history afloat.

item.title: [SCMP] Will China’s 4 peace principles for tackling African conflicts work?
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined Beijing’s formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues during a meeting this month with visiting Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, framing it around four principles linking peace to development.

The principles focus on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and long-term development.

Asked last week whether the principles could be applied to northern Ethiopia and the heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said they offered “practical guidance” for the Horn of Africa.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined Beijing’s formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues during a meeting this month with visiting Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, framing it around four principles linking peace to development.

The principles focus on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and long-term development.

Asked last week whether the principles could be applied to northern Ethiopia and the heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said they offered “practical guidance” for the Horn of Africa.

Days later, a joint statement following a meeting between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, said China would continue to play a constructive role in mediating regional disputes through its existing Horn of Africa peace and development initiative, subject to the wishes of the countries concerned.

Beijing has financed major infrastructure projects in the region under the Belt and Road Initiative, its China-centred trade and investment scheme. These include the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Standard Gauge Railway, as well as oil, fishing and maritime interests across Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Djibouti.

Yet, Beijing remains reluctant to intervene directly, opting instead to support African-led diplomacy to preserve its long-standing doctrine of state non-interference.

As conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, China seeks to strike a delicate diplomatic balance, advocating for peaceful, African-led solutions that align with Xi’s conflict-resolution principles.

The idea is to safeguard China’s billions in regional infrastructure and economic investments while carefully maintaining its core foreign policy pledge of non-interference.

But experts said lasting peace would ultimately depend on regional actors addressing internal factionalism, respecting state sovereignty and fostering inclusive dialogue alongside broader international peace efforts.

Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China programme at the Stimson Centre, a Washington-based think tank, said Beijing’s response reflected concern about what renewed fighting could mean for its interests in the Horn of Africa.

“I think it first and foremost points out China’s concern and aversion to instability,” Sun said. “War and conflicts fundamentally undermine China’s interests on the ground.”

China also faced a diplomatic constraint, she added, saying it sought to influence how conflicts were resolved without abandoning its stated principle of non-interference in other countries’ affairs.

Rather than lead a peace process itself, Beijing tends to support approaches led by countries in the region and their regional organisations.

“The balance they strike is through siding [with] and supporting [a] regional approach and the involvement of regional organisations,” Sun said. “That confers legitimacy and credibility to the Chinese approach.”

Ethiopian federal forces and fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) are battling again in northern Ethiopia, putting a 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement under severe strain.

Ethiopian federal forces entered Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, in early October after advancing on the city and prompting TPLF fighters to withdraw.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government has announced a six-month caretaker administration in the Tigray region to restore services, return displaced people and prepare for elections.

The conflict has also escalated Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of backing the TPLF and occupying its territory.

Eritrea rejects the claims and accuses Addis Ababa of threatening its territorial integrity to secure Red Sea access, which landlocked Ethiopia desperately seeks to reduce its dependence on Djiboutian ports.

According to Seifudein Adem, a visiting professor at Doshisha University in Kyoto, Ethiopia must address its internal divisions if it is to resist outside intervention.

“President Xi Jinping is correct to suggest that Ethiopia should put its house in order by resolving internal disagreements through dialogue because disorder is the ultimate justification for external intervention in Africa,” he said.

Adem argued that the obstacle was not an inability to resolve disagreements peacefully.

“Rather, these disagreements often take the form of militarised factionalism,” he said. “This, in turn, is because the Ethiopian state does not enjoy a monopoly over the means of violence in the society.”

“The problem is that some of these neighbouring countries seem to view their interference as a kind of African solution to African disorder, consistent with an ‘African-led’ solution,” Adem added.

Xi’s emphasis on sovereignty shifted the focus from Africa as a whole to the rights of individual states, he said.

According to Costantinos Berhutesfa Costantinos, a public policy expert at Addis Ababa University and former United Nations policy adviser, China has a clear stake in containing the conflict but must use its influence carefully.

“China is a friend and major trade partner and investor in the Horn,” Costantinos said, citing Beijing-backed roads, power-generation and transmission projects, and industrial estates in Ethiopia.

Those investments could not deliver their intended economic benefits without peace, he added.

Costantinos said China’s diplomatic initiative, together with its influence through the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, had raised expectations that Beijing would engage with countries in the region to help resolve their long-standing conflicts.

China appointed Xue Bing as its first special envoy for the Horn of Africa in 2022 and convened a conference on peace, governance and development in Addis Ababa that year.

Hu Changchun, who succeeded Xue last year, has continued to promote Beijing’s regional initiative.

Costantinos said governments in the Horn of Africa should put Xi’s principles into practice through diplomacy to reduce tensions, protect trade routes and secure local ceasefires.

“No conflict can be considered resolved if any group whose interests are affected has been left out of the negotiation or mediation,” he added, noting that the parties would not enter talks with equal influence.

China should work alongside existing peace efforts, Costantinos said.

“China will only add to the praiseworthy efforts by the [African Union], UN, US and [European Union],” he said.

“Its initiative will in no way gainsay the work of these venerable institutions and countries.”

item.title: [SCMP] Fandom vs flag: why young Chinese embrace Japanese pop culture but reject war-era symbols
item.description:
Young Chinese people enjoy Japanese pop culture such as anime and music, but many draw a firm line at symbols of Japanese militarism.

That line was tested recently at Moscow State University, where Chinese students confronted a classmate wearing Japan’s rising sun flag in class and called for his repatriation, state-run newspaper Global Times reported on Sunday.

Many countries, including China, view the flag as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression. Japan’s Self-Defence Forces still use the flag today.
item.content:encoded:
Young Chinese people enjoy Japanese pop culture such as anime and music, but many draw a firm line at symbols of Japanese militarism.

That line was tested recently at Moscow State University, where Chinese students confronted a classmate wearing Japan’s rising sun flag in class and called for his repatriation, state-run newspaper Global Times reported on Sunday.

Many countries, including China, view the flag as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression. Japan’s Self-Defence Forces still use the flag today.

The October 14 incident sparked an online backlash against the Chinese student and praise for those who reported him, following commentaries by People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s official newspaper, and the People’s Liberation Army.

“A disgrace to the Chinese people,” read one of the top comments under a post by Jun Zhengping, a social media account run by the PLA.

Among those condemning the student were people who enjoyed Japanese pop culture, including Lucy Huang, 24.

An anime fan since primary school, she has watched more than 200 anime series and read widely across manga – Japanese comic books and graphic novels.

“Japan in anime cannot really be called Japan but is an idealised utopia,” Huang said, adding that she drew a clear distinction between Japan in reality and the country as depicted in anime.

She said it was “unforgivable” for a Chinese person to wear the rising sun flag.

Japanese anime began appearing on Chinese television in the 1980s and gradually gained a larger audience over the following decades.

According to a 2018 report by Chinese consultancy iResearch, China had more than 200 million online anime users in 2018, with nearly 80 per cent of 803 surveyed anime consumers expressing a preference for Japanese animation.

Yet, for many young Chinese like Huang, an interest in Japanese pop culture does not mean an embrace of Japan as a whole.

Lillian Liu, a final-year university student in China’s Fujian province, echoed Huang’s anger over symbols associated with Japan’s wartime aggression against China.

Liu boycotted a September collaboration between WEGO – a popular Japanese fashion brand known for its anime merchandise and clothes – and Japanese anime series My Hero Academia.

Chinese platforms dropped the anime in 2020 after a character linked to Japan’s Unit 731, which conducted human experiments during World War II, appeared in the series.

“I really like Japanese anime and manga, but as Chinese people, we cannot allow our country’s political stance to be violated,” said Liu, who began watching Japanese anime in kindergarten.

In a September commentary, Beijing Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party’s Beijing Municipal Committee, described the collaboration as “an act of support for Japanese militarism”.

“This is shameful. I won’t buy anything from the store again,” said Liu, who estimated spending up to 20,000 yuan (US$2,995) a year on Japanese pop culture merchandise and had bought three transparent bags showing anime merchandise from WEGO before the incident.

WEGO Harajuku, the brand’s China subsidiary, later issued an apology, saying its Japanese parent company had cancelled the collaboration and removed related promotional posts.

But Yuki, 24, an anime fan who gave only her first name, said she had noticed a shift in how young people around her viewed Japan.

“The spread of anime has, to some extent, helped young people today avoid viewing all Japanese people as bad,” Yuki said.

Once a fan of My Hero Academia, Yuki stopped following the series after the 2020 controversy.

“Culture itself is also a form of politics. After the incident, I no longer engage with [My Hero Academia],” said Yuki, who regularly attends anime conventions where fans dress up as characters from animation and manga.

She has also seen how political tensions can affect the anime scene.

“The popularity of Japanese anime seems to rise and fall with China-Japan relations and political tensions,” she said, observing that a convention organiser had removed booths related to Japan after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s contentious remarks on Taiwan.

In November last year, Takaichi told Japan’s parliament that a Taiwan contingency could trigger the deployment of the Self-Defence Forces, eliciting heavy criticism from mainland Chinese officials and state media.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

China and Japan have long had a complex and evolving relationship, shaped by more than 1,000 years of exchanges in writing, religion, art and technology.

During several dynasties including the Tang, Japan sent envoys to China to study its political system, Buddhism, written culture and urban planning. The island country drew heavily on Chinese civilisation in shaping its own institutions and culture.

But Japan’s industrialisation and military expansion in the late 19th century led to war with China. Japan defeated the Qing dynasty in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95, forcing it to cede lands including Taiwan.

After Japan’s 1945 surrender at the end of World War II, China and Japan moved towards diplomatic relations, normalising them in 1972. Since then, ties have improved at times, only to be repeatedly strained by historical and territorial disputes.

Orna Naftali, an associate professor in the Department of Asian Studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said both recent geopolitical tensions and historical factors had contributed to hostility towards Japan in China.

“Every now and then, there is some kind of geopolitical tension about different issues, which is because of reasons including history,” Naftali said.

As for popular culture, she thought it did not necessarily lead people to “develop more positive attitudes” towards a country’s government or its policies.

Naftali said young people’s views of Japan were shaped by domestic influences and interactions with the country’s people and family members.

“What to think of a certain country [is shaped] not just through textbooks but also different rituals and ceremonies and whatever the teacher says,” she added.

Naftali observed that relatives’ memories of the war, whether young people had in-depth conversations with Japanese people, and their socioeconomic background also played an important role in shaping their understanding of the country.

Although “there is a constant sort of animosity towards Japan in terms of the nationalist rhetoric”, young people’s views were more complex, she said, adding that some held more favourable attitudes towards Japan, while even those with negative views had nuanced perspectives.

Shin Kawashima, professor in the University of Tokyo’s Department of International Relations, said young people in both China and Japan had shown considerable interest in one another’s cultures.

“In that sense, in the distant future, as the current younger generations come into contact with one another, Japan-China relations may take on a form different from what they are today,” he said.

However, Kawashima voiced pessimism about the prospects for building stable, positive ties between Chinese and Japanese societies through youth exchanges, noting that the “Chinese government has currently suspended most official exchanges with Japan”.

“At present, the influence of the political sphere on the economy and society is increasing, and such possibilities are not expected to expand,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Clashes flare at Paris protests as more than 400,000 march across France
item.description:
Protests across France were largely peaceful on Saturday, despite heightened tensions and sporadic clashes between protesters and the police, but authorities remained on high alert as night fell.

The French Interior Ministry counted 410,000 people who hit the streets across the country on Saturday, down from the 550,000 who protested last weekend.

The October 17 demonstrations descended into looting and the worst urban rioting France had seen in years.
item.content:encoded:
Protests across France were largely peaceful on Saturday, despite heightened tensions and sporadic clashes between protesters and the police, but authorities remained on high alert as night fell.

The French Interior Ministry counted 410,000 people who hit the streets across the country on Saturday, down from the 550,000 who protested last weekend.

The October 17 demonstrations descended into looting and the worst urban rioting France had seen in years.

A total of 249 protests took place in France on Saturday, just over half of the 430 protests that were recorded on October 17, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who added that police had detained close to 1,000 people by about 7.30pm on Saturday, with that number expected to go up.

“The marches unfolded well” despite the presence of certain “radical groups”, Nunez said.

In Paris, around 110,000 people took part in Saturday’s protest, according to Paris Police Prefecture, which said the situation across the city remained mostly “calm”.

The march started in the afternoon in a festive but uneasy mood at the southern edge of the city.

Towards Porte de Vincennes, the end point of the route, police clashed with groups of masked protesters dressed in black, an identity-hiding tactic known as the black bloc, firing tear gas and water cannon as the demonstrators set off fireworks and threw projectiles at officers.

Police also fired tear gas in Lyon and Nice, where demonstrations had been banned, and in Lille and Marseille, where a single march had been authorised in each city.

For many young students who gathered in Paris on Saturday, the main message was for the government to understand their struggle, their demand for better education and the general population’s suffering amid the rising cost of living.

Many of the protesters shared similar sentiments: they condemned the violence from looting and rioting, but also expressed anger at police conduct.

“Obviously I don’t support any kind of violence,” said Manon, a student.

“But we shouldn’t blame everything on the troublemakers who came from an underprivileged background and who probably suffer from more invisible forms of violence in their everyday life.”

Three friends had told Manon to be careful – not of the troublemakers, but of the police.

“It’s easy to see things burning, but people too have been burning on the inside,” she said.

Tensions surrounding Saturday’s demonstrations, already high, escalated further following a shooting of a “racist nature” in the western Paris suburbs of Trappes and La Verriere on Friday, which left one person dead and five injured.

The Paris police prefecture cited the attack as a primary reason for altering the authorised protest route late Friday afternoon, ordering the march shifted away from Place de la Bastille in central Paris to Porte d’Italie on the city’s outskirts.

Trade unions accepted the change after a failed legal challenge, but criticised the government for attempting to divide the movement and create chaos.

Police began clearing Place de la Bastille around noon, directing demonstrators towards Porte d’Italie, where some local residents learned only from journalists on the scene that their neighbourhood was now along the march route.

The abrupt re-routing deepened anxiety among local officials and businesses bracing for renewed unrest, with one official telling the South China Morning Post that the protest risked being “all over the place” and turning into “a mess”.

With 70,000 police and gendarmes deployed nationwide and soldiers also mobilised to protect public buildings and infrastructure, the government faced intense pressure to prevent a recurrence of the widespread violence and looting seen the previous weekend.

“A fiasco like this, two weekends in a row, I don’t know what explanation we could give the French. We really cannot afford to get this wrong,” an adviser to Interior Minister Nunez told broadcaster BFMTV on Saturday.

Across France, authorities moved to ban most demonstrations following French President Emmanuel Macron’s intervention on Thursday, in which he stated that “the general recommendation is to hold no demonstrations in the coming days”.

Protests were prohibited outright in regional cities including Bordeaux, Lyon and Nice, with only a single demonstration approved for each of Paris, Lille and Marseille.

In Paris, local businesses took aggressive security precautions.

Along Rue Beaurepaire and surrounding streets, storefronts were closed behind thick sheets of plywood.

Burn marks on the road and paper signs reading “Fermeture pour cause de sinistre” (Closed due to unforeseen circumstances) remained visible reminders of the previous Saturday’s riots, during which a bar was torched and multiple retail outlets were ransacked.

The few cafes and shops that chose to open planned to close by early afternoon.

Even luxury boutiques in the west of the French capital, located far from the designated protest route, boarded up display windows and reinforced entryways against potential roving bands of vandals. Major cultural landmarks including the Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay were also closed.

Sweeping restrictions have intensified national debate over civil liberties and the constitutionally protected right to protest as the French government tries to maintain social order.

“I want the interior minister to carry out his primary mission: guaranteeing the exercise of individual freedoms and the right to protest, and protecting people first and property second,” the green party mayor of Paris’ 11th arrondissement David Belliard told the SCMP. “That is simple and basic in a great democratic country.”

Belliard’s district encompasses both Place de la Bastille and Place de la Republique – covering some areas hardest hit by last Saturday’s riots and the exact corridor where organisers had originally planned to march.

France is the most prominent flashpoint in a wider wave of demonstrations over the cost of living, housing and government spending rippling across Europe this weekend, with rallies planned in Italy, Portugal, Spain, Belgium and Albania.

In Italy, a coalition called the “October 17 Movement” called protests across eight cities on Saturday.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni reinforced police and military deployments in Milan, one week after violent clashes and looting hit the country’s financial and fashion capital.

item.title: [SCMP] Ukraine’s Starlink woes should be a wake-up call for Taiwan, analysts say
item.description:
Taiwan should not rely on a single foreign satellite provider for critical wartime communications, analysts have warned, after sudden restrictions on the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.

The episode has renewed debate in Taiwan over the risks of entrusting essential communications to foreign commercial operators whose services could be restricted for political, military or business reasons.

Analysts said this was particularly relevant as Taipei was trying to strengthen the resilience of its communication networks against potential mainland Chinese attacks while simultaneously expanding its use of drones and other unmanned systems.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan should not rely on a single foreign satellite provider for critical wartime communications, analysts have warned, after sudden restrictions on the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.

The episode has renewed debate in Taiwan over the risks of entrusting essential communications to foreign commercial operators whose services could be restricted for political, military or business reasons.

Analysts said this was particularly relevant as Taipei was trying to strengthen the resilience of its communication networks against potential mainland Chinese attacks while simultaneously expanding its use of drones and other unmanned systems.
