“The lesson from this incident is that we cannot become overly dependent on satellite navigation services provided by a single company,” said Shu Hsiao-huang, a senior analyst at Taiwan’s government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research.

SpaceX this month imposed new speed restrictions on terminals in Ukraine connected to its Starlink satellite internet service, disrupting some Ukrainian drone combat operations.

The restrictions cut a terminal’s link to the internet when it travels faster than 160km/h (100mph), a speed often exceeded by Ukrainian drones equipped with Starshield, the military version of Starlink.

The restrictions forced some drones to fly more slowly, making them easier for Russian forces to target or evade and prompting Kyiv to seek changes to the limits.

Conflicting accounts have emerged over who was responsible for the restrictions and why they were introduced.

Musk suggested that US President Donald Trump had decided to implement the limits because the US government owns and controls Starshield. Trump denied this, but said he doubted Musk was responsible, while the Pentagon also denied it was involved.

Regardless of who made the decision, the episode showed the dangers of depending on a system ultimately controlled by an external provider, according to Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies in Taipei.

“Even the military-grade Starshield system funded or heavily supported by the US government could still potentially be disconnected or have its speed restricted at a critical moment because of political considerations or commercial interests,” Wang said.

He said the risks could be more complicated for Taiwan because Musk has substantial commercial interests on the Chinese mainland, including Tesla’s Shanghai factory.

While Taiwan’s military does not currently use Starlink, its legislature has eased rules that previously restricted foreign satellite communications companies from entering the local market, although detailed implementation arrangements have yet to be announced.

Taipei has already struck deals with providers willing to work within its restrictions, including Eutelsat OneWeb, while pursuing indigenous low-Earth-orbit satellite capabilities.

But analysts warned that replacing dependence on terrestrial and submarine networks with a single satellite constellation would merely exchange one vulnerability for another.

Wang called for a “multi-orbit, multi-provider” strategy combining indigenous satellites with commercial constellations from different international suppliers.

Taiwan should accelerate development of what he described as a “Taiwanese version of Starlink” to retain a communications channel beyond the control of foreign companies, while expanding cooperation with alternative operators such as OneWeb and Luxembourg-based SES.

He said the approach could also support Taiwan’s defence industry by encouraging the development of unmanned systems that did not rely on the US government-operated GPS as well as communications links less dependent on satellites.

Shu said redundancy would become increasingly important as Taiwan incorporated more unmanned systems into its armed forces.

Satellite systems support positioning, navigation and timing – or PNT – which are essential to operations ranging from unmanned aircraft and precision weapons to telecommunications and electricity networks.

Taiwan therefore needed alternatives to GPS as well as backup communication networks, Shu said.

The options include inertial navigation systems that can calculate an object’s position without external signals and AI-based visual navigation and terrain matching.

“The essence of satellite navigation redundancy is not putting all your eggs in the GPS basket,” Shu said, adding that weapons and critical infrastructure needed to remain functional during periods of “digital darkness”.

Developing unmanned systems capable of navigating without GPS would further reduce Taiwan’s dependence on satellite services, he added.

James Yifan Chen, a Taipei-based international relations and strategic studies scholar, said Taiwan’s situation differed from Ukraine’s because Taipei had “chosen not to depend on Starlink or Starshield because of its concerns about Musk’s close business ties with China”.

But that did not eliminate its reliance on foreign technology. Much of Taiwan’s advanced military equipment comes from the United States, meaning Taipei still needed to consider the possibility that externally supplied capabilities could be restricted during a conflict, he said.

Another challenge was whether “Taiwan’s own satellites could eventually provide sufficient connectivity and withstand electronic warfare and jamming by the People’s Liberation Army”, Chen added.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Analysts also cautioned against treating Ukraine as a direct template for a Taiwan Strait conflict.

Wang said Taiwan’s potential battlefield would be much smaller, while drones operating across the strait would face different geographical and weather conditions.

Many Taiwanese drones would probably operate around the island or in coastal areas, where microwave links and other terrestrial communications could provide alternatives if satellite connections failed, he said.

The controversy also raised a broader question about the reliability of US support, according to Huang Huei-hua, director of the Taiwan Global Talk think tank.

“If Taiwan found itself in Ukraine’s predicament during a cross-strait conflict, it could end up the biggest loser,” she said. “Like Ukraine, Taiwan could face the risk of being abandoned.”

Huang said relying too heavily on any single foreign partner, including the United States, carried considerable risks.

“Taiwan needs to prepare a range of contingency plans, or it risks becoming expendable when the interests of larger powers change,” she said.

“The crisis of trust between Ukraine and the United States should serve as a wake-up call: there is no permanent comfort zone, even between allies.”

item.title: [SCMP] Overseas Filipinos feel heartache over missing parcels for loved ones, demand answers
item.description:
At this time of year, Fatima Ramos would normally be preparing her balikbayan boxes. Overseas Filipinos typically fill these boxes with gifts, clothes, food and household items to send to their loved ones back home in the Philippines for Christmas.

Ramos has previously sent the tax-exempt parcels to her family and Philippine charity organisations from Abu Dhabi, where she is a domestic worker.

Now back in the Philippines, Ramos is seeking answers about the parcels she sent last year, some of which arrived severely damaged while others remain missing.
item.content:encoded:
At this time of year, Fatima Ramos would normally be preparing her balikbayan boxes. Overseas Filipinos typically fill these boxes with gifts, clothes, food and household items to send to their loved ones back home in the Philippines for Christmas.

Ramos has previously sent the tax-exempt parcels to her family and Philippine charity organisations from Abu Dhabi, where she is a domestic worker.

Now back in the Philippines, Ramos is seeking answers about the parcels she sent last year, some of which arrived severely damaged while others remain missing.

“I got one of my boxes, and it was completely soaked. The clothes were faded and mouldy. The items and the box were all crushed. It was heartbreaking. The food, such as the chocolates, had melted because it got wet,” Ramos told This Week in Asia.

Ric, an engineer in Saudi Arabia who asked to be identified only by his first name, has suffered a similar experience with a balikbayan – a compound word in Tagalog meaning return to a country – box.

According to him, he sent a balikbayan box from Jeddah in June, and a delivery company’s representative told him in July that the parcel was still awaiting shipment. When he followed up in September, his emails and calls went unanswered.

For many overseas Filipinos, balikbayan boxes often represent weeks or months of careful selection of items paid for with their hard-earned savings, and an expression of their love from afar. Their tax-exempt status reflects the Philippine government’s recognition of the role overseas Filipinos play in supporting their families.

But thousands of these boxes have been left in limbo as the Christmas season approaches, with some abandoned in shipping containers at Philippine ports and others stranded in their countries of origin amid problems involving cargo forwarding companies.

The boxes sent by Ramos and Ric were handled by Makati Express Cargo, a forwarding company serving customers in the United States and the Middle East.

The Philippines’ Bureau of Customs (BOC) revoked the company’s licence in January and filed criminal complaints against it in May over nearly 40,000 boxes left unclaimed at ports, involving more than 30 million pesos (US$1.6 million) in unpaid duties.

Ramos sent eight boxes between January and March before returning to the Philippines for good because of a heart condition that she said had worsened following Iran’s attacks on the United Arab Emirates, including Abu Dhabi.

She found out about the mounting complaints against the forwarding company only after she returned home.

“At first, I didn’t want to believe it. But then I started following up with my package online and through the company’s website in March. By April, I still couldn’t get an answer to verify whether my boxes had already arrived. They should have been in the Philippines by now,” she said.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Makati Express Cargo for comment.

On Sunday, the BOC said it had discovered 29 abandoned shipping containers holding at least 10,000 of the boxes at various ports in the Philippines, some of which had arrived in May.

In June, the BOC had earlier filed complaints against five cargo forwarding companies over 3,176 abandoned boxes.

Some of the boxes had already been opened, rummaged through and “slaughtered”, Ramos claimed.

This Week in Asia has also reached out to the BOC for comment.

Ramos, who has been gathering complaints from at least 300 overseas Filipinos in the Middle East over their unclaimed boxes, said she had spoken to officials from the BOC and the Department of Migrant Workers to help resolve the matter.

Labour of love

For migrant Filipinos, the unaccounted balikbayan boxes are a sore point as they symbolise their love and sacrifice, according to analysts.

Over 2 million Filipinos work as overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), part of a larger global diaspora of between 10 million and 15 million.

“Some Filipino families who decided to migrate to other countries may consider sending balikbayan boxes as a means of extending love and care to relatives in the Philippines. A balikbayan box could be viewed as a sustenance of relational closeness or to communicate thoughtfulness,” said Lenis Aislinn Separa, an intercultural communication researcher based in New Zealand.

“Each item they buy that fills a space in a balikbayan box has a backstory of how they struggled in prioritising between what they need to survive living abroad and providing what they believe their family needs back home.”

Hannah Nario-Lopez, an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman’s sociology department, said each box was a labour of love from migrant workers, who would curate items carefully over weeks or months.

“This simple, small, menial act converts the physical distance and the time spent abroad into tangible care, allowing the worker to remain present in the everyday life of their household,” she said.

The box also complements regular cash remittances from OFWs by offering items for household needs such as groceries, toiletries, school supplies, bags and shoes. For some, its loss could disrupt daily routines, such as health supplements for family members who were elderly or ill, Nario-Lopez said.

As such, the loss of the box would become a source of trauma for a family, according to Nario-Lopez.

“The non-arrival of a box feels like a broken promise, leading to guilt for the sender, and disappointment or a feeling of abandonment for the family,” she said.

Ramos said in one meeting with the Bureau of Customs, an OFW shared that she had sent a balikbayan box containing medicines for a family member, who later died. The box was lost along the way.

“The medicine never made it. The commissioner [of the bureau] was moved, because he had not realised how severe the impact had been,” she said.

Nario-Lopez said every loss of a balikbayan box would erode trust in Philippine institutions involved in its safe delivery, citing cases of looting at warehouses that stored such parcels.

“We have to remember that the balikbayan box is actually a grant to Filipinos working overseas. It’s tax-free because they’re sustaining the country through their remittances. So because of this, it becomes a manifestation of distrust in our logistics and governance,” Nario-Lopez said.

She warned that OFWs also faced unscrupulous scammers looking to exploit them.

“OFWs searching for cheap shipping alternatives become valuable targets for predatory forwarders. It seems like it gives an opening to people with bad intentions,” she added.

Nario-Lopez urged Philippine authorities to tighten regulations and online tracking of box movements to protect OFWs and their families.

“We could pressure the state through social media, for example, to have a more systematic or universal database to actively track container ships, expose fraudulent consolidators and [praise] lobby officials or leaders who would genuinely advocate for OFWs,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore embraces AI for cyber defence, with one caveat: breach transparency
item.description:
Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces.

Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous.

At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy that would see it progressively deploy AI across its cyber defence operations and work with industry partners to accelerate adoption, as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces.

Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous.

At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy that would see it progressively deploy AI across its cyber defence operations and work with industry partners to accelerate adoption, as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure.

The city state would take a “pragmatic” approach to AI adoption, allowing it to choose between the “best available” models, K. Shanmugam, coordinating minister for national security, said during a speech at Singapore International Cyber Week on October 13.

“We will not need to develop our own AI models for every use case. What we really need is the capability to evaluate the best available models and to adapt them to our own needs.”

Anthropic’s Claude is among the models Singapore is exploring as it seeks to strengthen its cyber defences. The US technology firm signed an agreement with Singapore on the sidelines of the summit, setting out areas of AI cooperation, including safety, security, responsible adoption and research into the impact of adoption.

“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Anthropic co-founder Benjamin Mann at the signing on October 13, a day before the firm opened its fifth Asia-Pacific office in the city state. Anthropic already has offices in Japan, India, South Korea and Australia.

“With this [memorandum of understanding], we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world,” Mann said.

Safety and transparency concerns

The partnerships offer governments access to emerging technologies and technical expertise, but also make transparency and oversight increasingly important as AI systems become more capable and autonomous.

On the sidelines of the event, Shanmugam told the media that Singapore had sought greater transparency from major technology companies, following meetings with firms including Anthropic, Google, Amazon and OpenAI.

“They need to notify us early on when something happens, taking a leaf from the experience in Australia and what happened there,” he said. “Generally, the companies have expressed an attitude of cooperation. But I would say it’s work in progress. It’s something that we are talking to them about.”

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese criticised OpenAI in September over what he called an “unacceptable” breach involving an AI agent that infiltrated a government health website and accessed public and non-public files in June. Albanese accused the firm of taking “way too long” to tell Canberra about the incident.

The San Francisco-headquartered company, which said it learned of the breach in August, apologised and acknowledged that its handling of the incident was “not enough”.

In July, open-source AI platform Hugging Face said it had been hacked by autonomous AI agents. Less than a week later, OpenAI revealed that the “unprecedented cyber incident” was driven by a combination of its models after it lost control of them during a security test.

Singapore had yet to encounter another attack like those attributed to cyberthreat group UNC3886, Shanmugam said. Last year, he revealed that the group had been targeting the city state’s critical infrastructure.

“We haven’t come across another attack like what we have heard from other countries,” he said. “But, you know, also, we don’t know what we don’t know.”

Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said closer cooperation with technology companies did not necessarily increase the risk of such breaches and could help mitigate threats through information-sharing and technical evaluation.

He warned, however, that expanding AI use in governance could create new vulnerabilities that existing cybersecurity arrangements might not address.

“AI agents could inadvertently access unauthorised systems, expose sensitive information or be manipulated through malicious inputs,” he said, urging the establishment of clear boundaries on AI autonomy and the use of controlled environments during deployment.

The partnerships could also make it harder to determine who was responsible when disruptions or breaches occurred, Gatra said.

“If an AI system makes a mistake that disrupts government services, who is accountable? The government agency deploying it, the company developing it, or the officials who authorised its use?”

Asean cooperation

Other Southeast Asian nations have also begun drawing on resources from major technology companies to strengthen their cyber defences, but industry experts warn that a widening digital divide could leave smaller states behind.

The Philippines and Google announced the expansion of a multi-year partnership in June aimed at strengthening Manila’s cybersecurity and subsea cable systems to ensure resilient digital connectivity. The country’s cyber-monitoring hub has also deployed Google Cloud’s security framework, which provides AI-driven cyber defence.

Last year, Thailand announced plans to adopt the Google framework, with the aim of enabling its cyberdefence centre to coordinate responses more effectively to online threats targeting government bodies and infrastructure.

But less developed states might lack the technical resources or negotiating leverage to secure timely disclosures from major technology firms through bilateral arrangements, said Gatra, who urged greater cooperation among members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

“Singapore could work with Asean partners to develop common expectations around incident notification and cross-border information-sharing,” he said.

The city state has said it wants to strengthen the bloc’s collective cyber resilience by deepening practical cooperation and capacity building when it assumes the Asean chairmanship next year.

Shanmugam told the media that Asean already had a framework for dealing with cyberthreats but acknowledged that it remained a “work in progress”. The Asean cybersecurity cooperation strategy outlines five pillars, including strengthening readiness, advancing regional policy coordination and building capacity.

“We are all catching up on this issue of AI, and each country is focused on its own issues,” he said. “Asean collectively has some work to do in trying to deal with it together too. So, these are discussions that have to carry on.”

item.title: [SCMP] Novel idea: Thailand, Vietnam take books on the road in reading drive
item.description:
Tran Dai Thang spotted two young people who had picked up their drinks at a pop-up cafe beside his travelling bookstore and were about to leave, so he called them over.

One of them said they did not read books, Thang recalled. But he kept the conversation going and eventually persuaded the visitor to buy a book for 10,000 dong (US$0.40) – heavily discounted from its original price of 45,000 dong.

For Thang, an artist and publisher, the small sale mattered far less than the fact that someone who said they did not read had chosen to pick up a book.
item.content:encoded:
Tran Dai Thang spotted two young people who had picked up their drinks at a pop-up cafe beside his travelling bookstore and were about to leave, so he called them over.

One of them said they did not read books, Thang recalled. But he kept the conversation going and eventually persuaded the visitor to buy a book for 10,000 dong (US$0.40) – heavily discounted from its original price of 45,000 dong.

For Thang, an artist and publisher, the small sale mattered far less than the fact that someone who said they did not read had chosen to pick up a book.

“Who knows, it might be the start of a new habit,” he said.

Thang, 53, is spending a year travelling across Vietnam in a truck with his “Books To Every Home” project, also known as “Roaming Turtle”.

In neighbouring Thailand, a similar book truck named “Somelee” (Cotton) is pursuing an equally ambitious mission: visiting all 77 provinces to take literature beyond Bangkok and the country’s other urban centres.

Their goal goes beyond selling books. By taking their trucks beyond the big cities, the two projects hope to spark curiosity, build connections through storytelling and turn chance roadside encounters into lasting reading habits for people who might otherwise never enter a bookshop.

But bringing books to the provinces comes at a cost – from fuel and accommodation to staff wages – and neither truck can guarantee a crowd at every stop.

‘Come with me for a year’

Thang’s decision to start Roaming Turtle followed the closure of the last branch of his Ca Chep bookshop chain on Ho Chi Minh City’s Vo Van Tan Street in June. Customers were increasingly buying online, he said, and he no longer had the time or focus to run the store.

As its closure approached, a former employee offered to help him sell books.

“Then come with me for a year,” Thang recalled replying.

With no advance plan, the truck set off on July 15 from Ho Chi Minh City on a journey scheduled to last until July 2027. By mid-October, Thang said the Roaming Turtle had reached its 27th stop – Nam Dinh in the Red River Delta – with Thai Binh next on the itinerary.

“The Ca Chep Bookstore may have closed its fixed location, but we don’t want the story of Ca Chep to end there,” he said, noting that Ca Chep means carp in Vietnamese. “Ca Chep only temporarily paused, but never stopped swimming.”

Growing up in mountainous Hoa Binh province, Thang loved reading and drawing. After graduating from the University of Industrial Fine Arts in 1995, he designed book covers at a state-owned publisher before establishing Dong A, his own book company.

On the road, those skills come together. Together with a driver and a sales assistant, Thang introduces readers to Dong A’s titles and hand-draws book covers upon request. Bystanders even help unload boxes, arrange displays and manage sales.

His autobiography has become a particular attraction. He initially brought five copies to sell at each stop, illustrating every cover differently. When those sold out, readers began ordering copies online and bringing them to his truck to be illustrated. In Da Nang, he hand-illustrated 22 covers.

“Each book cover is a unique illustration, connected to a person and a memory from my journey,” he said.

Other encounters have triggered deeper personal memories. In Quy Nhon, he met an unemployed mother who used her limited savings to buy books for her child – a scene that reminded him of his own childhood and mother.

Beyond the capital

In Thailand, the team behind the Somelee book truck began with a similar problem of access.

Bookshops and literary fairs were concentrated in Bangkok and other major urban centres, according to Yasawath Chuthivisitrathikul, a project manager at P.S. Publishing. The publisher was previously affiliated with Somewhere Bookshop and Home Cafe in Bangkok’s Yai district, which closed its doors last Sunday.

“We saw this as an opportunity to reach everyone – both readers and people who have never read books before,” Yasawath said.

Founded by Borisat Pongwat, or “Turk”, Somelee aims to reach regular readers and non-readers alike.

So far, the five-person Somelee team, including Yasawath and Borisat, has visited about 25 venues and plans to cover all 77 Thai provinces within two years.

Jarungdach Phosri, or “Ton”, who drives the truck, said journeys had grown rapidly, from three cafe visits in Nakhon Ratchasima (Korat) to a single tour covering 15 provinces over nearly three months.

Somelee’s inventory initially focused on Thai novels, short stories and poetry, before expanding into children’s literature. However, the team discovered reading preferences varied widely by region.

Jarungdach said some stops showed strong demand for translated literature, while others preferred short stories or Thai works. Unfulfilled reader requests are logged as feedback to guide future stock selection.

“What makes it worthwhile, beyond selling books, is meeting readers,” Jarungdach said. “Some are people we have only spoken to through a keyboard. We get to meet and exchange ideas.”

One reader travelled three hours on a motorcycle from another province just to visit the truck, Yasawath recalled.

At Natit Coffee and Crafts in Nong Khai province, proprietor Raviya Wongsathitana said the cafe connected with Somelee through a local community page on social media while taking part in the first Nongkhai Reading Week.

The cafe hosted activities alongside the truck, including a workshop on making simple handmade books or zines. Most visitors were existing customers, Raviya said, although the event also attracted wider local interest.

“I see Somelee as a living mobile bookstore,” she said. “They share stories of their travels and tell people who they’ll meet and where, allowing visitors to be part of an experience beyond simply buying books.”

Keeping things moving

Behind these encounters is a complex mobile supply chain. To keep inventory stocked, Somelee posts book shipments ahead to hotels along their route, while local cafe owners offer travel tips and help arrange accommodation.

Nevertheless, operational costs are a constant burden. Fuel, lodgings and equipment add up quickly, while turnout at remote stops can be unpredictable. Unfavourable weather, particularly heavy rain, can easily disrupt operations for days.

“We want to promote a reading culture, so we started driving out to meet people in the provinces, far from Bangkok,” Yasawath said. “Both readers and people who have never read books before are welcome, and we continue to stay in touch with them online.”

In Vietnam, Thang financed his truck with a bank loan of around 1.2 billion dong (US$46,360). Sales cover everyday living and operating expenses on the road, while Dong A handles staff salaries and vehicle loan repayments.

Both projects sometimes lower prices to keep books accessible. Somelee offers reductions of 15 to 30 per cent – sometimes exceeding 50 per cent for students – while Thang focuses sales in cities so he can give books away for free at schools in more remote locations.

For Thang, a year on the road has sharpened his approach to publishing.

“Making good, beautiful books remains important, but prices must allow them to reach people with different means,” he said. “People who truly want to read should not have to give up a book they love just because they lack money.”

item.title: [SCMP] Gulf economies accelerate diversification as recession looms over Iran war
item.description:
Before the outbreak of the war triggered by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, the Gulf monarchies were living the prosperity dream that was the envy of the world.

Their hydrocarbon-fuelled economies were glitzy oases of growth, inoculated from the conflict in Gaza that had rocked other parts of the Middle East for several years.

Underpinned by decades-old US security guarantees and conflict mediation by billionaire sheikhs, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar cultivated images as peaceful lands of opportunity as they invested staggering amounts of money in economic diversification programmes.
item.content:encoded:
Before the outbreak of the war triggered by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, the Gulf monarchies were living the prosperity dream that was the envy of the world.

Their hydrocarbon-fuelled economies were glitzy oases of growth, inoculated from the conflict in Gaza that had rocked other parts of the Middle East for several years.

Underpinned by decades-old US security guarantees and conflict mediation by billionaire sheikhs, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar cultivated images as peaceful lands of opportunity as they invested staggering amounts of money in economic diversification programmes.

Backed by sovereign wealth funds with trillions of dollars invested mostly in the West, these leading states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) embarked on transformative programmes to reposition their economies amid the global transition away from oil and gas. Similar diversification initiatives were also happening in Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain, the other three GCC members.

Such a shift towards long-term economic stability is important in maintaining the political legitimacy of the Gulf monarchies in the eyes of their burgeoning young populations, especially amid mounting public anger at the carnage in Gaza, according to analysts.

The GCC states, as well as other Muslim-majority governments such as Pakistan and Turkey, eventually persuaded US President Donald Trump to end the Gaza war in October 2025, renewing optimism about the Gulf economies.

However, everything changed soon after the Gaza ceasefire, when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu managed to convince Trump to go to war against Iran.

Rather than just retaliating against Israel, Iran has also vented its fury against the GCC states, attacking energy infrastructure, airports and ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.

With Trump weighing his options, including both another military escalation and a politically inconclusive end to the war with Iran after midterm congressional elections on November 5, uncertainty reigns in the Gulf region.

The eruption of war between Saudi Arabia and Tehran’s Houthi rebel allies in Yemen last month has exacerbated these anxieties.

Driven by necessity, GCC governments have unveiled plans to stabilise their economies. The two largest in the bloc – Saudi Arabia and the UAE – are on the verge of a potential technical recession caused by the Iran war, while Qatar is already in a recession.

In the second quarter of this year, Saudi Arabia’s economy – the largest in the GCC – fell by 4.8 per cent from 3 per cent growth in the first quarter. The UAE’s economy – the Gulf’s logistical hub – decreased by 2.1 per cent from an expansion of 3 per cent over the same period.

Qatar’s economic outlook worsened, with its GDP declining by 15.7 per cent in the second quarter, accelerating from a drop of 7 per cent in the first quarter.

According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) projections published on October 13, the UAE is expected to record a 3.9 per cent drop in its GDP in 2026 from a pre-war forecast of 3.1 per cent growth, while Saudi Arabia is projected to fall by 3.3 per cent this year from an earlier predicted 4.6 per cent growth.

Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are set to record double-digit GDP contractions in 2026.

Like the IMF, the World Bank has forecast the GCC economies to rebound in 2027 if hostilities end this year and unhindered passage through the Strait of Hormuz is restored by next March.

Tim Callen, a former chief of the IMF’s GCC division, expected the Gulf states to step up their economic diversification plans.

The development of new industries would move ahead with some adjustments, including “a new focus on diversifying and better protecting energy and transport infrastructure”, Callen said.

Karen Young, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Centre on Global Energy Policy in New York, said Gulf governments would continue to prioritise investments in natural gas production and its export in liquefied form, as well as the acquisition of such assets overseas.

They would also focus on other “essential” areas such as more localised defence manufacturing, AI and other technologies.

Young said the diversification of the power sector in the GCC to include nuclear and renewables would be crucial to reviving its economies, while other sectors like tourism could continue to come under pressure.

Sovereign wealth funds like Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, the UAE’s L’imad and the Oman Investment Authority would provide much of the funding and impetus needed to get the Gulf economies back on track, according to analysts.

“Those funds have already demonstrated a propensity to play a greater domestic role. But these funds can’t do it all alone,” said Robert Mogielnicki, founder of Paris-based Polisphere Advisory.

The involvement of foreign partners would be critical because of the considerable investments that would be needed to revive and grow the GCC economies, Mogielnicki said.

Analysts predict GCC members will spend hundreds of billions of dollars to expand infrastructure across major sectors in the coming years as part of their economic transformation.

One such initiative is a planned cross-GCC oil pipeline bypassing the Strait of Hormuz to be co-funded by all six members, which a report published by Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy estimated earlier this year to cost US$55 billion.

HSBC, Hong Kong’s biggest lender, recently projected the value of ongoing infrastructure projects in the UAE at US$190 billion.

The government of Dubai – one of the country’s seven emirates and its business centre – announced a US$572 billion pipeline of projects on October 13, including a massive new suburb and the construction of the world’s biggest airport.

Mognielicki said the GCC’s ambitious infrastructure roll-out was both expensive and complex. “For the moment, most Gulf governments see a compelling justification for paying the price.”

Callen said that despite these undertakings, it was far from certain whether the confidence of foreign investors in the GCC economies could rebound any time soon.

Investors would be assessing the post-war demand for both energy and non-oil goods and services from the Gulf states, as well as the outlook of their tourism, conference, logistics and aviation sectors, according to Callen.

“This is a very complex strategic project both because diversifying away from oil is anyway extremely difficult and to add to that now is the regional uncertainty,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Poster child’: why more Chinese firms have Thailand in their expansion plans
item.description:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a strategy largely designed as a hedge against tariffs and geopolitical risks.

Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.
item.content:encoded:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a strategy largely designed as a hedge against tariffs and geopolitical risks.

Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.

But the influx has also made Bangkok more mindful of risks, particularly those related to US measures intended to limit Chinese transshipment.

“Thailand is hailed as a new poster child of the ‘China plus one’ strategy of the new era,” said Donald Low, professor of public policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

As tech-intensive Chinese manufacturers flock there while the sun sets on export re-routing via Vietnam, the Land of Smiles may gain further ground over its neighbour.

“Thailand has a reasonably mature, sophisticated manufacturing base that is more advanced than Vietnam’s,” Low said.

From Vietnam’s perspective, “manufacturing saturation” and a perception change – aggravated by US trade scrutiny, including punitive tariffs of 40 per cent on Chinese goods found to have been diverted through the country – mean it may have run its course as a popular destination, the scholar added.

Thailand in, Vietnam out?

In 2025, Thailand attracted US$5.33 billion in Chinese investment, compared with Vietnam’s US$2.46 billion, according to data from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce.

Thailand’s location and established industrial infrastructure have allowed China-funded factories to plug straight into supply chains that are being extended from China to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), Low said.

“For tech-intensive manufacturing – like electronic components and machinery, electric vehicles [EVs] and solar panels – Thailand has the requisite capabilities to attract investments. BYD, for instance, runs an EV plant there,” he said.

In a success story now touted by Thai officials, the first EV made by BYD in Thailand rolled off the production line in 2024 in Rayong, the location of a US$490 million factory with an annual capacity of 150,000 units and a Thai workforce of 10,000.

On the other hand, BYD’s plan for a similar factory in Vietnam, unveiled in 2024, remains stuck in the slow lane, with construction delayed.

“Even before the US imposed tariffs on transshipped goods, there were already signs Vietnam was ‘saturated’ with manufacturing from China, especially in assembly,” according to Low.

“It was becoming less attractive to assembly manufacturing due to infrastructure bottlenecks and rising labour costs … American levies added to the pressures facing Chinese firms there.”

Some again see Thailand as the next Vietnam … They need a ‘Made in Thailand’ label

Thai trade official

Perception in Vietnam is also becoming less favourable towards Chinese investment. “A growing view is that Vietnamese domestic manufacturers weren’t benefiting from Chinese firms investing there for avoiding US tariffs,” Low said.

“There was little technology transfer, the investments weren’t helping the economy upgrade and worse, they may also squeeze out Vietnamese firms.”

In contrast, Thailand is anticipating a growing influx.

In the first half of 2026, Thai authorities approved 321 mainland China-funded investment projects for government incentives, representing one-quarter of the total. These projects brought in 45.7 billion Thai baht or 9.7 billion Chinese yuan (US$1.4 billion), according to Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI).

Between 2021 and 2025, total investments from mainland China reached 132.5 billion yuan, with an average year-on-year growth of 56 per cent.

Thailand has also entered the top four recipients of Chinese foreign direct investment in Asean, alongside Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia.

Thailand not becoming another Vietnam

Though more Chinese firms are making their way to Thai shores, their motives may still differ substantially, according to a trade official with Thailand BOI’s office in China, adding that some still sought only to divert exports.

“Some again see Thailand as the next Vietnam … They need a ‘Made in Thailand’ label,” she said, declining to be named as she was not authorised to speak to media.

The official said Bangkok’s relatively favourable trade ties with Washington presented an opportunity for companies looking to establish themselves in Thailand – as well as less scrupulous exporters searching for tariff loopholes.

She pointed to Bangkok’s 17 free trade agreements covering 24 partner economies, which would enable “broad export access”, as well as Bangkok and Washington’s reciprocal trade agreement, which included possible zero-duty treatment for certain products.

This stands in contrast with Vietnam’s higher US duty exposure, thanks to stricter transshipment rules and its trade surplus with the US – two times the size of Thailand’s.

Thailand, though also subject to rules of origin verification, experiences “relatively lower US scrutiny”, the official said.

These considerations are likely to have influenced Chinese manufacturers’ plans.

In a December stock exchange filing, Shandong Bailong Chuangyuan Bio-tech, one of China’s largest food ingredient producers, said it had raised 748 million yuan to expand its Thai operations.

“This is a strategic move … The Thai facility will not only boost profitability by leveraging low-cost raw materials and tariff advantages there … It can also circumvent trade barriers,” said the company.

Some analysts warned that a rush by Chinese manufacturers into Thailand could eventually turn the country into another Vietnam, with those seeking a new tariff haven getting squeezed all over again.

“With tools like Section 301 probes, Washington is looking through the map,” said Dan Martin, a Vietnam-based international business adviser with global consultancy Dezan Shira & Associates.

“Other countries like Thailand can also come under scrutiny, just like Vietnam. Exporters should stop hunting for the next loophole.”

But Thailand is not sitting idle, and appears to be heeding lessons from Vietnam’s experience over punitive measures targeting transshipment and “origin fraud”.

Minimal processing or simple relabelling before re-exporting has been under heavy scrutiny by the Thai Department of Foreign Trade, with the department heightening monitoring for products of Chinese origin and formulating watch lists for sectors vulnerable to tariff circumvention, according to Thai media reports.

To avoid US retaliation and access restrictions, and to protect legitimate local producers, Bangkok is collaborating with Washington to inspect suspected supply chains and mandate strict rules of origin certification.

Last year, Thailand’s Anti-Dumping and Subsidy Consideration Committee said it had determined certain Chinese steel pipe imports were slightly altered or transshipped through the country to bypass tariffs, a practice it deemed an evasion of anti-dumping rules.

In February, the US Department of Commerce also determined imported pipes, completed in Thailand but using steel billets from China, circumvented anti-dumping duties.

Thailand still beckons

As Bangkok takes steps to combat re-routing and other tariff avoidance practices, Thai diplomats in China stressed their country still “fully embraces” Chinese investments, adding that Bangkok was committed to helping companies tap Thailand’s potential.

Siwadee Suksawate, commerce consul with the Thai consulate in Guangzhou, said there were immense opportunities for Chinese firms who “invest local and sell local”.

“We have a huge domestic market of 66 million people. In areas like electronics and automotive, especially EVs, we are positioned to attract manufacturers seeking diversification and localisation,” she said.

“Rather than viewing Thailand as [only] for export, more Chinese firms now have long-term commitment and localised production and management.”

Unlike many in Vietnam, prominent Thai voices are continuing to call for infusions of Chinese capital. “Thailand is not wrong to welcome Chinese investment. The capital is real, the factories are being built, and the technology is arriving,” read a May editorial by the Thailand Business News.

“For a developing economy seeking to industrialise rapidly, that is not a relationship to squander.”

New era, new playbook

Underpinning their warmer economic ties after last year’s peak tariff levels, Beijing and Washington have extended their trade truce and pared back tensions, particularly after this year’s summits between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.

New Chinese investments coming to Thailand are lured by our real advantages, less likely for transshipment

Siwadee Suksawate, Thai commerce consul

The US has agreed to identify US$30 billion worth of “non-sensitive goods” from China, like toys, fireworks and daily necessities, for tariff exemption under the new Board of Trade mechanism. Beijing has agreed in principle to a similar exemption.

Officials and business leaders from Thailand, Vietnam and China said the friendlier atmosphere could reduce the incentive to divert exports.

“This means new Chinese investments coming to Thailand are lured by our real advantages, less likely for transshipment,” Suksawate said.

One type of Chinese investment being courted heavily is in hi-tech electronics, she said, adding that Bangkok had optimised tax and other incentives for them, particularly for those setting up shop in Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor, a special economic zone close to the Chinese border.

Liu Quanlei, chairman of the Chinese Enterprises Chamber of Commerce in Thailand, observed a similar shift towards local sales.

“Notably, more [Chinese firms] are going local, prioritising sales in Thailand and Asean … This is particularly evident in the tech and digital sector, led by Huawei and ZTE, in the home appliance sector represented by Haier, Midea and TCL, as well as EV makers like BYD and Chery,” Liu said at a business seminar held in September at the 23rd China-Asean Expo in Nanning.

He added some Chinese investors were shipping finished products and components back home, including rice, rubber and non-ferrous metal.

Liu said this demand was expected to bring more positive spillovers to Thailand, Vietnam and other countries in China’s periphery, including Chinese producers based there, in the form of more imports.

Though Thailand has gained a considerable lead on Vietnam, it is not all gloom in Hanoi, even as the momentum wanes for export re-routing.

“Vietnam is no longer a low-cost, low-income economy. It’s naturally looking to upgrade industrial structure and technology capabilities, rather than attract low-end manufacturing,” Low said.

At the China-Asean Expo in September, Vietnamese exhibitors occupied 170 booths spanning 3,000 square metres (32,290 square feet).

While attending the expo, Vietnam’s deputy prime minister Pham Gia Tuc made no reference to export re-routing, but said Hanoi would welcome Chinese trade and investment in artificial intelligence, smart manufacturing and industrial estate development.

Meanwhile, China’s launch of the massive river-to-sea Pinglu Canal in September, a waterway connecting southwest China with the Gulf of Tonkin – and several nearby Vietnamese ports – could again redraw trade in Hanoi’s favour.

The canal is expected to slash tens of billions of yuan in annual logistics costs and spur more two-way flows between China and Asean, potentially positioning Vietnam as the beachhead for trade between the bloc and the world’s second-largest economy.

item.title: [SCMP] Katie Zacharia and Mao Ning – a study in contrasts in US and China media strategies
item.description:
Katie Zacharia may have lasted just five days as the White House press secretary but still managed to set off a diplomatic incident with China.

In an interview with a conservative commentator on Thursday, Zacharia referred to China as a place that “doesn’t even have proper toilets”.

Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded a day later with a smile and a brief, pointed invitation.
item.content:encoded:
Katie Zacharia may have lasted just five days as the White House press secretary but still managed to set off a diplomatic incident with China.

In an interview with a conservative commentator on Thursday, Zacharia referred to China as a place that “doesn’t even have proper toilets”.

Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded a day later with a smile and a brief, pointed invitation.

“We welcome her to visit China more often when she has the opportunity,” said Mao, a veteran diplomat.

Like Mao, Zacharia was – if only for less than a week – the highly visible public face of her government, speaking on issues that could shape how her country was perceived.

But Mao and Zacharia are the products of vastly different systems and took contrasting paths to the podium, using very different ways to tell two very different stories.

Worlds apart

Zacharia’s debut – and final – official White House briefing lasted fewer than 15 minutes on Tuesday, with much of her presentation delivered from a prepared script.

By then, questions had surfaced about her legal credentials after she had presented herself as a lawyer in media appearances.

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm, one of China’s biggest, in Beijing from 2011 to 2013.

Before joining the White House, she was a frequent commentator on conservative networks Fox News and Newsmax, where she defended US President Donald Trump and his agenda. She had also briefly held a communications role at the Department of Homeland Security.

As she stepped into one of the most visible communications positions in the US government, Zacharia found herself becoming the story.

Asked about her legal credentials, she said she had received them “when I moved to China”, before later saying she had misheard the question.

By the weekend, she was no longer in the White House job.

In China’s foreign ministry spokesperson system, officials generally have extensive diplomatic experience and undergo substantial preparation before taking on the position.

Another difference is in the scope of their roles.

A foreign ministry spokesperson is among the Chinese government’s most prominent and regular public-facing representatives, communicating Beijing’s positions on diplomacy and international affairs.

By contrast, the White House press secretary’s responsibilities extend beyond explaining domestic and foreign policy.

As a presidential appointee, the spokesperson is also expected to defend the president’s agenda and respond to political criticism on their behalf.

Zacharia was appointed to the role just three weeks before the midterm elections, at a politically sensitive time with Trump’s approval ratings at near-record lows. Her debut briefing on October 13 combined praise for Trump and his “America first” agenda, taking questions from just three reporters before wrapping up.

She left a question about Ukraine unanswered, saying she would have to return to it, prompting further doubts about her readiness for the position.

Her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had also used her first briefing to frame a major development involving China through the lens of US domestic politics.

Describing the emergence of Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) company DeepSeek as a “wake-up call” for the US AI industry, she blamed the previous Joe Biden administration for allowing China to develop the technology so rapidly.

Different paths

China’s foreign ministry formally established its spokesperson system in March 1983, during the country’s reform and opening-up drive.

A year earlier, Qian Qichen had held what is regarded as the ministry’s first press conference. He later rose through the diplomatic ranks to become foreign minister and vice-premier.

The ministry’s spokespersons are career diplomats who typically gather years of experience in foreign affairs before taking on the high-profile role.

Mao became the ministry’s 33rd spokesperson in September 2022 and was appointed director general of its information department in January 2025.

Before taking on the chief spokesperson role, Mao had spent more than 27 years in diplomatic service, focusing mainly on Asian affairs. She had also briefly served in a local government position as deputy mayor in 2020.

Qin Gang, who was later removed from office, also served two stints as a ministry spokesman before rising to become foreign minister in 2022.

By contrast, White House press secretaries often come from political communications, campaign work or media backgrounds.

Leavitt, for example, worked in Trump’s first administration, served as communications director for Republican congresswoman Elise Stefanik and was national press secretary for Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign before taking the White House job in January 2025.

The contrast reflects the different institutional functions of the two positions.

The White House press secretary speaks mainly for the president and his administration, defending its policies while responding to domestic political scrutiny.

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, by comparison, communicates the government’s positions on international affairs through regular briefings, which have been held each weekday since 2011.

Method and manner

For Beijing, public communication is part of a broader effort to shape how China is understood abroad, with the foreign ministry enlisted to “tell China’s story well”.

To this end, Chinese spokespersons’ comments are measured and carefully scripted, sometimes using subtle and indirect language.

A 2022 commentary in Shanghai news outlet The Paper defended this style of communication as a strategic buffer, saying that avoiding definitive statements left room for manoeuvre without boxing officials into a position that could prove difficult to defend.

That is poles apart from the more combative style associated with some US White House press secretaries. Leavitt, for instance, became known for her sharp retorts and rapid-fire responses, which also won praise from some Chinese social media users impressed by her verbal agility. Her language was direct and combative, consistent with the political messaging that had defined her work on Trump’s campaign.

But the Chinese spokesperson is usually more measured – something Mao in particular is known for.

Nevertheless, China’s roster of spokespeople has also included more controversial figures, most notably Zhao Lijian, who became a prominent face of the Wolf Warrior style of diplomacy.

The style, named after a Chinese nationalist action-film franchise, is commonly used to describe an assertive and confrontational approach to defending China’s interests and responding to foreign criticism.

Critics argue that such confrontational messaging risks damaging China’s diplomatic relationships, while supporters see it as a forceful response to Western criticism.

item.title: [SCMP] How Japan’s innovative Nakagin Capsule Tower is finding new life
item.description:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.
item.content:encoded:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.

Nakagin’s scattered course would have pleased its avant-garde architect Kisho Kurokawa (1934-2007), who conceived the design to emancipate what he called Homo movens (mobile humans). Many fans still demonstrate their unbridled enthusiasm for the building by donning zany get-ups inspired by its form – often described as a stack of front-loading washing machines.

In my mind’s eye, however, Nakagin had always been a colony of barnacles. That analogy borrows from the free movement of these crustaceans before anchoring themselves in place. But unfortunately, it was the unexpected immobility of Kurokawa’s capsules during their first phase of life that ultimately thwarted his vision that they be modular, interchangeable and recyclable.

That idea of impermanent permanence remains irresistible, however – at least in Japan. Which was one reason Metabolism captured the imagination of many during the country’s buoyant post-war expansion, making its name and ethos heard at the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo. Adaptable buildings and cities – with renewable nodes fed by circulation systems – sparked interest. Adding excitement was the promise of Expo ’70, whose theme was “progress and harmony for mankind”.

At that landmark event in Osaka, futuristic pavilions, including several by Kurokawa, allowed the forward-thinking to see for themselves the biomimetic potential of a movement whose proponents included other eminent architects, Kenzo Tange and Fumihiko Maki among them.

Nakagin, however, earned the kind of cult status accorded few other buildings in Japan. One reason was the charisma of Kurokawa, also a media personality and, towards the end of his career, a politician. His building was among the few examples of Metabolist architecture ever realised.

In late 2022, Ikko Yokoyama visited a warehouse in Chiba, near Tokyo, where salvaged Nakagin capsules, resembling pet Cyclops, awaited adoption. As lead curator of design and architecture at M+, she was there to see one of 23 pods that had been saved by the Nakagin Capsule Tower Preservation and Restoration Project, founded by former resident Tatsuyuki Maeda.

Hong Kong’s museum of contemporary visual culture was prepared for this inevitable moment, according to Yokoyama. Debate had raged for years about whether to preserve Nakagin whole, with Kurokawa himself shifting from yes to no. Ultimately, land value outweighed legacy, says Dytham, who had tried without success to persuade developers and hospitality groups to turn Nakagin into a boutique hotel. “It wasn’t sustainable to keep it there,” he says.

The decision to tear it down was made despite its uniqueness. Unlike anything the West had produced – except, perhaps, in the minds of Britain’s Archigram group of architects – Nakagin consisted of capsules “plugged” into the building’s towers, or cores, one 11 storeys high, the other two floors taller. Tight spaces between each pod impeded access and meant that repairs were difficult because “you couldn’t get in”, says Dytham. Worse, owners were unwilling to pay the high cost of detaching their capsules for upkeep every 25 years, as Kurokawa had warned they must. Decay set in, leaks appeared and damage from Japan’s frequent earthquakes saw the building’s exterior netted for safety. Additionally, the presence of asbestos complicated matters.

But M+’s capsule speaks volumes about their enduring appeal. A806 now stands beside another of the museum’s inspired acquisitions, Kiyotomo (1988), the sushi bar designed by Shiro Kuramata. Unlike that 656 sq ft restaurant – which was disassembled in Japan, shipped to Hong Kong and later put together again by the original contractors and an M+ team of restorers – Kurokawa’s capsule was purchased fully reconditioned.

The 2.78 metre x 2.69 metre x 4.21 metre capsule in the East Galleries is one of six standard units, complete with their famous round window at one end accommodating a circular blind that folds open like a hand fan. Also included within the 121.9 sq ft space are mod cons and a dinky unit bath, those tiny waterproof rooms sold as a single product in Japan.

“Like organ donation”, as Yokoyama puts it, parts for the capsule were harvested from others in the building because none of the pods survived with all of its original fittings intact. Kiyotomo’s neighbour now also boasts a new blue carpet and mattress, in addition to a fold-down desk, television and reel-to-reel tape deck, among other integrated features. Combine the service and payload modules of a spaceship and you get the idea.

Of the capsules plucked to safety by Maeda’s group, 14 have been sold to companies and museums, including M+ and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which purchased Kurokawa’s prized personal unit. Of the nine remaining, he says, four are to stay in Japan while five will head abroad.

Some have already been turned into display modules and mobile units and, next year, hotel-room conversions are expected, which should come as no surprise: in 1979, Kurokawa’s ideas also gave birth to the world’s first capsule hotel. New Japan Umeda continues to offer budget accommodation in Osaka.

Maeda’s is not the only group intent on giving the (in) famous corner building a second life. The Nakagin Capsule Tower A606 Project is named after the pod that another ex-resident helped restore several years before the building came down. This group, which owns seven units, has even more ambitious, albeit firmly parochial, aims.

“We plan to reconstruct a mini-tower using several capsules we own,” the group reveals via core member, architect Akiko Ishimaru.

“We aim to keep the reconstructed ones for 50 years [100 years after their completion] by continuing to use them ourselves. We want to utilise the capsules that were born in Japan and rebuild them in Japan.”

Crowdfunding has helped pay for the work so far. “The cost of asbestos control and investigation during the survey and dismantling, transportation and storage of seven capsules, storage of original parts, printing of a book with records, restoration of the interior of capsule A606, crowdfunding gifts [such as the aforementioned book], and fees consumed most of the total 8,673,000 yen [HK$443,000],” the group says.

Ishimaru’s efforts to keep Nakagin from history’s scrapheap underscores the passion in the project. But that’s not to say she fully enjoyed her year living in the building (and seven more working in two other capsules).

“One of my fond memories is drawing the actual survey plan for Nakagin Capsule Tower on my laptop at the original desk of Capsule A606 in August 2021,” she recalls, adding, “The 1.3-metre-diameter round window meant that the small room didn’t feel cramped.”

Having been designed as “hotel-like second homes” – or crash pads for salarymen – none of the capsules came with a kitchen. It was “very quiet”, Ishimaru recalls. The prefabricated steel modules didn’t share walls and, by 2013, when she moved in, there were only a few residents left. “Since it was so old and there was no hot water, I couldn’t even take a shower inside the capsule, so I stopped living there and used it as a shared office.”

Other assessments were bleaker. “From outside, the tower looked like a dying animal, sweating and greasy in the heat, trapped inside its wire netting,” reads an account by The Paris Review of Nakagin’s condition in 2016. “Looking up, you could see that some capsules had been half-filled with rotting garbage, a rippling line of trash drawn across their single windows. Inside, panels peel from the ceilings and mold crawls underneath; grime and seepage scorches the concrete with strange, bubbling forms.”

The reviewer added: “Kurokawa’s masterpiece was an utter, unsalvageable failure.”

And there’s the rub.

On whether Metabolism remains relevant in the 21st century, few can deny the importance of urban development that hews closely to principles of sustainability and flexibility. “The idea that buildings can change, grow and regenerate over time within a city may be increasingly needed to adapt to urban population growth and environmental issues,” the A606 group argue.

But how to label Kurokawa’s achievement remains as polarising as the fractious debates about whether the building should have been protected for posterity.

“It was an amazing success because he made it happen,” says Yokoyama, referring to how Kurokawa turned theory into reality and created a prototype. “It wasn’t just imagination.”

Dytham also believes Kurokawa got it “pretty right”, explaining that Nakagin was an early model. “If you’re building 10 of them, you get it. That was the first one.”

He adds that, for him, the building’s success had much to do with a design so simple that even a child could read and recognise it. “That would be a totally protected building if it was in the UK,” he posits. “Traditionally, here [in Japan], things are built in a temporary way.”

However, the recent wide dispersal of Nakagin capsules underscores the fact that Kurokawa’s vision has come to fruition. As Dytham says, “How many buildings have been taken apart and put all around the world?

“Taking [Nakagin] to the rest of the world is as important as just being all in one place.”

Metabolism was simply operating at its own pace.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s ‘stolen’ cultural relics: why the numbers just don’t add up
item.description:
More than 150 years after British and French troops sacked and razed the Summer Palace, in Beijing, the incident is regularly revisited in the Chinese press. Articles usually appear around the October anniversary of the destruction, after yet another announcement of plans to catalogue looted antiquities now overseas, or when Summer Palace items appear at foreign auction houses.

As well as their incomplete and inaccurate descriptions of the palace and its destruction, these stories often contain transparently false accusations against foreign institutions holding collections of Chinese treasures, as well as unsustain­able claims of a legal right to them and demands for their uncompensated return.

Even the most outrageously distorted claims often go unrefuted by timid governments and cultural institutions, perhaps for fear of complicating more important diplomatic negotiations or voiding loan arrangements and cultural exchanges.
item.content:encoded:
More than 150 years after British and French troops sacked and razed the Summer Palace, in Beijing, the incident is regularly revisited in the Chinese press. Articles usually appear around the October anniversary of the destruction, after yet another announcement of plans to catalogue looted antiquities now overseas, or when Summer Palace items appear at foreign auction houses.

As well as their incomplete and inaccurate descriptions of the palace and its destruction, these stories often contain transparently false accusations against foreign institutions holding collections of Chinese treasures, as well as unsustain­able claims of a legal right to them and demands for their uncompensated return.

Even the most outrageously distorted claims often go unrefuted by timid governments and cultural institutions, perhaps for fear of complicating more important diplomatic negotiations or voiding loan arrangements and cultural exchanges.

Museum public relations departments keep curators away from the press and mention of the Summer Palace is omitted from catalogue and cabinet label alike. Requests for a response to the Chinese campaign for repatriation of just about anything Chinese, with its insinuation that even legally purchased items are loot, are answered slowly, if at all.

As a result, it’s easy to conclude that museums, particularly those in the English-speaking world, must indeed have a lot to hide, although just how much is hidden away is itself the subject of considerable distortion. The French are more outspoken about both their possessions and their plans to retain them, yet receive less criticism.

For many years it has been claimed in the mainland Chinese press (as well as the South China Morning Post), with minor variations, that 1.64 million Chinese antiquities reside in 200 museums in 47 foreign countries.

On a 1998 visit to Beijing, Britain’s then prime minister Tony Blair was asked by a local journalist how he could justify the British Museum’s continued possession of 23,000 of these antiquities, a question still being posed when successor David Cameron visited 15 years later.

The China Centre for International Economic Exchanges, a “super think tank” headed by former vice-premier Zeng Peiyan, took up the invitation to ask Cameron questions via his newly created Sina Weibo microblog account.

“When will Britain return the illegally plundered artefacts?” was the inquiry, with the implication that the museum’s entire Chinese collection had been acquired by military force.

How an old palace and a historic railway station lay bare China’s conflicted relationship with its past

By last year, the source for these figures was repeatedly claimed to be “a Unesco study”, although in fact an information pack by the UN’s heritage body on the illicit trafficking of cultural property merely quoted a 2009 article in the magazine Art Antiquity and Law, by author Ji Ling. There is no such Unesco study.

In 2009, the Summer Palace’s then director, Chen Mingjie, claimed that 1.5 million antiquities had been looted in 1860 alone, and that they were in 2,000 museums, 10 times as many as previously suggested. By last year, the China Cultural Relics Academy was estimating that 10 million Chinese items were overseas, including those in private collections.

Among public institutions, London’s British Museum is often said to be the chief culprit, with its holdings now sometimes magically increased tenfold to 230,000 items, all now claimed to be from the Summer Palace. Eventually, the museum meekly responded to Post Magazine, claiming that, among its 23,000-item Chinese collection, purchased from or donated by myriad sources over a long period, just 15 pieces might possibly be of Summer Palace origin.

The French are typically more forthright. When asked in a 2011 interview how many items in Paris’ Château de Fontainebleau collections were from the plundering of the Summer Palace, the then director of patrimony and collections at the French museum, Xavier Salmon, answered immediately and unblushingly, “We think between 600 and 800.”

With an eye to national identity, Beijing vows to stem loss of cultural treasures

As the ponderous shutters of Fontainebleau’s Chinese Museum are unbarred and swung open, gleams of gold in the dark interior swell into a display of dazzling magnificence. Jades, porcelains and bronzes jostle for shelf space around a jewel-encrusted golden stupa flanked by two upright elephant tusks. The walls are lined with landscapes in gold and black lacquer, and the ceiling is draped with silk tapestries. The chamber buzzes with beauty, and it is difficult for the eye to know where to rest.

Here, then, is the magnificence that otherwise exists only in the imaginations of those keen to magnify for political purposes the wonders of the now-vanished Summer Palace.

The complex’s decay was already apparent in 1793, when it was visited by Lord Macartney, King George III’s ambassador to the Qianlong emperor. The best of the palaces, wrote Macartney, “is so much out of repair that I already see it will be impossible to reside in it comfortably during the winter”.

The looting and destruction of 1860 was intended, according to official and much personal correspondence, as a reprisal for the torture and murder of British and French envoys who had been under a prearranged flag of truce (a fact always omitted from Chinese accounts).

The French boxed up the best of the treasures they plundered from the Summer Palace and shipped them to Emperor Napoléon III. The Empress Eugénie is said to have been present in person at the opening of the crates.

She selected items to display in a purpose-built museum, mixing them with gifts from other parts of Asia, purchases from Parisian antiques shops and treasures confiscated from aristocratic families during the French revolution. She commissioned the building of display cabinets inset with Chinese panels and gave pieces of Chinese cloisonné to a master craftsman to incorporate in a vast chandelier that, 150 years on, still glitters overhead.

“She didn’t have an historic or artistic vision for these objects, she had a very personal vision,” said Salmon. “It is she who created this ambience, mixing up techniques and colours in a manner to which her eye responded and which was of the China of her imagination.”

Eugénie’s creation, he firmly asserted, was now part of French patrimony and “to return the objects would be to destroy a little bit of French history”.

But if the items were stolen, is this a sufficient defence?

“The question of plunder in war remains a question with a history as long as that of the planet,” said Salmon. “The history of the world has been regularly marked by these events, and the Chinese with their politics of conquest have also taken objects from their proper culture.”

In fairness, wild claims about the grandeur of the Summer Palace and the quality of the items stored therein began not with the Chinese but with Jesuit missionaries keen to justify the costs of maintaining their mission in the Manchu empire’s capital, and who compared the Summer Palace to Versailles.

There were also conflicting overestimates of the Summer Palace’s size from foreign travellers anxious to impress their readers.

Official descriptions of the now-much-built-over site continue this tradition in order to exaggerate the losses, increase criticism of foreign powers and enhance support for the Communist Party as the only bulwark behind which the Chinese can effectively unite and resist foreign exploitation.

The truth is, the number of surviving Summer Palace antiquities is unknowable, although no expert credits the figure of 1.5 million looted items overseas. There are no records of the palace’s original contents, much was destroyed on site and several eyewitnesses describe extensive looting by both local Chinese and the 2,500 coolies from southern provinces who were aiding the foreign forces (information also omitted from Chinese accounts).

Those forces were welcomed with open arms by Peking shopkeepers and items both with palace provenance and without were purchased and mixed together. Chinese traders in Canton and Hong Kong were willing purchasers of loot from the French troops who passed through on their way home.

The French expeditionary force provided lists of what it had packed, but these contain very little in way of description: “A vase, a vase, a vase,” quoted Salmon, from one of these lists, which makes individual identification impossible.

Furthermore, little in the Summer Palace was unique to its collection and, according to those present, the most easily identifiable items were of foreign manufacture, such as the field guns given by Macartney’s late-18th century embassy and French clocks and watches in such numbers that French looters sold them for pocket money to British soldiers, whose own looting opportunities had been relatively limited.
