Chen never contacted the institutions he had accused of holding the largest collections, according to Salmon and other museum officials. Instead, a visit to museums in nine American cities in 2009 was deemed a success for the “discovery” of several previously unknown items. Chen declined to provide details except for those of a single Song-dynasty painting at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, which bore 18 seals, including those of the Chun Hua Xuan, a hall in the Summer Palace complex.

At first, the museum claimed difficulty in identifying the painting in question, and gave a carefully anodyne response: “We have many strong connections to cultural institutions in China and look forward to continued collaborations.” It eventually emerged that the painting had been purchased from a Chinese seller within China in December 1913. And while the museum is apparently shy of labelling the painting in English as being of Summer Palace origin, Herd-boys with Water Buffaloes Under Willow Trees can clearly be seen on its website complete with identifying seals.

Peking University accused of not protecting Summer Palace relics

Chen’s “discovery” could have been made from a comfortable chair anywhere in the world, including Beijing. The painting had not been on public display since 1997, and a museum spokeswoman said in an e-mailed response that she could find no record of Chen’s visit.

In recent years, auctions of Jesuit-made bronze animal heads from the 1860 looting have brought ever more strident demands for their return. There have been futile legal attempts and the intervention of state actors willing to pay any price for national pride. This has driven up bidding for other Summer Palace items to well beyond what the state is willing to pay, leading to claims in Chinese media that prices are “unfair”.

When acquired instead by Chinese nouveaux riches, these pieces sometimes disappear into private collections and remain as invisible to ordinary Chinese as they were in Europe – or were back in 1860. Foreign museums are willing to lend items for exhibition but a willingness to accept them would also suggest acceptance of foreign ownership, and the political campaign has made this impossible, even where antiquities were legally purchased from Chinese sellers. Rather than achieving its aim of acquiring Chinese treasures, the carefully orchestrated brouhaha has put them further out of reach.

As Anglo-French forces progressed towards Beijing in 1860, Henry Loch, secretary to British plenipotentiary Lord Elgin, was one of the parley party imprisoned and tortured, and so did not participate in the looting. According to the accounts of various witnesses, the British watched the French carry off the largest part of the loot but subsequently pooled their finds of art, costumes and silks for auction, producing a fund of £8,000 – nearly US$1 million in today’s money – for distribution among the British forces.

Eighteen of his party were murdered but Loch survived to bid successfully for a pair of cloisonné double crane censers. In 2010, these were auctioned again and their Summer Palace connections helped push their sale price to US$16.7 million, a new record for cloisonné and roughly 17 times the value of the entire original British haul.

This was not a quirk. A month earlier, a gaudy Qing-dynasty porcelain vase from the Summer Palace had been sold by a small English auction house to a Beijing-based bidder for US$85.9 million, including tax and fees – 50 times its estimate.

While many museums now shy away from discussing the Summer Palace provenance of items in their collections, Chinese cataloguers and foreign auctioneers claim it wherever they can because it adds both political and financial value.

In May 2011, Bonhams promoted the auction of a white jadeite seal sold by the descendants of a 19th-century medical missionary to China, William Lockhart. The auction house sought to add Summer Palace lustre by mentioning the entirely irrelevant “unequivocal support” for British actions shown in Lockhart’s memoirs, and stating that he was “possibly” in Beijing during the sacking.

Norwegian art museum to return seven columns from Old Summer Palace to Beijing

Lockhart’s concise chapter of history on Anglo-Chinese relations from 1839 to 1860 contains not even a hint that he was at the Summer Palace. He moved to Beijing only in 1861. The price obtained was only double the estimate, suggesting that bidders found Bonhams’ claims no more credible than those of Chen.

In April 2011, complaints about unfair auction prices gave way in the official China Daily to the headline “Asian art market sizzles”. A surprisingly outrage-free article oozed with national pride because there were now Chinese sufficiently wealthy to pay record-breaking sums for Summer Palace jade, cloisonné and ceramics, while still avoiding any suggestion that state interference had increased the need for such deep pockets.

This was finally acknowledged in assorted articles in November last year that quoted Song Xinchao, deputy director of the State Administration of Cultural Heritage (SACH), as decrying the private purchase of “lost relics”, because “purchasing them will, in a way, confirm the legitimacy of such thefts, and make the prices of these items even higher in the international market”.

As with the inquiries made to the British prime ministers, there was also the implication that all Chinese treasures “lost” overseas must be, in some sense, stolen.

The main purpose of the 2016 articles was to trumpet SACH’s success in suppressing an auction in Japan of frescoes and manuscripts taken from a cave-temple site outside Dunhuang, on the Silk Road, as part of China’s supposedly growing success in repatriating treasures using diplomatic and legal persuasion rather than purchase. But Chinese propaganda has elevated Silk Road artefact prices also and, without it, there might be more to see in China’s museums.

Around the rim of the lens-shaped Taklimakan Desert, signs at cave-temple sites condemn by name the foreign explorers who plundered frescoes, paintings and manuscripts during an Indiana Jones-style archaeological free-for-all in the early 20th century.

At Dunhuang, where sheer cliffs are pitted with hundreds of hand-carved caves dating back as far as 366CE, it is again the British and French who come in for most criticism. In 1907, Britain’s Marc Aurel Stein purchased thousands of documents recently discovered in a hidden library cave. The following year, France’s Paul Pelliot did the same, as did subsequent Russian and Japanese expeditions.

The seller was a Taoist monk, Abbot Wang, the caves’ self-appointed guardian, who had been unable to interest local officials in the documents he had discovered and who wanted funds for the preservation of the caves and their frescoes.

The sums paid by foreigners were large for what local people regarded as useless papers in assorted scripts they could not read, but derisory in terms of their cultural significance. The Chinese authorities now cry foul.

Amazing journey: how China hid palace artefacts from Japanese invaders

The November 2016 articles, in assorted Chinese media and a paid-for soft-power supplement to The Washington Post, claimed China had triumphed by suppressing a Yokohama International Auction sale of Tang-dynasty frescoes and manuscripts from Dunhuang “stolen by Otani Kozui, a Japanese abbot who was part of expeditions to China between 1902 and 1913”, according to SACH.

Accuracy is once again of little interest here. The records of the exhibitions financed by Otani make it clear he did not travel to Dunhuang in person but those he’d sponsored did purchase the scrolls directly from Abbot Wang.

These Dunhuang manuscripts were catalogued before financial trouble led Otani to sell the remainder of his collection in 1915, but take the Dunhuang items to Lüshun, in Japanese-occupied northeast China. After Japan’s 1945 defeat, these manuscripts ended up in museums in Lüshun and Beijing, except for 49 later discovered in Japan, which are now at the Ryukoku University, in Kyoto, and not for sale.

It is not entirely clear, then, what Yokohama International Auction intended to sell at the suppressed auction, but this is one of the exports of antiquities about which China has least to complain, since almost all are already back in the country.

It’s not impossible that other manuscripts may turn up, but these will most likely not be from Dunhuang, says Cambridge University Otani expert Dr Imre Galambos.

“[Otani] is often vilified for his acquisition of antiquities, even though his collection was quite modest in comparison to that of Aurel Stein, but he was Japanese and, on top of that, related by marriage to the imperial house, all of which have a very bad resonance with the Chinese public.”

Records of three Otani-sponsored expeditions show that frescoes were acquired not from Dunhuang but from Miran, hundreds of kilometres further west, and these are now in the National Museum of Korea, in Seoul.

“We are not conditioned by guilt,” said a forthright Jacques Giès, when interviewed at the Musée Guimet in Paris in 2011. Giès had spent more than 30 years curating the museum’s magnificent Silk Road displays. “Our duty is to present the best of the Chinese creation, to testify to the excellence of this civilisation, and to let our public have respect for Chinese history and civilisation.”

China bans looted antiques from going under hammer at mainland auction houses

Indeed, Giès points out that Silk Road studies were a foreign invention. It was the 1890 discovery by a British Indian Army officer of ancient texts on birch bark in an unknown language that sparked multiple arduous desert expeditions to discover more of the same.

It was principally European, Russian, Japanese and American scholars who pieced together the history of the trade routes, deciphering scripts and translating forgotten languages.

“We, who have worked for almost one century on these materials, represent the best of the best of the scholarship in all these countries, and these materials were essential not only for the history of China, but also for all High Asia and the Indian subcontinent,” said Giès.

In other words, there are many other Asian cultures that might lay claim to the Silk Road treasures, including those of the local minority and the Tibetans who controlled Dunhuang for centuries and compelled the local Chinese to wear Tibetan clothing and speak Tibetan.

Of the Otani Dunhuang documents already back in China, it’s the Chinese-language ones that have been taken to Beijing, with those in other languages left tucked away in distant Lüshun.

“History is not made of ‘if’,” said Giès. Due to the French revolution, the most important French royal furniture collections are in England. “But that’s history. I am very grateful because they preserved these pieces which could have been destroyed.”

Dr Frances Wood, formerly head of Chinese collections at the British Library, says she is familiar with that sentiment.

“In private, most Chinese scholars are much happier that the material is in England,” she says. The Dunhuang scrolls remaining in Japan are dwarfed in number by those in the British Library’s collection, purchased by Stein from 1907.

“There are about 7,000 fairly complete scrolls, so they’re reasonably substantial. Six thousand of those are rolls of paper anything from five to 30 feet long, mostly Buddhist. And then when you get towards the other end, they’re very tiny fragments because they’re really the bottom of the sacks.”

No sooner had China begun to open up in the 1970s than Chinese scholars were invited to work on this “Stein debris”, carefully flattening pieces for analysis.

Continuing cooperation by members of the British Library-based International Dunhuang Project has seen thousands of documents from collections around the world digitally photographed and made freely available online. The British Library’s entire Dunhuang collection is now being published in a 150-volume catalogue by the Guangxi Normal University Press.

In private, most Chinese scholars are much happier that the material is in England

Dr Frances Wood

In 2014, China drafted an international rule on the return of cultural property – China’s first such effort, reported the China Daily, in November. “The Dunhuang Recommendation has led to more success in China’s efforts since then.”

However, this home-made “international rule” is merely wishful thinking and China has been party to a 1970 Unesco convention on the illicit transfer of stolen cultural property since 1989. It is this that provides a proper legal basis for reclaiming stolen antiquities, but it doesn’t apply to those taken before 1970, and the Dunhuang Recommendation, as the 2014 rule is known, changes nothing.

Yokohama International Auction is registered in Hong Kong and its owner is reportedly a Japanese national of Chinese descent. On its Japanese webpages – although not those in Chinese – the company makes clear that its very purpose is the return of Chinese antiquities to China.

Before being cancelled, the November auction had been won by a Japanese national, but the items were returned to their owner, not passed to China. This was, in fact, the opposite of progress, and nothing to do with any “international rule”.

Threats against foreign auction houses with Chinese connections have been seen before, such as in another quoted example of “more success in China’s efforts”, the 2013 return of two bronze animal heads originally from a fountain in the Summer Palace.

These were returned free of charge by French billionaire François-Henri Pinault, whose Kering group owns luxury brands such as Gucci and Saint Laurent that now rely on China for a significant portion of their income.

Through the holding company Groupe Artemis, Pinault also owns auction house Christie’s. The heads had appeared in a Christie’s-run auction of the late Yves Saint Laurent’s effects in Paris in 2009, leading SACH to threaten “serious effects” on Christie’s’ future in China. It was widely reported that the company began to experience difficulties with Chinese customs inspections.

Pinault was accompanying then French president François Hollande on a trade visit to China at the time of the announcement of his donation. It may only be coincidence that Christie’s became the first international fine-art auction house to receive a licence to operate independently in China that very same year.

Return of Old Summer Palace statues seen as Kering group PR exercise

Other claimed Chinese successes concern antiquities stolen recently by Chinese themselves and smuggled overseas, their repatriation subject to existing conventions and not to any newly coined domestic rule. But the Communist Party ensures that only its own version of events is heard domestically, and stories of foreign destruction and looting certainly help to distract from the infinitely greater ruination brought about by the party itself.

During the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, Red Guards confiscated 613,600 antiques and jade pieces from their Beijing owners in just one month, according to the book Mao’s Last Revolution (2008), few of which were ever seen again. More than 70 per cent of 6,843 officially designated places of cultural or historical interest in the city were destroyed, and what remained or had been rebuilt of the Summer Palace sustained further damage.

According to SACH itself, destruction in recent times has continued apace. Of about 225,000 historic sites in China on an incomplete list compiled in 1982, 30,995 had disappeared by 2009.

That foreign destruction, looting and purchase of China’s cultural heritage is statistically insignificant compared with the towering catastrophe the Chinese have achieved for themselves does not provide any excuse for it.

The Greeks, the Egyptians and the people of Benin in West Africa are among others pressing more honestly for the return of “stolen” antiquities, and engaging in debate. It’s long past time certain museums also stood up for their own reputations and against Chinese propaganda, and demanded that accurate and complete accounts be given of both historical events and existing collections.

item.title: [SCMP] What will China’s fifth plenum mean for the root-and-branch corruption drive?
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the third part of this series, William Zheng and Alcott Wei examine how the fight against corruption is shaping the party’s future.

When China’s political elites gather for a key conclave in Beijing later this month, the increasingly empty auditorium will speak loudly to the event’s theme – the ruling Communist Party’s strict self-discipline and its never-ending fight against corruption.

The fifth plenum of the party’s 20th Central Committee will also serve as an important venue for the political momentum of next year’s quinquennial leadership transition and ratify disciplinary verdicts against dozens of fallen cadres.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the third part of this series, William Zheng and Alcott Wei examine how the fight against corruption is shaping the party’s future.

When China’s political elites gather for a key conclave in Beijing later this month, the increasingly empty auditorium will speak loudly to the event’s theme – the ruling Communist Party’s strict self-discipline and its never-ending fight against corruption.

The fifth plenum of the party’s 20th Central Committee will also serve as an important venue for the political momentum of next year’s quinquennial leadership transition and ratify disciplinary verdicts against dozens of fallen cadres.

The four-day closed-door meeting comes roughly one year ahead of the 21st National Party Congress in late 2027 and is poised to formalise one of the most extensive turnovers of senior party, state and military personnel in modern Chinese political history.

According to a tally by the South China Morning Post, 20 full and seven alternate members are facing corruption investigations and await formal expulsion from the Central Committee.

The SCMP’s research also shows that about 35 full and alternate members who did not appear at last year’s plenum have made no public appearances in the current cycle, indicating potential trouble for their political careers.

The fifth plenum, from October 26 to 29, is also set to endorse a key document outlining a long list of measures by the party to maintain internal discipline, ensure political loyalty and fight corruption.

Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Strategic Studies at Tsinghua University, noted that this focus on the party’s governance came seven years after a similar document that zeroed in on modernising the nation’s governing capacity.

“In 2019, the focus was on how to run the government and manage society better. Now, the focus is on the party ruling China,” Xie said.

“The reason is simple: China’s overall governance starts from the ruling party. The party’s successful and effective self-governance is a prerequisite for China’s long-term governance.”

Cutting down sick trees

As the countdown to 2027 begins, the fifth plenum is set to see a fresh push to cement better party governance control and ensure uncompromised loyalty ahead of the next party congress.

Beijing issued a series of blunt warnings via the script of a January speech by President Xi Jinping, published in the party’s top theoretical journal Qiushi on October 15. It was the first time some of the details had been made public.

In the speech, Xi argued that internal regulations had long been too vague. He demanded systemic reforms to prevent “using a cattle pen to confine a cat” – a traditional idiom for lax rules that fail to restrain misbehaviour.

Emphasising that corruption remained widespread and prone to recurring within the party, Xi pledged to uproot or cut down “sick trees” wherever necessary.

The metaphor, from ancient Chinese poetry, suggests that new life will flourish beyond decaying trees, with the new replacing the old.

Fighting corruption is also a major focus of “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building”, a new addition to the paramount leader’s expanding theoretical canon that was made public just months ahead of the plenum.

Officially introduced to the party in June, the political doctrine is aimed at building a “Marxist party with long-term governance”.

Besides the relentless drive to ensure officials “do not have the audacity, opportunity or desire to commit corruption”, the doctrine calls for the party’s centralised leadership to avoid divisions that will weaken the party.

It insists on comprehensive and rigorous self-governance to enforce discipline and continuous self-reform across all levels, as well as solid political and theoretical bases to enhance loyalty and avoid weakening the party’s ideological foundations.

The doctrine also demands a robust organisational system to train and select high-calibre officials who strictly follow party directives.

According to Xie from Tsinghua, strict and comprehensive party governance is a “key pillar” of Xi’s party building thought, especially at the juncture of the transition period for leading officials.

“With the party’s self-governance system in place, the next batch of leading cadres will have a unified code of conduct and they can have a cleaner start,” he said.

A Nanjing-based analyst said that while Xi’s sustained, hard-hitting efforts may address the symptoms, the plenum’s agenda suggested he was willing to go deeper and wider to address the causes of China’s chronic corruption problems, but in his own way.

The political analyst, who asked not to be named as his school required him to seek approval when speaking to media, detailed some of the opportunities for corruption that the country still faced.

“In China, areas like promotion of officials, public projects, military equipment acquisition and natural resources development remain highly lucrative black boxes in which one or a few key persons can dictate the decisions involving billions of dollars, despite the relentless anti-corruption fight,” he said.

“While Western analysts would suggest the scrutiny of the public and the media to be part of the equation, it will not be the party’s priority as Xi firmly believes strengthening the party’s self-governance is sufficient.”

Expected absences

At the 20th party congress in October 2022, 205 full Central Committee members were appointed, along with 171 alternate members. Four years later, the number of empty seats at next week’s conclave could highlight an extraordinary level of attrition.

The anti-corruption campaign has taken a heavy toll on the committee, with 35 of its full members either under investigation or stripped of their seats in the National People’s Congress, China’s top legislature.

The precedent for mass adjustments was set during last year’s fourth plenum, which confirmed the expulsion of 14 full and alternate members – including former senior generals He Weidong and Miao Hua – and elevated 11 alternates to full membership.

The party is set to appoint a cascade of replacements to the vacant or compromised seats as it deals with the large backlog of the remaining 21 full members and seven alternate members who are facing investigation but are yet to be expelled from the committee.

The vacancies reflect a sprawling anti-corruption and political disciplinary campaign that is cutting across both party and government systems as well as the People’s Liberation Army.

The SCMP’s tally shows that Xi’s anti-corruption machinery clearly accelerated after 2020, when 19 “tigers” or senior officials were caught. The number of top officials facing investigation has been on a rising trend, reaching a new high of 65 last year.

Most officials in the group, supervised directly by the party’s top anti-graft body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), belonged to a pool of officials known as “centrally managed cadres”, meaning they typically ranked at deputy ministerial level or above.

A smaller number held slightly lower ranks but occupied sensitive positions in important sectors.

Unlike their subordinates, who are managed and supervised by local branches of the party’s organisation and disciplinary agency, senior officials are under the direct management of the Central Organisation Department, its top personnel body.

The Central Committee has yet to confirm the expulsion of a slew of prominent former ministerial and regional chiefs occupying full member seats who were snared in corruption investigations over the past few months or are facing legal procedures.

Among them are Jiangxi’s former party chief Yi Lianhong and provincial governor Ye Jianchun, former Inner Mongolia party secretary Sun Shaocheng and government chief Wang Lixia.

They include Hu Henghua, who was mayor of Chongqing, Lan Tianli, former Guangxi government chairman, Yi Huiman, who chaired China’s securities regulator, and emergency management minister Wang Xiangxi.

Several lower-ranked alternate members are facing investigations but have yet to be formally removed: ex-mayor of Shenzhen Qin Weizhong, as well as the former Xian and Hefei party bosses Fang Hongwei and Fei Gaoyun, respectively, and ex-railway chief Fei Dongbin.

And with just a week to go before the plenum, Xia Maolin, vice mayor of Beijing and an alternate member of the Central Committee, has come under investigation.

Bijie party secretary Wu Shenghua, who was expelled from the party and dismissed from public duties in January, became a target of name-and-shame campaigns in September when Beijing made him an exemplary case of failing to address local government debts incurred by predecessors.

Missing generals

There was even more turbulence in the PLA, where the anti-corruption and political rectification campaign has reached the pinnacle of its command structure, the Central Military Commission (CMC).

The CMC’s former deputy chairman Zhang Youxia and member Liu Zhenli were both accused of severe political disloyalty and factionalism.

A broad swathe of CMC, theatre-command and service-branch chiefs holding Central Committee seats were also implicated. Many were expelled from the national legislature before their term ended, usually a sign of serious career setback.

They included Wang Peng, who was director of the CMC’s training department, its political and legal affairs committee chief, Wang Renhua, as well as the head of equipment development, Xu Xueqiang.

Logistics Support Department chief Zhang Lin, General Office director Zhong Shaojun and Ju Qiansheng, who commanded the PLA’s Strategic Support Force, were also removed from their positions.

Other senior expulsions included ground forces commander Li Qiaoming and four political commissars: Li Wei, from the information support force, Western Theatre Command’s Li Fengbiao, Zhang Hongbing from the armed police and the air force’s Guo Puxiao.

Wang Kangping, the former commander of the Joint Logistics Support Force who was removed from the national legislature in June, is the only uniformed alternate member waiting for the Central Committee’s decision.

The vanished ones

There are also civilian officials who have disappeared from the public eye without explanation, which could suggest some career hiccups or that they have quietly stepped down from their positions.

Among the most prominent abrupt departures was ex-agriculture minister Han Jun, who was unexpectedly removed from his position in April.

Also noteworthy was the sudden exit of former international liaison department head Liu Jianchao, who vanished from public view following an overseas trip last summer. He was subsequently replaced by Liu Haixing.

Two critical positions bridging Beijing’s military-civilian fusion statecraft were left vacant with the departure of Jin Zhuanglong, former industry and information technology minister, and Lei Fanpei, who chaired state-owned conglomerate China State Shipbuilding Corporation. Beijing has made no announcements about their status.

The replacement dynamic

Under party statutes, vacancies on the Central Committee are filled by alternate members, who are ranked based on votes received at the previous congress.

However, recent sessions indicate that promotions are no longer strictly aligned with the ranking of alternate members and could even become the latest indicator of further downfall.

During last year’s fourth plenum, as alternate members were promoted to fill vacancies, several were bypassed – including Wang Jiayi, Shi Yugang and Fang Hongwei, with the latter subsequently expelled from the party.

Any candidate skipped in the line-up at this year’s event is likely to face intense scrutiny regarding their political standing.

The round of replacements in the previous plenum did not strictly follow the established ranking of alternate members. Instead, four military and three civilian alternate members were “skipped over”.

The military alternates were Wang Liyan, then-deputy commander of PLA Rocket Force, Wang Kangping, who commanded the Joint Logistics Support Force, Fang Yongxiang, ex-head of the CMC’s General Office, and Shi Zhenglu from Northern Theatre Command.

The skipped-over civilian officials were the then deputy education minister Wang Jiayi, former Xian party secretary Fang Hongwei and Shi Yugang, deputy chief of the provincial political advisory body in Yunnan.

Several of the skipped alternate members were later officially confirmed to be facing disciplinary investigations.

Wang Kangping was stripped of his seat in the national legislative body while Xian’s Fang Hongwei was detained by the CCDI just days after the fourth plenum and expelled from the party and public office in July.

item.title: [SCMP] Is Washington misreading Beijing? Decline in US visits to China sparks concern
item.description:
When Grant Newsham, a retired US Marine colonel and security analyst, sat down for an interview that aired last month, he called China’s economic rise illusory and said there were “600 million Chinese at least who live on US$5 a day or less”.

His remarks quickly drew online criticism as well as accusations that he was using outdated figures from 2020 while ignoring differences in purchasing power.

Some commenters argued that uneven development was common across countries. Others questioned how much on-the-ground China experience Newsham had before making the statement to the Epoch Times, a right-wing outlet associated with Falun Gong and banned in China.
item.content:encoded:
When Grant Newsham, a retired US Marine colonel and security analyst, sat down for an interview that aired last month, he called China’s economic rise illusory and said there were “600 million Chinese at least who live on US$5 a day or less”.

His remarks quickly drew online criticism as well as accusations that he was using outdated figures from 2020 while ignoring differences in purchasing power.

Some commenters argued that uneven development was common across countries. Others questioned how much on-the-ground China experience Newsham had before making the statement to the Epoch Times, a right-wing outlet associated with Falun Gong and banned in China.

However, the debate went beyond a dispute over China’s living standards: it highlighted a need for Americans – including policymakers and academics – to gain first-hand experience of China, while drawing attention to their shrinking opportunities to gain that exposure.

A report issued by the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) last month documented a sharp decline in congressional delegations to China between 2010 and 2026, a period marked by persistent bilateral tensions.

A separate analysis published by the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) later in September highlighted a parallel downturn in American students studying in China and the erosion of programmes designed to train future China specialists.

Observers warn that the loss of direct, on-the-ground exposure could threaten America’s ability to assess and engage its primary rival, particularly as China’s strategic importance to US foreign policy continues to grow.

A broad retreat

According to the CSIS report, visits by congressional delegations to mainland China and Hong Kong have fallen since the late 2010s as bilateral relations deteriorated.

Tensions deepened during US President Donald Trump’s first term from 2017 to 2021, marked by a full-blown trade war, intensifying technological rivalry and recurring military stand-offs in the contested South China Sea.

The report showed that visits plunged at the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic and had yet to return to earlier levels.

Congressional travel to Taiwan has also dropped since 2022. The report attributed the decline to lingering fallout from then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s 2022 visit to Taipei – which triggered major People’s Liberation Army drills – and subsequent caution in Washington around such delegations to avoid further provoking Beijing.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The ripple effects will spread from academia into government, media and business, heightening the risk of miscalculation

Sun Chenghao, Chinese academic

CSIS found that only 32 per cent of the 535 sitting US lawmakers had travelled to mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan, based on its tracking of congressional delegations between 2010 and 2026.

The report expected that share to shrink further as veteran members left office and newer lawmakers arrived without that first-hand experience.

US Senator Steve Daines is among the few lawmakers who still make such trips. He concluded his most recent visit to China in late August, just weeks ahead of President Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington from September 23 to 25.

After Daines visited artificial intelligence and space firms in China’s tech hub Hangzhou and the southern city of Guangzhou, he told Bloomberg the US risked underestimating “both the quality and the scale of the tech innovation ecosystem in China”.

Isabella McCallum, co-author of the CSIS report, noted that the small 32 per cent share – the 172 current lawmakers who have visited mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan – suggested on-the-ground engagement was becoming less common among the people responsible for shaping US policy towards China.

“With less direct experience of China, Congress will become more reliant on second-hand information for one of the country’s most consequential relationships,” McCallum said in an interview.

Meanwhile, lawmakers continued to introduce legislation concerning Beijing, creating a growing gap between how much Congress acted on China and how well its members knew the country, she added.

To Beijing, the concern is not simply that US lawmakers may hold unfavourable views of China. It is that their assessments may be made without enough contact with the people, businesses and institutions affected by their decisions.

Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said limited direct experience could make American policymakers more likely to rely on political labels and a narrow security-focused view of China.

“This could lead them to overestimate certain threats while overlooking opportunities for cooperation,” Sun said.

The decline in congressional visits is part of a wider retreat in exchanges between the two countries.

According to the CSIS report, fewer than 2,000 Americans are estimated to be studying in China, compared with a peak of about 11,000 in 2019.

Likewise, the number of Chinese students enrolled at US universities had continued to fall from its 2019 peak of 372,532 amid tightening visa restrictions and curbs on research exchange, the report said, without stating current figures.

According to the Institute of International Education’s most recent annual survey, nearly 266,000 Chinese students were in the US in 2024.

The drop in academic exchange was also underscored in an analysis released by CFR on September 23.

It highlighted the suspension in China of US government-backed exchange projects, including the Fulbright programme and the Critical Language Scholarship. The author, political scientist Rush Doshi, noted that these programmes had helped to cultivate generations of specialists equipped to study China through its language, society and political institutions.

Meanwhile, some study-abroad programmes at US universities have been halted following a Pentagon directive in August instructing institutions to review relationships with foreign counterparts over national security concerns.

The loss of these opportunities could have consequences beyond universities.

Doshi noted that American government agencies and businesses largely relied on China expertise to interpret China’s actions, from geopolitics and security to trade and supply chains.

“A United States that no longer trains people who can read Chinese primary sources, sit in Chinese classrooms, track policy implementation on the ground, is hardly more secure and is substantially less capable,” he wrote.

Sun said the decline in China expertise could also hurt Beijing, depriving the country of interlocutors who could accurately interpret its intentions.

“In the long run, the ripple effects will spread from academia into government, media and business, heightening the risk of miscalculation and narrowing the scope for cooperation,” he said.

Rebuilding channels

The CSIS report called for renewed congressional travel, arguing that visits could help lawmakers understand how China’s policies and economic decisions affected their constituents.

McCallum said such trips could give Congress members a better understanding of issues they raised with Chinese officials, connecting foreign policy with practical concerns at home.

She cited Daines, whose home state of Montana is a major beef producer. Daines has used his visits to press for restored Chinese market access for American beef producers.

But visits must go beyond carefully arranged itineraries showcasing economic development, the CSIS report noted. McCallum said Beijing should allow visitors to have greater access to China’s economy and society, and make room for frank conversations with a range of counterparts.

She also identified Chinese sanctions against US officials as a possible deterrent to congressional travel.

“Sanctions on even a limited number of members can discourage others from travelling,” McCallum said, adding that expanding congressional travel took effort from both sides.

Sun similarly argued that Beijing should ease visits by lawmakers from both parties and chambers of Congress, including their staff.

“Exchanges should directly address constituency concerns, including agriculture, jobs and trade, while establishing follow-up mechanisms to turn single visits into sustained dialogue, preventing communication from snapping whenever the political climate cools,” he said.

The need for sustained, first-hand engagement with China extends beyond Congress to education and academia.

The CFR analysis called for Washington to rebuild funding and institutional support for China studies, while clarifying federal rules so that non-sensitive academic activities, such as language learning, could continue.

The report also urged Washington and Beijing to protect educational programmes from the wider tensions in their relationship.

Diao Daming, a professor in international studies at Renmin University of China, said efforts to strengthen Americans’ first-hand understanding of China would also benefit Beijing.

“They would help both sides develop a clearer, more objective and accurate understanding of each other, deepen their appreciation of the vital importance of stable China-US relations to both countries and the wider world, and ultimately contribute to greater stability in bilateral ties,” he said.

There have been signs of renewed interest in exchanges, but the larger question is whether these efforts can help rebuild American expertise on China.

At his summit with Trump in September, Xi invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange or study programmes in the coming five years.

The initiative doubles an earlier target announced in 2023 – to bring 50,000 young Americans to China by 2028. Chinese authorities said that target had been reached ahead of schedule.

Diao said the 2023 initiative’s early completion showed strong demand for youth and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.

“These efforts incrementally build goodwill in a subtle, quiet way,” Diao said. “They lay a solid foundation for people-to-people ties and play a crucial role in stabilising the broader bilateral relationship.”

Sun, while echoing Diao’s view, cautioned that short-term visits alone could not reverse the decline in American expertise on China.

Developing specialists required sustained engagement with the country, rather than brief exposure through organised exchange programmes, Sun noted.

He said visits should be connected to longer-term opportunities, including Chinese-language courses, semester exchanges, graduate study and field research.

Sun added that credit recognition, scholarships and academic supervision could help participants continue their studies after returning home.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s Huanggang crossing absorbs 366% surge as travellers stream back
item.description:
Inbound crossings at Hong Kong’s revamped Huanggang Port surged by 366 per cent on Monday afternoon over comparable periods in September, as the first long weekend since its reopening came to a close, with authorities expecting an even greater rush later in the evening.

A steady stream of travellers returned to Hong Kong through the checkpoint on Monday, with crowds growing noticeably by 5pm, peaking at around 6.15pm, and tapering off by 7pm, as observed by the South China Morning Post.

Unlike Sunday, when departing travellers complained on social media about long wait times during peak hours, Monday’s inbound flow remained orderly.
item.content:encoded:
Inbound crossings at Hong Kong’s revamped Huanggang Port surged by 366 per cent on Monday afternoon over comparable periods in September, as the first long weekend since its reopening came to a close, with authorities expecting an even greater rush later in the evening.

A steady stream of travellers returned to Hong Kong through the checkpoint on Monday, with crowds growing noticeably by 5pm, peaking at around 6.15pm, and tapering off by 7pm, as observed by the South China Morning Post.

Unlike Sunday, when departing travellers complained on social media about long wait times during peak hours, Monday’s inbound flow remained orderly.

“It’s a very nice port – the bathrooms are clean, it’s huge and spacious … what a great thing to see in our lifetime,” said 66-year-old retiree Adam Ko, who was with his wife, Mary.

The couple said they were aware of the large crowds at the crossing over the weekend.

“It’s still early in the night, so we decided to come here hoping to skip the peak hours. It was very smooth and we just breezed through,” said Ko.

However, he noted minor traffic congestion while approaching the port by taxi in Shenzhen at around 4.30pm. “We were stuck on the roads for maybe 10 minutes. Acceptable, but I’d think twice if it was any later in the day.”

A Shenzhen resident in her forties who works in the garment industry and gave only her surname, Tang, said she preferred the revamped port for its convenience.

“This new arrangement saves me about 20 minutes crossing the border,” she said.

According to the Security Bureau, 9,401 travellers entered Hong Kong via Huanggang Port between 2pm and 4pm on Monday, a 366 per cent surge from the average number of inbound crossings through the former Huanggang/Lok Ma Chau control point during the same hours across the four weekends in September.

It expected the number of inbound travellers to rise further in the evening.

With the expected surge in crossings, all immigration clearance channels were opened, while authorities prepared crowd-control measures and designated waiting areas for passengers using public transport.

The holiday marked the first major test for the revamped crossing between Hong Kong and mainland China, which reopened on October 12 with a new joint immigration clearance system designed to cut processing times from about half an hour to as little as five minutes.

Travellers can complete clearance by presenting a single identity document and passing through an automated channel with three gates.

Yung Ka-wai, deputy commander of the Immigration Department’s Lok Ma Chau Division, said clearance at Huanggang had been smooth on Monday and expected the afternoon-to-evening period to be the busiest for foot traffic.

“We will continue to monitor the situation at the control points in real time and flexibly deploy manpower according to passenger flows to speed up the clearing of crowds,” Yung said.

“Travellers are advised to plan their journeys early, choose a suitable control point and avoid crossing the border during peak hours.”

He also reminded eligible residents to register in advance if they wished to use the new clearance model.

Commissioner for Transport Winnie Tse Wing-yee inspected Huanggang Port on Monday morning, instructing officers and public transport operators to closely monitor passenger and traffic flows and deploy resources flexibly. She also asked bus companies to run additional short-haul special services to clear travellers more quickly.

The Transport Department said about 120 franchised buses, 40 minibuses and 130 cross-border buses had been deployed for service and standby on Monday.

Headways for franchised buses would be shortened to two to three minutes during peak hours, and to three to four minutes for minibuses and cross-border buses.

Huanggang handled more than 152,000 crossings on Sunday, with some travellers waiting up to two hours amid congestion that lawmakers attributed to unfamiliarity with new clearance procedures, a surge in traffic and computer system reboots.

Immigration Department figures showed the port handled 152,068 crossings, the highest daily total since it opened on October 12. These comprised 77,166 outbound trips and 74,902 inbound journeys.

Hongkongers accounted for 133,265 crossings, while mainland visitors made 16,832 trips.

The facility is designed to handle up to 300,000 travellers and 15,000 vehicles a day, with daily passenger numbers initially expected to range from 100,000 to 200,000.

As the Chung Yeung Festival break fuelled a surge in cross-border travel over the weekend, the Security Bureau issued a “busy” advisory for Huanggang on its “Easy Boundary” portal on Sunday afternoon, warning that clearance could take up to 45 minutes. Some mainland visitors, however, reported queuing for as long as two hours.

Lawmaker Ben Chan Han-pan, chairman of the Legislative Council’s transport panel, said travellers’ unfamiliarity with the new “collaborative inspection and joint immigration clearance” model was the main cause of congestion on Sunday, with some attempting to use the automated channels without registering beforehand.

He added that the sudden surge in passenger numbers had also overwhelmed the control point.

Chan said computer systems at the immigration counters had slowed after running for extended periods and needed to be rebooted, further lengthening queues.

Lawmaker Chong Ho-fung said the long queues at the newly reopened port over the weekend were inevitable given the large number of travellers crossing the border during the Chung Yeung Festival peak.

He said that close to 40,000 people crossed at Huanggang between 10am and 2pm on Sunday, averaging nearly 10,000 an hour, and even with each passenger taking just a minute to complete clearance, queues could easily result in an hour-long wait.

“The government’s projections and my own both forecast this would happen. It is a chaotic situation that was within expectations,” Chong told a radio programme.

He urged authorities to step up publicity about registration procedures and eligibility requirements for the new “joint clearance” automated channels.

Children under seven cannot use the automated channels and must be accompanied by their parents to staffed counters to complete clearance. Those aged seven to 17 can use the “joint clearance” channels once their parents have registered them.

Chong said clearer information would help prevent families with young children from reaching the front of the queue only to discover they were ineligible and had to move to staffed counters, adding to their clearance time.

“There were too many different reasons why a passenger could not complete clearance, and staff on the ground may not be able to identify the exact reason immediately, causing a chaotic situation,” he said.

He also suggested designating more clearance lanes for use by both foreign travellers and Hong Kong residents to speed up the process.

Chong said he had also observed system reboots on Sunday in the “joint one-stop” vehicle clearance lane because of mismatches between Hong Kong and Shenzhen data.

But he said the congestion was unlikely to persist, as clearance should become smoother once more travellers had registered properly.

item.title: [SCMP] Abby Choi’s partner tells murder trial she hid ex-in-laws’ financial reliance on her
item.description:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s partner told a court this week she initially misled him about her former in-laws’ wealth before describing them as horrible and ungrateful after a bitter family dispute.

Chris Tam Fong-chun’s testimony also shed light on his complex relationship with Choi and his former classmate Alex Kwong Kong-chi. The three remained connected through their four children, as Choi had two with each man.

During the third week of the murder trial, Tam told the High Court that the 28-year-old model had initially portrayed her former in-laws as financially independent and comfortable. She feared her two children from her first marriage would be looked down on in their new home because of their background, the court heard.
item.content:encoded:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s partner told a court this week she initially misled him about her former in-laws’ wealth before describing them as horrible and ungrateful after a bitter family dispute.

Chris Tam Fong-chun’s testimony also shed light on his complex relationship with Choi and his former classmate Alex Kwong Kong-chi. The three remained connected through their four children, as Choi had two with each man.

During the third week of the murder trial, Tam told the High Court that the 28-year-old model had initially portrayed her former in-laws as financially independent and comfortable. She feared her two children from her first marriage would be looked down on in their new home because of their background, the court heard.

After an acrimonious row over parenting in mid-2022, Choi allegedly told Tam for the first time that she had been supporting the Kwong family financially and urged him and his father to cut ties with them.

But Tam said he and Choi had kept up a friendly facade in front of her former in-laws while seeking to sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) home registered in Kwong’s father’s name.

He acknowledged he had been “a bit sneaky”, but said this was unavoidable as the couple tried to recover what belonged to them gradually and through diplomatic means.

Asked whether he still viewed his former classmate in the same way after the dispute, Tam said: “I would say the friendship was no more.”

Kwong, 31, is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35.

The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial began last month.

Prosecutors argued that the murder stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of the luxury flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin.

They said Choi had registered her former father-in-law as the owner to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty but had never intended to give the property to her former in-laws.

The court heard that Choi had a heated argument with her former mother-in-law, Jenny Li Sui-heung, at the Kadooria flat in June or July 2022, when the influencer’s elder daughter had a fever.

Li allegedly told her son Alex to stay away from the child because she could infect him, prompting Choi to accuse her of favouring sons over daughters.

Kwong Kau allegedly joined the row, twice attempted to attack Choi, swore at her and called her a “birthing machine”.

The elder Kwong was subsequently barred from visiting the flat and seeing his two grandchildren, the court heard.

But the children were allegedly taken to see him and his girlfriend while Choi was attending a fashion event in France during the Chinese New Year holiday in 2023, much to her dismay.

Tam became friends with Alex Kwong in 2008, when they were studying at Concordia International School in Kowloon Tong, the court heard. Tam later continued his studies in Australia, while Kwong moved to Sear Rogers International School, where he met Choi, the court was told.

Tam appeared surprised when Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, suggested he had wanted a “romantic and sexual relationship” with his client when they were schoolmates.

“Definitely disagree,” the witness said.

Tam said he first met Choi in late 2013 or early 2014, during a brief holiday visit to Hong Kong to see Kwong, who was then married to her.

He said his relationship with Choi changed after Kwong “totally disappeared” one day in 2015. That year, Kwong began divorce proceedings and absconded from a trial over his alleged involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case.

Tam and Choi began dating in December 2015 and held a wedding banquet a year later, although they never registered their marriage, the court heard. Their daughter was born in September 2016 and their son three years later.

“After Abby and I were together, I knew through Abby that Kwong Kong-chi was fine with our relationship and sent us his blessing. I also know his relationship with Abby was something in the past,” Tam said.

He added that he and Choi would meet Kwong during leisure trips to mainland China. The three saw one another more often at family gatherings after Kwong returned to Hong Kong in 2022.

Asked whether they had remained close until Choi’s disappearance, Tam said it was reasonable for them to do so because of their children.

He said the Kwong brothers and their mother appeared calm and unconcerned after Choi disappeared on February 21, 2023.

Li allegedly suggested that her former daughter-in-law had been abducted and that they should delay reporting her disappearance to police until the supposed kidnappers made their demands.

Anthony Kwong, who was working as Choi’s stand-in driver at the time, allegedly evaded questions about her whereabouts and pretended to help by driving Tam around to look for her.

Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains were found at a rental flat in Lung Mei village, Tai Po, on February 24.

The trial also shed light on the Tam family’s wealth and financial dealings with Choi and her former in-laws.

Tam’s father, Tam Chak-kwan, founded the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian and received a share of the proceeds from its HK$1 billion sale to a Japanese company.

In 2019, the family moved into their current 4,000 square foot home on Begonia Road in Kowloon Tong, which the elder Tam bought for HK$168 million.

He said he had given his previous home, a 1,800 square foot flat valued at HK$41 million at the Manhattan Hill private estate in Lai Chi Kok, to Choi in 2018. But he had not expected his de facto daughter-in-law to live there, as he wanted to share a home with his grandchildren.

The court heard that the elder Tam gave Choi at least HK$200,000 a month to cover living expenses for her and his son. He also gave her more than HK$80 million in total to invest.

Chris Tam said Choi had made money investing in luxury watches, although he was unsure whether she had done so through her ex-husband.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, accused Alex Kwong of failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million her daughter had given him to invest. She also called him a “brute” and dismissed his claim that he had supported her financially as “a pack of lies”.

Choi also allegedly put money into the Kadooria flat and an egg waffle shop run by Anthony Kwong, but Chris Tam said both had proved poor investments.

The court also heard how Kwong Kau had helped settle a dispute over a HK$5 million gambling debt Chris Tam incurred in Macau in August 2021.

The younger Tam said he had refused to repay the loan because he knew the casino, run by SunCity Group, was about to close following the arrest of its founder and CEO, Alvin Chau Cheok-wa.

Tam’s father said he had approached Kwong Kau for help because he wanted to resolve the dispute.

He said he had transferred HK$5 million to Kwong Kau’s personal bank account in March 2022 and paid him a further HK$450,000 in gratuities for people with triad affiliations who had stopped debt collectors from harassing his family.

The elder Tam said Kwong Kau later asked him for a HK$400,000 loan, saying police had frozen his account. Tam agreed to lend him HK$250,000, which had yet to be repaid, the court heard.

He added that he had ignored Kwong’s request for help with legal fees after the former officer was remanded in custody in connection with the case.

The trial continues on Tuesday before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] What Indonesia’s warnings of energy cuts mean for Asean
item.description:
Indonesia’s warnings of curbing energy exports to countries it deems disrespectful amid regional tensions have put Singapore and other Southeast Asian buyers on notice, exposing the risks of relying on a neighbour increasingly protective of its resources.

But analysts see little chance of Jakarta following through on the threat, given its own economic interests and the mutual benefits of regional energy cooperation, including the long-planned Asean Power Grid.

On Thursday, Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia said he would not hesitate to consider halting exports to countries that did not respect Indonesia.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s warnings of curbing energy exports to countries it deems disrespectful amid regional tensions have put Singapore and other Southeast Asian buyers on notice, exposing the risks of relying on a neighbour increasingly protective of its resources.

But analysts see little chance of Jakarta following through on the threat, given its own economic interests and the mutual benefits of regional energy cooperation, including the long-planned Asean Power Grid.

On Thursday, Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia said he would not hesitate to consider halting exports to countries that did not respect Indonesia.

“Don’t come asking for help only when you’re in need, but when other issues that can actually be discussed arrive, act like you have no sense of propriety, like someone who doesn’t know how to conduct yourself properly,” said Bahlil at the launch of a gas facility, as reported by local media.

A day earlier, he told reporters that Indonesia was considering not renewing natural gas export contracts with neighbouring countries to prioritise domestic energy needs. Bahlil, who is also the minister of energy and mineral resources, did not name any countries on either occasion.

Mirza Huda, a senior research fellow at the climate and sustainability programme at think tank ODI Global, said Indonesia’s remarks were likely to put neighbouring countries who imported natural gas from Jakarta – such as Singapore, Thailand and the Philippines – on notice.

But while the warnings “warranted attention”, they should not be interpreted as a decision to disrupt supplies, he added.

Among member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), Singapore was the largest importer of natural gas from Jakarta last year at 3.22 million tonnes, according to statistics agency BPS. Thailand and the Philippines imported 291,000 tonnes and 138,000 tonnes respectively.

Victor Nian, founding co-chairman of the Centre for Strategic Energy and Resources, cites Singapore as arguably the most exposed to potential non-renewal of natural gas contracts, given that its deal with Indonesia is set to expire at the end of 2028.

But the city state had diversified supplies through liquefied natural gas imports for global markets, and losing the Jakarta pipeline was likely to risk higher energy costs rather than a supply crisis, he said.

Dinita Setyawati, senior Asia energy analyst at Ember, pointed out that breaching gas contracts before expiry would lead to losses for Indonesia.

The warnings underscored the vulnerability of being dependent on imported gas, she said, urging investments in renewable energy and relevant technologies to serve as buffers. “Fossil fuels are molecules that cannot be reproduced.”

Resource nationalism

Bahlil’s remarks come as Indonesia grapples with a stock-market rout and its worst haze episode in over a decade.

Jakarta has responded to the crises with public shows of nationalism. President Prabowo Subianto this week called out global index MSCI, which warned that Indonesia’s economy could be downgraded from emerging-market to stand-alone-market status. “MSCI wants to scare us, but I say to them: Indonesia fears no one and will not be intimidated!”

During a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prabowo also slammed countries he said liked to snub his nation over intensifying wildfires. “Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” he said.

Jakarta has reportedly held off accepting offers of help from Singapore and Malaysia to tackle the fires, which have plagued many countries in the region.

Melinda Martinus, a fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s Asean Studies Centre, noted that the current transboundary haze situation might lead to the perception that Indonesia was targeting Singapore with its latest warnings.

She said resource nationalism was not new in Indonesia, citing recent moves such as the establishment of Danantara Sumber Daya Indonesia by the Indonesian government to supervise commodity exports.

The mineral-rich country has also banned the export of unprocessed nickel, bauxite and raw copper to encourage companies to refine minerals domestically and boost the local economy. Jakarta has also restricted palm oil exports on several occasions to safeguard domestic supply and prevent excessive price rises.

“This form of resource nationalism is often framed by politicians as a means of helping Indonesia achieve its ambition of becoming a high-income country,” she said.

Jakarta’s warnings reflected a broader and intensifying trend towards resource sovereignty among commodity producers, said Kaho Yu, head of energy and resources research at Verisk Maplecroft.

“Southeast Asian countries reliant on Indonesian gas will need to strengthen supplier engagement and diversify their energy sources,” he said, urging states to vary suppliers and start early negotiations for long-term contracts.

Nian cautioned that Bahlil’s remarks risked setting the precedent of attaching prerequisites to energy exports.

On Thursday, the minister said Indonesia remained open to signing energy export agreements with countries that treated it as an equal, even if they did not have existing contracts with Jakarta.

“Indonesia has every right to prioritise domestic energy security and maximise the economic benefits of its natural resources,” Nian said. “But making energy exports conditional on political ‘respect’ goes beyond legitimate resource nationalism and raises the troubling prospect of weaponising strategic resources.”

Impact on Asean cooperation

Observers say while Indonesia’s warnings are unlikely to hinder progress on regional frameworks such as the Asean Power Grid, they highlight the need for stronger dispute resolution mechanisms.

The regional grid, first conceptualised in 1997, aims to connect the electricity networks of all 11 member states through overland and undersea links. It is expected to boost the economy of exporters while strengthening the energy security of those who receive the supply.

“The fundamental premise of the power grid remains strong,” Martinus said. “Under such arrangements, everyone should benefit.”

But Nian said Jakarta’s warnings risked impeding the advancement of the regional grid, which required substantial investment and mutual confidence in the long term. “The prospect of politically motivated supply disruptions could increase investment risks, financing costs and hesitation over deeper regional energy integration.”

Mirza said the incident highlighted the need for long-term agreements, continued dialogue and a regional dispute resolution mechanism to address potential disagreements over electricity trade.

The grid has seen gradual progress – only eight of 18 planned interconnection projects were operational in 2024, according to the Asean Power Centre – but leaders of member states seem to be pushing it up the agenda list. The Asean summit in May set out a new target of full operationalisation across all member states by 2045.

Dinita was confident that discussions on the power grid would continue as usual. “As long as Indonesia stands to benefit, be it from electricity exports or toll rates for transmission lines, negotiations will continue,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Opportunistic’: experts weigh Manila’s minilateral agenda ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
item.description:
The Philippines’ dual push for stronger “minilateral” defence links and a more robust Asean security role is dividing analysts, with one calling the move “opportunistic”.

Some experts view Manila’s advocacy for the “Squad” alliance as a strategic opportunity to deepen core security partnerships while chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Others question how much actual weight is carried by this informal defence grouping – comprising the United States, the Philippines, Japan and Australia – which aims to counter China’s influence in the region.

They also caution that a flurry of US-led small-group diplomacy could undermine Asean’s centrality in a coming summit and leave Manila with less strategic leeway ahead of next month’s Trump-Xi talks.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines’ dual push for stronger “minilateral” defence links and a more robust Asean security role is dividing analysts, with one calling the move “opportunistic”.

Some experts view Manila’s advocacy for the “Squad” alliance as a strategic opportunity to deepen core security partnerships while chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Others question how much actual weight is carried by this informal defence grouping – comprising the United States, the Philippines, Japan and Australia – which aims to counter China’s influence in the region.

They also caution that a flurry of US-led small-group diplomacy could undermine Asean’s centrality in a coming summit and leave Manila with less strategic leeway ahead of next month’s Trump-Xi talks.

In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Philippine ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez indicated that the Squad could meet on the sidelines of next month’s Asean summit in Manila.

If realised, the talks would come just days before US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the Apec forum sidelines, in what would be their third summit meeting this year.

In the interview, Romualdez also expressed hope that Asean could one day take greater responsibility for its own security, much like Nato.

Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has confirmed that the Quad will hold its first summit in more than two years during the Manila gathering.

Characterised as a “diplomatic partnership” by the US, the informal bloc with Japan, Australia and India – aimed at “fostering a free and open Indo-Pacific” – has not held a summit since Trump returned to power in 2025. As reported by the SCMP, Trump refused to travel to India for a Quad meet last year after the two sides failed to strike a trade deal to his liking.

The timing of the meetings has led analysts to question whether the US and its allies were seizing an opportune window to highlight minilateral security cooperation and how this push might affect Asean unity and regional flexibility towards Beijing.

Arrizal Jaknanihan, a researcher with the Asean Studies Programme at The Habibie Centre in Jakarta, said the prospect of Squad meetings signalled “the Philippines’ long-standing pursuit of expanding and deepening its network of security partnerships across the Indo-Pacific”.

Given the recurring maritime clashes with rival claimant Beijing in the South China Sea and limited guarantees from other Asean members, “it is only natural that leaders in Manila eye the US, Japan and Australia as trusted partners”, he added.

Hosting the meetings while chairing Asean, Jaknanihan contended, offered “a strategic opportunity to show its commitment to both deepening security partnership with extra-Asean countries, while remaining committed to the regional grouping in Southeast Asia”.

Maritime tensions between China and the Philippines have escalated under President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, who has been more assertive regarding Philippine claims compared with his predecessor.

Beijing claims most of the islands and rocks in the South China Sea and rights over their adjacent waters, with rival claimants including Malaysia, Vietnam and Brunei, in addition to the Philippines.

Manila also asserts sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone, a position upheld by a 2016 international arbitral ruling that China rejects.

Chinese coastguard and militia vessels have repeatedly used water cannons and blocking manoeuvres against Philippine resupply missions to Second Thomas Shoal and around other disputed features, resulting in a series of collisions and injuries.

Manila has responded by expanding US military access under the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement, while increasing joint patrols with Squad members.

He Xianqing of the Haikou-based National Institute for South China Sea Studies described the proposed Squad meetings as “both opportunistic and deliberate”.

“It’s simply convenient to hold this gathering on the sidelines of the Asean summit, with so many key officials already in town,” he said. “But it also shows Manila clearly favours a smaller, tighter group built on formal US alliances, different from the Quad.”

The format of the Squad grouping was “far more military-focused and centred on deterrence”, He said, noting that the Philippines, Japan and Australia were all formal US treaty allies.

He added that scheduling the talks just before the Trump-Xi meeting in southern China allowed Manila to “show it stands with US security support” without looking “like a troublemaker ahead of the crucial bilateral summit”.

Jennifer Kavanagh of Defence Priorities, a think tank in Washington, questioned the actual geopolitical weight of the Squad.

“Despite reports of a meeting of the Squad on the sidelines of Asean, I see no evidence the Trump administration has prioritised or is investing in this vehicle,” she said.

“It is not mentioned in any US strategic documents issued in recent years,” Kavanagh added, cautioning that without sustained joint training and institutional work, “the Squad will remain most irrelevant to Asian security, as it has been since it was announced under the [Joe] Biden administration”.

Pointing to Trump’s preference for bilateral engagement, she said: “A meeting of regional powers without the US would send a stronger signal to Beijing than a formulaic meeting of the Squad at this point.”

Commenting on the Quad meeting confirmed by Rubio, Ken Moriyasu of the Hudson Institute said: “If the leaders of the US, Japan, India and Australia were in the same venue and they didn’t hold a Quad, that would send quite the negative signal.”

But he cautioned against reading too much into a meeting alone, urging observers to focus instead on “the length and substance of the discussion, including the wording used in the joint statement”.

On the Squad, he said a gathering of US treaty allies “would provide an important opportunity for the Trump administration to demonstrate to the world that America’s alliance network in Asia remains ironclad”.

Ambassador Romualdez’s suggestion that Asean could evolve towards a Nato-style security alliance drew the sharpest scepticism from analysts.

Jaknanihan called the idea “both unrealistic and unnecessary”, as members held “differing perceptions regarding what they consider as a security threat, including China”.

An alliance built around a single threat “will be the complete opposite of Asean’s approach for decades”, he noted.

He of the National Institute for South China Sea Studies said an Asean Nato was “simply not realistic strategically”, pointing to the Asian group’s diverse political systems, non-aligned tradition and resistance to binding collective defence.

Manila is trying to walk a very fine line ... but right before the Trump-Xi summit, this delicate balance can easily break down

He Xianqing, National Institute for South China Sea Studies

Kavanagh was more blunt in her assessment. “Asean will never function like Nato,” she said, noting that Nato was a US-led collective defence alliance organised around blocs, while Asean operated on consensus and had no collective defence role.

On Asean centrality, Jaknanihan said the grouping had long accommodated differing external alignments as long as it did not “directly harm the security interest of other Asean members”.

Provided the Philippines continued to engage Asean-led processes during its chairmanship, deeper minilateral ties “will not substantially undercut Asean centrality”, he contended.

But He took the opposite view, saying that concurrent Quad and Squad activity alongside talk of an Asean Nato “looks like US-led small group diplomacy [is] taking over regional security” and this “weakens Asean’s central role”.

From Beijing’s perspective, Jaknanihan said that given the proximity of the Trump-Xi summit, it would be less likely to “express frontal opposition or punitive measures in response to the potential Squad meeting to avoid escalating tension, but China will definitely signal displeasure towards the development”.

According to Kavanagh, Beijing “sees the Philippines as a US puppet and will interpret the ambassador’s comments as either directed by Washington or motivated by a desire to tell Washington what it wants to hear”.

Looking ahead to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen and potential talks on the sidelines between Marcos and Xi, analysts expect a familiar Philippine hedging posture complicated by the surrounding optics.

Jaknanihan said the meetings “offer an opportunity to find the pathway towards a more stable relationship, while still maintaining a mitigation through deeper security partnerships with Indo-Pacific partners”.

He in Haikou called the dual approach “exactly the Philippines’ hedging style”, but cautioned that if Squad coordination dominated the narrative, “the Marcos-Xi meeting will end up being nothing more than a symbolic photo opportunity, with little chance for real tension reduction”.

“Manila is trying to walk a very fine line: it wants both military deterrence and diplomatic dialogue with China,” He said. “But right before the Trump-Xi summit, this delicate balance can easily break down.”

item.title: [SCMP] What Beijing’s 2-to-1 shipbuilding lead means for the US in war over Taiwan
item.description:
Mainland Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice as much naval tonnage as their US counterparts in 2024 and 2025, according to a new survey, exposing a growing production gap that analysts say could weigh heavily in a prolonged conflict over Taiwan.

Tonnage alone is an imperfect measure of naval power, specialists cautioned, pointing to ongoing US advantages in submarine technology, aircraft carriers and operational experience. They also highlighted China’s ability to draw on commercial shipyards, unmanned systems and dual-use civilian vessels during a conflict. But they differed on how far the balance between the two had already shifted.

The Chinese mainland turned out 636,208 tonnes of military, paramilitary and auxiliary vessels over the two years, against 270,509 tonnes from American builders, the survey showed.
item.content:encoded:
Mainland Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice as much naval tonnage as their US counterparts in 2024 and 2025, according to a new survey, exposing a growing production gap that analysts say could weigh heavily in a prolonged conflict over Taiwan.

Tonnage alone is an imperfect measure of naval power, specialists cautioned, pointing to ongoing US advantages in submarine technology, aircraft carriers and operational experience. They also highlighted China’s ability to draw on commercial shipyards, unmanned systems and dual-use civilian vessels during a conflict. But they differed on how far the balance between the two had already shifted.

The Chinese mainland turned out 636,208 tonnes of military, paramilitary and auxiliary vessels over the two years, against 270,509 tonnes from American builders, the survey showed.

The survey, compiled by maritime intelligence publication Flottes de Combat and the French Naval Industry Association, found China accounted for more than 43 per cent of global naval production tonnage in the two years, compared with just over 18 per cent for the US.

Chinese yards delivered 84 vessels, up from 31 in 2022 and 2023, while American deliveries rose from 32 to 38, said the report, which was presented in Paris on Tuesday ahead of next month’s Euronaval defence exhibition.

While the US Navy’s combat fleet remains more than double the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) by tonnage, China is catching up. But analysts have questioned whether total tonnage alone would prove decisive in a war fought near China’s coast.

China has had the world’s largest navy by number of ships since at least 2020, according to the Pentagon, with the new survey counting 418 PLA Navy combat vessels on January 1. But at 1.44 million tonnes, they displaced less than half the 3.11 million tonnes of the US Navy’s 283 ships. The US had 11 aircraft carriers to China’s three.
